papers.title: SoundWeaver: Compositional Warm-Starting for Text-to-Audio Diffusion Serving
papers.abstract: Text-to-audio (T2A) diffusion models generate high-quality audio but require tens of neural function evaluations (NFEs), resulting in substantial inference latency. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize each generation trajectory independently, even when reusable acoustic structure exists in prior examples. We introduce SoundWeaver, the first training-free framework for compositional cross example acoustic reuse. Rather than generating from pure noise, SoundWeaver constructs a prompt-conditioned acoustic prior from segments distributed across cached audios and warm-starts diffusion from an intermediate noise level. We introduce an Acoustic Composition Graph (ACG), which uses neural codec representations and segment-level identification to identify candidate cross-cache transitions and structured path search to jointly optimize prompt relevance and acoustic continuity. We further establish a warm-start error bound showing how prior quality and diffusion SNR jointly govern the admissible skip depth, motivating an adaptive contextual-bandit Skip Gater that selects the warm-start level for each request. Across T2A diffusion backbones, SoundWeaver achieves 1.48-3.74x generation speedup with only a 1K-clip cache while improving generation quality.
papers.summary: Text-to-audio (T2A) diffusion models need tens of neural function evaluations per clip, and existing accelerators treat every generation independently. `SoundWeaver` is a training-free serving framework that stitches segments from cached audio clips into a prompt-conditioned prior and starts diffusion from an intermediate noise level instead of pure noise. An `Acoustic Composition Graph` searches for segment paths that balance prompt relevance and acoustic continuity, and a contextual-bandit `Skip Gater` picks how many steps to skip per request, motivated by a warm-start error bound. Across T2A backbones the authors report **1.48-3.74x generation speedup with only a 1K-clip cache**, alongside improved generation quality.

papers.title: Harnessing Dephasing for Quantum Reservoir Computing with a Minimum Complexity Architecture: Applications to Nonlinear Time-Series Prediction
papers.abstract: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) exploits quantum dynamics for temporal information processing. Quantum noise affects the reservoir dynamics and can either impair computational performance or serve as a computational resource. However, the role of pure dephasing in Hamiltonian encoding QRC remains unclear. In this work, we propose a minimum complexity QRC model that harnesses pure dephasing in an open uniform XX chain. We show that, under suitable input encoding, pure dephasing can ensure the echo state and fading memory properties even without amplitude damping. Furthermore, in the presence of amplitude damping, the proposed quantum reservoir has distinct stationary states for distinct inputs, and introducing pure dephasing alters these states, thereby affecting the reservoir dynamics. Information processing capacity analysis shows that joint control of the two decoherence mechanisms regulates memory and nonlinearity, providing access to diverse capacity profiles. The proposed QRC achieves promising performance on synthetic benchmarks, while its 6-qubit configuration outperforms all three multi-reservoir echo state network baselines on over half of the real-world prediction tasks. These findings highlight pure dephasing as a computational resource for QRC.
papers.summary: Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) uses quantum dynamics for temporal information processing, but the role of pure dephasing noise in Hamiltonian-encoding QRC has been unclear. The authors propose a minimum-complexity reservoir built on an open uniform XX spin chain and show that, with suitable input encoding, pure dephasing alone can guarantee the echo state and fading memory properties without amplitude damping. Jointly tuning dephasing and amplitude damping regulates the trade-off between memory and nonlinearity. A **6-qubit configuration outperforms all three multi-reservoir echo state network baselines on over half of the real-world prediction tasks**.

papers.title: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
papers.abstract: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. We propose C2, a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout: every other parameter, and the readout's singular values, norms and entry multiset, are unchanged, and the function can change in an exactly recomputable way; we verify that each evaluated permutation does. C2 separates fingerprinting from computation only under three conditions, which we state as an eligibility protocol: a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries must already predict the target; C2 must change a property specific to the rewiring; and the reader's identity must be attested. No natural setting we tested is eligible. On tiny MLPs a frontier reader route followed the rewired function on all 24 networks, but invariant baselines were near chance and its backend could not be attested. In two public CNN zoos the conditions traded off: weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution, but C2's effect on accuracy was not specific to the swap, while per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries. On a constructed population where a planted fingerprint rule works, all conditions hold and C2 separates a rule-following reader from an executor. A self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut, and showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled. A registered replication on fresh networks confirmed both findings (tracking minus stuck 0.875, 95% interval [0.750, 1.000]), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B also followed the rewiring (tracking minus stuck 0.729 [0.552, 0.885]). The transforms, audits and raw records are available from the authors.
papers.summary: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but that could reflect recognizing weight-space fingerprints rather than actually computing the function. `C2` is a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout, changing the function in an exactly recomputable way while leaving the readout's singular values, norms and entries unchanged, paired with a three-condition eligibility protocol for when the test is valid. **No natural setting tested met all three conditions**, including tiny MLPs and two public CNN zoos. On a constructed population with a planted fingerprint rule, a self-hosted `Qwen3.8-27B` followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut (tracking minus stuck 0.875 in a registered replication), as did `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B`, and `Qwen3.8-27B` showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled.

papers.title: Verifiable On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) gives language models only a sparse sequence-level signal, while on-policy distillation (OPD) gives dense per-token teacher feedback that is not grounded in verified outcomes. `VOPD` (Verifiable On-Policy Distillation) couples the two by treating teacher supervision as an implicit reward, projecting the verifier's preference onto that reward direction, and Rao-Blackwellizing the signal over the full vocabulary so that unsampled tokens also receive verifier-grounded supervision. The objective can be read as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher-verifier agreement. Across two teacher-student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, **`VOPD` consistently improves final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD** and other on-policy distillation baselines.

papers.title: Local subspace encoding for spectral prediction: from TabPFN to operator-adaptive calibration
papers.abstract: TabPFN has already shown useful predictive performance on near-infrared spectra. RamanPFN subsequently proposed two spectral representations for tabular inference: Global Compositional Unmixing (GCU) and Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding (LVSE). We assess whether these representations also help on datasets assembled through the nirs4all ecosystem, and whether their value extends to classical calibration. We reanalyse completed experiments from a public spectral dataset catalogue. On a post-hoc subset of 61 matched numerical prediction tasks, after excluding ten class-code, metadata or semantically ambiguous targets, LVSE reduces RMSE relative to raw-spectrum TabPFN by 10.22%, 12.80% and 14.52% on average for checkpoints 2.5, 3 and 3.5, respectively, with median reductions of 4.99%, 4.74% and 7.82%. Across 76 classification datasets, weighted F1 increases by 2.22, 2.56 and 3.81 percentage points. The 2.5 classification procedure uses output coding on 15 datasets exceeding the checkpoint's native class limit. GCU alone is less reliable in this implementation. LVSE also improves PLS and Ridge in many cases, with median RMSE reductions of 4.75% and 1.89%. Adding LVSE candidates to an operator-adaptive model is feasible, but a separate 35-task panel derived from the public AOM benchmark shows only small median gains. These results motivate evaluating LVSE alongside existing representation choices. They do not establish that a selector choosing between raw and LVSE inputs will improve every task.
papers.summary: The study tests whether two spectral representations proposed by `RamanPFN`, Global Compositional Unmixing (GCU) and Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding (LVSE), help tabular foundation models and classical calibration on spectral datasets from the `nirs4all` ecosystem. Reanalysing completed experiments on a post-hoc subset of 61 regression tasks, **`LVSE` reduces RMSE relative to raw-spectrum `TabPFN` by 10.22% to 14.52% on average** across three checkpoints, with median reductions of roughly 5-8%, and raises weighted F1 by 2.22 to 3.81 points on 76 classification datasets. `LVSE` also gives smaller median gains for PLS and Ridge regression, while `GCU` alone is less reliable. Adding `LVSE` candidates to an operator-adaptive model yields only small median gains on a separate 35-task panel, and the authors caution that a raw-versus-LVSE selector is not shown to help on every task.

papers.title: InletScope: Multiscale pressure-based inlet unstart monitoring under changing sensor configurations
papers.abstract: Supersonic inlets capture and compress air for aeroengines, and unstart can disrupt the air supply and compromise propulsion-system stability. Pressure-based monitoring must accommodate flow responses that vary with operating condition and measurement location. InletScope combines shared multiscale pressure encoding, learned scale fusion and sensor-probability averaging, allowing measurement sets to change without retraining. Separate models evaluate unstart detection and new-onset prediction within a 0.5-s future interval. Seven Mach-2.9 runs, each with one annotated event, cover downstream throttling, throat regulation and splitter adjustment; three are held out with fixed weights and source-derived settings. Across three training seeds, full-sensor detection achieves run-wise mean window $F_1$ scores of 0.834--0.964. Eight-sensor aggregation reduces detection-score variation across sensor subsets in both splitter runs while retaining mean scores close to those of the full sets. Regional detection favors cowl and high-speed-channel measurements during splitter adjustment and compression-side measurements during downstream throttling, consistent with their respective pressure responses. Complete-record evaluation shows that configurations with comparable window scores can produce different alarm timing and persistence. These findings connect sensor count and regional coverage to pressure discrimination and sequential alarm behavior, providing experimental guidance for configuring inlet monitoring systems.
papers.summary: Unstart in supersonic engine inlets disrupts air supply, and pressure-based monitoring has to cope with flow responses that vary by operating condition and sensor location. `InletScope` combines a shared multiscale pressure encoder, learned scale fusion and averaging of per-sensor probabilities, so the set of sensors can change without retraining; separate models handle unstart detection and prediction of onset within a 0.5-second future interval. On seven Mach-2.9 runs, three of them held out, **full-sensor detection reaches run-wise mean window F1 scores of 0.834-0.964** across three training seeds. Eight-sensor aggregation reduces score variation across sensor subsets, and the most informative sensor regions differ between splitter adjustment and downstream throttling.

papers.title: Actionwave: A Systematic Benchmark for Waveform-Centric Clinical Prediction Across Care Scenarios
papers.abstract: Continuous bedside waveforms record rapid physiological changes that can inform clinical decisions. Existing benchmarks examine selected prediction conditions, but it remains unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time, and available inputs across care settings. We introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across intensive-care, operating-room, and emergency-department settings. Actionwave uses a common decision-time prediction interface and groups clinically grounded tasks by what is inferred and when. It varies conditions relevant to clinical use, including the warning required before an intervention. We compare diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under specified model-size and compute budgets. The protocol requires patient-level splits, strict information cutoffs, and comparisons that isolate individual modeling factors. Across 20 tasks and 1.4M task-labelled windows from source datasets, the experimental grids account for over 87,000 model fits. These comparisons identify task-specific choices and show why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are necessary when interpreting waveform model performance.
papers.summary: Existing benchmarks for clinical prediction from bedside waveforms test selected conditions, leaving unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time and available inputs. `Actionwave` defines a common decision-time prediction interface across intensive-care, operating-room and emergency-department settings, with patient-level splits, strict information cutoffs and comparisons that isolate individual modeling factors. It covers **20 tasks and 1.4M task-labelled windows, with experimental grids totalling over 87,000 model fits** across diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under fixed size and compute budgets. The comparisons surface task-specific modeling choices and show that matched cohorts, unimodal controls and explicit timing are needed to interpret waveform model performance.

papers.title: Validation Bias in Large Language Model Responses to Cancer Treatment Queries: A Factorial Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly used by patients seeking cancer information, but their safety when users present evidence-misaligned beliefs about treatment remains uncharacterized. We hypothesized that LLMs exhibit validation bias, affirming rather than correcting such beliefs, and evaluated this with a 2x2x2 factorial design crossing conversation format (single-turn vs multi-turn), treatment type (evidence-based vs alternative), and query valence (positive vs negative). Framing was evidence-aligned (supporting evidence-based treatments or questioning alternative therapies) or evidence-misaligned (promoting alternative treatments or questioning evidence-based therapies). We analyzed 1,272 conversations (6,360 interactions) across 14 LLMs from 6 vendors, scored by an LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) validated against human annotation on a 6-dimension safety rubric. The primary outcome was the unsafe response rate, defined as a Weak classification or any critical failure. Evidence-misaligned framing increased unsafe response rates compared with evidence-aligned framing (14.4% vs 5.1%; OR 3.14, 95% CI 2.07-4.78; P < .001), and the association persisted after accounting for clustering by LLM. Among 429 conversations classified as Strong under evidence-aligned framing, 22.6% were downgraded in their paired evidence-misaligned counterpart. Multi-turn conversations had lower unsafe response rates than single-turn conversations (5.2% vs 14.7%; P < .001). Unsafe response rates varied by vendor from 1.8% to 36.8%. LLMs exhibited significant validation bias in oncology, with unsafe responses nearly tripling under evidence-misaligned framing. Evaluations limited to neutral, fact-seeking queries may overestimate real-world safety, and safety testing of medical AI systems should include evidence-misaligned user framing.
papers.summary: The study asks whether large language model (LLM) chatbots affirm rather than correct patients' evidence-misaligned beliefs about cancer treatment, which the authors call validation bias. A 2x2x2 factorial design crossed conversation format, treatment type and query valence over 1,272 conversations with 14 LLMs from 6 vendors, scored by a `GPT-5-mini` judge validated against human annotation on a six-dimension safety rubric. **Evidence-misaligned framing raised the unsafe response rate to 14.4% from 5.1% (odds ratio 3.14)**, and 22.6% of conversations rated Strong under aligned framing were downgraded in their misaligned counterpart. Multi-turn conversations were safer than single-turn ones (5.2% vs 14.7%), and unsafe rates ranged from 1.8% to 36.8% by vendor.

papers.title: DAGGER: Deployment-Free Quality Estimation for Generative AI Workflows
papers.abstract: Estimating the quality of generative AI workflows is challenging because these workflows comprise multiple stages, and errors can propagate across them, making end-to-end performance depend not only on the accuracy of individual models but also on how their outputs affect downstream stages. Each stage can use one of many candidate models. Estimating end-to-end workflow quality by deploying and evaluating every resulting model configuration is therefore prohibitively expensive. As a result, existing approaches face a tradeoff between estimation cost and accuracy: inexpensive methods often produce unreliable quality estimates, while accurate methods require deploying and evaluating many workflow configurations. In this paper, we introduce DAGGER, a framework for estimating the quality of generative AI workflows without exhaustive deployment and profiling. DAGGER represents a workflow as a graph, in which nodes correspond to stages and edges capture how outputs from one stage affect subsequent stages. It then decomposes workflow quality into per-node accuracy terms and per-edge dependency terms. Using a novel analytical formulation and SVD-based matrix completion, DAGGER estimates workflow quality from sparse observations without executing every candidate workflow. We evaluate DAGGER on three generative AI workflows across three datasets. DAGGER estimates workflow quality with a median error of 6.8 percentage points while reducing profiling cost by 10.2$\times$ relative to BenchPress, a state-of-the-art baseline, and selects workflow configurations competitive with state-of-the-art frameworks such as LLMSelector.
papers.summary: Choosing which model to use at each stage of a multi-stage generative AI workflow is expensive because errors propagate between stages, so end-to-end quality normally has to be measured by deploying each configuration. `DAGGER` represents the workflow as a graph, decomposes quality into per-node accuracy terms and per-edge dependency terms, and uses an analytical formulation plus SVD-based matrix completion to estimate quality from sparse observations. On three workflows across three datasets it estimates workflow quality with a **median error of 6.8 percentage points while cutting profiling cost 10.2x relative to `BenchPress`**. The configurations it selects are competitive with frameworks such as `LLMSelector`.

papers.title: Instantiation of Human Values in Image Generation
papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models are increasingly embedded in everyday visual culture, yet little is known about how they translate abstract human values into visual scenes. We address this gap by introducing a framework, grounded in Schwartz's theory of basic human values, for studying value instantiation: the process by which ideals such as success, care, or freedom are visually realized. Using person-centered prompts from 70 positive and negative value items, we generate 28,000 images across four state-of-the-art T2I models. We identify visual prototypes, recurring combinations of subjects, actions, and settings, and use them to quantify how narrowly models instantiate these values and how this breadth compares with human descriptions of the same items. We then map these prototypes onto a taxonomy of social configurations spanning setting, sociality, mode of engagement, and social register, revealing what is systematically foregrounded or omitted. Our results show that T2I models produce far more concentrated representations than humans do when describing the same values. They default to a hyper-individualistic, adult-centric worldview, reproducing value-specific associations, such as achievement tied to formal institutional settings or hedonism rendered as affluent consumption, while marginalizing everyday labor, relational care, and non-adult perspectives. As a proof of concept, we show that these structural gaps can guide a steering method that diversifies outputs without modifying the original prompt.
papers.summary: Little is known about how text-to-image (T2I) models turn abstract human values such as success, care or freedom into concrete scenes. Using person-centered prompts built from 70 positive and negative value items in Schwartz's theory of basic human values, the authors generate 28,000 images from four T2I models, extract recurring visual prototypes of subjects, actions and settings, and map them onto a taxonomy of social configurations. **The models produce far more concentrated representations than humans do when describing the same values**, defaulting to a hyper-individualistic, adult-centric view, for example tying achievement to formal institutions and hedonism to affluent consumption while marginalizing everyday labor and relational care. A proof-of-concept steering method uses these gaps to diversify outputs without modifying the prompt.

papers.title: The Date You Didn't Set: The System-Prompt Date as a Hidden Variable in LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract: The system prompt of many instruction-tuned models carries a date, usually today's, filled in automatically for conversational and agentic requests alike, so an unchanged evaluation can send a different prompt each day. In this paper, we explore how much this hidden input changes evaluation outcomes. Across six instruction-tuned models and four benchmarks, with prompts, decoding, and configuration fixed, every model is affected: two plausible dates (2024--2026) switch a median $6.6\%$ of test items between correct and incorrect. Even rerunning the evaluation one day later flips about as many items as changing the batch size, although nothing in the setup was changed. In addition, using a grammar-constrained variant of Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to search dates of any year, we find dates that cost the Llama-3.x models up to $36.5$ points of held-out accuracy. Beyond accuracy, switching to another plausible date alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes $15$--$32\%$ of reproduced jailbreak successes on Llama-3.2-3B. Yet none of the eleven evaluation stacks we audit pins the date. With the date and the rest of the setup fixed, reruns reproduce byte-for-byte; we therefore recommend pinning, logging, and reporting the date.
papers.summary: Many instruction-tuned models have today's date auto-filled into the system prompt, so an otherwise unchanged evaluation sends a different prompt each day. Across six models and four benchmarks with prompts, decoding and configuration fixed, **switching between two plausible dates (2024-2026) flips a median 6.6% of test items between correct and incorrect**, and rerunning one day later flips about as many items as changing the batch size. A grammar-constrained variant of `Greedy Coordinate Gradient` finds adversarial dates that cost `Llama-3.x` models up to 36.5 points of held-out accuracy, and changing the date also alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes 15-32% of reproduced jailbreak successes on `Llama-3.2-3B`. None of eleven audited evaluation stacks pins the date, and with the date fixed reruns reproduce byte-for-byte, so the authors recommend pinning, logging and reporting it.

papers.title: INCLUDE-2.0: Disentangling Knowledge Gaps in Multilingual LLM Evaluation
papers.abstract:
Current multilingual benchmarks cover only a fraction of the languages represented in modern pretraining corpora and often conflate language proficiency with the ability to answer questions grounded in specific regions and communities. We introduce INCLUDE-2.0, a large-scale benchmark for region-aware multilingual factual evaluation, which covers 91 languages from 86 countries (127 total language--country pairs), comprising over 220K curated samples drawn from native regional sources. Unlike existing benchmarks that often treat language as a proxy for region, IINCLUDE-2.0 distinguishes between questions whose answers are independent of context, vary by country, concern widely documented facts about a place, or depend on knowledge primarily expressed through local linguistic and cultural sources. Each item is annotated with its regional knowledge type and domain, and paired with an English translation, enabling controlled analysis of the relationship between language proficiency and possession of regional knowledge.
  Evaluating frontier and open-weight models on IINCLUDE-2.0, we find that aggregate multilingual accuracy masks substantial variation across regional knowledge types, languages, and regions. We find that frontier models perform worse on locally embedded knowledge than on widely documented facts about regions, with an average drop of ~14.5 points. We also show that for open-weight models, scale improves accuracy but does not reliably make performance invariant to whether a question is asked in English or its original language. INCLUDE-2.0 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/epfl-nlp/include-2.0
papers.summary: Multilingual benchmarks often treat language as a proxy for region, conflating language proficiency with knowledge grounded in specific places and communities. `INCLUDE-2.0` covers 91 languages from 86 countries with over 220K curated samples from native regional sources, each annotated by regional knowledge type and domain and paired with an English translation. The knowledge types separate context-independent questions, answers that vary by country, widely documented facts about a place, and knowledge mainly expressed in local sources. **Frontier models score about 14.5 points lower on locally embedded knowledge than on widely documented regional facts**, and for open-weight models scale raises accuracy without making performance reliably invariant to whether a question is asked in English or its original language.

papers.title: Directly Maximizing On-policy Expected Accepted Length for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose tokens for verification by a target model. Draft training commonly optimizes token-level distribution alignment, but this does not directly optimize the length of the accepted prefix: once a draft token is rejected, all subsequent draft tokens are discarded. We propose FreDraft, an on-policy training method that directly maximizes the expected accepted length of drafts sampled from the current draft model. This objective accounts for first-rejection truncation and induces prefix-aware credit assignment, weighting each token by its contribution to the acceptance of the current and subsequent tokens. To optimize the objective efficiently, we analytically marginalize token-level acceptance rate, using the target model's vocabulary distribution to reduce gradient variance. We further redistribute part of this distribution-level gradient into an explicit penalty for sampled tokens whose probabilities are overestimated by the draft model, while preserving the expected gradient. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and target models show that FreDraft improves accepted length and decoding speedup over strong baselines, achieving faster on-policy training convergence.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model inference by having a small draft model propose tokens that the target model verifies, but draft models are usually trained for token-level distribution alignment rather than for how many tokens survive before the first rejection. `FreDraft` trains the draft on-policy to **directly maximize the expected accepted length** of its own sampled drafts, which weights each token by its effect on the acceptance of itself and later tokens. The method analytically marginalizes the token-level acceptance rate using the target model's vocabulary distribution to reduce gradient variance, and adds an expectation-preserving penalty on sampled tokens the draft overestimates. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and target models show longer accepted prefixes, higher decoding speedup than strong baselines, and faster on-policy training convergence.

papers.title: scOPD: Routed On-Policy Self-Distillation for LLM-Based Single-Cell Annotation
papers.abstract:
Motivation: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for single-cell annotation, but existing training methods mainly rely on scalar outcome rewards that provide limited supervision for intermediate biological reasoning. Batch-level annotation is particularly challenging because it requires jointly resolving local cell identities and a global one-to-one matching constraint, such that one local error can affect the entire assignment. Moreover, a single inference pass provides insufficient evidence for locating uncertain predictions. These limitations call for fine-grained reasoning supervision during training and uncertainty-aware refinement during inference.
  Results: To address these challenges, we propose scOPD, an on-policy self-distillation framework for LLM-based single-cell annotation. After reasoning fine-tuning, scOPD adaptively routes qualified rollouts to reward-based optimization, while erroneous rollouts receive privileged token-level supervision from successful sibling trajectories. During inference, rollout disagreement triggers constraint-aware pairwise refinement of uncertain assignments. Across CellPuzzles and four out-of-domain disease datasets, scOPD consistently improves the performance of diverse LLM backbones, achieving average cell-level and batch-level accuracies of 81.71% and 44.49% with Qwen3-8B.
  Availability and Implementation: Code and data are available at https://github.com/YuZhiyin/scOPD.
papers.summary: Annotating batches of single cells with large language models requires resolving each cell's identity under a global one-to-one matching constraint, and scalar outcome rewards give little supervision for the intermediate biological reasoning. `scOPD` is an on-policy self-distillation framework that routes successful rollouts to reward-based optimization while erroneous rollouts receive token-level supervision from successful sibling trajectories. At inference, disagreement between rollouts triggers constraint-aware pairwise refinement of uncertain assignments. On `CellPuzzles` and four out-of-domain disease datasets it improves several LLM backbones, reaching **average cell-level and batch-level accuracies of 81.71% and 44.49% with `Qwen3-8B`**.

papers.title: RECAP: Training Long-horizon LLM Agents with Context Compaction
papers.abstract: Context compaction enables large language model agents to tackle long-horizon tasks within limited context budgets by replacing interaction histories with compressed summaries. However, learning effective compaction jointly with the agent policy remains challenging, as summaries affect task success over many subsequent interactions. We introduce RECAP, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework based on the principle that a summary should preserve the behavior induced by the original interaction history. We formalize this principle with a behavior distortion objective that measures the divergence between the agent's subsequent behavior under compressed and original contexts. We show that the gradient of the distortion objective decomposes into two complementary learning signals: distortion-based reward for summary generation and self-distillation for subsequent actions. Experiments on Qwen3.5-4B show that RECAP consistently outperforms the task-reward-only RL baselines on both environments, leading to an absolute improvement of 4.6% and 4.3% on BrowseComp-plus and SWE-bench Verified, respectively. Ablations further highlight the value of jointly supervising summary generation and post-compaction behavior for RECAP.
papers.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents rely on context compaction, replacing interaction history with summaries, but learning good compaction jointly with the agent policy is hard because a summary affects many later steps. `RECAP` is a reinforcement learning framework built on the principle that a summary should preserve the behavior the original history would have induced, formalized as a behavior distortion objective measuring divergence between the agent's subsequent behavior under compressed and original contexts. The gradient of this objective decomposes into a distortion-based reward for summary generation and a self-distillation signal for post-compaction actions. With `Qwen3.5-4B`, it beats task-reward-only RL baselines by **4.6% absolute on `BrowseComp-plus` and 4.3% on `SWE-bench Verified`**.

papers.title: RecipeADQA: A User-aware Question-Answering Dataset for Multi-Constraint Recipe Recommendation
papers.abstract: Question-answering recipe recommendation tasks lack datasets with ground-truth labels. Existing methods often generate datasets from simple combinations of ingredient or tag constraints, leading to unnatural expressions and unreasonable constraints that are hard to reflect users' real preferences. This paper proposes a construction method for a benchmark-style QA dataset for natural-language recipe recommendation. Driven by real user behavior, our method integrates external user query and review data to extract fine-grained preference signals by LLMs and maps them onto a knowledge-graph-based tag schema, thereby constructing QA data consisting of preference and ingredient constraints. Besides, a greedy strategy for constraint selection is also used to control the answer size, while tag-based re-ranking is applied to improve data quality. The generated dataset RecipeADQA contains natural-language questions, structured constraints, and answer sets, resulting in 128,465 instances. Experiments compare RecipeADQA with baseline datasets from two perspectives: data quality and retrieval-recommendation performance. The results show that ours outperforms existing methods on the same recipe knowledge graph in coverage, higher question quality in naturalness and constraint rationality, and better queryability. Moreover, we design a noise-augmented retrieve-and-rerank model, in which a lightweight parser first retrieves candidate recipes, and a small language model then selects and ranks relevant recipes from a noisy candidate pool. The model trained on RecipeADQA outperforms the same model trained on the baseline datasets. The relevant construction code and data have been open-sourced at a GitHub repository https://github.com/MorimoLab/RecipeADQA.
papers.summary: Question-answering recipe recommendation lacks datasets with ground-truth labels, and existing ones are built from simple combinations of ingredient or tag constraints that read unnaturally. The construction method here uses LLMs to extract fine-grained preference signals from real user queries and reviews, maps them onto a knowledge-graph tag schema, and applies greedy constraint selection and tag-based re-ranking to control answer-set size and quality. The resulting `RecipeADQA` dataset contains **128,465 instances** of natural-language questions, structured constraints and answer sets, and scores better than baseline datasets on coverage, naturalness, constraint rationality and queryability. A noise-augmented retrieve-and-rerank model with a small language model performs better when trained on it than on the baseline datasets.

papers.title: Capability and Interpretability of Transformers on Multi-task Recurrence
papers.abstract: Transformers are widely used in various language tasks, with limited understanding of their internal mechanisms. Motivated by the recurrent structure of many linguistic rules, we study the capability and interpretability of Transformers through a controlled family of linear recurrence tasks over finite cyclic groups. These tasks range from executing a single fixed rule to identifying a latent rule from context and switching between explicitly specified rules, with and without input masking. Through extensive experiments across different configurations, we find that switching specified rules is simpler than identifying latent rules for Transformers in general. We also identify how several key factors affect the generalization capability of Transformers, including the depth, width, and the algebraic structure of the linear recurrence. Curriculum training is extremely useful when the number of rules is large. With standard tools in mechanistic interpretability like linear probing and input patching, our study reveals how Transformers represent, identify, and execute multiple rules.
papers.summary: To study what Transformers can learn and how they represent rules, the authors use a controlled family of linear recurrence tasks over finite cyclic groups, ranging from executing one fixed rule to inferring a latent rule from context and switching between explicitly specified rules, with and without input masking. Experiments across configurations show that **switching between specified rules is generally easier than identifying latent rules**. Depth, width and the algebraic structure of the recurrence all affect generalization, and curriculum training helps substantially when the number of rules is large. Linear probing and input patching are used to show how the models represent, identify and execute multiple rules.

papers.title: Does Item Response Theory Generalize Across Languages? Evidence from Cross-Lingual LLM Benchmarks
papers.abstract: The application of Item Response Theory (IRT) for data selection in benchmarks has mostly been limited to monolingual settings. In this work, we ask: how does IRT generalize when the same benchmark is translated across languages? We conduct experiments on Multilingual GSM and Global MMLU, covering over 100 language models and 11 languages. Fitting 1PL, 2PL, and 3PL IRT models per language, we assess cross-lingual consistency of parameters and whether IRT-filtered subsets preserve model rankings across languages: item difficulty emerges as the most stable parameter followed by guessing and then discrimination. A differential item analysis also shows that lack of stability can be tracked to specific items shifting under translation across languages. Our findings suggest IRT-based selection in multilingual settings must be both parameter-aware and item-aware, validating model choice and screening individual items before assuming cross-lingual generalization.
papers.summary: Item Response Theory (IRT) is used to select informative benchmark items, but mostly in monolingual settings, leaving open whether fitted parameters carry over when a benchmark is translated. The authors fit 1PL, 2PL and 3PL IRT models per language on `Multilingual GSM` and `Global MMLU`, covering over 100 language models and 11 languages, and check parameter consistency and whether IRT-filtered subsets preserve model rankings. **Item difficulty is the most stable parameter across languages, followed by guessing and then discrimination**, and a differential item analysis traces instability to specific items that shift under translation. They conclude that multilingual IRT-based selection should validate the model choice and screen individual items before assuming cross-lingual generalization.

papers.title: RegioZH: Unveiling Comprehension Disparities across Regional Chinese Varieties in LLMs
papers.abstract: Current evaluations often treat Chinese varieties as monolithic, obscuring failures for regional users. We introduce RegioZH, a 2,607-item multiple-choice benchmark for regional lexical reasoning across Mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia. Built by region-specific annotators and expert-validated, it targets localized idioms, slang, code-mixing, politeness conventions, and sociocultural expressions. Zero-shot results on eleven LLMs show large disparities, including a 29.4-point average accuracy gap between Taiwan and Singapore. Persona and structured chain-of-thought prompts for five models yield selective gains, suggesting that some errors stem from retrieval or framing rather than only missing knowledge. Representation, attention, calibration, and surface-feature analyses show a dissociation between marker attention and semantic grounding, overconfident forced-choice errors, and localized lexical density as a consistent difficulty predictor. Qualitative analysis finds terminology misunderstandings, sociocultural inference gaps, and cross-regional semantic divergence. RegioZH demonstrates that apparent Chinese proficiency can mask uneven understanding across regional varieties, motivating intra-language robustness evaluation alongside multilingual generalization.
papers.summary: Evaluations usually treat Chinese as a single language, hiding failures on regional varieties. `RegioZH` is a 2,607-item multiple-choice benchmark of regional lexical reasoning covering Mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia, built by region-specific annotators and expert-validated to target idioms, slang, code-mixing, politeness conventions and sociocultural expressions. Zero-shot results on eleven LLMs show large disparities, including a **29.4-point average accuracy gap between Taiwan and Singapore**. Persona and structured chain-of-thought prompts give only selective gains, and further analyses find overconfident forced-choice errors and localized lexical density as a consistent predictor of difficulty.

papers.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on Iranian Doctoral Entrance Exams in Electrical and Computer Engineering
papers.abstract: We evaluate four large language models (LLMs) on multiple-choice questions from the 2024 and 2025 Iranian national Ph.D. entrance examinations in Electrical Engineering (EE) and Computer Engineering (CE). Of the 440 questions in the four official booklets, 7 were excluded because the question statement or its figure was ambiguous, leaving 433 questions (186 EE, 247 CE), of which 171 (39.5\%) depend on a figure. Each question was presented in the original Persian and in an English translation, giving 3,464 scored responses. GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Grok 4 were queried zero-shot, with reasoning enabled, through a single commercial web interface (Perplexity) in October 2025, using an automated script. Because every model answers the same items, all inferences use paired tests or question-clustered models. Accuracy separates into two tiers: GPT-5 (79.9\%, 95\% CI 76.6--83.1) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (78.4\%, 74.8--81.9) are statistically indistinguishable, and both outperform Grok 4 (71.7\%) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (71.3\%) by 6.7--8.7 percentage points (Holm-adjusted $p < 0.001$). The English--Persian accuracy difference is small for every model ($-0.2$ to $+2.5$ points; exact McNemar $p \ge 0.28$). For three models the 90\% confidence interval lies within $\pm 5$ points, so differences larger than this can be excluded. Questions with figures are much harder: the odds ratio is 0.30 (95\% CI 0.21--0.43) after adjusting for discipline. The apparent EE deficit of two models disappears once the larger share of figure-based EE items is accounted for. We describe the dataset, the protocol and its limitations, including the uncontrolled web-retrieval and decoding settings of the interface, and release item-level responses and analysis code.
papers.summary: Four large language models were tested on 433 multiple-choice questions from the 2024 and 2025 Iranian national Ph.D. entrance exams in Electrical and Computer Engineering, each posed in Persian and in English translation, queried zero-shot with reasoning enabled through the Perplexity web interface. **`GPT-5` (79.9%) and `Gemini 2.5 Pro` (78.4%) are statistically indistinguishable and beat `Grok 4` (71.7%) and `Claude Sonnet 4.5` (71.3%) by 6.7-8.7 points**. The English-Persian accuracy difference is small for every model (-0.2 to +2.5 points), while questions that depend on a figure are much harder (odds ratio 0.30). The authors note limitations including the interface's uncontrolled web-retrieval and decoding settings, and release item-level responses and analysis code.

papers.title: How Persona Conditioning Changes Open-Ended Task Execution: A Paired Evaluation of Behavioral Gains and Reliability Costs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often prompted with role- or persona-based instructions, yet persona conditioning has mainly been evaluated through character fidelity or aggregate benchmark accuracy. We study persona conditioning as a task-execution steering signal that changes how models interpret, structure, and sustain responses. Using paired instances derived from real user role-play logs and expanded into simulated multi-turn continuations, we compare with-persona and no-persona conditions while fixing task content, constraints, user simulation, and evaluation criteria. Across eight models, persona conditioning improves expert content depth and procedural fidelity, and these gains survive length control. At the same time, it lowers strict instruction-following accuracy by 17 to 30 points in every model evaluated, and increases unsupported real-world specificity through persona-induced elaboration. These results suggest that persona prompting is not a general-purpose performance improvement technique, but a selective task-execution policy shift with both behavioral gains and reliability risks.
papers.summary: Persona or role prompts for large language models (LLMs) are usually judged by character fidelity or aggregate accuracy, not by how they change the way a task gets carried out. Using paired instances built from real user role-play logs and extended into simulated multi-turn conversations, the authors compare with-persona and no-persona conditions while holding task content, constraints, user simulation, and evaluation criteria fixed. Across eight models, personas improve expert content depth and procedural fidelity even after controlling for length, but they **lower strict instruction-following accuracy by 17 to 30 points in every model** and increase unsupported real-world specifics. The authors conclude that persona prompting shifts how a task is executed, with both gains and reliability costs, and is not a general performance booster.

papers.title: SD-Cache: Learnable Memory Consolidation with State-Guided Dynamic Caching
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as persistent services that must reason over large volumes of external knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds model responses in relevant documents, but the retrieved content must still be encoded and stored in the key-value (KV) cache. As this content accumulates, the cache grows linearly, increasing memory consumption and inference cost. Existing memory-compression methods address this problem either by retaining a subset of cached states or by learning context compressors that map documents to compact latent representations. Despite these advances, consolidating information under tight memory budgets while preserving its usefulness for future queries remains challenging. We investigate how the model's native KV states can be selectively consolidated into a fixed-size working memory without access to future queries. To this end, we introduce SD-Cache (State-guided and Dynamically updated Cache), a query-agnostic KV-memory consolidation framework that operates alongside a frozen generator LLM. SD-Cache learns to consolidate layer-wise KV states into fixed-size memory through selective anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement, processing new contexts in a single forward pass without context-specific optimisation. Experiments on retrieval-augmented question answering and synthetic long-context benchmarks show that SD-Cache maintains competitive downstream performance under constrained memory budgets.
papers.summary: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), retrieved documents must be encoded into the model's key-value (KV) cache, which grows linearly as content accumulates and drives up memory and inference cost. `SD-Cache` (State-guided and Dynamically updated Cache) is a learned module that runs alongside a frozen generator and consolidates layer-wise KV states into a fixed-size working memory, using anchor-based pooling and state-guided refinement, without knowing future queries. New contexts are processed in a single forward pass with no per-context optimisation. On retrieval-augmented question answering and synthetic long-context benchmarks, the authors report that it **maintains competitive downstream performance under constrained memory budgets**.

papers.title: Agentic Systems Need Multi-Run Evaluation: A Study of Retrieval and Response Variability in a Deployed Enterprise RAG System
papers.abstract: Previous RAG systems have mostly been evaluated in a single-run setting, and with the advent of agentic RAG, systems are still often evaluated the same way. However, agentic RAG systems introduce a source of run-to-run variability, since several of their components make decisions non-deterministically. Such systems typically comprise a retrieval stage followed by a generation stage, and the retrieval stage in particular can behave differently across runs. For example, the agent might issue a different number of parallel searches from one run to the next, which alters the retrieved documents and therefore the final answer. In this paper we study this behavior in a deployed agentic RAG system for product-documentation questions, running each of 739 questions ten times and analyzing the execution traces to find where different runs first diverge. We find a substantial gap between success in any run and success in every run: the retrieval hit rate is 69.4% when the correct page is found in at least one run, but 50.9% when it must be found in all ten. Responses also stay similar in meaning while varying in wording, with an average BERTScore of 0.90 and a BLEU of 0.49. Trace-level analysis shows that retrieval is the largest source of divergence (43.9%), and the number of parallel searches at the first retrieval step alone accounts for 20.1% of divergent pairs. Taken together, these results show that single-run evaluation can hide reliability and consistency issues in agentic RAG systems, and that multi-run evaluation is necessary to reveal them.
papers.summary: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems make non-deterministic decisions, such as how many parallel searches to issue, yet are still mostly evaluated from a single run. The authors ran each of 739 product-documentation questions ten times through a deployed enterprise system and analysed the execution traces to find where runs first diverge. The **retrieval hit rate is 69.4% when the correct page is found in at least one run but only 50.9% when it must be found in all ten**, while answers stay similar in meaning but vary in wording (`BERTScore` 0.90, `BLEU` 0.49). Retrieval is the largest source of divergence at 43.9%, and the number of parallel searches at the first retrieval step alone accounts for 20.1% of divergent run pairs.

papers.title: ToneMamaba: Learning Contextualized Tonal Contours with Boundary-Reset State Space Models
papers.abstract: Mandarin tone recognition in connected speech is challenging because contextual and durational variation reshapes F0 contours. We propose ToneMamba, a boundary-aware state space model that replaces static boundary embeddings with bidirectional state resets at syllable, word, and IPU levels. Fixed weights fuse multi-level representations, while shared-weight bidirectional scans use channel-wise directional fusion to reduce parameters. Dynamic syllable pooling forms tonal contours, and rhythm-conditioned gating incorporates durational information. ToneMamba achieves 97.9% and 74.8% accuracy on FCU-VOICE-360 read and MCDC-8 conversational speech, outperforming the baseline (ToneNet) by 0.9 and 15.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that word-level resets are particularly effective, while rhythm conditioning provides greater gains in conversational speech, underscoring the role of durational variation in spontaneous speech.
papers.summary: Recognising Mandarin tones in connected speech is hard because context and duration reshape pitch contours. `ToneMamba` is a state space model that, instead of using static boundary embeddings, resets its bidirectional state at syllable, word, and inter-pausal-unit boundaries, and adds dynamic syllable pooling and rhythm-conditioned gating to bring in durational information. It reaches 97.9% accuracy on `FCU-VOICE-360` read speech and **74.8% on `MCDC-8` conversational speech, 15.9 percentage points above the `ToneNet` baseline**. Ablations indicate that word-level resets help most and that rhythm conditioning matters more for conversational speech.

papers.title: AhaPro: A Process-level Rebus benchmark for probing Aha moments in LLM reasoning
papers.abstract: Existing research on Aha moments in large language models has largely focused on reflective expressions or final revision outcomes, leaving their role in the visible reasoning process insufficiently characterized. Rebus puzzles encode answers through character forms, spatial arrangements, and homophony. Reinterpreting key details may trigger Aha moments and shifts in the reasoning process and candidate answers. We introduce AhaPro, a process-level benchmark that uses rebus puzzles to examine how models reorganize evidence and revise answers through Aha moments. The framework represents CoT as sequences of candidate answers, evidence, and verification states, using hierarchical metrics to assess conflict detection, state improvement, and subsequent adoption. Across eleven models, we observe frequent failures to adopt better states discovered during Aha moments, alongside adopted revisions that leave state quality unchanged or reduce it. Models also detect conflicts without subsequently achieving an effective revision. Further paired interventions suggest that prior reasoning context may hinder effective revision after conflict detection, while multi-branch search highlights answer selection as a bottleneck between correct-answer discovery and successful correction.
papers.summary: Studies of sudden insight, or Aha moments, in large language models have mostly looked at reflective phrases or final revised answers, leaving the visible reasoning process itself uncharacterised. `AhaPro` is a benchmark built on rebus puzzles, which hide answers in character forms, spatial layout, and homophony, and it represents chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning as a sequence of candidate answers, evidence, and verification states scored for conflict detection, state improvement, and adoption. Across eleven models, the authors find that **models frequently fail to adopt better states they discover during Aha moments**, make revisions that leave quality unchanged or worse, and detect conflicts without then revising effectively. Paired interventions suggest that prior reasoning context can hinder revision, and multi-branch search points to answer selection as the bottleneck between finding the correct answer and committing to it.

papers.title: Reliability of Language-Model Judges for Quantitative Scientific Question Answering: Evidence from Perovskite Photovoltaics
papers.abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented language models increasingly relies on automated model judges, yet their reliability on quantitative scientific synthesis remains largely unmeasured. Here, we evaluate automated grading on a quantitative benchmark for perovskite photovoltaics, where all 755 ground-truth answers are deterministically computed from 45,441 experimental device records. We evaluate a frontier judge (Claude Opus 5.5) alongside two local open-weight judges (Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-8B) across 4,530 free-text answers from six retrieval architectures under three regimes: reference-augmented (with the computed key), evidence-augmented (with retrieved passages and query logs), and unassisted (question and answer alone). Equipped with the reference key, Claude Opus reproduces ground truth near-perfectly (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.982 \pm 0.003$) and preserves exact architectural rankings ($\tau = 1.00$). Withholding the reference causes evaluation fidelity to collapse: frontier agreement drops to $\kappa = 0.557 \pm 0.022$, and providing retrieved literature passages yields virtually no improvement ($\kappa = 0.576 \pm 0.024$). Without reference keys, local judges degrade to near-random agreement ($\kappa = 0.087$ and $0.112$), inverting the leaderboard to rank a hallucinating closed-book baseline first ($\tau \le 0.20$). Furthermore, SQL-augmented generations induce severe evaluative blind spots: absent a reference, the frontier judge accepts 46.6% of erroneous SQL answers, overestimating architecture accuracy as 66.4% against its true 52.6%. These findings demonstrate that model-based evaluation in the physical sciences cannot rely on unstructured text inspection; rigorous benchmarking requires reference ground truth precomputed from structured measurement records.
papers.summary: Automated model judges are widely used to grade retrieval-augmented systems, but their reliability on quantitative scientific questions is largely unmeasured. On a perovskite photovoltaics benchmark whose 755 ground-truth answers are computed deterministically from 45,441 device records, the authors test `Claude Opus 5.5` and two local judges (`Qwen3-14B`, `Qwen3-8B`) on 4,530 answers, with a reference key, with retrieved evidence, or with nothing. With the key, `Claude Opus 5.5` matches ground truth almost perfectly (Cohen's kappa 0.982), but **without it agreement falls to a kappa of 0.557, and adding retrieved passages barely helps (0.576)**. The local judges drop to near-random agreement without a key and rank a hallucinating closed-book baseline first, and the frontier judge accepts 46.6% of erroneous SQL-generated answers.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) allows language models to verbalise multi-step rationales before producing their final answer. While this technique often boosts task performance and offers an impression of transparency into the model's reasoning, this position paper argues that rationales generated by current CoT techniques can be misleading and are neither necessary nor sufficient for trustworthy interpretability. We analyse faithfulness as whether CoTs are not only human-interpretable but also reflect the model's underlying reasoning well enough to support responsible use. By synthesising evidence from prior work, we systematically show that verbalised chains are frequently unfaithful, diverging from the critical hidden computations that drive a model's predictions. As CoT is increasingly relied upon in application domains, including high-stakes ones such as medicine, law, and autonomous systems, we further argue that this unfaithfulness is not taken seriously enough in these settings: our analysis of 1,000 recent CoT-centric papers finds that approximately 21.7% explicitly treat CoT as a load-bearing interpretability technique, building pipelines or safety arguments that would not hold if CoT is unfaithful to the model's actual reasoning. They include papers in high-stakes domains that heavily hinge on such interpretability claims. Building on prior work, we make three proposals: (i) avoid treating CoT as being sufficient for interpretability without additional verification, (ii) adopt rigorous methods that assess faithfulness for downstream decision-making, and (iii) report such assessments alongside any interpretability claims based on CoT, while continuing to use CoT for its communicative and monitoring benefits.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales give an impression of transparency, but this position paper argues they are neither necessary nor sufficient for trustworthy interpretability. Synthesising prior evidence, the authors argue that verbalised chains are often unfaithful to the hidden computations that actually drive a model's predictions. Their review of 1,000 recent CoT-centric papers finds that **about 21.7% explicitly treat CoT as a load-bearing interpretability technique**, including work in high-stakes domains such as medicine and law. They propose not treating CoT as sufficient without additional verification, adopting rigorous faithfulness assessments, and reporting those assessments alongside any CoT-based interpretability claim.

papers.title: Agentic Optimization: LLM Agents Select and Configure Algorithms for Engineering Design
papers.abstract: Engineers solving new multi-objective design problems commonly commit to a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) before seeing a result. The best MOEA differs from benchmark to benchmark. We propose agentic optimization, placing an LLM agent outside the optimization loop, where it reads a natural-language problem description to configure and launch algorithms, drawing on parametric knowledge rather than on a performance history that a novel problem lacks. We compare five LLMs in a fixed harness on four engineering benchmarks and a real-world SARS-CoV-2 molecular docking task, using hypervolume (HV) and IGD+ with multiple comparison-corrected tests. Three models (GPT, DeepSeek, Qwen) dominate every baseline on combined HV and IGD+, and each is significantly better than the best baseline on at least one benchmark, sometimes by applying the same baseline algorithm they surpass, showing the importance of both algorithm configuration and selection. Agent behavior is strongly model-dependent, but even the weakest agents dominate three of the four baselines overall.
papers.summary: Engineers facing a new multi-objective design problem usually have to pick a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) before seeing any results, and the best choice varies by problem. The proposed approach places an LLM agent outside the optimisation loop, where it reads a natural-language problem description and uses its parametric knowledge to select, configure, and launch algorithms. Five LLMs are compared in a fixed harness on four engineering benchmarks and a SARS-CoV-2 molecular docking task, scored by hypervolume and `IGD+`. **Three models (`GPT`, `DeepSeek`, `Qwen`) dominate every baseline on the combined metrics**, sometimes by better configuring the very algorithm they beat, and even the weakest agents dominate three of the four baselines overall.

papers.title: Lexical Tone and Word Order Matter in Translation: Prosodic Correspondence Across Languages
papers.abstract: Prosody conveys emphasis, emotion, and intent, yet its correspondence across translation remains underexplored, especially when languages differ in lexical tone and word order. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic word-level analysis of prosodic correspondence in translated speech spanning tonal and non-tonal Asian languages, with comparisons to European-language findings and explicit analyses of lexical tone and word reordering. Building on prior evidence of fine-grained prosody correspondence in European-language pairs, we investigate how these linguistic factors relate to word-level pitch and energy correspondence between English and five languages: Mandarin Chinese, Thai, and Vietnamese, which have lexical tone, and Japanese and Korean as additional comparisons. Correspondence is generally lower than previously reported European-language estimates. Adjusting for lexical tone increases pitch correspondence for English-Mandarin Chinese, English-Thai, and English-Vietnamese. However, English-Japanese and English-Korean also exhibit lower correspondence than the European-language estimates, indicating that tonal status alone does not explain the observed pattern. Greater word reordering is associated with weaker local correspondence even under semantic alignment, suggesting that semantic alignment does not fully account for differences in prosodic organization. These findings characterize the limits of fine-grained acoustic correspondence across translation and motivate prosody modeling that accounts for lexical pitch constraints and the structural context of translated content.
papers.summary: How prosody (pitch and energy patterns that carry emphasis and intent) carries over in translated speech is poorly understood for languages that differ from English in lexical tone and word order. The authors run a word-level analysis of pitch and energy correspondence between English and Mandarin Chinese, Thai, Vietnamese, Japanese, and Korean, and compare against earlier European-language results. **Correspondence is generally lower than the estimates previously reported for European language pairs**; adjusting for lexical tone raises pitch correspondence for the three tonal languages, but Japanese and Korean are also low, so tone alone does not explain the gap. More word reordering is associated with weaker local correspondence even under semantic alignment.

papers.title: LLM Genetic Feature Engineering
papers.abstract: Feature Engineering is the (traditionally manual) process of constructing derived variables from an existing dataset by combining, transforming, or otherwise manipulating the original data fields to reduce statistical noise and extract meaningful, domain-specific quantities of interest from the raw dataset. Recent work demonstrates promising progress toward the au tomation of this process through the integration of large language models (LLMs) and various metaheuristics to guide the search for useful features. We build on this approach by introducing a novel genetic algorithm that implements selection, crossover, and mutation at the individual feature level, rather than at the level of the entire engineered feature set. In doing so, we enable in-process statistical analysis of newly-generated features, thereby enabling the genetic algorithm to simultaneously integrate individual and group-level feature metrics into its selec tion process. We demonstrate this capability using state-of-the-art feature importance metrics, and show that this approach yields superior predictive performance while driving meaningful improvements in feature relevance, algorithm robustness, and overall model interpretability.
papers.summary: Automated feature engineering with large language models typically pairs the model with a search heuristic that evolves whole sets of engineered features. This work introduces a genetic algorithm that applies selection, crossover, and mutation to individual features instead, which allows each newly generated feature to be statistically analysed during the search. Selection can then combine per-feature and group-level metrics, demonstrated with feature importance measures. The authors report that the approach **yields superior predictive performance** along with gains in feature relevance, robustness, and interpretability, though the abstract gives no figures.

papers.title: Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition
papers.abstract:
Autonomous agent governance is commonly framed as a problem of enforcing correct execution. However, in multi-agent systems, an equally fundamental question precedes execution: which agents are allowed to act.
  In this paper, we show that allocation is not an auxiliary concern but a structural component of governance. When multiple agents compete for execution under constrained resources, any allocation mechanism introduces unavoidable trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and resistance to strategic manipulation. We formalize this through a set of impossibility results, including Sybil amplification and the incompatibility of desirable allocation properties.
  We then show that these allocation constraints cannot be resolved within a single layer of control. Instead, they propagate across the system, interacting with execution atomicity, state enforcement, and behavioral drift. This leads to a multi-scale governance structure composed of four orthogonal dimensions: temporal (atomicity), state (enforcement), behavioral (drift monitoring), and population (allocation).
  Our main result is an irreducibility theorem: under finite observability, no governance architecture can collapse these dimensions without loss of correctness or stability. Allocation, in particular, acts as a first-class constraint that prevents simplification of the governance stack.
  We validate these results through a series of analytical constructions and empirical ablations, showing that removing or approximating any layer leads to systematic failure modes.
  This work reframes agent governance as a structural problem: not only how actions are executed, but how access to execution is determined, and why these decisions impose irreducible architectural requirements.
papers.summary: Governance of autonomous agents is usually framed as enforcing correct execution, but the authors argue that deciding which agents get to act under constrained resources is an equally structural part of the problem. They formalise impossibility results for allocation mechanisms, including Sybil amplification and incompatibilities among fairness, efficiency, and resistance to strategic manipulation. From these they derive a governance structure with four orthogonal dimensions: temporal (atomicity), state (enforcement), behavioural (drift monitoring), and population (allocation). The main result is an irreducibility theorem stating that, **under finite observability, no governance architecture can collapse these four dimensions without losing correctness or stability**, which the authors support with analytical constructions and ablations.

papers.title: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End
papers.abstract:
Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts.
  The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.
papers.summary: Drawing on the 1970s argument by DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis that mathematical proofs gain their standing through a social process of human critique and understanding, this essay critiques what it describes as OpenAI's October 2026 release of 722 automated manuscripts claiming full or partial solutions to 372 open problems. The authors examine the automated approach under three headings (Specification, Regress, and Utility) and contend that separating mechanical solving from human understanding yields logical artefacts nobody has digested. Their central claim is that **flooding the literature with unexamined proofs guarantees that finite human attention cannot separate signal from noise**. They conclude that posting a result is not the same as submitting it to the community processes that vet mathematics.

papers.title: Hidden Clues in WM-811K: Uncovering the Spatial Signals Behind Wafer Map Prediction
papers.abstract: WM-811K (also known as LSWMD) is a wafer map dataset first made publicly available in a 2015 paper by Wu et al. Convolutional neural networks have been used to achieve high classification accuracy on this dataset, yet it's not easy to decipher which features of the dataset are driving that performance. This study attempts to answer this specifically for WM-811K: how much of the predictive performance results from the wafer layout, the count of failed dies, their distance from the center and their exact 2-D location. After analyzing duplicate wafer maps, removing same wafer maps with conflicting labels and ensuring that the same manufacturing lot or exact same map doesn't appear in training, validation and test data, we were left with 25,513 defect-labeled wafer maps from eight classes. We then constructed four variations of each wafer map. The Original was the actual wafer map present in the dataset. The Layout-only kept only the layout of the non-background dies. The Global-shuffle kept the count of failed dies while shuffling them around. The Radial-shuffle randomized the locations of failed dies only in their radial bin, which was chosen out of 8 radial bins based on distance from the center. The data split, preprocessing and CNN architecture remained the same for all four of them. Macro-F1 progressed like this: 0.3829 (Layout-only), 0.5803 (Global-shuffle), 0.7439 (Radial-shuffle) and 0.8563 (Original). These results show that WM-811K contains useful information at several levels: wafer layout, number of failures, distribution of failed dies in a given radius, and exact 2-D locations of the failed dies. Therefore, high classification performance on this benchmark does not come only from learning the exact defect configuration.
papers.summary: Convolutional networks score well on the `WM-811K` wafer map defect dataset, but it is unclear which properties of the maps drive those scores. After removing duplicates and conflicting labels and preventing lot-level leakage across splits, the authors train the same network on 25,513 defect-labelled maps in four variants: wafer layout only, failed dies shuffled globally, failed dies shuffled within radial bins, and the original. **Macro-F1 rises from 0.3829 (layout only) to 0.5803, 0.7439, and 0.8563 (original)**, so layout, failure count, and radial distribution each carry predictive signal. High accuracy on the benchmark therefore does not come only from learning the exact two-dimensional defect pattern.

papers.title: PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL: Polarization-Keyed Examination Papers and Mandatory Issued Eyewear that Displace AI Glasses and Extend Universal Design
papers.abstract: Camera-equipped AI glasses turn an examination page into a query for a remote vision-language model. Device detection targets possession, and our companion work SEOYUN targets the model. PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL instead changes who owns the eyewear. Every candidate wears authority-issued glasses for the whole session, and the question paper is printed so that it can be read only through them. As in cinema stereoscopy, a patterned laminate encodes the text in the handedness of circular polarization rather than in brightness. The page looks uniformly grey to the naked eye and to unfiltered cameras, and the issued circular analyzer reveals the text. Compulsory issued eyewear turns the smart-glasses form factor against itself. The face position is occupied by a device the authority supplies and collects, and a camera anywhere else needs its own analyzer. Spectacle wearers receive prescription inserts in the issued frame, low-vision candidates may use an offline assistive mixed-reality tier, and blind candidates keep braille, audio, and screen-reader formats.
