We derive the luminance and contrast budget and show why circular keying tolerates head tilt. A simulation study supports the analysis. A spectral Mueller model confirms tilt invariance and invisibility to linear-polarization cameras, but a 1 degree axis misregistration leaks a few percent of contrast. A capture-and-OCR experiment on English and Korean text shows that video averaging can recover leakage too weak to read in a single frame, so leakage must be bounded against the adversary's total photon budget. Data from 151 observers and 28 cameras show that spectral (metameric) keys are visible to all of them. The key carries no secrecy, and filtered covert cameras remain possible. All results are simulations; no prototypes, physical measurements, or human-subject results are reported.
papers.summary: Camera-equipped AI glasses let an exam candidate send the question page to a remote vision-language model. `PEACE-TEST-PROTOCOL` proposes that every candidate wear authority-issued eyewear and that papers be printed with a laminate encoding the text in the handedness of circular polarization, so the page looks uniformly grey to the naked eye and to unfiltered cameras. Simulations confirm tolerance to head tilt and invisibility to linear-polarization cameras, but a 1 degree axis misregistration leaks a few percent of contrast, and video averaging can recover leakage too weak to read in a single frame. The authors state that filtered covert cameras remain possible and that **all results are simulations, with no prototypes, physical measurements, or human-subject results**.

papers.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
papers.abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/
papers.summary: Most audio-video deepfake benchmarks ask only whether a clip is real or fake, which hides whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. `MOZAIC` releases every source clip in all four combinations of real or fake video and audio, giving 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks covering authenticity, manipulation type, identity verification, and explanation. Of 12 audio-video multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) tested, **the best reaches only 35.6% on four-way authenticity** and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% versus 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4%, but the best falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training.

papers.title: Differential evolution with perturbation for continuous function optimization
papers.abstract: This paper presents differential evolution with perturbation (DEP) for continuous function optimization. Differential evolution is a simple and efficient algorithm. Perturbation is the phenomenon that the motion by the contribution of the main force is disturbed by the influence subsidiary power. In order to show the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, we compare it to existing algorithms by CEC2017 datasets.
papers.summary: Differential evolution is a simple population-based method for optimising continuous functions. The authors propose a variant, `DEP`, that adds a perturbation step to the search, and they **compare it against existing algorithms on the `CEC2017` benchmark functions**. The abstract reports no numerical results.

papers.title: Set-based comprehensive learning and particle swarm optimization with memory for discrete optimization problem
papers.abstract: This paper describes a novel algorithm of set-based comprehensive learning and particle swarm optimization with memory for discrete optimization problem. Our algorithm is an approach of searching for the best position in a set by referring to the current position when updating the solution. In order to show the validity of our algorithm, we examine numerical experiments compared to existing algorithms.
papers.summary: For discrete optimisation problems, the authors propose a set-based particle swarm optimisation algorithm that combines comprehensive learning with a memory mechanism. When updating a solution, it searches for the best position within a set by referring to the current position. Validation consists of **numerical experiments comparing it with existing algorithms**, with no specific results given in the abstract.

papers.title: When Successful Collaboration Becomes an Attack Surface: Insider Memory Poisoning in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Recent Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) increasingly use shared memory to store and reuse successful collaboration records, enabling teams to improve across tasks. However, this memory introduces a new attack surface for malicious insiders. Unlike existing insider attacks that inject misleading information directly into the current collaboration, misinformation stored in shared memory can later appear as successful team experience and gain greater credibility and influence. We propose MIMPA (Multi-Agent Insider Memory Poisoning Attack), which exploits this vulnerability using only normal participation privileges, without direct memory access. During an earlier task, the malicious agent embeds a target-specific payload while helping the team answer correctly, allowing the payload to be retained in a successful collaboration record. When retrieved for a later target task, this poisoned record can steer benign agents toward a designated wrong answer, further amplified by malicious triggering. Across three benchmarks and two LLM backbones, MIMPA substantially outperforms existing insider attacks and remains effective under hierarchical memory management, while auditing only partially mitigates it. These results reveal that shared memory intended to accumulate team experience can become a persistent channel for insider attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ahnji0520/MIMPA-code.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) increasingly store successful collaboration records in shared memory for reuse, which gives a malicious insider a persistent channel. `MIMPA` (Multi-Agent Insider Memory Poisoning Attack) needs only normal participation privileges: the malicious agent helps the team answer an earlier task correctly while embedding a target-specific payload, so the payload is saved as part of a successful record. When that record is later retrieved for the target task, it steers benign agents toward a designated wrong answer. Across three benchmarks and two LLM backbones the attack outperforms existing insider attacks and survives hierarchical memory management, and **auditing only partially mitigates it**.

papers.title: Evolutionary AI Control: Population-Level Safety Under Reproduction, Heredity, and Selection
papers.abstract:
An AI agent can satisfy every individual safety check and still give rise to a population that violates a collective safety limit. This risk arises in open multi-agent systems, where agents copy themselves, modify their successors, and change system membership during a run. Selection then shifts the population toward traits outside the developers' optimization targets. We prove conditions under which safety guarantees persist through reproduction, inheritance, and selection, and we characterize how they fail.
  Four counterexamples illustrate these failures. Unauthorized copies, which violate a specified reproductive restriction, can each leave fewer than one successor on average while their expected number grows without bound under continued production from an expanding authorized population. Two lineages can each decline in isolation yet grow exponentially when they interact. Alternating between reproductive rules can drive growth even when each rule, applied alone, suppresses it. Selection can raise the population's average rate of unauthorized reproduction above a certified limit even though every agent's rate remains fixed.
  Whereas existing verification methods assume fixed or registered membership, we prove safety certificates, under stated assumptions, for populations whose agents create successors during a run. The main result bounds the expected cumulative harm over a run, including when a scheduler adapts the reproductive rules to the observed history. Further conditions cover every population state reachable through evolution and preserve reproductive restrictions as descendants inherit modifications. Drawing on the mechanisms by which multicellular organisms control cell reproduction, the framework enables developers to specify and verify these controls before deployment.
papers.summary: In open multi-agent systems where agents copy themselves and modify their successors, every agent can pass its individual safety checks while the population as a whole violates a collective limit. The authors prove conditions under which safety guarantees persist through reproduction, inheritance, and selection, and give four counterexamples of failure, such as lineages that each decline in isolation but grow exponentially when they interact. Their main result **bounds the expected cumulative harm over a run, even when a scheduler adapts the reproductive rules to the observed history**. Further conditions cover every reachable population state and preserve reproductive restrictions as descendants inherit modifications, with the framework modelled on how multicellular organisms control cell reproduction.

papers.title: SlotFill: Repairing Lossy SoC Communication Traces for Post-Silicon Validation
papers.abstract: Post-silicon validation relies on traces of messages exchanged by SoC components, but trace buffers and monitors drop messages, often leaving no mark of what was lost. We present SlotFill, which puts each deleted message back in the right gap, with the right type and order. SlotFill gives every gap between the remaining messages a fixed number of slots, and a Transformer-based model fills each slot with a message or leaves it empty when nothing was deleted there, so the input never reveals how much was lost. The model also uses monitor fields (timestamps, transaction IDs, addresses) from surviving messages. On whole-program gem5 traces of 4- and 8-core systems (2.07 billion messages), SlotFill restores up to 97% of deleted messages exactly at 15% loss and up to 87% at 50% loss, and 76-83% at 15% loss when timestamps are coarse.
papers.summary: Post-silicon validation depends on traces of messages exchanged between system-on-chip components, but trace buffers and monitors silently drop messages. `SlotFill` assigns a fixed number of slots to every gap between surviving messages, and a Transformer-based model fills each slot with a message or leaves it empty, so the input never reveals how much was lost. It also uses monitor fields such as timestamps, transaction IDs, and addresses from the surviving messages. On whole-program `gem5` traces of 4- and 8-core systems totalling 2.07 billion messages, it **restores up to 97% of deleted messages exactly at 15% loss** and up to 87% at 50% loss.

papers.title: Scoring Recovery-Time Agent Security: Proposals, Effects, and Retry Instructions
papers.abstract: A timed-out tool write may be absent, committed, or still in flight. Evaluating an agent only on whether its goal exists can hide harmful recovery actions: auditing 12 supplied traces changes apparent completion from 10/12 to 8/12. We introduce an executable evaluation that separately records tool proposals, runtime decisions, and committed effects. In 3,456 model episodes, the original task wording produces only 39/576 valid recoveries when the initial write is absent; a combined clarification produces 576/576. A further 1,584 episodes test stronger attacks and separate the effect definition from the recovery recipe with three rollouts per absent-state cell. Definition alone yields 276/288 valid recoveries; recipe alone yields 288/288. For Luna, malicious text is associated with 11.1 percentage points fewer valid recoveries under both original and definition-only wording, an availability signal limited by shared tasks and templates. The stronger attacks produce no attempted unauthorized or changed-key action and no unsafe effect. A trajectory audit finds six original-key retries after observing pending status: five denied and one deduplicated. Bounded checks distinguish atomic key enforcement from a delayed-commit race; stale negative reads also invalidate the evidence gate. A separate Claude Code program adds 720 successful episodes: 288 under the original attacks and 432 stronger-attack calibration episodes across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 5.5, with no observed proposal or effect deviations. The contribution is a measurement design and a diagnosis of availability, specification, and contract sensitivity, with no demonstrated general defense efficacy.
papers.summary: When an agent's tool write times out, the write may be absent, committed, or still in flight, and scoring only whether the goal state exists can hide harmful recovery actions. The authors build an executable evaluation that separately records tool proposals, runtime decisions, and committed effects, then run several thousand model episodes with varied task wording and injected malicious text. With the original wording only 39 of 576 recoveries were valid when the initial write was absent, while **a combined clarification of the effect definition and recovery recipe produced 576 of 576 valid recoveries**, and the stronger attacks produced no unauthorized actions or unsafe effects. The authors frame the contribution as a measurement design and a diagnosis of specification sensitivity, with no demonstrated general defense.

papers.title: Conformalized Tree-Based Gradient Ensembles for Out-of-Distribution Detection and Plausible Recourse
papers.abstract: Counterfactual recourse provides actionable feature adjustments that reverse unfavourable predictions made by automated decision models. However, when recourse search optimizes purely against classifier confidence or narrow proxy scores over gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT), search procedures can exploit boundary artifacts and low-density regions---an instance of Goodhart's law---yielding out-of-distribution (OOD) recommendations that appear favourable nominally while lacking manifold plausibility. In this paper, we study conformalized OOD gating coupled with actionability-constrained counterfactual search across two tabular benchmarks: Adult and Give Me Some Credit (GMSC). Calibrating finite-sample anomaly gates (gate_IF, gate_LOF, and the conjunctive gate_ALL) at significance level delta = 0.05 over isolation forest, local outlier factor, and k-nearest-neighbor signals, we audit generated counterfactuals against held-out GMM and OCSVM detectors alongside ablation studies (gen10, gen100, and relax). Across matched recourse pairs where both constrained and unconstrained searches succeed, gate_ALL significantly reduces held-out OCSVM flags on Adult (N=541, Delta flag_OCSVM = -0.0296, p_Holm = 4.0e-4) and lowers both held-out flags on GMSC (N=540, Delta flag_OCSVM = -0.0346, p = 1.0751e-4; Delta flag_GMM = -0.1663, p = 3.5679e-16) while increasing matched recourse cost (Delta cost = +0.3035, p = 1.3365e-5) and narrowing overall feasibility. Our findings formalize the cost--feasibility--plausibility trade-off and demonstrate how conformal OOD gating audits recourse reliability on tabular ensembles.
papers.summary: Counterfactual recourse searches over gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT) can exploit boundary artifacts and low-density regions, producing out-of-distribution (OOD) recommendations that look favourable but are implausible. The authors pair conformally calibrated anomaly gates built on isolation forest, local outlier factor, and k-nearest-neighbor signals with actionability-constrained search, and audit the results against held-out detectors on the `Adult` and `Give Me Some Credit` datasets. The conjunctive gate `gate_ALL` **significantly reduces held-out outlier flags on both datasets while raising recourse cost and narrowing feasibility**, which the authors describe as a cost, feasibility, and plausibility trade-off.

papers.title: Layer-Readout Interfaces in EEG Foundation Models: Predictive Accessibility and Cross-Dataset Transfer
papers.abstract: Intermediate layers often outperform final layers when foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors, but the source of this advantage is unclear. We study this question in EEG foundation models by separating three factors: how representations are read out, whether intermediate layers provide predictive utility beyond the final-layer interface, and whether useful depth structure transfers across datasets. Across five models and three tasks, improving the final-layer readout consistently recovers substantial predictive performance, yet intermediate layers remain advantageous within frozen extraction. We also find that layers selected on one dataset remain useful on another across five dataset pairs and four task families, and that a compact set of source-derived task directions retains predictive value after transfer in sleep staging. Together, these results show that predictive utility varies across depth, and its usefulness depends on how representations are read out and transferred. More crucially, source-selected layers provide a reusable feature interface across datasets, reducing the need for target-side layer search while outperforming final-layer baselines on target datasets.
papers.summary: Intermediate layers of frozen foundation models often beat the final layer as feature extractors, and this study asks why in the setting of electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models. It separates three factors: how representations are read out, whether intermediate layers add predictive value beyond the final layer, and whether useful depth structure transfers across datasets. Across five models and three tasks, a better final-layer readout recovers much of the gap, yet intermediate layers remain advantageous. In addition, **layers selected on one dataset stay useful on another across five dataset pairs and four task families**, reducing the need for layer search on the target dataset.

papers.title: Flagging Batch Shift in Flow Cytometry using Jeffreys Divergence between Gaussian Mixtures
papers.abstract: Machine learning models for clinical flow cytometry are usually evaluated on data drawn from their training distribution. In routine practice, however, acquisition conditions and reagents may change, potentially making predictions unreliable without warning. We propose a model agnostic criterion for prediction reliability based on a notion of distance from the training distribution: each patient sample is represented by a Gaussian mixture model, and its Jeffreys divergence to a reference fitted on the training data is estimated using Monte Carlo integration. We illustrate our approach on real-life shifted cohorts of acute myeloid leukaemia patients, using a classifier trained to predict NPM1 mutation status. First, we show graphically and statistically that pairwise divergences capture acquisition cohort structure. We then calibrate a rejection threshold on a subset of shifted cohort samples and evaluate it on held-out subjects. Across 20 runs, the misclassification rate of rejected samples was 2.5 times larger than for retained samples. These results suggest that input divergence can help identify unreliable predictions, providing a strong candidate component for abstention frameworks, along with quality control measures and classifier confidence.
papers.summary: Classifiers for clinical flow cytometry can become unreliable without warning when acquisition conditions or reagents change. The proposed model-agnostic check represents each patient sample as a Gaussian mixture model and estimates its Jeffreys divergence to a reference fitted on the training data using Monte Carlo integration, rejecting samples above a calibrated threshold. On shifted cohorts of acute myeloid leukaemia patients with a classifier predicting `NPM1` mutation status, **rejected samples were misclassified 2.5 times as often as retained samples** across 20 runs.

papers.title: Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data
papers.abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.
papers.summary: Missing values break the equivalence-class structure that rough set theory relies on for attribute reduction. The Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (`COFRS`) model measures similarity as a weighted overlap on attributes present in both objects divided by the total attribute count, so missing values are penalised instead of treated as wildcards, and it finds reducts by greedy backward elimination. On 11 UCI benchmarks **`COFRS` yields the smallest reducts on average, at 4.1 attributes against 5.0 to 11.2 for the alternatives**, though the difference from `Tolerance-RS` is not statistically significant. Classification accuracy does not improve, and with an RBF support vector machine `COFRS` ranks last, so the gain is compactness only.

papers.title: Fusion Gains Depend on the Implementation and the Calibration Target: An 18-Task Study of Prediction Intervals with a Single-Source Fallback
papers.abstract: A fused model can benefit from an extra learning stage as well as from a second data source. We compare four fusion implementations with matched single-source learners on 18 regression tasks with prediction intervals. Across ten refits under group-wise calibration, linear stacking improved the interval score by 6.0% against a source model without a second stage and by 0.1% against its matched single source. The four implementations agreed on 3 of 18 tasks and gave opposite clear verdicts on 12, including 8 of the 10 tasks with naturally distinct sources. With pointwise calibration, they agreed on 5 tasks and gave opposite clear verdicts on 9. A development-set selector with a matched single-source fallback improved ten-refit task-averaged scores by 2.2--6.3% in every implementation under both calibrations. Adding fused arms to the pool of single-source candidates improved the mean relative score by about 5 percentage points. Under group-wise calibration, the gradient-boosted selector met the criterion frozen before evaluation on eight held-out tasks. In post-opening refits, selectors lost to the matched single source in 4.4--6.1% of task-level runs under group-wise calibration. Under signed pointwise calibration, three implementations lost in 19--23% of runs. Fusion evaluations should compare matched candidates on held-out data and report how often the selector loses alongside its average gain.
papers.summary: A fused model can gain from an extra learning stage as well as from a second data source, which makes fusion benefits easy to overstate. The authors compare four fusion implementations with matched single-source learners on 18 regression tasks with prediction intervals, under group-wise and pointwise calibration. Linear stacking improved the interval score by 6.0% over a source model without a second stage but by **only 0.1% over its matched single source**, and the four implementations gave opposite clear verdicts on 12 of the 18 tasks. A development-set selector with a single-source fallback improved task-averaged scores by 2.2 to 6.3%, though it still lost to the matched single source in a measurable share of runs.

papers.title: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability: A Weakest-Link Analysis of Tool Manifests
papers.abstract: Runtime controls for tool-using agents depend on manifests that state what each tool may read and where its output may go. Evaluations of these controls, including ChainCaps, report per-attack blocking: the share of attacks a set of manifests stops. We show that this is the wrong unit. A catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy: if $M$ independently authored policies are each wrong with probability $p$, the chance that the catalog contains an accepted exfiltration path is $1-(1-p)^M$, while per-attack blocking stays at $1-p$. Three lines of evidence agree. In synthetic catalogs run through two enforcement engines, ChainCaps and OpenAPPA, per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200, and composition provides no protective effect. A fifteen-model authoring pilot shows that real errors cluster by author, so a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions rather than 60 (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2). On 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules, the models' own manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, as the author-effect model predicts and independence does not. Evaluations should report catalog vulnerability, the sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.
papers.summary: Runtime controls for tool-using agents rely on manifests stating what each tool may read and where its output may go, and evaluations usually report the share of individual attacks blocked. The authors argue a tool catalog is only as safe as its weakest policy, so the chance of at least one accepted exfiltration path grows with catalog size even when per-attack blocking stays constant. In synthetic catalogs run through `ChainCaps` and `OpenAPPA`, **per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200**. On 114 real Model Context Protocol tools, model-written manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, and errors cluster by author so that a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions.

papers.title: Exact Volume-Preserving Diffeomorphic Shear Splitting: Continuous-Discrete Geometric Bounds, Reversible Memory Backpropagation, and Expressivity Frontiers in Volumetric Mapping
papers.abstract:
Incompressible diffeomorphic registration requires continuous spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume (det(D\Phi) = 1) without topological folding (det(D\Phi) > 0). Standard velocity-field methods (SVF, LDDMM) approximate incompressibility via numerical ODE integration or soft penalties, exhibiting numerical volume drift (~10^-4 to 10^-1), iterative grid inversions, and linear backpropagation memory O(L * N_vox).
  We formulate an exact structure-preserving framework for 3D registration based on cascaded coordinate shears. By decomposing the divergence-free Lie algebra sdiff(\Omega) into six coordinate-shear generators whose convective non-linearities vanish identically, each elementary stage integrates analytically to a closed-form triangular shear with det(DS_k) = 1 and exact machine-precision inverse requiring zero iterations and zero spatial interpolations. Multi-stage compositions generate the connected volume-preserving group SDiff_0(\Omega). We establish: (i) an unconditional global diffeomorphism proof closing the Hadamard-Caccioppoli injectivity gap; (ii) a Dirichlet boundary confinement lemma; (iii) an anisotropic Riemannian similarity invariance; (iv) a Sobolev H^2 spectral budget preventing chaotic mixing; and (v) an exact reversible backpropagation engine eliminating O(L) trajectory storage (0.00 MB intermediate activations).
  We prove second-order O(h^2) sub-voxel convergence across 16^3 to 64^3 lattices and second-order trajectory accuracy for palindromic Strang splitting (468.1x error reduction vs. Lie-Trotter; drift |det(D\Phi)-1| <= 2.22e-16). Execution is 2.1x-4.0x faster than SVF with 78.4% GPU memory reduction. On cardiac cine-MRI (ACDC, N=100) and brain MRI (OASIS-1, N=414), our model achieves competitive Dice (0.884 and 0.841) while strictly maintaining 0.0000% folding and zero volume drift.
papers.summary: Incompressible image registration needs spatial mappings that preserve local tissue volume without folding, but standard velocity-field methods only approximate this and show numerical volume drift and memory that grows with integration depth. The proposed framework composes six kinds of coordinate shears, each integrating in closed form to a volume-preserving map with an exact inverse, and uses reversible backpropagation to avoid storing intermediate activations. The authors prove global invertibility and second-order convergence, and report 2.1 to 4.0 times faster execution than stationary velocity fields with 78.4% less GPU memory. On `ACDC` cardiac MRI and `OASIS-1` brain MRI the model reaches competitive Dice scores of 0.884 and 0.841 with **zero folding and volume drift at machine precision**.

papers.title: Beyond Static Charts: Benchmarking Interactive Chart-to-Code Generation for MLLMs
papers.abstract: In recent years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved significant progress in chart-to-code generation. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on static charts, overlooking interactive charts that enable richer and more expressive data exploration. Unlike static chart-to-code generation, which emphasizes visual consistency, interactive chart-to-code evaluation targets behavioral consistency, requiring chart states to evolve correctly under sequences of user interactions, thereby rendering traditional one-step evaluation paradigms ineffective. To address this gap, we introduce ChartInt, the first benchmark specifically designed for interactive chart-to-code generation. ChartInt consists of 2,779 carefully annotated examples covering common interaction patterns such as hover, highlight, and tooltips. Additionally, ChartInt incorporates editing tasks such as data updates, style adjustments, and cross-chart style transfer to expand real-world application scenarios. To enable reliable evaluation of interaction behavior, we propose a preset state snapshot protocol that predefines target interaction states and deterministically triggers interaction events, transforming dynamic behaviors into reproducible evaluation targets. Based on this protocol, we design a multi-dimensional evaluation framework measuring semantic and stylistic consistency. Experiments show that while current MLLMs perform well on static charts, their performance drops significantly on interactive tasks, highlighting the need for interaction-aware benchmarks.
papers.summary: Chart-to-code benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) focus on static charts, ignoring interactive charts whose state must evolve correctly under sequences of user actions. `ChartInt` provides 2,779 annotated examples covering interactions such as hover, highlight, and tooltips, plus editing tasks such as data updates, style adjustments, and cross-chart style transfer. A preset state snapshot protocol predefines target interaction states and triggers events deterministically, making dynamic behavior reproducible to evaluate. Experiments show that **current MLLMs do well on static charts but drop significantly on interactive tasks**.

papers.title: What People Choose Not to Say: A Multimodal Benchmark for Fine-Grained Information Manipulation in Conversations
papers.abstract: Recent advances in MLLMs have improved social understanding, enabling models to recognize emotions and distinguish truthful from deceptive behaviors. However, existing benchmarks largely focus on coarse-grained emotion recognition or binary truth-deception detection, overlooking the diverse ways people manipulate information in conversations, such as withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim. Understanding these behaviors requires reasoning about underlying facts, participant knowledge, and conversational context, making them difficult to evaluate reliably. To address this gap, we introduce InfoCon, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained information manipulation in conversations. InfoCon identifies six fine-grained strategies and derives a coarse consistency label from their factual and interactional relations. We develop an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework to construct and verify reliable labels from rich contextual evidence. We benchmark representative multimodal models and systematically analyze their fine-grained information manipulation understanding, providing a testbed beyond binary truth-deception judgments.
papers.summary: Benchmarks of social understanding in multimodal models mostly test coarse emotion recognition or binary truth-versus-deception detection, missing the varied ways people manipulate information in conversation. `InfoCon` is a multimodal benchmark that labels **six fine-grained strategies, including withholding, leakage, fabrication, evasion, and defensive counterclaim**, and derives a coarse consistency label from their factual and interactional relations. Labels are built and verified with an evidence-grounded multi-agent annotation framework, and representative multimodal models are benchmarked on the resulting testbed.

papers.title: Antares-Smaug: Adversarial Names, Tokens and Attack Rewrites: Sanitisers Miss Unseen Generalisations
papers.abstract: Laya is an open decision model: given a text, a question and K named options with descriptions, it returns one probability per option in a single pass, and software may act on the answer unseen. We attack six Laya models with 81 programmatic edits of 566 synthetic items (injected sentences, label leaks, edited descriptions, decoy options, invisible and look-alike characters, floods) and report the share of correctly answered items hijacked or lost, with bootstrap intervals. Attack wordings that no defence was built from win the attacker's option on 59% of items for released Laya and 36% for fine-tune v1 (trained on 109 written injections). An injection works through the option name: a sentence naming an option steers the released model even when negated (32%), while an imperative naming no option does not (5%). Option descriptions barely matter (2%). Character edits alone cost v1 up to 72% of right answers. A sanitiser frozen before any held-out result cuts the attacks it was built from by 72% but held-out sentence attacks by 27%, and an attacker who picks the best of 34 held-out strings per item restores success to 84% (mean string 18%). The same oracle takes the model fine-tuned on the four build families of injected sentences from 5% (mean string) to 58%. Fine-tuning on build families only (against an unchanged-rows control) cuts held-out sentence attacks (three held-out families) from 33% to 3% but character edits only from 25% to 20%. A label-free check that deletes the option names and measures the shift flags held-out sentence attacks (AUROC 0.95) but not character edits (0.46), and thresholds set on dev schemas for 5% false alarms gave 8% to 18% on an unseen schema and other languages. All data are synthetic with LLM labels, on one backbone. Several planned runs (other checkpoints, a second seed, some fine-tunes) were not run.
papers.summary: `Laya` is an open decision model that returns one probability per named option for a text and question, and downstream software may act on its answer without review. The authors attack six `Laya` models with 81 programmatic edits of 566 synthetic items, covering injected sentences, label leaks, decoy options, invisible and look-alike characters, and floods. Attack wordings that no defence was built from **hijack the answer on 59% of items for the released model** and 36% for a fine-tune, with injections working mainly by naming an option, even when negated. A sanitiser cuts the attacks it was built from by 72% but held-out sentence attacks by only 27%, and fine-tuning reduces held-out sentence attacks from 33% to 3% while barely helping against character edits.

papers.title: GHC:Expanding Residual Interfaces in Hyper-Connections
papers.abstract: Hyper-Connections expand residual capacity across parallel streams, yet restrict every branch to narrow read and write interfaces: each branch still reads a single stream mixture and writes scaled copies of one output vector to all streams. To lift this bottleneck, we propose Grouped Hyper-Connections (GHC). By partitioning each branch into parallel groups along attention heads or FFN channels, GHC supplies each group with a distinct stream mixture and aggregates their separate outputs into each stream with learned weights. Extensive experiments across dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models show that GHC consistently improves upon Identity Hyper-Connections (IHC) with negligible parameter and memory-access overhead, increasing training efficiency by 35% over Pre-Norm and 10% over IHC. Moreover, expanding residual interfaces overcomes the diminishing returns of adding streams, allowing wider residual states to yield further gains.
papers.summary: Hyper-Connections widen a network's residual pathway into parallel streams, but each branch still reads a single stream mixture and writes scaled copies of one output vector to all streams. Grouped Hyper-Connections (`GHC`) split each branch into groups along attention heads or feed-forward channels, giving each group its own stream mixture and aggregating group outputs into each stream with learned weights. Across dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, `GHC` **improves training efficiency by 35% over `Pre-Norm` and 10% over Identity Hyper-Connections (`IHC`)** with negligible parameter and memory-access overhead. It also removes the diminishing returns of adding more streams.

papers.title: Detecting Harmful Short Videos in Toxic Diet Culture: A Governance-Ready Evidence Framework with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Algorithmic content moderation is increasingly important for governing short-form video content, yet harmful-content detection research focuses primarily on prediction or limited explanations. This leaves a governance challenge underexplored: producing decision-linked evidence that supports the review and justification of moderation decisions. Using toxic diet culture as an empirical case, we conceptualize governance-ready evidence as computational traceability, evidence localization, policy grounding, and evidence inspectability. We develop the Sparse Autoencoder-based Policy-Aligned Contrastive Evidence (SPACE) framework in a pretrained SAE feature space derived from a large multimodal model. A global relevance gate and decomposable linear evidence head identify decision-linked evidence; segment supervision and within-video ranking localize this evidence; policy alignment maps it to platform guidelines; and Pareto-efficient selection yields a compact, task-specific evidence vocabulary. On 3,711 labeled TikTok videos, SPACE achieves the highest harmful-category Macro F1 among benchmarks across four families, at 0.8507. Its highest-scoring observation overlaps a ground-truth harmful span for 88.0% of harmful test videos, while its evidence representation retrieves the corresponding policy category for 87.0%. Stakeholder evaluations indicate that the SPACE evidence report is perceived as useful for understanding, reviewing, documenting, and responding to moderation decisions. The study contributes computational design science knowledge for embedding governance-ready evidence within predictive content-moderation systems.
papers.summary: Harmful-content detectors for short videos mostly output predictions or limited explanations, leaving moderators without evidence they can review and justify. Using toxic diet culture as the case, the Sparse Autoencoder-based Policy-Aligned Contrastive Evidence (`SPACE`) framework works in a sparse autoencoder feature space from a large multimodal model, identifying decision-linked evidence, localizing it to video segments, and mapping it to platform policy categories. On 3,711 labeled TikTok videos, `SPACE` reaches **a harmful-category Macro F1 of 0.8507, the highest among the compared baselines**. Its top-scoring segment overlaps a ground-truth harmful span in 88.0% of harmful test videos, and its evidence retrieves the matching policy category for 87.0%.

papers.title: Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation: Pixel as Code for Agentic Visual Creation
papers.abstract: Visual creation demands expressive imagery together with precise control over text, layout, and structure. We introduce Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation, an agentic framework that connects these capabilities through Pixel as Code. Raster images are represented by learned discrete visual tokens, while structured artifacts use explicit programs. A shared generation-and-rendering interface connects these representations to visual feedback across images, vector graphics, webpages, and documents. A Nemotron-native harness coordinates planning and raster candidate selection, with targeted repair for editable structured and hybrid artifacts. To support this interface, we develop Nemotron-Labs-Image-Tokenizer, the autoregressive raster generator Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B, and the structured-code model family Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode. On approximately 178K images spanning six visual domains, our tokenizer improves reconstruction PSNR from 26.08 to 29.57 dB over Emu3.5 IBQ. It also provides 7.13x faster encoding and 10.93x faster decoding at batch size one on A100. In standalone evaluation, one Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode variant surpasses Kimi K3.1 Pro on the aggregate across Chart2Code, MMSVG, Design2Code, and Image2Struct. At the system level, the Nemotron-native configuration raises GenEval2 Soft-TIFA GM from 31.71 to 52.56 using the same raster generator. With our best setting, Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation achieves performance competitive with GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana Pro across most benchmarks with available comparisons.
papers.summary: Visual creation needs expressive imagery along with precise control over text, layout, and structure. `Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation` is an agentic framework that represents raster images as learned discrete visual tokens and structured artifacts as explicit programs, joined by a shared generation-and-rendering interface with visual feedback across images, vector graphics, webpages, and documents. Its components include a new image tokenizer, the autoregressive generator `Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B`, and the `Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode` code models. The tokenizer raises reconstruction PSNR from 26.08 to 29.57 dB over `Emu3.5 IBQ`, and the agentic harness **lifts the `GenEval2` Soft-TIFA score from 31.71 to 52.56 using the same raster generator**, with overall results reported as competitive with `GPT Image 2` and `Nano Banana Pro`.

papers.title: CoRe: Jointly Learning Contextual Representations for Understanding and Generation
papers.abstract: We introduce CoRe, in which understanding and generation jointly shape one contextual representation for images and one for text, trained from scratch. Each representation is read for understanding, conditions the other modality, and is the space in which that modality is generated by a continuous flow from Gaussian noise. With 383M parameters trained on CC12M and no pretrained language model, text encoder, or VAE at inference, CoRe matches a same-data contrastive-only baseline in global understanding and reaches COCO-30K FID 10.10, comparable to much larger generators built on pretrained components. In controlled comparisons at equal data and architecture, CoRe generates better in both directions (text to image and image to text) than a representation shaped by understanding alone and then frozen, and follows prompts better than generating in a space that understanding does not shape. In the other direction, with an attentive segmentation probe, on monocular depth, and when read by a frozen language model, CoRe surpasses the contrastive-only baseline: generation adds information that stronger readouts reach. Because generation runs inside the understanding representation, frozen real-image probes read and steer intermediate states and the model ranks its own samples without extra training. Because both modalities use continuous flows, both also distill to a few steps. Our controls indicate why one representation suffices: understanding organizes the representation semantically, while generation makes it retain more information.
papers.summary: `CoRe` trains from scratch one contextual representation for images and one for text, each shaped jointly by understanding and generation. Each representation is read for understanding, conditions the other modality, and serves as the space in which its modality is generated by a continuous flow from Gaussian noise. With 383M parameters trained on `CC12M` and no pretrained language model, text encoder, or VAE at inference, it matches a contrastive-only baseline on global understanding and reaches **a `COCO-30K` FID of 10.10, comparable to much larger generators built on pretrained components**. Controlled comparisons indicate that understanding organizes the representation semantically while generation makes it retain more information.

papers.title: OmniX: A first jet and event model
papers.abstract: Foundation models are a new approach to building machine learning algorithms for particle physics. Their central idea is that a single model can be adapted to a variety of downstream tasks, amortizing training costs. So far, most foundation model prototypes have operated on the constituents of a single jet. This limits their usefulness for physics problems at the scale of full events, such as distinguishing different processes, and restricts their performance, as global correla- tions are invisible to the model. Here, we introduce OmniX, an architecture that operates on both single jets and whole events within a single model. Using the jet-level JetClass and Top-tagging datasets and the event-level Collide-2V dataset, we demonstrate that OmniX trained jointly on single jets and full events matches or exceeds otherwise equivalent jet-only and event-only models in generation and classification.
papers.summary: Foundation model prototypes in particle physics have mostly operated on the constituents of a single jet, which hides global correlations and limits their use for problems at the scale of full collision events. `OmniX` is an architecture that handles both single jets and whole events within one model. Using the jet-level `JetClass` and `Top-tagging` datasets and the event-level `Collide-2V` dataset, the authors show that joint training **matches or exceeds otherwise equivalent jet-only and event-only models** in generation and classification.

papers.title: ContextLure: Exploiting Benign Conversation History for Indirect Prompt Injection
papers.abstract: As LLMs become more capable, agents can perform more complex tasks with tools and maintain longer interactions with users. These benign conversations contain evidence on task results, user concerns, and operational constraints. The risk is that attackers who can observe benign conversations (evidence) may construct stronger indirect prompt injections without increasing the attackers' control over prior turns or the later injection. However, we still lack a clear study of how effectively attackers can select and use this evidence. To address this gap, we introduce ContextLure, a red-teaming framework in which an attacker silently observes an existing benign conversation, extracts evidence, and constructs an injection. The challenges are twofold: (a) selecting useful evidence and (b) presenting it as reasons for an unauthorized action, without changing the prior benign conversation. To efficiently exploit (a) the effect of evidence on attack success, our framework selects evidence across 2 dimensions: User/System Preferences with 3 selection policies. And to enhance (b) the process of turning the selected information into the malicious request, we introduce an Urgency/Priority matrix with 4 rewriting strategies. Across the evaluated conditions, we reach 67.4% ASR on AgentDojo and 87.3% on InjecAgent. These results show that attackers can use benign interaction evidence in later attacks without first poisoning the benign conversation.
papers.summary: Long agent conversations accumulate evidence about task results, user concerns, and operational constraints, which an attacker who can observe them might use to craft stronger indirect prompt injections. `ContextLure` is a red-teaming framework in which the attacker silently observes a benign conversation, selects evidence along user and system preference dimensions, and rewrites it into reasons for an unauthorized action using urgency and priority strategies, without altering prior turns. The attack reaches **a success rate of 67.4% on `AgentDojo` and 87.3% on `InjecAgent`**.

papers.title: Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training
papers.abstract: LLM agents operate through harnesses that define system prompts, action formats, feedback loops, and resource constraints. A model may possess the knowledge needed to solve a task yet fail to express that knowledge through a particular harness. This raises a basic question: when a policy fails under a given harness, is it missing task knowledge or the competence to operate the interface? We distinguish two components of agentic competence: task competence, the knowledge and reasoning needed to solve a task, and interface competence, the ability to act on that knowledge through a given harness. Across four reasoning and agentic benchmarks, we show that harness-conditioned training yields vastly different outcomes depending on how these interact. Multi-harness distillation aggregates task knowledge from trajectories collected through different harnesses into a shared policy, but this knowledge is realised only when training preserves or improves competence on the inference-time interface. Otherwise, single-harness training can induce interference in interface competence, sometimes catastrophically collapsing performance on a held-out harness despite improvements in underlying task knowledge. To disentangle task and interface supervision, we introduce harness rehearsal: distillation on traces that carry minimal task knowledge while exercising the target interface. Cross-harness task supervision or rehearsal alone yields little gain, but their combination yields gains far larger than either: on BFCL V3 multi-turn with Qwen3-4B, they achieve 8.5% and 32.5% respectively, versus 58.8% together. Finally, on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is more robust than distillation to single-harness training: it does not substantially degrade performance on other harnesses, and interface competence acquired through multi-harness distillation persists through subsequent RL.
papers.summary: LLM agents act through harnesses that define system prompts, action formats, and feedback loops, so a failure may reflect missing task knowledge or an inability to operate the interface. The authors separate task competence from interface competence and show across four benchmarks that distilling on a single harness can collapse performance on a held-out harness even as task knowledge improves. They introduce `harness rehearsal`, distillation on traces that exercise the target interface while carrying minimal task knowledge. On `BFCL V3` multi-turn with `Qwen3-4B`, cross-harness task supervision alone and rehearsal alone reach 8.5% and 32.5%, **while combining them reaches 58.8%**, and on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) proves more robust than distillation to single-harness training.

papers.title: Leaks by Installments: Cross-Session Answer Disclosure in LLM Tutors and a Ledger-Based Defense
papers.abstract: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner does not have to ask for the answer all at once. Existing safeguards judge each reply within the current conversation, so a learner can open a new session, reword the problem, or request a worked solution to the same problem with different numbers. We call this cross-session disclosure and propose a defense: a persistent, per-learner disclosure ledger. For every problem a learner brings, the system builds a typed solution graph. Before a reply is released, a gate matches the reply's own content, not the learner's wording, against the ledger by result values and by type-labeled solution structure, then computes which steps the learner could now derive. The reply is withheld if that set reaches the final answer or exceeds a budget. In a simulation of 3,000 problems, the ledger reduced leakage through renumbered practice variants from 100% to 10.6% while honest learners completed 94-99.5% of problems. With two real LLM tutors (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) on 60 problems, leakage through renumbered variants fell from 0.58 to 0.08 and from 1.00 to 0.18, with 98% honest completion. The ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate in the live runs. All acceptance criteria were fixed before each run.
papers.summary: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner can extract one piecemeal by opening new sessions, rewording the problem, or asking for a worked solution with different numbers. The proposed defense keeps a persistent per-learner disclosure ledger with a typed solution graph for each problem, and a gate matches each reply's content against the ledger to compute which steps the learner could now derive, withholding replies that would reach the final answer. In a simulation of 3,000 problems, **leakage through renumbered practice variants fell from 100% to 10.6%** while honest learners completed 94 to 99.5% of problems. With `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` and `Phi-3.5-mini-instruct` on 60 problems, leakage fell from 0.58 to 0.08 and from 1.00 to 0.18, though the ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate.

papers.title: CaLA: Causal Latent Adjustment for World Models under Adaptive Policies
papers.abstract: World models is answering ``imagine" answers to ``what-if'' questions via imagined rollouts. But rollouts collected by adaptive policies induce treatment-outcome confounding in imagined rollouts. We study this problem in Match-3 difficulty adjustment, where latent player skill influences both assigned difficulty and churn. We build a fully specified Match-3 SCM with sequential mechanics, adaptive assignment, and paired ground-truth interventions, on which unadjusted models fit to the logged trajectories select difficulty settings that raise churn. We then introduce Causal Latent Adjustment (CaLA), a DAG-constrained world model that infers a variational player representation from pretreatment history. Across our evaluations, CaLA provides the most reliable population-level intervention estimates and competitive individualized decisions, although rich handcrafted histories can remain advantageous for individual-level adjustment. We further find that residual correction can degrade causal decision quality despite improving predictive fit, highlighting the need to distinguish predictive accuracy, confounding adjustment and the behavior of downstream causal estimators.
papers.summary: World models answer what-if questions through imagined rollouts, but data logged under adaptive policies confounds treatment and outcome. The authors study this in Match-3 difficulty adjustment, where hidden player skill drives both assigned difficulty and churn, and build a fully specified structural causal simulator with ground-truth interventions, on which unadjusted models choose difficulty settings that raise churn. Causal Latent Adjustment (`CaLA`) is a world model constrained by a causal graph that infers a variational player representation from pretreatment history. It gives **the most reliable population-level intervention estimates** and competitive individualized decisions, and the authors find that residual correction can worsen causal decisions even while improving predictive fit.

papers.title: The Recycler: In-Transit Machine Learning on High-Fidelity Data from Simulation Campaigns as an Optimized Approach for Building Frontier Models
papers.abstract: We report on the first realization of in-transit machine learning using data streamed from multiple simulations running in parallel to the training on the same exascale high performance computing system. This workflow can be commonly applied to a broad variety of scenarios in which simulation campaigns play an important role. Unlike single simulations, campaigns run several simulations in parallel. This is interesting for finding an optimum operation point of a machine like a particle accelerator or a fusion reactor, quantifying the variation in model predictions e.g. in climate research, or discovering new capabilities e.g. in materials or drug design. Such campaigns produce huge amounts of high-fidelity data at high rates. File system bandwidth and capacity prohibit retaining all of that data, usually requiring orders of magnitude in reduction before it can be stored. We demonstrate a workflow that streams the data from multiple simulations to train a frontier model in parallel, thereby maximizing data throughput. We demonstrate that this can use a much larger amount of high-fidelity data as training data for the model compared to storage in files, essentially replacing file IO by in-transit training of large-scale frontier models. This will allow to create AI-informed feedback loops to steer simulation campaigns while reducing the overall computation time needed and provide high-fidelity frontier models for reuse by the scientific community.
papers.summary: Simulation campaigns on exascale systems produce high-fidelity data faster than file systems can store it, so most of it is discarded before it can be used for training. The authors report a workflow that streams data from multiple simulations running in parallel straight into model training on the same high-performance computing system, which they describe as the first realization of in-transit machine learning of this kind. They claim that **streaming lets training use a much larger amount of high-fidelity data than storing it in files would allow**, effectively replacing file IO with training. The intended uses are AI-informed feedback loops that steer campaigns and reusable scientific models.

papers.title: Is 4 Bits Enough for EEG Sleep Staging? A Subject-Level Benchmark of MXFP4, NVFP4 and FP8
papers.abstract: Staging sleep on a wearable device keeps the raw electroencephalogram (EEG) private and saves the energy needed to transmit it. It also requires small, energy-efficient neural networks. We benchmark 13 post-training quantization (PTQ) configurations, from FP16 to the block-scaled 4-bit formats MXFP4 and NVFP4, for five-stage sleep staging from single-channel Fpz-Cz EEG. We use Sleep-EDF-78 (78 subjects), subject-wise cross-validation, three training seeds, value-exact emulation, and per-subject paired statistics. All 8- and 16-bit formats stay within 0.45 percentage points (pp) of FP32 Macro-F1. With 4-bit weights and activations, an epoch-wise CNN loses 1.98 to 3.04 pp, and a temporal-context network loses at most 1.19 pp. A same-encoder ablation shows that temporal context explains little of this gap. At equal block size, NVFP4 outperforms MXFP4. The first layer, which quantizes the raw EEG, is the most sensitive layer in both networks. Keeping the first and last layers in FP8 brings both tested 4-bit formats within 0.48 pp of FP32. This recipe adds at most 2.1% weight storage, needs no retraining, and is equivalent to quantization-aware training (QAT) within an exploratory 1-pp margin. The 4-bit losses fall on the same subjects across architectures (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.69 to 0.79), and they reduce N3 recall the most. On the nested Sleep-EDF-20 subset, NVFP4 with FP8 first and last layers again stays within 0.25 pp of FP32. Under MXFP4, however, the ranking of the architectures reverses, and FP8 first and last layers do not fully recover two of the three tested models. In our emulation, NVFP4 with FP8 first and last layers thus loses little accuracy without QAT in both cohorts.
papers.summary: On-device sleep staging from single-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) needs very small networks, so the authors benchmark 13 post-training quantization (PTQ) configurations from FP16 down to the block-scaled 4-bit formats `MXFP4` and `NVFP4` on `Sleep-EDF-78` with subject-wise cross-validation. All 8- and 16-bit formats stay within 0.45 percentage points of FP32 Macro-F1, while full 4-bit quantization costs an epoch-wise CNN 1.98 to 3.04 points and a temporal-context network at most 1.19 points. The first layer, which quantizes the raw signal, is the most sensitive, and **keeping the first and last layers in FP8 brings both 4-bit formats within 0.48 percentage points of FP32** with at most 2.1% extra weight storage and no retraining. `NVFP4` beats `MXFP4` at equal block size, and on the `Sleep-EDF-20` subset the recipe does not fully recover two of three models under `MXFP4`.

papers.title: Transformers with Signatures: Towards Universal In-Context Learning in Path Space
papers.abstract:
In-context learning (ICL) enables transformers to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations without updating their parameters. However, theoretical guarantees for transformers remain limited in general, and elusive in particular when target responses depend nonlinearly on the evolution of observed paths. We establish an ICL framework for path space, using path signature features. Building on the universal linear approximation property of signatures, we construct explicitly a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso. Under sparse signature approximation and suitable moment and concentration conditions, we establish finite-sample prediction error bounds. Our analysis goes beyond the IID data setting in the existing ICL theory, allowing dependence among demonstrations and the query.
  Experiments on in-context sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference demonstrate robustness to changes in observation grids and adaptation to unseen market environments. Across these prediction tasks, transformers with signatures match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of signature-based ICL.
papers.summary: Theoretical guarantees for in-context learning (ICL) in transformers are limited, especially when targets depend nonlinearly on the evolution of observed paths. The authors build an ICL framework for path space on path signature features and explicitly construct a causal softmax transformer with two attention heads per layer that emulates in-context Lasso, with **finite-sample prediction error bounds that hold when demonstrations and the query are dependent rather than IID**. In experiments on sparse recovery, nonlinear path regression, execution-cost prediction, and financial payoff inference, signature-based transformers match or outperform vanilla transformer baselines with substantially fewer trainable parameters.

papers.title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.
papers.summary: Dense retrievers can be fooled by a near-copy of the correct document that differs only by a small meaning-reversing edit: raw cosine similarity over `E5-Large-v2` puts such a trap document in the top 10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. The authors train a small projection from 1024 dimensions down to 11 or 32 on a declared set of cases, and for those cases **no trap appears in the top 10 in any of twelve domain and pool-size settings** across legal, medical, patent, and financial data with pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases. They also describe an accelerated variant of spectral graph retrieval (`SpectRAG`) that serves the projection at about 2-4 ms per query, with indexes roughly 90x smaller than the full embedding. The claim is limited to declared cases, the correct-answer rate falls to about 0.79 for reworded queries, and projections transfer only partly across domains.

papers.title: Learning from Human Corrections through Temporal Preferences
papers.abstract: When people intervene to correct a robot, they provide information not only through how they correct its behavior, but also through when they choose to intervene. Existing approaches to Learning from Corrections focus on comparing the new trajectory to the robot's originally intended behavior, thus underutilizing the context of the robot's behavior before the intervention. In this work, we investigate how both pre- and post-intervention behavior can be translated into preference pairs for learning value functions that approximate a human's latent reward. We construct post-intervention preferences by comparing corrected behavior with the behavior it replaces, and pre-intervention preferences from temporal relationships among states leading up to an intervention. We evaluate the learned value representations through two downstream tasks: goal inference and correction forecasting. Our results show that post-intervention preferences are particularly effective for goal inference, while pre-intervention preferences provide strong correction-forecasting performance. Combining both sources of information performs strongly across both tasks, even when generalizing to participants unseen during training. These findings demonstrate that both when and how humans correct provide complementary information for learning value representations from corrective interactions.
papers.summary: Methods for learning from human corrections of a robot usually compare the corrected trajectory with the robot's original plan and ignore what the timing of the intervention reveals. The authors turn both sources into preference pairs for learning a value function that approximates the human's latent reward: post-intervention preferences compare corrected behavior with the behavior it replaces, and pre-intervention preferences come from temporal relationships among the states leading up to the intervention. Post-intervention preferences work best for goal inference and pre-intervention preferences for forecasting corrections, and **combining both performs strongly on both tasks, including for participants unseen during training**.

papers.title: Taxi: Analyzing Agents at (Real) Scale
papers.abstract: In this technical report, we present Taxi -- a system for debugging, clustering, and monitoring agents at scale. Taxi scales to millions of steps efficiently. This is made possible by a combination of scalable analysis methods. Taxi relies primarily on clustering to generate a taxonomy over steps for a structured overview of the data, and provides full SQL access for engineers and automated agents to ask complex questions. Clustering and querying are best used together in a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent. Taxi also includes an experimental integration of Jev-style decision models: models that map state and bounded questions directly to typed, probabilistic decisions. They add low-cost semantic routing and evaluation where embeddings or literal queries alone are insufficient. In addition, Taxi provides an extensible ecosystem, including built-in evaluators and daily reports. To accommodate growth, Taxi is designed to be modular, hackable, and easy to plug-and-play for individuals and teams.
papers.summary: `Taxi` is a system for debugging, clustering, and monitoring AI agents whose traces run to millions of steps. It **clusters steps into a taxonomy for a structured overview and exposes full SQL access**, with the two meant to be combined in a hybrid pipeline guided by a coding agent. The technical report also describes an experimental integration of `Jev`-style decision models, which map state and bounded questions to typed, probabilistic decisions for low-cost semantic routing and evaluation, along with built-in evaluators and daily reports.

papers.title: Below the Stopwatch: Checking the Performance Claims of Coding Agents in the Kernel
papers.abstract: Coding agents open many pull requests (PRs) that claim to make software faster. Most such claims also give a reason, such as "cache the result" or "read the file once". A stopwatch can show that code got faster, but not that it got faster for the stated reason. We present Below, a pipeline that checks these reasons at the kernel level. From 1,343 runtime-performance PRs in the AIDev dataset, Below extracts the mechanism each PR claims and maps it to the kernel and hardware signals that must change if the claim is true. A build agent that never sees the claim rebuilds the code before and after each PR. Below then measures both versions with plain timing runs, hardware counters and LTTng kernel traces. Most claims are not measured: 57.3% of the PRs offer only reasoning or no evidence, and only 31.4% state an effect size. Of 82 analyzed PRs, 32 ran faster, 28 showed no clear change and 22 ran slower. The expected signal of the claimed mechanism appeared in 34 PRs (20 in kernel-trace signals alone), and 42 PRs also changed their output. Kernel signals move about 1.7 times as often for a faster PR's claimed mechanism as for mechanisms it did not claim; the instruction count barely separates them (1.15 times).
papers.summary: Coding agents often open pull requests claiming a speedup for a stated reason, such as caching a result, and timing alone cannot confirm that the stated reason is what changed. `Below` extracts the claimed mechanism from 1,343 runtime-performance pull requests in the `AIDev` dataset, maps it to the kernel and hardware signals that should move, has a build agent that never sees the claim rebuild the code before and after, and measures both versions with timing runs, hardware counters, and `LTTng` kernel traces. Most claims are unmeasured, with 57.3% offering only reasoning or no evidence, and **of 82 analyzed pull requests 32 ran faster, 28 showed no clear change, and 22 ran slower**, while 42 also changed their output. The expected signal of the claimed mechanism appeared in 34 of them, and kernel signals separated claimed from unclaimed mechanisms better than instruction counts did.

papers.title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval
papers.abstract: Retrieving images of patients clinically similar to a given patient can support diagnosis, teaching and research. Training and evaluating retrieval systems requires knowing which images of different patients show the same finding, and existing datasets are small or narrow in scope. We construct PMC-PaIR, a dataset of 86,144 pairs of clinically similar images from 56,013 open-access PubMed Central case reports, which often document rare or challenging presentations. We develop an approach that follows citations, which often link case reports of similar patients. To determine what two linked cases share clinically, it prompts large language models to generate and answer hierarchical questions, from modality to diagnosis and findings, and to match images by caption using the answers. Experts find the pairs highly accurate, and this question-guided approach finds twice as many correct pairs as direct matching. Fine-tuning BiomedCLIP on PMC-PaIR improves retrieval in all modality, anatomy and diagnosis categories tested, for image-only queries and image queries with a short text naming the finding. We release the dataset and the automated pipeline, which can extend PMC-PaIR as new case reports are published.
papers.summary: Training and evaluating medical image retrieval requires knowing which images from different patients show the same finding, and existing datasets are small or narrow. `PMC-PaIR` contains **86,144 pairs of clinically similar images drawn from 56,013 open-access PubMed Central case reports**, built by following citations between case reports and prompting large language models to generate and answer hierarchical questions, from modality to diagnosis and findings, before matching images by caption. Experts rate the pairs as highly accurate, and the question-guided approach finds twice as many correct pairs as direct matching. Fine-tuning `BiomedCLIP` on the dataset improves retrieval in every modality, anatomy, and diagnosis category tested.

papers.title: AdProducer: Towards Agentic Advertising Video Generation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have made automated advertising production increasingly feasible. However, an effective advertisement must faithfully represent the product and communicate its selling points through compelling visual storytelling, which requires more than visual synthesis: it calls for deeper product understanding and strategic decisions about how to present product value. Crucially, product research and creative design are closely intertwined, as the information gathered about a product determines which features can be faithfully demonstrated and how they should be presented. In this paper, we introduce AdProducer, the first end-to-end agentic framework for advertising video creation, transforming concise creative briefs into finished advertisements. Our multimodal agent autonomously researches products through web and image search and translates its findings into selling-point-driven storyboards that guide a frozen video generator. To achieve this, we develop a dedicated data construction pipeline that yields two training datasets, AdProducer-SFT and AdProducer-RL, and train the agent through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with joint optimization of storyboard- and video-level rewards. We further introduce AdCreation-Bench, comprising 305 advertising briefs across eight domains, with two complementary metrics: PG-Score for product correctness and creative execution, and Ad-Score for overall advertising effectiveness assessed by an independent judge. Experiments demonstrate that AdProducer improves the PG-Score of MiniMax H3 from 17.3 to 51.3 and generalizes to Veo 3.1 without additional training, improving its score from 28.0 to 35.9, with consistent gains in Ad-Score, VideoScore2, and human evaluations. Code, models, and data are released.
papers.summary: Producing an advertising video requires understanding the product and deciding how to present its selling points, not only synthesizing visuals. `AdProducer` is a multimodal agent that researches a product through web and image search and turns its findings into selling-point-driven storyboards that guide a frozen video generator, trained with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on storyboard- and video-level rewards. The authors also introduce `AdCreation-Bench`, with 305 briefs across eight domains and two metrics, `PG-Score` and `Ad-Score`. The agent **raises the `PG-Score` of `MiniMax H3` from 17.3 to 51.3** and transfers to `Veo 3.1` without further training, lifting it from 28.0 to 35.9.
papers.highlight_summary:
