Good-looking ad videos often show the wrong product, garbled specs, or no real demonstration of the selling point, because direct prompting gives a video model no product knowledge. `AdProducer` trains a multimodal agent to research the product through web and image search and write a shot-level storyboard with reference images, which a frozen video generator then renders.

- The agent is a `Qwen3.5-9B` model fine-tuned on 3,710 teacher trajectories and then optimised with `GRPO` on 1,000 briefs, using a reward that averages a video-level `PG-Score` with a judged storyboard score.
- The accompanying `AdCreation-Bench` has 305 briefs across eight domains, split into recent, long-tail and evergreen products, and is scored by `PG-Score` (product correctness, judged by Gemini 3.1 Pro) and `Ad-Score` (viewer-side ad quality, judged by a separate model).
- With `MiniMax H3` as the frozen generator, `PG-Score` rises from **17.3 to 51.3** and `Ad-Score` from **2.72 to 4.70** on a 10-point scale, while 15 human raters score product fidelity at **4.75** versus 2.46 out of 5.
- Supervised fine-tuning alone reaches 48.4 and the joint-reward RL stage adds **2.9 points**, whereas the best untrained search-enabled agent, a larger 35B model, reaches only 34.7.
- Transfer to `Veo 3.1` without retraining is weaker, at **28.0 to 35.9**, with text accuracy flat, and even the best configuration scores only 36.5 on visual correctness and 40.4 on text accuracy out of 100 on a metric that also served as the RL reward.

papers.title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from task difficulty, and Experiences with consistently positive utility are consolidated into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings, showing that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience.
papers.summary: Spatial reasoning agents that call tools such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation depend on orchestrating those tools well, and a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. `SpatialCraft` lets a frozen agent built on a multimodal large language model (MLLM) improve without parameter updates by maintaining Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts, and consistently useful Experiences are folded into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones it **achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings**.

papers.title: Transferable, Time-Parallel Graph Dynamics via Space-Time Factorization
papers.abstract: Time-parallel neural operators (FNO and successors) have transformed PDE surrogates on regular grids. Mesh-based operators (MeshGraphNets, Transolver) extend operator learning to irregular geometries, but jointly learning across diverse topologies while retaining non-recurrent temporal evaluation remains challenging. We propose space-time factorization: partition the model into local temporal operators (learned, graph-independent) and a spatial mixer that propagates information across nodes without graph-dependent learned parameters. This structural condition lets the same parameters run on unseen graphs; non-recurrent instances also admit time-parallel evaluation. Accurate zero-shot transfer further depends on controlling three information leaks (graph-dependent weights, graph-specific features, and graph-correlated training distributions) and on suitable task physics and training coverage. The protocol applies to two distinct spatial-mixer families, fixed-spectral and learned-attention. We validate the principle in three domains. For floodwave propagation in river networks, a 27K-parameter model trained on the Yangtze transfers zero-shot to the Mississippi with median NSE 0.998 in boundary-conditioned operational evaluation, training 5.5x faster than a stabilized recurrent baseline. On cross-geometry Navier-Stokes, the three-seed SepFNO mean relative vorticity error on five unseen targets falls by about 28% from 5 to 12 training geometries, with a consistent single-run SepTransolver trend. On cross-city traffic forecasting, zero-shot transfer reaches within 12.9% of an oracle trained on the target city. Across settings, cross-geometry error decreases with both the number of training geometries and their relatedness to the test, at a rate depending on the spatial mixer. This opens the path to pooled-data, foundation-style models for graph dynamics on irregular topologies.
papers.summary: Neural operators for irregular meshes and graphs struggle to learn jointly across different topologies while keeping non-recurrent, time-parallel evaluation. The authors propose space-time factorization, which splits the model into learned, graph-independent local temporal operators and a spatial mixer with no graph-dependent learned parameters, so the same weights run on unseen graphs. A 27K-parameter floodwave model trained on the Yangtze **transfers zero-shot to the Mississippi with a median NSE of 0.998** and trains 5.5x faster than a stabilized recurrent baseline. On cross-geometry Navier-Stokes, `SepFNO` error on unseen targets falls by about 28% when training geometries increase from 5 to 12, and zero-shot cross-city traffic forecasting comes within 12.9% of an oracle trained on the target city.

papers.title: Evaluating Frontier-Model Agent Skills with Open-Weight Models in a Science Gateway
papers.abstract: Scientific analyses that span many jobs and computing sites depend on workflow management systems to run reliably, but writing a production workflow requires expertise in such a system, which many domain scientists do not have. Coding agents can supply this expertise when they are guided by skills and packaged procedures for recurring tasks. We wrote skills and specialist agents for the Pegasus workflow management system with a frontier model, and the PegasusAI Studio science gateway offers them to scientists through a chat interface. New users without frontier-model credits need an open-weight model, served at no cost on research cyberinfrastructure, but skills written for a frontier model may not work with an open-weight solution. This paper presents a method for adapting such skills. An evaluation harness drives the real gateway as a user would, scores the workflows the agent builds, and feeds recurring failures back to the frontier model that maintains the skills. We evaluated 21 open-weight models on 17 tasks. The five highest-scoring models are close in quality after one trial per task, and their median response times differ twelvefold. In repeated trials with the best of the three open-weight models, we repeated scores of 0.76 on workflow building against 0.82 for Claude. The harness led to five changes to the initial skills. We also identify challenges in evaluating agents within operational systems: evaluation failures can be mistaken for model failures, and agents can circumvent experimental controls within their privilege domain. In a controlled ablation, an initially significant effect disappeared when the restrictions were properly enforced.
papers.summary: Skills and specialist agents written with a frontier model for the `Pegasus` workflow management system may not work when the `PegasusAI Studio` science gateway serves users with free open-weight models instead. The authors build an evaluation harness that drives the real gateway as a user would, scores the workflows the agent builds, and feeds recurring failures back to the frontier model that maintains the skills, then evaluate 21 open-weight models on 17 tasks. The five highest-scoring models are close in quality but differ twelvefold in median response time, and in repeated trials an open-weight model **scored 0.76 on workflow building against 0.82 for `Claude`**. They also report that evaluation failures can be mistaken for model failures and that agents can circumvent experimental controls, with one initially significant ablation effect disappearing once restrictions were properly enforced.

papers.title: SwiftLoop: Selective Refinement for Adaptive Implicit Reasoning in Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Looped Transformers advance implicit chain-of-thought reasoning through recurrent latent refinement. However, existing looped reasoners typically employ fixed-depth recurrence, updating all latent positions at every iteration and incurring redundancy when further refinement is unnecessary. We introduce \textsc{SwiftLoop}, an inference-time framework for selective recurrent refinement through position-wise freezing, enabling adaptive computation allocation across both recurrent depth and active width. SwiftLoop learns lightweight freezing policies through hindsight-guided supervision derived from two complementary criteria: K/V reusability at the internal representation level and functional impact at the output level. At inference time, these policies guide adaptive freezing based on observed hidden states. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SwiftLoop achieves favorable accuracy--computation trade-offs over fixed-loop inference and adaptive baselines, with measured inference acceleration. Beyond implicit reasoning, we further demonstrate its applicability to recurrent prompt prefilling in general looped models.
papers.summary: Looped Transformers perform implicit chain-of-thought reasoning by repeatedly refining latent states, but they typically run a fixed number of loops and update every position each time, even when further refinement is unnecessary. `SwiftLoop` is an inference-time framework that freezes individual positions, adapting both recurrent depth and active width, using lightweight freezing policies trained with hindsight supervision based on key/value reusability and impact on the output. The authors report that it **achieves better accuracy-computation trade-offs than fixed-loop inference and adaptive baselines, with measured inference acceleration**, and that it also applies to recurrent prompt prefilling in general looped models.

papers.title: CHORD: Learning Latent Spaces for Constrained Stellarator Design
papers.abstract: In high-dimensional, PDE-constrained design, interpolating between known feasible solutions can reveal trade-offs without repeating expensive optimization campaigns. In stellarator design for fusion energy, direct interpolation of plasma boundary parameters can violate physical constraints even when both endpoints are feasible. Learned latent representations can capture nonlinear relationships among design variables, but latent interpolation can still cross infeasible regions, and conditioning on target metrics can become inconsistent with the decoded design. We introduce CHORD, a conditional variational autoencoder that penalizes predicted constraint violations along decoded latent interpolants during training, paired with self-consistent inference that aligns conditioning with the decoded design's predicted metrics. Geometric benchmarks show the benefit of regularizing latent interpolants. In stellarator interpolation between distinct geometry families, CHORD reaches up to 81% simulator-validated mid-segment feasibility, compared with 50% for an unregularized conditional VAE and 28% for direct interpolation of boundary parameters. Ablations show that both ingredients are needed for this gain. Beyond interpolation, latent-space optimization finds simulator-feasible designs, while self-consistent sampling produces more diverse feasible alternatives. On the ConStellaration benchmark, chord-regularized models with linear conditioning reuse data from five optimization campaigns and simulator-labeled rescalings to populate the Pareto front more densely. After low-fidelity screening, 93% of 1.2k generated candidates pass the benchmark's high-fidelity feasibility test. We release code and over 600k designs for stellarator generation, surrogate training, and front-filling evaluation. These results support feasibility-aware latent learning for exploring constrained design trade-offs.
papers.summary: In stellarator design for fusion energy, interpolating between two feasible plasma boundary designs can violate physical constraints, and learned latent spaces can still cross infeasible regions. `CHORD` is a conditional variational autoencoder that penalizes predicted constraint violations along decoded latent interpolants during training and uses self-consistent inference to align the conditioning with the decoded design's predicted metrics. Interpolating between distinct geometry families, it **reaches up to 81% simulator-validated mid-segment feasibility, compared with 50% for an unregularized conditional VAE and 28% for direct interpolation**. On the `ConStellaration` benchmark, 93% of 1.2k generated candidates pass the high-fidelity feasibility test after low-fidelity screening, and the authors release code and over 600k designs.

papers.title: Trust-Region Optimization for Performative Prediction without Response Modeling
papers.abstract:
Performative prediction studies learning problems in which deployed decisions change the distribution of future data. Existing methods often impose structure on the population response, which limits their applicability when a fixed model class poorly captures that response. Generic black-box optimization avoids response modeling but does not exploit the known loss function.
  We introduce Performative Trust-Region Optimization (PTRO), which bridges these two approaches by optimizing performative risk without specifying or fitting a response model while still exploiting the known loss. The key idea is sampling from the current population to evaluate the known loss at nearby decisions, and use additional deployments only to estimate the effect of population response. This gives a local approximation of performative risk without committing to a model of how the population responds. PTRO then uses a trust-region mechanism to determine and adapt how far this local information can be trusted.
  Under moment-bounded losses and suitable smoothness and estimator-accuracy conditions, we establish high-probability convergence to an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the performative risk in $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ iterations, with $O(d^{3}\epsilon^{-4})$ samples per iteration, where $d$ is the decision dimension and $q\geq2$ is the loss-moment order.
  Experiments illustrate methods built around a specified response model can be more sample-efficient when their structural assumptions are accurate, whereas PTRO remains effective as the population response is poorly captured by a fixed model class. Ablations further show that both exploiting the known loss and adaptive trust-region updates are important for controlling the accuracy and efficiency.
papers.summary: Performative prediction covers learning problems where deployed decisions change the distribution of future data, and existing methods either assume a structured model of the population's response or use black-box optimization that ignores the known loss. Performative Trust-Region Optimization (`PTRO`) samples from the current population to evaluate the known loss at nearby decisions, spends extra deployments only on estimating the response effect, and uses a trust region to adapt how far that local approximation is trusted. Under smoothness and estimator-accuracy conditions, the authors prove **high-probability convergence to an epsilon-stationary point of the performative risk in O(epsilon^-2) iterations**, with O(d^3 epsilon^-4) samples per iteration for decision dimension d. In experiments, methods built on a specified response model are more sample-efficient when their assumptions hold, while `PTRO` remains effective when the response is poorly captured by a fixed model class.

papers.title: ModernELECTRA: Replaced-Token Detection with Boundary-Window Reconstruction for Compact Encoders that Classify and Embed
papers.abstract: ELECTRA-style replaced-token detection (RTD) is a sample-efficient objective for pre-training text encoders, and RTD-trained models such as DeBERTaV3 are strong on classification benchmarks. The same models, however, are known to be poor backbones for embedding tasks such as retrieval and semantic similarity: the binary "original vs. replaced" signal does not ask the final layer to retain the token identity and contextual content that dense representations rely on. We introduce ModernELECTRA, a pre-training recipe that keeps RTD as the main objective and adds a lightweight auxiliary task, boundary-window reconstruction. For every token, we sample a window of 3-12 tokens that strictly contains it and reconstruct the token's original identity only from the discriminator's hidden states at the two window boundaries. The task costs one small FFN at training time and is discarded afterwards, yet it forces every final-layer state to carry information about its neighbourhood. Combined with a frozen, separately pre-trained generator, a temperature curriculum for hard negatives and a 512-to-8192 length curriculum, we train two compact encoders: EdgeCoder-31M, an 8-layer English model, and EdgeCoder-Multilingual-61M, a 16-layer model covering 46 languages, each on about 1T tokens. They reach 86.0 and 85.1 on GLUE. The English model outperforms Ettin-Enc-32m (83.5) and MiniLM-L12 (84.6) on GLUE while matching them on MTEB English v2 (51.1), and the multilingual model outperforms the 2.3x larger mmBERT-small on GLUE and Multilingual MiniLM and mDistilBERT on XTREME over the languages it covers. We also describe FlashDeBERTa, our open-source fused implementation of DeBERTa's disentangled attention that stores no $n \times n$ score matrix: at 4096 tokens it is 10x faster and uses 93% less memory than the reference implementation, and it loads existing DeBERTa checkpoints unchanged.
papers.summary: Text encoders pre-trained with ELECTRA-style replaced-token detection (RTD), such as `DeBERTaV3`, are strong classifiers but poor backbones for retrieval and semantic similarity, because the binary objective does not require final-layer states to retain token identity and context. `ModernELECTRA` keeps RTD as the main objective and adds boundary-window reconstruction, which recovers each token's identity from the hidden states at the two edges of a sampled 3-12 token window, and combines it with a frozen generator and temperature and length curricula. The resulting `EdgeCoder-31M` English encoder **reaches 86.0 on `GLUE`, ahead of `Ettin-Enc-32m` at 83.5 and `MiniLM-L12` at 84.6, while matching them on `MTEB` English v2**, and the 61M-parameter multilingual model covering 46 languages reaches 85.1. The authors also release `FlashDeBERTa`, a fused implementation of disentangled attention that is 10x faster and uses 93% less memory at 4096 tokens.

papers.title: Reading Between the Layers: Where Representation Quality Lives, and What Geometry Reveals
papers.abstract: Representation quality in pretrained text foundation models is not concentrated at the final layer, yet practitioners routinely probe it there because layer selection without labels has remained an open problem. We present a large-scale empirical study of where layer quality lives across 25 models spanning four architectural families and four pretraining strategies, evaluated on 13 datasets across classification, pair classification, semantic textual similarity, and multiple-choice question answering. Peak probing layers depend systematically on pretraining strategy and architecture: masked encoders peak in late-middle layers, sequence-to-sequence models shift their peak with task type, contrastive sentence encoders concentrate signal at the final layer under CLS and last-token readouts but peak early under mean pooling, and decoder-only models exhibit distinct phase structure tied to depth. We distill these findings into the Stable Geometry Index (SGI), a closed-form, fully label-free selector with no fitted coefficients combining power-law fit quality, effective-rank capacity, spectral stability, and a weak depth prior. Across 383 evaluation groups SGI improves over the last-layer baseline and lifts Hit@3 from 0.39 to 0.52, recovering 40% of the gap to the oracle without using any labels, and exceeds a supervised ELMo-style layer mix on the matched subset despite using strictly less information. Our ablations also reverse a common assumption in the spectral-decay literature: power-law fit quality is a stronger predictor of layer quality than the exponent's proximity to one.
papers.summary: The best layer to probe in a pretrained text model is often not the last one, but choosing a layer without labels has been an open problem. A study of 25 models across four architectural families and four pretraining strategies on 13 datasets finds that peak layers depend systematically on pretraining strategy and architecture, for example masked encoders peak in late-middle layers and contrastive sentence encoders peak at the final layer under CLS and last-token readouts but early under mean pooling. The authors distill this into the Stable Geometry Index (`SGI`), a closed-form, label-free selector combining power-law fit quality, effective rank, spectral stability, and a weak depth prior. Across 383 evaluation groups it **lifts Hit@3 from 0.39 to 0.52 over the last-layer baseline, recovering 40% of the gap to the oracle**, and ablations indicate that power-law fit quality predicts layer quality better than the exponent's proximity to one.

papers.title: XRL4T1D: A Post-hoc Explainability Framework for Reinforcement Learning in Type 1 Diabetes Management
papers.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) requires lifelong insulin therapy, and reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for automated dosing in the UVA/Padova simulator. However, the decisions of RL controllers remain difficult to interpret. We present XRL4T1D, a post-hoc explainability framework for evaluating pretrained insulin-dosing policies without retraining. Each policy uses 60 minutes of continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and administered-insulin history, sampled every 5 minutes, to recommend insulin. We use SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to compare the importance of CGM and insulin-history inputs and summarize insulin-history attributions over three 20-minute windows motivated by insulin-on-board. We assess whether these attributions correspond to policy-output sensitivity through targeted input replacement and compare temporal rankings with TimeSHAP. In all 80 patient-policy-mask-size cases, replacing the highest-attribution inputs changes the normalized insulin recommendation more than replacing the lowest-attribution or random inputs. The highest-attribution insulin-history window is also the most output-sensitive in 115 of 120 patient-policy-scenario configurations, and KernelSHAP and TimeSHAP select the same top window in 111 of 120. Applying XRL4T1D to PPO and G2P2C across 20 virtual patients, we find that both controllers rely predominantly on CGM history, especially G2P2C. However, the distribution of insulin-history importance across recent, middle, and older windows varies by cohort, explainer, and analysis settings, without a consistent separation between controllers. Global feature-attribution rankings remain stable under the tested observation corruptions. These results show why attribution fidelity, temporal reproducibility, and controller-comparison robustness should be assessed separately.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) controllers for insulin dosing in type 1 diabetes are hard to interpret, so `XRL4T1D` provides a post-hoc explainability framework for pretrained policies that needs no retraining. It uses SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to compare the importance of continuous glucose monitor (CGM) history and insulin history, checks the attributions against output sensitivity through targeted input replacement, and compares temporal rankings with `TimeSHAP`. **In all 80 patient-policy-mask-size cases, replacing the highest-attribution inputs changes the insulin recommendation more than replacing the lowest-attribution or random inputs.** Applied to `PPO` and `G2P2C` across 20 virtual patients in the `UVA/Padova` simulator, both controllers rely mostly on CGM history, while the distribution of insulin-history importance over time varies by cohort, explainer, and settings.

papers.title: Measuring Counterfactual Credit in a Replayable Wildfire-Suppression Benchmark
papers.abstract: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, learned critics are usually evaluated by how well they predict the team's return. Yet predicting a team's return and assigning credit to individual actions are distinct tasks. To test credit directly, we introduce FLARE (Fireline Learning Agents in a Replayable Environment), a stochastic wildfire suppression benchmark in which any moment of a fire can be replayed with different actions under the same random events. Replaying one step measures the immediate effect of each agent's suppression, which we call simulator credit and use for training. Replaying to the end of the episode measures the effect of each action, which we use for grading critics. In a comparison over eight seeds with multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO), simulator credit reduces the interquartile mean burn score (each cell's burning time, capped and averaged over the map; lower is better) from 26.6% with shared reward to 20.9%. Learned credit from a centralized COMA-style critic does no better than the shared reward. Four trained critics predict the team's return well, yet the credit they assign is 9 to 42 times larger than the credit measured by replay. The critics also give heterogeneous agents nearly identical action rankings. These results show that a good fit to the team's return is a weak test of a critic's credit.
papers.summary: Critics in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning are usually judged by how well they predict team return, which is a different task from assigning credit to individual actions. `FLARE` (Fireline Learning Agents in a Replayable Environment) is a stochastic wildfire-suppression benchmark in which any moment can be replayed with different actions under the same random events, giving a one-step simulator credit for training and an end-of-episode measurement for grading critics. With multi-agent proximal policy optimization (`MAPPO`) over eight seeds, simulator credit lowers the interquartile mean burn score from 26.6% with shared reward to 20.9%, while learned credit from a `COMA`-style critic does no better than shared reward. Four trained critics predict team return well, yet **the credit they assign is 9 to 42 times larger than the credit measured by replay**.

papers.title: Near-Zero Forgetting Is Not Enough: Out-of-Distribution Robustness in Continual Learning of Pretrained VLAs
papers.abstract: Recent work shows that pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit near-zero forgetting in specific continual learning settings with experience replay. However, robustness to domain shift of learned tasks remains unexplored. In this work, we study the robustness of Pi0 fine-tuned with experience replay under out-of-distribution (OOD) data using the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. While the in-domain (ID) setup achieves near-zero catastrophic forgetting, OOD performance on previous tasks quickly collapses. Specifically, we show that during the continual learning process, the OOD capabilities of the model degrade, following a shared representational pattern across domain shifts, which is also visible behaviorally in the two simpler suites. Representational analysis shows that drift concentrates in the multimodal and action features. Linear probes indicate that OOD features still retain task-relevant information, but appear unreadable, consistent with representation misalignment. These findings suggest that even when ID stability remains intact, severe OOD forgetting can still occur, accompanied by representational drift during continual learning.
papers.summary: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have been shown to exhibit near-zero forgetting in some continual learning settings with experience replay, but whether learned tasks stay robust to domain shift has not been examined. The authors fine-tune `Pi0` with experience replay and test it on `LIBERO` and `LIBERO-Plus`, finding that **in-domain performance shows near-zero forgetting while out-of-distribution performance on earlier tasks quickly collapses**. Representational analysis locates the drift mainly in the multimodal and action features, and linear probes indicate that out-of-distribution features still hold task-relevant information that the model can no longer read, consistent with representation misalignment.

papers.title: How to build and train your recurrent-depth model: A fixed-point perspective
papers.abstract: Recurrent-depth models are trained with truncated backpropagation, yet it remains unclear why this works. We show that input injection, commonly used in recurrent-depth models, is exactly Halpern iteration, and that a slowly vanishing stepsize provably converges with a backpropagation window polylogarithmic in the depth. The guarantees require a Lipschitz operator, which for SwiGLU leads to a weight constraint in both row and spectral norm, while only a row norm constraint for gates. Based on these constraints, we develop an optimizer tailored to each parameter group, Sparrow, which provides a drop-in replacement of Muon/MuonH with no overhead, that speeds up training even beyond recurrent models.
papers.summary: Recurrent-depth models are trained with truncated backpropagation without a clear account of why that works. The authors show that input injection is exactly Halpern iteration, and that a slowly vanishing stepsize **provably converges with a backpropagation window polylogarithmic in the depth**. The guarantee needs a Lipschitz operator, which for `SwiGLU` translates into row-norm and spectral-norm weight constraints (row norm only for gates). From these constraints they derive `Sparrow`, a per-parameter-group optimizer offered as a no-overhead drop-in replacement for `Muon`/`MuonH` that is reported to speed up training even for non-recurrent models.

papers.title: PatientFlowSynth: Evaluating FHIR Agents with Matched Patient Charts
papers.abstract: Agents that search patient charts must classify claims from retrieved records, including cases with missing or conflicting evidence. In Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), status fields can change how those records should be interpreted. PatientFlowSynth provides 18,000 tasks from 225 synthetic patients and 18 templates that hold the patient, question, and retrieval program fixed across chart variants representing four evidence states. Re-executing the program verifies each variant's reference answer, evidence sets, and search requirements. Strict success requires a completed response with correct labels and citations exactly matching an accepted evidence set retrieved during the episode. Where required, a tool response must also show a complete search at the specified scope. In a study using GPT-5.6 Luna and 225 synthetic patients (3,600 matched pairs), explicit Encounter-status guidance increased strict success from 40.7% to 51.3% (+10.6 percentage points; 95% patient-bootstrap confidence interval, 8.4 to 12.8). Among cases whose primary reference label was insufficient evidence, label agreement fell from 49.2% to 29.3%. A prespecified two-model replication reproduced both changes. Failed retrieval can mask interpretation errors by producing a correct insufficient-evidence label without examining the relevant records. Additional model comparisons showed that the benefit of guidance was model-dependent. Retrieval, citation, and classification should be evaluated separately.
papers.summary: Agents that search patient charts stored as Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) must classify claims even when evidence is missing or conflicting, and status fields change how records should be read. `PatientFlowSynth` supplies 18,000 tasks from 225 synthetic patients and 18 templates, holding patient, question, and retrieval program fixed across chart variants for four evidence states, with strict scoring that requires correct labels plus citations matching an accepted evidence set. With `GPT-5.6 Luna`, explicit Encounter-status guidance **raised strict success from 40.7% to 51.3%**, yet label agreement on insufficient-evidence cases fell from 49.2% to 29.3%, a pattern reproduced in a two-model replication. The authors note that failed retrieval can mask interpretation errors and argue that retrieval, citation, and classification should be scored separately.

papers.title: One Step, Four Clocks: How GUI Agents Fall Out of Step
papers.abstract: GUI agents can choose correct actions yet fail as interfaces change during deliberation. Latency alone cannot explain these failures because actions may become invalid at different interaction stages. We model four events: environment change, observation availability, decision commitment, and action receipt (EODA). We introduce ChronotopeGym to study these failures under Paused, Replay, and Live execution. Across five tasks, agents can fail in Live despite succeeding when responses remain valid, even when actions meet deadlines. On Moving Balloon, updating a pending click raises success from 0% to 100% without changing response time. Our accelerator-resident GUI controller, Chronotope, maintains compact interaction history and selectively keeps, updates, or redecides pending actions. Compared with Agent S3, Chronotope reduces median end-to-end latency by 85.5% for a 27B model, expanding its performance envelope to 100% Live success at an 8-second deadline versus 0%. Chronotope enables real-time GUI control through compact interaction history, knowing when to preserve, revise, or replace actions, and an overall efficient architectural design that obviates verbose reflection, reasoning, and grounding calls.
papers.summary: GUI agents can pick the right action and still fail because the interface changes while they deliberate, which latency alone does not explain. The authors model four events per step, environment change, observation availability, decision commitment, and action receipt (EODA), and introduce `ChronotopeGym` to test agents under Paused, Replay, and Live execution. On the Moving Balloon task, updating a pending click lifts success from 0% to 100% without changing response time. Their accelerator-resident controller `Chronotope`, which keeps a compact interaction history and chooses to keep, update, or redecide pending actions, **cuts median end-to-end latency by 85.5% versus `Agent S3` for a 27B model**, reaching 100% Live success at an 8-second deadline where the baseline gets 0%.

papers.title: SOTS: Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection
papers.abstract: Training data selection for machine learning models is a critical bottleneck in industrial applications where expert annotation is costly and time-consuming. Existing coreset selection methods for time series either ignore temporal structure entirely or cannot handle variable-length, irregularly sampled, multi-channel signals, the setting most common in industrial monitoring and testing. We introduce SOTS (Signature-based Optimal Transport Selection), an unsupervised coreset selection framework for irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) classification. Each sample is mapped to a truncated path signature, capturing the joint geometric structure of its channels, and the coreset is selected by greedily minimizing the Sliced Wasserstein distance between the empirical signature distributions of the candidate subset and the full dataset, a criterion for which we establish a convergence guarantee for random coresets. We validate SOTS on a real-world, highly imbalanced industrial I&C testing dataset, where SOTS-Greedy exceeds 95% of full-dataset accuracy using only 30% of the training data, outperforming standard coreset baselines at most budgets. This advantage generalizes to public UEA regular multivariate time series benchmarks specifically when class-discriminative information is purely geometric.
papers.summary: Choosing which time series to send for costly expert annotation is hard when signals are variable-length, irregularly sampled, and multi-channel. `SOTS` is an unsupervised coreset selection method for irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) classification that maps each sample to a truncated path signature and greedily picks a subset minimizing the Sliced Wasserstein distance to the full dataset's signature distribution, with a convergence guarantee shown for random coresets. On an imbalanced industrial instrumentation-and-control testing dataset, `SOTS-Greedy` **exceeds 95% of full-dataset accuracy using 30% of the training data** and beats standard coreset baselines at most budgets. The advantage carries over to the public `UEA` benchmarks only when the class-discriminative information is purely geometric.

papers.title: Diagnosing Epistemic Uncertainty in Neural Operators: Effects of Initialization, Discretization, and Function Sampling
papers.abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for mappings between function spaces, but their reliability cannot be characterized by the performance of a single trained model. Existing neural operator uncertainty quantification approaches often characterize predictive uncertainty without separately identifying the contributions of individual sources of epistemic uncertainty. Finite sampling of the training function space, output discretization, and model initialization can produce substantial variation among learned operators even when the underlying physical problem is deterministic. We systematically investigate these sources of epistemic uncertainty across a diverse set of operator learning architectures. Across our experiments, we train approximately 46,000 neural operator models and construct ensembles over training datasets, model initializations, and output discretizations to characterize distributions of relative $L_2$ error rather than individual trained realizations. We find substantial architecture-dependent differences in epistemic uncertainty, with model initialization often accounting for the largest proportion of variance in relative $L_2$ error. The ranked performance of neural operator architectures can invert as the number and spatial distribution of output samples change, with the best architectures under sparse or randomly sampled observations differing from those at higher-resolution or structured discretizations. Furthermore, ensembles that reliably characterize aggregate operator error can provide unreliable estimates of error quantiles for individual test functions. These results highlight the importance of distinguishing the sources of epistemic uncertainty when evaluating neural operator reliability and establishing robust benchmarking practices.
papers.summary: Neural operators serve as surrogates for mappings between function spaces, but a single trained model says little about reliability. The study trains roughly 46,000 neural operator models and builds ensembles over training datasets, model initializations, and output discretizations to separate the sources of epistemic uncertainty in relative L2 error across architectures. **Model initialization often accounts for the largest share of error variance**, and architecture rankings can invert as the number and spatial layout of output samples change. Ensembles that describe aggregate error well can still give unreliable error quantiles for individual test functions.

papers.title: ECLIPSE: Embedding-Centered Foundation-Model Federated Knowledge Transfer for Data-Free Edge Intelligence
papers.abstract: Foundation Models (FMs) are envisioned to become an integral component of intelligent federated edge networks because of their strong representation and generalization capabilities. However, their integration into resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive edge environments remains challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced in data-free settings, where no shared, public, or server-accessible reference dataset is available to establish a common reference space for aligning distributed knowledge. To address this challenge, we propose ECLIPSE, which is an embedding-centered FM-based federated knowledge transfer framework developed for data-free edge intelligence. ECLIPSE enables edge intelligence capitalizing on a server-hosted FM without sharing raw data, local models, or a public reference dataset. It establishes a shared embedding reference space through which edge devices encode their local task knowledge. Only the resulting embeddings are transmitted to the server for alignment and aggregation. Using the aggregated embeddings, the server constructs a task-aware surrogate dataset through an embedding-guided generative process. This surrogate dataset is then used to adapt the server-hosted FM to the downstream task. The adapted FM is subsequently distilled into a lightweight global model and distributed to the edge devices. This process allows edge devices to benefit from both distributed task knowledge and the generalization capabilities of the FM. Experimental results across diverse classification datasets show that ECLIPSE outperforms conventional Federated Learning (FL) and data-free Federated Knowledge-Transfer (FKT) baselines. It also achieves competitive performance compared with databased approaches. Furthermore, the framework remains robust under statistical and model heterogeneity across different data distributions and local architectures.
papers.summary: Bringing foundation models (FMs) into federated edge networks is difficult when no shared or public reference dataset exists to align knowledge across devices. In `ECLIPSE`, edge devices encode local task knowledge into a shared embedding space and send only embeddings to the server, which aggregates them, generates a task-aware surrogate dataset through an embedding-guided generative process, adapts a server-hosted FM on it, and distills the result into a lightweight global model for the devices. Across several classification datasets it **outperforms conventional Federated Learning (FL) and data-free Federated Knowledge-Transfer (FKT) baselines** and is competitive with approaches that use real data. It is also reported to stay robust under heterogeneous data distributions and local architectures.

papers.title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; their variance, which indicates whether responses contain meaningful variation; and differences between subpopulations, which indicate whether questions capture distinctions between relevant groups within a population. We introduce a preregistered, prospective evaluation that commits model predictions before target human responses exist, ruling out memorization of those responses by design. Using two waves of a local survey (2025: N = 1,271; 2026: N = 1,161), we built simulated respondents from 2025 participants and preregistered GPT-4.1 predictions for 22 questions introduced in 2026. Simulations accurately ranked questions by mean responses (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.71) and anticipated which questions distinguished city from county residents (\r{ho} = 0.88), Black from White residents (\r{ho} = 0.68), and employed from unemployed residents (\r{ho} = 0.57), suggesting simulations can help prioritize questions before fielding. More broadly, our prospective, preregistered design provides a general framework for evaluating AI simulations without contamination from memorized target outcomes.
papers.summary: Whether simulated survey respondents built from large language models (LLMs) can help pre-test new questions before fielding is tested here with a preregistered, prospective design that commits predictions before human answers exist, ruling out memorization. Simulated respondents were built from 1,271 participants in a 2025 local survey, and `GPT-4.1` predictions were registered for 22 questions newly added to the 2026 wave of 1,161 respondents. The simulations ranked questions by mean response with a Spearman correlation of 0.71 and **anticipated which questions separated city from county residents with a correlation of 0.88**, with weaker agreement for Black versus White (0.68) and employed versus unemployed (0.57) residents.

papers.title: JevBench: Metamorphic Coherence Testing for Typed Probabilistic Decision Models
papers.abstract: Typed probabilistic decision models return distributions over specified answers, such as yes or no, a set of options or levels on an ordered scale. We ask whether their probabilities remain coherent when questions about the same input are reworded, negated, combined, given different options or placed in different batches. JevBench tests this coherence without gold labels. Its 50 metamorphic relations each test one law of probability or choice across five dimensions: representation, batch independence, probability measure, logical order and choice-set conditioning. Each test changes the question or batch while keeping the input fixed. Every model receives the same requests, fixed in advance. JevBench-240 contains 12,000 tests across 240 synthetic cases in 12 decision domains. A fixed subset of 1,200 tests, JevBench-mini, closely reproduces the full-suite ranking (Spearman 0.983). Across 21 openly released models, coherence scores range from 56.5 to 83.9. Batch independence holds for most models. Additivity fails broadly, particularly for complements, where the probabilities of a proposition and its negation should sum to one. A uniform reference model ignores the input and scores 89.4 at chance accuracy, exceeding every evaluated model's coherence score. Among decoders, accuracy ranges from 82.4% to 89.2%, while coherence ranges from 64.2 to 83.9. These results show why both measures are needed to assess decision models. JevBench is available as an open-source Python package.
papers.summary: Typed probabilistic decision models return distributions over fixed answer sets, and `JevBench` checks without gold labels whether those probabilities stay coherent when a question is reworded, negated, combined, given different options, or batched differently. It applies 50 metamorphic relations across five dimensions, giving 12,000 tests over 240 synthetic cases in `JevBench-240`, plus a 1,200-test `JevBench-mini` that reproduces the full ranking with Spearman 0.983. Across 21 open models coherence scores run from 56.5 to 83.9, with batch independence mostly holding and additivity failing broadly, especially for a proposition and its negation. **A uniform reference model that ignores the input scores 89.4 on coherence, higher than every evaluated model**, which the authors use to show that coherence and accuracy must be reported together.

papers.title: Tempering and few-shot calibration of pathology foundation models improve digital biomarker reproducibility across slide scanners
papers.abstract: Pathology foundation models underpin a growing number of histology-based cancer biomarkers, but sensitivity to slide scanner-specific image signatures degrades cross-center reliability and reproducibility. We developed a foundation model fine-tuning method that improved consistency in head-and-neck cancer human papillomavirus (HPV) prediction, colorectal cancer microsatellite instability (MSI) identification, prostate cancer grading and breast cancer phenotyping. This tempering method decreased cross-scanner prediction differences by 67.5% for HPV (95% CI 59.0-73.9%), 69.3% for MSI (95% CI 51.9-76.5%) and 63.4%-81.2% for breast signatures. Cross-scanner prostate grade agreement rose from 42.5% to 92.7%. Under full scanner-HPV confounding during training, AUROC fell from 0.80 to 0.68 with original model features but only from 0.86 to 0.84 with tempering. Unlike post hoc feature calibration, tempering used only public data yet matched or exceeded on-site calibration. These findings support tempering to reduce scanner dependence of pathology foundation models.
papers.summary: Pathology foundation models are sensitive to slide-scanner-specific image signatures, which hurts the reproducibility of histology-based cancer biomarkers across centers. The authors propose a fine-tuning method called tempering and test it on head-and-neck human papillomavirus (HPV) prediction, colorectal microsatellite instability (MSI) identification, prostate grading, and breast cancer phenotyping. Tempering cut cross-scanner prediction differences by 67.5% for HPV and 69.3% for MSI, and **raised cross-scanner prostate grade agreement from 42.5% to 92.7%**. It uses only public data yet matched or exceeded on-site post hoc feature calibration, and under full scanner-label confounding AUROC dropped only from 0.86 to 0.84 instead of from 0.80 to 0.68.

papers.title: Agent Evaluation Without Ground Truth: A Null Proportion Perspective
papers.abstract: The correctness of actions taken by agents is typically evaluated against known, externally verified ground truth labels, such as whether a proof is correct or whether code compiles and passes unit tests. However, as coding and science agents are entrusted with more end-to-end autonomy -- proposing interventions, running experiments, and deciding what to deploy and investigate next -- whether an agent's actions genuinely improve an outcome must be inferred from noisy, often inconclusive experiments. To evaluate agents in this setting, we define agent quality as a weighted sum of correct decisions along its trajectory, using sequences of $e$-values as statistical evidence regarding correctness in place of ground-truth labels. Our framework accommodates arbitrarily dependent decisions, data-dependent trajectory termination, dynamically generated hypotheses, and quality measures defined after the trajectory concludes. We construct upper and lower bound estimators and confidence sets for agent quality with statistical guarantees that hold uniformly over agent trajectory distributions and establish instance-wise sharpness of our estimator class. We demonstrate our methods with a case study comparing the success of Claude Opus and Claude Haiku in improving the runtime of an open-source Python package.
papers.summary: As coding and science agents propose interventions and run their own experiments, whether an action actually helped must be inferred from noisy, inconclusive results instead of ground-truth labels. The authors define agent quality as a weighted sum of correct decisions along a trajectory and use sequences of e-values as statistical evidence of correctness, allowing arbitrarily dependent decisions, data-dependent stopping, dynamically generated hypotheses, and quality measures chosen after the fact. They construct **upper and lower bound estimators and confidence sets with guarantees that hold uniformly over agent trajectory distributions**, and show instance-wise sharpness of the estimator class. A case study applies the method to compare `Claude Opus` and `Claude Haiku` on improving the runtime of an open-source Python package.

papers.title: ExitLUT: Boolean Early Exits for Efficient FPGA-Based Neural Network Inference
papers.abstract: Early exit neural networks reduce average inference cost by terminating once sufficient confidence is reached. On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly matched to LUT fabrics, consuming resources that could otherwise support the main datapath. We present ExitLUT, which replaces softmax-style exit decisions with learned Boolean functions mapped directly into FPGA LUTs. In our CNN evaluation, fpgaConvNet is the static spatial-dataflow baseline, while ATHEENA is its softmax-based early exit extension. ExitLUT reduces ATHEENA's exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58$\times$ over the softmax path and eliminates decision-path DSP usage, while preserving accuracy and exit behavior. Rerunning design-space exploration reinvests these savings into the datapath, improving throughput by up to 4.08$\times$ over fpgaConvNet and 1.82$\times$ over ATHEENA. For LUT-based NNs, embedded ExitLUT exits achieve 1.41-1.89$\times$ average time-to-decision speedup over static NeuraLUT-Assemble designs with under 1% LUT overhead.
papers.summary: Early-exit neural networks on FPGAs normally decide when to stop using softmax-style confidence checks, whose arithmetic maps poorly onto lookup-table (LUT) fabric. `ExitLUT` replaces those checks with learned Boolean functions placed directly in LUTs, cutting exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58x relative to the softmax path in `ATHEENA` and removing DSP usage from the decision path while keeping accuracy and exit behavior. Reinvesting the saved resources in the datapath **improves throughput by up to 4.08x over `fpgaConvNet` and 1.82x over `ATHEENA`**. For LUT-based networks, embedded exits give a 1.41-1.89x average time-to-decision speedup over static `NeuraLUT-Assemble` designs with under 1% LUT overhead.

papers.title: Where Agent Defenses Fail: A Case Study of Policy Compositions and Measurement Limits
papers.abstract: A coding agent may need to upload a report while its sandbox blocks network access. A host mediator can restore delivery, but an injected instruction may add a secret to the approved request. We study this interaction using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects independently of control logs. Two prospective frozen-input cohorts comprise 110 and 300 runs on previously explored authored tasks. Restrictive sandboxing produces no observed attack harm but reduces benign utility to 6/8 and 12/24. Mediation restores uploads and admits disclosure; complete-line matching retains full benign utility but misses two value-only disclosures in the expanded cohort. A separate 72-run boundary study identifies encoded disclosure, observer misses, and formatting checks that obscure benign refusals. An 80-run SafeAgents/OpenShell follow-up shows that containment stops the tested guard misses among valid observations, while mediation restores benign uploads and delivers both encoded-attestation attacks. Twelve judge-error rows remain unscored. A separate response-capture diagnostic reproduces their failures at the native token budget. A 12-run exact-publication-contract experiment blocks both attacks but also rejects both benign formatting variants; a 4-run normalized follow-up restores both benign uploads while still rejecting both attacks. These small, single-model studies identify delivery-path and measurement limits; they do not establish general attack resistance.
papers.summary: A sandboxed coding agent that needs to upload a report may be given a host mediator to restore network delivery, which also lets an injected instruction smuggle a secret into the approved request. The authors measure this trade-off from files and HTTP receipts across several small cohorts of runs, including 110-run and 300-run frozen-input sets and an 80-run `SafeAgents`/`OpenShell` follow-up. Restrictive sandboxing showed no attack harm but cut benign utility to 6/8 and 12/24, while **mediation restored uploads and also delivered disclosures, including encoded ones that complete-line matching missed**. An exact-publication contract blocked both attacks but rejected benign formatting variants until a normalized version was used, and the authors state that these single-model studies expose delivery-path and measurement limits without establishing general attack resistance.

papers.title: Reproducible Social Structure Emerges From Free-Form Interaction Among LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM simulations are increasingly used as models of social systems, but most published findings are anecdotal, i.e., drawn from a single run. It is therefore unclear which observed phenomena are robust findings of the simulated system itself, and which were random events in one particular run. Here, we introduce a repeatable, goal-free, proactive multi-agent framework in which fifty persona-conditioned agents with persistent memory choose whether, with whom, and how to communicate across three social platforms. The framework supports non-perturbative measurements across temporal snapshots and repetitions. Running the same world ten times from identical initial conditions for a total of 700 hours, we find that most measured network- and agent-level parameters are stable across repetitions. Throughout a run, initially broad communication contracts into sparse sustained dyads in all ten worlds. Importantly, we find that many identical dyads re-form across worlds significantly more often than expected by chance or from agent-specific sociability alone. Static personality similarity largely fails to predict these dyads. Instead, alignment and extremity in the emotions and traits expressed during first contact predict whether a pair later forms a sustained dyad. Additionally, individual agents' emotion and trait expression in their chain-of-thought predicts their future behavior. Finally, swapping either persona prompts or accumulated memories between agents causes recipients to exhibit behavior more similar to donors. Both kinds of transplant move the recipients about 60% of the way toward its donor personality, and state-transplanted agents start behaving similar to their donor agent from their next turn on. Overall, we show that repeated worlds enable robust, statistically-grounded conclusions about emergent within-configuration behavior in agent societies.
papers.summary: Findings from multi-agent LLM social simulations usually come from a single run, leaving it unclear which phenomena are robust. The authors build a goal-free framework in which fifty persona-conditioned agents with persistent memory decide whether, with whom, and how to communicate on three social platforms, and run the same world ten times from identical initial conditions for 700 hours in total. Most network- and agent-level measures were stable across runs, communication contracted into sparse sustained pairs in all ten worlds, and **the same pairs re-formed across worlds significantly more often than chance or individual sociability would predict**. Emotions and traits expressed at first contact predicted pair formation better than static personality similarity, and swapping persona prompts or accumulated memories moved recipients about 60% of the way toward the donor's personality.

papers.title: Agent Recovery Gone Wrong: Measuring Harm Beyond Duplicate Calls
papers.abstract: Code-executing LLM agents submit blocks of code that issue several API writes. If a block fails after some of its writes have taken effect, the agent rewrites the block and continues. It is unknown how often such a recovery harms the external state when the failure occurs naturally in the code written by the agent. In this paper, we measure it on recorded trajectories of AppWorld agents. In a stratified random sample of 200 candidate episodes across ten models, 145 are partial executions confirmed by the database state. In the sample, 30 of 143 confirmed partial executions with a determinable outcome are followed by a harmful recovery, and its violation remains at the end of the run, which gives a stratification-weighted estimate of 24.6%. Two thirds of the harmful recoveries duplicate an effect, and the rest delete user data or make a wrong first-time write, e.g., an order of a wrong product. A rule that searches for repeated calls finds 75% of duplications but only 41% of all harm. We also examine two sources of operation identity for an idempotency contract. In a small pilot (17 episodes, one local model), identifiers supplied by the model do not detectably reduce harm, because the model issues a new identifier for the same operation. Identity derived from the call content, evaluated counterfactually on the sample, would have matched every harmful write in 14 to 18 of the 30 harmful recoveries, but in none of those with a wrong first-time write, and it would also have matched writes required by the task in 30 episodes. Based on these results, we outline design requirements for safer agent recovery.
papers.summary: Code-executing LLM agents often submit blocks that issue several API writes, and when a block fails partway the agent rewrites it and continues, possibly corrupting external state. Using recorded `AppWorld` trajectories from ten models, the authors confirm 145 partial executions in a stratified sample of 200 episodes and estimate that **24.6% of partial executions are followed by a harmful recovery whose violation persists to the end of the run**. Two thirds of harmful recoveries duplicate an effect and the rest delete user data or make a wrong first-time write, so a repeated-call detector catches 75% of duplications but only 41% of all harm. Model-supplied idempotency identifiers did not detectably help in a small pilot, and content-derived identity would have covered 14 to 18 of the 30 harmful cases while also matching legitimately required writes in 30 episodes.

papers.title: Denoising Diffusion with Progressive Posterior Sampling
papers.abstract: Diffusion models provide effective generative priors for solving noisy linear inverse problems. However, existing posterior sampling methods may require singular value decomposition (SVD) of the measurement operator or prior knowledge of the measurement noise variance, while guidance based on local gradients provides only a limited view of posterior geometry. We propose progressive posterior sampling (PPS) with manifold projection, which automatically estimates the measurement noise variance and avoids SVD. During reverse diffusion, PPS constructs a Gaussian approximation to the posterior distribution in closed form and guides a sample drawn from the local prior toward the approximate posterior mean. We then project the guided sample onto a spherical level set that approximates the local noisy image manifold, promoting consistency with the local geometry of the diffusion prior. Experiments on FFHQ and ImageNet across four restoration tasks and three measurement noise levels demonstrate competitive reconstruction accuracy and perceptual quality by PPS.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based solvers for noisy linear inverse problems often need a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the measurement operator or a known measurement noise variance. Progressive posterior sampling (`PPS`) avoids both by estimating the noise variance automatically, building a closed-form Gaussian approximation of the posterior during reverse diffusion, and guiding a sample from the local prior toward the approximate posterior mean. The guided sample is then projected onto a spherical level set that approximates the local noisy image manifold. On `FFHQ` and `ImageNet`, across four restoration tasks and three noise levels, the method reports **reconstruction accuracy and perceptual quality competitive with existing approaches**.

papers.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
papers.abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.
papers.summary: Standard computer-use agents are tuned to complete tasks, not to reproduce how people perceive, reason, and act, which limits their use for simulating users. `COGENT` is a modular cognitive architecture for desktop user simulation that draws on Norman's action cycle and `ACT-R`, splitting the process into modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. Six demonstrations trace how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a module propagates into a behavioral change. Across `AgentNetBench`, `A11y-CUA`, and `SENSE-42`, it shows **statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior** and recovers the relational structure among self-reported psychological states.

papers.title: CLAIMGATE: Cautious On-Device Checking of Spoken Legal and Clinical Claims
papers.abstract: In law and medicine, a misstated rule can shape a decision before anyone has time to check it. Checking such claims in real time helps only if the checker keeps pace with conversation, keeps sensitive audio on the device, and stays silent rather than mislead. We present CLAIMGATE, an on- device assistant that listens to a conversation, detects checkable claims, retrieves the relevant official rule, and labels each claim as supported, contradicted or not covered, with a citation. CLAIMGATE is designed to fail towards silence: its 4-bit 7B- parameter language model may cite only retrieved rules, and the verdict is derived in code from the claim and rule the model quotes. We evaluate it on traffic stops and medical visits using real official rule text (5,742 Florida and Texas statute subsections; CDC, FDA and MedlinePlus guidance), real transcripts, live speech and author-written gold-labelled claims. On 141 held-out traffic-stop claims, CLAIMGATE reaches 80.1% accuracy and cuts serious errors (a true claim called false, or the reverse) from 20 to 5 compared with the same model without retrieval; deriving the verdict in code alone reduces them from 13 to 5 at no cost to accuracy. The claim gate passes 95.7% of held-out claims and rejects all 30 everyday sentences, and feedback arrives a median 1.86 s after a speech window closes on an 8 GB consumer GPU. On 148 allergy claims, with only the claim gate to rebuild, CLAIMGATE reaches 87.8% accuracy with 5 serious errors, against 20 without retrieval.
papers.summary: `CLAIMGATE` is an on-device assistant that listens to a conversation, detects checkable legal or clinical claims, retrieves the relevant official rule, and labels each claim as supported, contradicted, or not covered, with a citation. It is built to stay silent when unsure: a 4-bit 7B-parameter language model may cite only retrieved rules, and the verdict is computed in code from the claim and rule the model quotes. On 141 held-out traffic-stop claims checked against 5,742 Florida and Texas statute subsections, it reaches 80.1% accuracy and **cuts serious errors from 20 to 5 compared with the same model without retrieval**, with feedback arriving a median 1.86 s after a speech window closes on an 8 GB consumer GPU. On 148 allergy claims it reaches 87.8% accuracy with 5 serious errors versus 20 without retrieval.

papers.title: Off-the-Shelf Autonomous Agents for Game Playtesting
papers.abstract: In playtesting games, a human operator is typically required to test most gameplay elements. In this work we present Buddy, an autonomous game solving agent which can solve long time horizon objectives in an unseen 3D role-playing game using off-the-shelf language model systems. Buddy will take actions, receive feedback on those actions, and pursue a goal across many turns. No written walkthrough or model training of any kind is required, and we show that this paradigm holds in a novel environment where the agent must discover solutions via exploration rather than recalling them from pretraining. We demonstrate three downstream capabilities: game solving with no provided walkthrough, logging bug tickets for encountered difficulties, and conversion of successful agent traces into scripted hierarchical task networks for regression testing. Unlike existing playtesting solutions, our framework is fully modular: language models and harnesses can be easily swapped out as capabilities improve over time.
papers.summary: Game playtesting usually needs a human operator to exercise most gameplay elements. `Buddy` is an autonomous agent built from off-the-shelf language model systems that takes actions, receives feedback, and pursues long-horizon objectives in an unseen 3D role-playing game. The authors report that it **solves the game with no walkthrough and no model training, in a novel environment where solutions must be found by exploration instead of recalled from pretraining**. It also files bug tickets for difficulties it encounters and converts successful traces into scripted hierarchical task networks for regression testing, with models and harnesses designed to be swappable.

papers.title: Safe Autoformalization: Sufficiency and Necessity with Entailment Graphs
papers.abstract: Autoformalization translates a natural-language statement into a formula that captures its intent, which depends on the statement's context: the background that disambiguates it. LLMs make autoformalization practical, but their probabilistic output carries no formal guarantees. We propose techniques for safe autoformalization that certify one-sided logical adequacy: a formula sufficient for the intent is safe to enforce, and a formula necessary for it is safe to rely on. We use LLMs to generate candidate formulas and order them by logical strength in an Entailment Graph (EG), an ordering a solver decides. Each edge carries a residual and a co-residual, the two adjoints of the entailment order, all fixed by the candidate pool alone. In a context, two searches return the sufficient frontier, the weakest candidates that entail the statement, and the necessary frontier, the strongest candidates the statement entails; each step is one local check against an edge's residual or co-residual. The frontiers bracket the statement and yield the ambiguity residue, which holds exactly of the situations the candidates certify neither as satisfying nor as violating it; the statement is ambiguous precisely when the residue is satisfiable. For natural-language statements and contexts, an LLM entailment oracle decides the checks; it is sound if it accepts only checks that hold, and complete if it accepts every check that holds. We prove that a sound oracle makes the search safe regardless of pool quality, and that a complete one makes the frontiers tight. On security-critical AWS properties, EGs are safe in all 20 cases of an expert-adjudicated study, where majority vote over equivalence clusters and Universal Self-Consistency are unsafe in 25% and 10%. An ablation with the same oracle but no graph is unsafe in 25% and rejects every candidate in another 30%. We machine-checked our proofs in Lean.
papers.summary: Autoformalization with LLMs turns natural-language statements into formulas but offers no formal guarantee that the result matches the intent. The authors have an LLM generate candidate formulas, order them by logical strength in a solver-decided Entailment Graph (EG), and search it for a sufficient frontier (weakest candidates that entail the statement) and a necessary frontier (strongest candidates it entails), which together bracket the statement and expose any residual ambiguity. They prove, with proofs machine-checked in `Lean`, that a sound LLM entailment oracle makes the search safe regardless of candidate quality and a complete one makes the frontiers tight. On security-critical AWS properties, the method was **safe in all 20 expert-adjudicated cases**, whereas majority vote over equivalence clusters and `Universal Self-Consistency` were unsafe in 25% and 10%.

papers.title: The Paradox of Agency-Preserving AI: Negotiating Learner Agency in Layered Human-AI Interactions
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used by learners in cognitively demanding tasks, but its capacity to provide immediate solutions raises concerns about decreased learner agency. Meta-level AI systems that provide reflective and metacognitive scaffolding have emerged as a promising approach to supporting learners' self-regulation. However, these systems introduce a fundamental paradox: AI intended to preserve learner agency can itself constrain that agency by regulating when, how, and why learners should reflect. To investigate this challenge, we conducted a co-design workshop with 18 students engaged in programming and academic writing tasks using ChatGPT extended with ChatWise, a meta-level AI system providing self-regulated learning-aligned feedback. Drawing on 185 prompt-feedback entries, 174 written reflections, and participants' design artifacts (17 storyboards and 5 group design proposals), we identified four interconnected design tensions: assistance vs reflection, immediate intervention vs space for self-regulation, visibility vs attention competition, and system adaptation vs user control. The study contributes a multidimensional account of learner agency that includes task, cognitive, and interaction agency, along with empirically grounded interaction-design mechanisms to negotiate these tensions.
papers.summary: Meta-level AI systems that prompt learners to reflect are meant to protect learner agency, yet they can constrain it by dictating when, how, and why reflection happens. The authors ran a co-design workshop with 18 students doing programming and academic writing in `ChatGPT` extended with `ChatWise`, a system that gives feedback aligned with self-regulated learning, and analyzed 185 prompt-feedback entries, 174 written reflections, and the participants' design artifacts. They identify **four design tensions: assistance versus reflection, immediate intervention versus space for self-regulation, visibility versus attention competition, and system adaptation versus user control**. The study also offers an account of learner agency spanning task, cognitive, and interaction agency, along with interaction-design mechanisms for negotiating the tensions.

papers.title: Latent Channel Completion for Forecasting in Sensor Networks with Failed Detectors
papers.abstract: Monitoring networks for traffic and utility infrastructure lose sensors routinely, and forecasting models that couple sensors together to gain accuracy also inherit an exposure to those losses. When a detector stops reporting, the substituted value is embedded as though it were a reading and propagates through the shared representation that couples the network, degrading forecasts for sensors that are still healthy. Because these models are selected on benchmarks where every sensor reports, the exposure is absent from the numbers used to choose them. We introduce Latent Channel Completion, a channel-axis joint embedding predictive objective that reconstructs missing sensors' latent representations rather than their values, since a coupling operator consumes embeddings and never sees raw readings. Channels are masked during training and their representations predicted from surviving channels against stop-gradient targets; at inference the operator fills in whichever sensors the monitoring system reports as dark, using parameters shared with the forecaster. On three highway detector networks, after half of each network goes dark, the accuracy advantage of coupling changes by -1.0, -0.5 and +8.8 percentage points, against losses of 10.2 to 50.3 points for the unmodified forecaster, which on one network falls behind an uncoupled reference entirely. Against cross-channel ridge imputation drawing on the same surviving sensors, completing the latent lowers error by a further 13.9% and 28.6%, and on complete inputs, the method matches its backbone. The benefit tracks how much a network gains from coupling when intact, giving operators a criterion evaluable before any outage occurs.
papers.summary: Forecasting models that couple sensors in traffic and utility networks degrade when detectors fail, because substituted values are embedded as if they were real readings and spread through the shared representation. `Latent Channel Completion` trains a joint-embedding predictive objective over the channel axis: sensors are masked during training and their latent representations, not their raw values, are predicted from the surviving channels. On three highway detector networks with half the sensors dark, **the accuracy advantage of coupling changes by only -1.0, -0.5 and +8.8 percentage points, against losses of 10.2 to 50.3 points for the unmodified forecaster**. The method also lowers error by a further 13.9% and 28.6% relative to cross-channel ridge imputation and matches its backbone on complete inputs.

papers.title: PazaBench: Large-Scale ASR Benchmark for Low-Resource Languages in Africa
