papers.abstract: Low-resource languages remain underrepresented in ASR benchmarks, limiting the ability to reliably assess and compare model performance. We present a large-scale benchmark for automatic speech recognition (ASR) on low-resource languages in Africa. The benchmark harmonizes six public corpora into a unified, reproducible evaluation framework and evaluates 52 state-of-the-art ASR models spanning three model architectural paradigms across 39 African languages on diverse datasets. Models are evaluated using standard accuracy and efficiency metrics, word error rate (WER), character error rate (CER), and inverse real-time factor (RTFx). This benchmark introduces architecture-aware comparison that systematically analyzes both individual models and broader model families. In addition, we quantify linguistic variance across language families, revealing how these factors shape ASR performance across diverse African languages. We also provide a comprehensive accuracy and efficiency trade-off analysis directly relevant to deployment in low-resource settings. Together, the benchmark, evaluation pipeline, and results support transparent, reproducible, and deployment-aware evaluation of ASR models for low-resource languages.
papers.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) benchmarks underrepresent low-resource languages, which makes it hard to compare models reliably for them. `PazaBench` harmonizes six public corpora into one reproducible evaluation framework and evaluates **52 ASR models from three architectural paradigms across 39 African languages**. Models are scored on word error rate (WER), character error rate (CER) and inverse real-time factor (RTFx), with comparisons at the level of both individual models and model families. The analysis also quantifies variance across language families and the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency for deployment in low-resource settings.

papers.title: Provably Near-Optimal PQ in the Extended Zador Model
papers.abstract: This paper investigates Product Quantization (PQ) Optimization with Gaussian data. It offers three key contributions (i) a proof that SVD is the optimal preconditioning rotation for PQ; (ii) a new Extended Zador (EZ) estimator of the $k$-means quantization cost that is accurate in low bit rates and low dimensions; and (iii) a novel segmentation algorithm based on 1-d bin packing of global bit allocations. The result is a simple algorithm (EZPQ) with strong approximation guarantees. It matches OPQ's empirical accuracy while providing a per-instance distortion lower bound certificate under the Gaussian EZ cost model. On typical real embedding spectra, EZPQ with 2 bits per coordinate is often certifiably within 1% of the optimum in this model. It also consistently achieves a lower reconstruction error than all random-rotation-based algorithms such as EDEN, E-RaBitQ, and TurboQuant.
papers.summary: Product Quantization (PQ), a standard way to compress embedding vectors, is studied here for Gaussian data with the aim of provable guarantees. The authors prove that SVD is the optimal preconditioning rotation, introduce an Extended Zador (EZ) estimator of k-means quantization cost that stays accurate at low bit rates and low dimensions, and segment dimensions with an algorithm based on one-dimensional bin packing of bit allocations. The resulting `EZPQ` algorithm matches the empirical accuracy of `OPQ` while providing a per-instance distortion lower bound, and on typical real embedding spectra at 2 bits per coordinate it is **often certifiably within 1% of the optimum under the model**. It also achieves lower reconstruction error than random-rotation methods such as `EDEN`, `E-RaBitQ` and `TurboQuant`.

papers.title: Frequency-Conditioned Privacy Auditing of Fine-Tuned Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly fine-tuned on sensitive data, where the same person's information may appear multiple times across records. This can cause models to memorize sensitive information, but memorization does not necessarily mean that the information can be recovered. A more serious privacy risk arises when the model begins to reproduce that information during generation. In this paper, we study how often sensitive information must appear in the fine-tuning data before it becomes recoverable. Across four language models, we vary the frequency of email addresses and phone numbers from $1\times$ to $50\times$ and compare standard fine-tuning, gradient clipping, and differentially private training. We find that the number of repetitions required before sensitive information becomes recoverable varies substantially across models. Gradient clipping can delay extraction, but it does not consistently prevent leakage at high repetition. DP-SGD at $\varepsilon=5$ produces zero observed extraction through $50\times$ repetition across all four models under the attacks we test, although the utility cost varies by model. These findings characterize how observed extraction varies across sensitive-data frequencies, model families, and training mechanisms, and highlight substantial differences in extraction behavior across models. Code and data are publicly available.
papers.summary: Language models fine-tuned on sensitive data can memorize personal information, and the question studied here is how many times a piece of information must appear before it can actually be extracted during generation. Across four language models, the authors vary the frequency of email addresses and phone numbers from 1 to 50 repetitions and compare standard fine-tuning, gradient clipping and differentially private training. The repetition count needed for recovery varies substantially across models, and gradient clipping delays extraction without consistently preventing it at high repetition. **`DP-SGD` at epsilon = 5 produced zero observed extraction through 50 repetitions on all four models** under the attacks tested, with a utility cost that differs by model.

papers.title: LatentLens: Rethinking Latent Interface in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Latent interfaces let agents in a multi-agent system communicate through continuous representations rather than decoded text. Prior work reports performance and efficiency gains, but neither separates latent communication from the agent harness nor examines its internal components, leaving its actual contribution unclear. We propose LatentLens, a framework that decouples the latent interface at two levels: externally from the agent harness, to measure its contribution to overall performance (RQ1), and internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility, and propagation dynamics, to identify the benefits and limitations of each (RQ2). Across seven benchmarks with Qwen3 models, adding the latent interface to the same harness does not improve and can even substantially degrade accuracy. Internally, latent representations retain some domain information, but incompatible realignment can substantially degrade performance, and repeated latent steps can amplify representation-level failures. Thus, while latent representations may preserve information, they do not necessarily ensure effective communication, which also requires compatible realignment, information accessibility, and stable propagation.
papers.summary: Latent interfaces let agents in a multi-agent system exchange continuous representations instead of decoded text, and earlier reports of gains did not separate the interface from the surrounding agent harness. `LatentLens` isolates the latent interface from the harness to measure its contribution, and breaks it internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility and propagation dynamics. Across seven benchmarks with `Qwen3` models, **adding the latent interface to the same harness does not improve accuracy and can substantially degrade it**. Latent representations retain some domain information, but incompatible realignment hurts performance and repeated latent steps can amplify representation-level failures.

papers.title: SecondChance: Benchmarking Reliable Error Recovery in AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents make errors while they act, and their reliability depends on what they do afterwards. Existing recovery benchmarks mostly inject faults, involve no user and score whether the task is eventually completed, so they cannot show whether an agent undid its own silent error, told the user, or faced an error that could not be fixed. We introduce SecondChance, an error checkpoint dataset and evaluation harness that profiles and measures error-recovery behaviour of AI agents. The errors are natural: they come from agents' own task attempts in $\tau^2$-bench, BFCL and AppWorld. Different agents then resume from the same checkpoints under one of four conditions: no assistance, an error notice, the error location, or repair guidance. We measure error correction, task success, policy compliance, preservation of environment state, repair durability and cost. We evaluate 12 models under all four conditions in 5,760 continuations. Recovery is rare: across its environments, the best model completes only 16% of recoveries unaided and 27% with repair guidance. Correcting is not recovering: with repair guidance, Llama-3.3-70B corrects 26% of $\tau^2$ errors but completes none, and 40 of 84 successful AppWorld continuations leave the error in place. SecondChance exposes these differences that task success alone cannot capture.
papers.summary: Existing error-recovery benchmarks for AI agents mostly inject artificial faults and score only eventual task completion, so they cannot show whether an agent undid its own silent mistake or told the user. `SecondChance` is a checkpoint dataset and harness built from natural errors made by agents in `τ²-bench`, `BFCL` and `AppWorld`; different agents resume from the same checkpoints with no assistance, an error notice, the error location, or repair guidance. Across 12 models and 5,760 continuations, **the best model completes only 16% of recoveries unaided and 27% with repair guidance**. Correcting an error is also distinct from recovering: with repair guidance `Llama-3.3-70B` corrects 26% of `τ²-bench` errors but completes none, and 40 of 84 successful `AppWorld` continuations leave the error in place.

papers.title: One Phase Is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable. We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly backpropagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation rendering. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT's relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer. Project website: https://jmarangola.github.io/one-phase-visual-rl/
papers.summary: Vision-based robot policies are commonly trained in two phases, with a reinforcement learning (RL) teacher that uses privileged state and a vision student distilled from it, and the student often underperforms the teacher. `DRIFT` trains the visual policy directly with RL in a single phase by using frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, which avoids backpropagation through the vision backbone and supports transfer from fast rasterized simulation rendering. Under matched architectures, observations and compute, it outperforms two-phase distillation with a **58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks**. In simulation its relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts.

papers.title: GoldiBench: Right Tools, Wrong Amount -- Benchmarking Agents on Effect Judgement in Professional Editing
papers.abstract: Real editing requests describe a look, not the steps to reach it, so an agent that serves them must judge how much of each tool the look takes. Existing benchmarks do not measure this: their tasks either state the tools and values, or leave the amount open and are scored by VLM judges that pass more than half of half- and triple-strength results. We introduce GoldiBench, a benchmark of 500 editing tasks in five professional applications (darktable, RawTherapee, GIMP, Inkscape, Blender), solvable by writing a program or by operating the GUI. Each task pairs a START image with a TARGET rendered from a hidden program, so the amount is fixed by a known target; the agent's edit is re-rendered and compared with TARGET, and the same task is posed with the tools and values, the tools only, or the goal only, separating operation from effect judgement. Across 25 open, GUI and closed models, agents operate well (99-100% with programs from 4B up when told the values) but fall off a cliff when they must judge the amount: given only the tools, the best model passes 19% of the tasks with programs and 33% through the GUI, and scale does not close the gap. Manuals barely help; the measured TARGET-START difference more than doubles the pass rate, but the same difference shown as an image does not for open models. Allowed four renders, agents almost always stop after the first; forced to compare, the strong models double their pass rate. Agents know the tools, but neither read nor check the amount.
papers.summary: Editing requests describe a desired look rather than the steps to reach it, so an agent has to judge how much of each tool to apply, which existing benchmarks do not measure. `GoldiBench` contains 500 editing tasks across `darktable`, `RawTherapee`, `GIMP`, `Inkscape` and `Blender`, each pairing a start image with a target rendered from a hidden program, and poses every task with the tools and values, the tools only, or the goal only. Across 25 models, agents pass 99-100% of program-based tasks when told the values, but **given only the tools the best model passes 19% of tasks with programs and 33% through the GUI**, and larger models do not close the gap. Agents allowed four renders almost always stop after the first, while forcing a comparison doubles the pass rate of strong models.

papers.title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation
papers.abstract: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). Without retraining or weight access, LUCID calibrates binary step ratings by aligning predicted and expert soundness rates. From a small expert-labeled set, LUCID summarizes rater bias in plain text and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps. For example, on PRM800K, GPT-5-mini grades too strictly, under-rating computation, verification, and late-trace steps most acutely. In one pass, LUCID shrinks GPT-5-mini's calibration gap from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points in absolute predicted-expert rate difference. LUCID also halves false alarms (sound steps rated unsound) and lifts error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. LUCID retains these gains with 1,000 diagnostic steps or overall-gap feedback alone. The loop also transfers across models and domains: it applies GPT-5-mini's bias profile to lift GLM-5.2's PRM800K accuracy, and it narrows calibration gaps for overly strict but capable raters across math, science, web, and logic benchmarks. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced sound/unsound discrimination, LUCID filters re-grading with pre-/post-checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes. Finally, we reuse that expert set with raw corpus ratings in DSL for calibration and regression debiasing, and apply DSL to pair-labeled steps for sound-step transitions. DSL's out-of-fold soundness probabilities lift best-of-K selection to match expert labels, while its doubly-robust estimators beat expert-only regression fits at small budgets and cut sound-step transition error by nearly two-thirds.
papers.summary: Cheap language-model raters that grade chain-of-thought reasoning steps make systematic errors that can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. `LUCID` (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis) summarizes a rater's bias in plain text from a small expert-labeled set and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps, and pairs this with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL) for statistical debiasing, all without retraining or weight access. On `PRM800K`, one pass **shrinks the calibration gap of `GPT-5-mini` from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points**, halves false alarms and raises error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced discrimination, the loop includes checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes.

papers.title: RePT: 3D Geometry Emerges from 2D Relational Pretraining
papers.abstract: Learning spatial representations often relies on explicitly predicting geometric quantities, but how physical geometry is organized within learned representations remains less understood. We ask whether 3D structure can emerge from learning relations across 2D observations, without 3D prediction targets. We introduce RePT, which learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction. The learned relation space develops a geometric organization in which magnitudes, angles, and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes without refitting (Pearson r = 0.72 and 0.78). The ARKitScenes-trained checkpoint also retains strong geometric organization on ScanNet++, showcasing generalizability. In controlled comparisons, distinct-point relational prediction consistently yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning. This organization depends on additive relations and adaptive scene context, and higher point-transfer accuracy does not by itself produce stronger organization. More broadly, our results suggest that 3D geometry need not be an explicit prediction target and can instead emerge as a structural property of representations trained to relate 2D observations, pointing to relational prediction as a complementary route to learning the representations that spatial intelligence builds on.
papers.summary: Whether 3D structure can arise in learned representations without any 3D prediction targets is the question addressed here. `RePT` learns compact relations between distinct physical points through cross-view 2D point prediction, and the resulting relation space organizes itself so that magnitudes, angles and neighborhoods reflect physical 3D displacement. **A single linear readout fitted on 16 scenes recovers displacement length and angle on 39 held-out scenes with Pearson r of 0.72 and 0.78**, and a checkpoint trained on `ARKitScenes` retains this organization on `ScanNet++`. Controlled comparisons show that predicting relations between distinct points yields stronger geometric organization than matched same-point correspondence learning.

papers.title: Noise-Level Adjacency in Diffusion Training
papers.abstract: Diffusion models train one network across all noise levels, although their training objective is pointwise in the noise level. If training on each pair of adjacent levels were an independent problem, separate networks with the same total parameter count would be expected to match one shared network. But in practice, on images, sharing weights across levels gives better results, which hints at an implicit dependence on their order. An order fixes both which levels are adjacent and the direction in which they run. In this paper, we show that, of the two, the benefit of sharing rests on adjacency in the noise-level embedding. The fitting error of a shared network is bounded below by the distances between neighbouring posterior means, minus the change the network can make between neighbouring embeddings. We first distinguish adjacency from direction: on a Gaussian mixture and CIFAR-10, reversing the embeddings keeps every neighbour and leaves the fitting error unchanged, whereas shuffling them raises it. Second, we rule out sharing between distant levels as the source of the benefit: separate networks on contiguous ranges match the shared network at its width, and with the parameters fixed, breaking adjacency at the same places costs less than 40\% of a full shuffle. Dividing the levels at equal shares of these distances lowers the error of all but the smallest networks. We therefore show that the order of the noise levels enters a diffusion model through adjacency, with its direction being a design choice. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/Noise-Level-Adjacency-in-Diffusion-Training.
papers.summary: Diffusion models share one network across all noise levels even though the training objective is defined separately at each level, and the reason sharing helps has been unclear. The authors show that the benefit rests on adjacency in the noise-level embedding rather than on the direction of the ordering, and derive a lower bound on a shared network's fitting error in terms of distances between neighbouring posterior means. On a Gaussian mixture and `CIFAR-10`, **reversing the embeddings leaves the fitting error unchanged, whereas shuffling them raises it**. Separate networks on contiguous ranges match the shared network at its width, and dividing the levels at equal shares of these distances lowers the error of all but the smallest networks.

papers.title: Instance-Dependent Bandit Convex Optimization in One Dimension
papers.abstract: We study the instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization in the fixed-confidence setting. First, we consider minimizer localization, where the learner seeks to identify a point within distance $\varepsilon$ of the unique minimizer. We introduce a new instance-dependent quantity $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)$, corresponding to the threshold for which the sublevel set of $f-\min f$ has length $2\varepsilon$. We prove a lower bound of order $\Delta_\varepsilon(f)^{-2}$ and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches this rate up to logarithmic factors. We then revisit the simple-regret setting, where the goal is to identify an $\varepsilon$-optimal point. Surprisingly, no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm has sample complexity of order $\varepsilon^{-2}$ on every instance, matching the minimax rate up to constants. Together, these results separate the statistical complexity of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization in one-dimensional convex bandits.
papers.summary: The instance-dependent sample complexity of one-dimensional stochastic bandit convex optimization is analyzed in the fixed-confidence setting. For locating a point within distance epsilon of the minimizer, the authors define an instance-dependent quantity based on the threshold at which the sublevel set has length 2 epsilon, prove a lower bound of order the inverse square of that quantity, and give a bisection-style algorithm that matches it up to logarithmic factors. For the simple-regret goal of finding an epsilon-optimal point, **no comparable instance-dependent improvement is possible: every correct algorithm needs on the order of 1/epsilon² samples on every instance**. The two results separate the statistical difficulty of minimizer localization from that of simple-regret optimization.

papers.title: Monitorable-by-design architectures for a post-Astra world: a compartmentalization-based approach
papers.abstract: Frontier models like GPT-6 Astra are increasingly able to do substantial reasoning without a monitorable chain of thought, chains of thought are becoming less legible, and are often monitored asynchronously to reduce cost. With the future of chain of thought monitoring unclear, it may be necessary to design LLMs with monitorability in mind. We propose a modification to existing LLM architectures based on GRAM, SGTM, DEMix, BTS, and similar methods to compartmentalize dangerous capabilities so that their use, especially in combination with dangerous reasoning types that may indicate strategic adversarial use, can be monitored more cheaply than chain of thought in a way that might outlast monitorable chain of thought. We propose several variants of this architecture designed to balance tradeoffs and discuss other benefits, such as capability removal.
papers.summary: Chain-of-thought monitoring is becoming less dependable as frontier models such as `GPT-6 Astra` do more reasoning without a legible chain of thought and as monitoring is often run asynchronously to save cost. The authors propose modifying language-model architectures, building on methods such as `GRAM`, `SGTM`, `DEMix` and `BTS`, to **compartmentalize dangerous capabilities so that their use can be monitored more cheaply than chain of thought**, particularly when combined with reasoning types that may indicate strategic adversarial use. Several variants of the architecture are presented to balance trade-offs, along with other potential benefits such as capability removal. The abstract reports no experimental results.

papers.title: Multi-agent System for Automatic Discovery of Pareto-optimal Meta-solvers for PDEs
papers.abstract: Designing linear solvers for discretized partial differential equations requires problem-specific expertise. We present a multi-agent framework, in which language-model agents propose, critique, implement, and evaluate solver configurations assembled from Krylov methods, preconditioners, block factorizations, and neural operators. Inside the proposing agent, a non-dominated sorting genetic evolutionary algorithm evolves the population of meta-solvers toward the Pareto front of six measured quantities, so that one run returns a front of trade-offs rather than a single tuned solver. The system runs on small open-weight language models served on a single laptop, and we compare it with a single agent on four problems. For three-dimensional acoustic scattering and elasticity, it delivers 47 and 48 convergent hybrid solvers out of 60 candidates. Relative to the Jacobi-preconditioned Krylov baselines, the best of the discovered solvers reduce the iteration counts by factors of 4.7 and 60 and the online solve time by factors of 2.3 and 3.0, whereas the single agent produces no executable plan. For coupled dynamic thermoelasticity in two and three dimensions, where the baselines fail, it completes 98 of 100 transient candidates and, compared with the single agent, reaches a given accuracy 15 times faster in two dimensions and a displacement error 20 times lower in three dimensions.
papers.summary: Designing linear solvers for discretized partial differential equations normally requires problem-specific expertise. In this multi-agent framework, language-model agents propose, critique, implement and evaluate solver configurations built from Krylov methods, preconditioners, block factorizations and neural operators, while a non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm inside the proposing agent evolves candidates toward the Pareto front of six measured quantities. The system runs on small open-weight language models served on a single laptop. For 3D acoustic scattering and elasticity it delivers 47 and 48 convergent hybrid solvers out of 60 candidates, and **the best discovered solvers cut iteration counts by factors of 4.7 and 60 relative to Jacobi-preconditioned Krylov baselines, whereas a single agent produces no executable plan**.

papers.title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
papers.abstract: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis, and randomized experiments. However, synthetic choice data from off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference. Neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably reduces this bias. We investigate decision models (System One architectures) for silicon sampling. Using choice training, we update KEV model weights on historical respondent-level choice microdata by conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without target-study data. Across three model scales, training on two discrete choice experiments lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% on four held-out studies from new domains (vaccines, nutrition labels, consumer rights, and AI) and new response formats. A small choice-trained model outperforms a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four studies. Although training on single studies lowers cross-entropy, it can exacerbate treatment-effect error. Choice training thus complements post-inference calibration by providing a stronger starting point for estimating human preferences.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) used as synthetic survey respondents produce choice data that biases downstream econometric inference, and neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably fixes this. The authors update the weights of `KEV` decision models on historical respondent-level choice data by conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without any data from the target study. Across three model scales, training on two discrete choice experiments **lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% on four held-out studies** from new domains and response formats, and a small choice-trained model beats a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four. Training on a single study can lower cross-entropy while making treatment-effect error worse.

papers.title: Tablassert: Declarative Extraction of Knowledge Graphs from Biomedical Tables
papers.abstract: Tables published in biomedical research papers, particularly supplemental tables, capture knowledge assertions that may not be in the main text of the manuscript for several reasons, including low statistical significance, space limitations, and narrative scope. These tables include data (e.g., association statistics, assay readouts, curated gene lists, and omics) encoding relationships between biological entities. Tablassert converts such tabular data (Excel, CSV, TSV, Parquet) into knowledge graphs ready for the NCATS Biomedical Data Translator (Fecho et al. 2025). A user declares in YAML how each table's data map to subject-predicate-object-qualifier statements; Tablassert resolves free text (e.g., ''lung cancer'') to standard identifiers, attaches provenance and statistics, and emits graph files conforming to Translator standards (D. Unni, Bruskiewich, and Moxon 2026; D. R. Unni et al. 2022).
papers.summary: Tables in biomedical papers, especially supplemental ones, contain relationships between biological entities that often never appear in the main text. `Tablassert` **converts tabular data in Excel, CSV, TSV or Parquet form into knowledge graphs ready for the `NCATS Biomedical Data Translator`**. A user declares in YAML how each table maps to subject-predicate-object-qualifier statements, and the tool resolves free-text terms to standard identifiers, attaches provenance and statistics, and emits graph files that conform to Translator standards.

papers.title: Eliciting sandbagged LLM capability via structural interventions on attention-head functional networks
papers.abstract: Reliably evaluating the capabilities of advanced AI systems is critical for safe development and deployment, yet such evaluations may be undermined by sandbagging, a situation in which a model strategically suppresses capabilities it possesses. Existing work has developed controlled sandbagging settings and methods for detecting or eliciting hidden capabilities, but comparatively little is known about how a model's internal neural computation changes when its capabilities are suppressed. In this work, we study sandbagging through the lens of internal functional organization. Inspired by network neuroscience, we construct functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions while holding the model architecture and weights fixed. Surprisingly, across model architectures and community detection methods, we find a consistent structural signature in which sandbagging is associated with reduced functional connectivity within detected communities. We further demonstrate that this reorganization can guide capability elicitation. Ablating attention heads that exhibit the largest connectivity changes substantially recovers suppressed performance while largely preserving performance under honest behavior. Moreover, incorporating these structural signals further improves existing inference-level and weight-level elicitation methods. Together, our results show that sandbagging is accompanied by systematic reorganization of internal computation and demonstrate that functional network structure can provide both a mechanistic lens for understanding capability suppression and a practical signal for recovering hidden capabilities.
papers.summary: Sandbagging, where a model strategically suppresses capabilities it has, can undermine capability evaluations, and little is known about how internal computation changes when it happens. Borrowing from network neuroscience, the authors build functional graphs from attention-head activations and compare their organization under honest and sandbagging conditions with architecture and weights held fixed. Across model architectures and community detection methods, sandbagging is associated with reduced functional connectivity within detected communities. **Ablating the attention heads with the largest connectivity changes substantially recovers suppressed performance while largely preserving honest performance**, and the same structural signals improve existing inference-level and weight-level elicitation methods.

papers.title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
papers.abstract: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier
papers.summary: Leaderboards for zero-shot time-series foundation models do not state how small a score difference their datasets can actually detect. `Vernier` computes this quantity, called the resolution of a board, from the files a board already publishes, and reports which entries cannot be separated from the leader and whether rankings shift when unrelated parties submit. **`GIFT-Eval` resolves 6.8 rank places while its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart**, and `fev-bench`, `Chronos Benchmark II` and `TIME` show the same pattern, with resolution 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours; `BOOM` is the only board that resolves its top ten. Across four boards, pool-relative ranking rules reversed 43 top-ten pairs without either entry being rerun, and shortening the history given to a model raised the error of three of four open models.

papers.title: Self-Improving Long-Horizon Reasoning by Learning Summaries from Local Continuations
papers.abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.
papers.summary: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer traces do not on their own extend the effective reasoning horizon. The authors train a separate summarizer with `Delta-KL`, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference with `TruSuCo`, which truncates the trace, summarizes it and continues from the summary. Training needs a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and no answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget the trained summarizer beats vanilla reasoning in all nine settings by up to 7.7 points, and **at 128k tokens it outperforms vanilla reasoning by 10 points on `AIME 2024-2026`**.

papers.title: What You See Is What You Certify: Concept-Based Certificates for Unseen Compositions
papers.abstract: Concept-based models justify a decision by concepts they claim to see, decoded through an explicit ontology. Yet concept predictions are known to leak label information, ignore locality, and be poorly grounded on new attribute combinations. A decision decoded from such concepts can satisfy the ontology and still be wrong, so we ask when it can serve as a certificate. On unseen combinations of familiar parts, a joint concept bottleneck model and a concept embedding model, trained as is standard, certify wrong classes 93-94% of the time despite a correct ontology (60% for a joint model trained only on visible parts and gated by a localizer). The joint model's part errors copy co-occurring values more often than chance (cross-concept shortcutting). Treating the ontology as an error-detecting code, we show that a certificate needs visible evidence excluding every rival, unseen parts reported as such, and rare misreads not driven by a shared shortcut. A minimal reference design, OCVE, reads each part from a local crop in its own forward pass. On unseen FunnyBirds classes, it certifies 52% of images at 0.4% risk, against 14% for mask-pooled features and 33% for full-image part readers (5.6% when trained and gated alike), at similar zero-shot accuracy. The best baselines, even calibrated or restricted to unseen classes, and a decoder counting only agreeing parts remain about 3-8 times riskier. On CUB, isolated region readers are more accurate than an attribute-prototype model (63.1% vs. 55.3%) and certify unseen species at about 6 points less risk than it and about 10 points less than features pooled in the same keypoint boxes. On real traffic signs, isolated readers lower certified risk from 99.8% to 67%, which is still far too high; most remaining errors are misread pictograms. On seen classes the ontology brings no gain over a fairly trained black box, and isolation costs accuracy.
papers.summary: Concept-based models justify decisions through predicted concepts decoded by an explicit ontology, and the question here is when such a decision can serve as a certificate on unseen combinations of familiar parts. Standard joint concept bottleneck and concept embedding models certify wrong classes 93-94% of the time on unseen compositions despite a correct ontology. Treating the ontology as an error-detecting code, the authors derive requirements for a valid certificate and build a reference design, `OCVE`, that reads each part from a local crop in its own forward pass. On unseen `FunnyBirds` classes it **certifies 52% of images at 0.4% risk, against 14% for mask-pooled features and 33% for full-image part readers**, though on real traffic signs certified risk only falls from 99.8% to 67%.

papers.title: Wavefront: Low-Rank Drafting with Parallel Causal Refinement for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Parallel block drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE propose a whole block in one forward pass, but they lose the dependence between tokens in the block; DSpark restores part of it with a lightweight correction head that runs sequentially. Measuring DSpark, we find that this head overrides the base prediction on most slots, so the expensive base readout through the target's full lm_head mostly provides a seed. We therefore propose Wavefront, which follows a simple principle: shrink the base and strengthen the correction head. Wavefront replaces the full lm_head with a learned low-rank base, conditions the correction head on the whole drafted prefix within the same block, and resolves it with a few parallel Jacobi passes. A fixed pass budget makes the draft step free of data-dependent control flow, so we capture it as a single CUDA graph in vLLM with fused kernels. On Qwen3-8B, Wavefront improves throughput over xPress, DSpark and DFlash by 2.6%, 10.7% and 23.6% on average across math, code, chat and agentic benchmarks, and by 9.6%, 14.3% and 28.9% on SPEED-Bench long-context prompts. On Qwen3.8-27B it leads DFlash2, DSpark and xPress by 7.6%, 10.6% and 5.0%, and by 7.4%, 5.8% and 6.0% on the same long-context prompts. The gains persist as serving load grows to concurrency 32.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model inference by having a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, but block drafters lose the dependence between tokens in a block. Measurements of `DSpark` show its sequential correction head overrides the base prediction on most slots, so `Wavefront` replaces the full output head with a learned low-rank base, conditions the correction head on the whole drafted prefix, and resolves it with a fixed number of parallel Jacobi passes captured as a single CUDA graph in `vLLM`. On `Qwen3-8B` it **improves throughput over `xPress`, `DSpark` and `DFlash` by 2.6%, 10.7% and 23.6% on average** across math, code, chat and agentic benchmarks, with larger margins on `SPEED-Bench` long-context prompts. Gains also hold on `Qwen3.8-27B` and as serving load grows to concurrency 32.

papers.title: Reward Basis Decomposition for Interpreting Preference Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Canonical reward models specify the optimization target for AI policies, so understanding the values they encode is important for ensuring AI alignment. Existing interpretability techniques interpret reward models with a single reward head, which cannot distinguish between the values that a population shares and those that vary among individuals. We introduce Reward Basis Decomposition (RBD), which splits per-user weights into a population term and a per-user term. This yields a shared population direction and individual user directions that are analyzed separately via concept alignment and sparse autoencoder decomposition. We verify that RBD can recover artificially planted per-user directions on a synthetic control, then apply it to two real-world multi-preference datasets, PRISM and Community Alignment. In both, we find no individual-user structure, suggesting that a single direction in the reward embedding space accounts for most preferences. We verify that RBD can recover artificially planted per-user directions on a synthetic control, then apply it to two real-world multi-preference datasets, PRISM and Community Alignment. In both, we find no reliable predictive benefit from the fitted per-user terms beyond the shared population direction under our setup. Code and the synthetic dataset are available at https://github.com/RachelFreedman/RBD.
papers.summary: Interpretability methods for reward models usually analyze a single reward head, which cannot separate values a population shares from those that differ between individuals. Reward Basis Decomposition (`RBD`) splits per-user weights into a population term and a per-user term, then analyzes the resulting directions with concept alignment and sparse autoencoder decomposition. After confirming that it recovers planted per-user directions on a synthetic control, the authors apply it to the `PRISM` and `Community Alignment` datasets and find **no reliable predictive benefit from the per-user terms beyond the shared population direction** under their setup.

papers.title: E2SIM: Long-Horizon Simulation of Everyday Human Behavior with Evolving States
papers.abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to support users over long periods, across work, and daily life. This requires modeling not only who users are, but also how their goals, interests, activities, and interactions evolve over time. A challenge in longitudinal user simulation is maintaining consistency between these evolving states and the consequences of actions in a shared environment. We introduce E2SIM, a longitudinal user simulation framework that jointly models evolving actor states and a dynamic shared environment. E2SIM connects actor-state updates with shared-world changes through a feedback loop linking immediate actions, delayed outcomes, and actor-specific observations across work and life. This allows the consequences of earlier actions to shape later behavior, while preserving differences in what each actor knows. We further propose a suite of longitudinal trajectory diagnostics, measuring dynamic consistency, coherent event progression and collaboration, and non-degenerate trajectory development rather than static consistency alone. In one 60-day simulation, E2SIM produced more extracted event threads judged meaningful by our evaluator and fewer near-duplicate actions than four direct-generation baselines. The framework and evaluation methods provide a basis for studying longitudinal user simulation, with potential applications in training and evaluating AI agents that assist users over extended periods.
papers.summary: Simulating users over long periods requires keeping their evolving goals, interests and activities consistent with the consequences of their actions in a shared world. `E2SIM` jointly models evolving actor states and a dynamic shared environment, linking immediate actions, delayed outcomes and actor-specific observations through a feedback loop so earlier actions shape later behavior while each actor keeps its own knowledge. The authors also propose trajectory diagnostics for dynamic consistency, coherent event progression and non-degenerate development. In a single 60-day simulation, it produced **more event threads judged meaningful by the authors' evaluator and fewer near-duplicate actions than four direct-generation baselines**.

papers.title: Anchoring VAE Fine-Tuning to Its Latent Diffusion Prior
papers.abstract: Pretrained latent diffusion models are effective priors for transfer learning, from geometry estimation to physics simulation. Existing approaches fine-tune the diffusion backbone but freeze the encoder of the VAE to preserve the latent distribution. However, a frozen encoder may miss salient details in non-RGB inputs and is limited to three channels. We introduce Diffusion Prior Anchoring (DPA), a regularizer applied during VAE fine-tuning that uses a score-distillation update to steer latents toward the high-density manifold on which the pretrained diffusion model denoises accurately. We validate DPA across three image and video models (FLUX 3, LTX-Video, Wan2.2) and four tasks: monocular depth estimation, MRI reconstruction, wind-flow simulation, and surface normal estimation, where DPA lowers the prediction error by 7.5% relative to the frozen VAE, 4.9% to decoder-only fine-tuning, and 4.0% to unanchored VAE fine-tuning. Its gain grows the further the target data lies from the RGB training distribution, from 3.3% on monocular depth estimation to 7.2% on complex-valued MRI. DPA also applies to modified VAEs, including pruned and multi-channel variants. With a four-channel VAE that encodes depth and surface normals, it lowers depth estimation error by 9.3%.
papers.summary: Transfer learning with pretrained latent diffusion models usually freezes the encoder of the variational autoencoder (VAE) to preserve the latent distribution, which can miss details in non-RGB inputs and limits inputs to three channels. Diffusion Prior Anchoring (`DPA`) is a regularizer for VAE fine-tuning that uses a score-distillation update to keep latents on the high-density manifold where the pretrained diffusion model denoises accurately. Across `FLUX 3`, `LTX-Video` and `Wan2.2` on depth estimation, MRI reconstruction, wind-flow simulation and surface normal estimation, it **lowers prediction error by 7.5% relative to the frozen VAE** and by 4.0% relative to unanchored fine-tuning. The gain grows as the target data moves further from RGB, and the method also works with pruned and multi-channel VAEs.

papers.title: Constructing physical mechanisms with artificial intelligence
papers.abstract: Mechanisms recur across the sciences: the equation for heat in a solid also describes molecular diffusion or a Brownian particle. A mechanism is rarely written in one equation; its operation, boundaries, parameters and closures are stated at different steps of a derivation, where methods that read text or fit formulas miss it. We built an equation-native system that reads the equations of all 2.5 million arXiv manuscripts, and show that mechanisms can be compiled from them and constructed by deterministic calculation. A constructor detaches, transfers, unfolds, composes and joins their parts across disciplines; where parts do not fit, the failure is an equation for the missing term. Constructions turn a threshold reactor into a memory that a weak signal writes, an oscillator into a switch through two changes that each fail alone, and a rhythm into the regulator of a chemical amount, each with conditions for an experimental test.
papers.summary: Physical mechanisms, such as the diffusion equation that describes both heat and Brownian motion, are typically spread across several steps of a derivation, where text-reading and formula-fitting methods miss them. The authors built an equation-native system that reads the equations of all 2.5 million arXiv manuscripts, compiles mechanisms from them, and uses a deterministic constructor to detach, transfer, compose and join their parts across disciplines. Where parts do not fit, the failure is expressed as an equation for the missing term. The reported constructions **turn a threshold reactor into a memory written by a weak signal, an oscillator into a switch, and a rhythm into a regulator of a chemical amount**, each with conditions for an experimental test.

papers.title: Stranded Compute in AI Inference Workloads: Recovering Value Through Demand Aggregation
papers.abstract: AI inference infrastructure is commonly analyzed as an energy business. Under full total cost accounting it is not: in the reference deployment modeled here, capital recovery is 87.3% of fully loaded cost per token and electricity 3.7%. Because capital accrues per unit time irrespective of use, accelerator value is destroyed by non-utilization rather than by consumption. Yet, SLO qualified goodput reaches only 59.6% of nameplate throughput, and the decomposition of the loss chain shows that 25.2 of the 40.4 lost percentage points arise from scheduling idleness and stranded burst reserve. Both are properties of a tenant's demand portfolio rather than of its silicon, and neither is diversifiable by a single tenant acting alone. Modelling reserve and idle capacity as diversifiable risk, pooling demand across eight imperfectly correlated tenants (rho = 0.3) recovers 7.3 pp of goodput, approximately $0.75M per annum per megawatt of IT capacity, or between 2.8x and 4.9x the entire annual interconnection spend of the deployment that produced it. The implication for neutral colocation and interconnection providers is that the switching and interconnection layer aggregating tenant demand functions as an instrument of capital productivity while being priced as transport.
papers.summary: A total-cost model of AI inference infrastructure argues that it is a capital business rather than an energy one: in the reference deployment, capital recovery makes up 87.3% of the fully loaded cost per token and electricity only 3.7%. Goodput that meets service-level objectives reaches just 59.6% of nameplate throughput, and 25.2 of the 40.4 lost percentage points come from scheduling idleness and stranded burst reserve, which depend on a tenant's demand pattern rather than its hardware. Treating that idle capacity as diversifiable risk, the model finds that **pooling demand across eight imperfectly correlated tenants recovers 7.3 percentage points of goodput**, about 0.75 million dollars per year per megawatt of IT capacity.

papers.title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.
papers.summary: Methods that improve retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by learning from retrieval feedback are mostly separate heuristics with no account of when each is appropriate. `BRAG` is a generative model of retrieval in which each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its embedding and has a latent utility that drifts over time, yielding a closed-form online filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback, frequency reranking, `NUDGE` and `LADER` fall out as special cases. `BRAG` matches them on repeated queries, and when a new chunk makes an old one obsolete it **retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time while the others stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 of 0.67-0.71)**; on nine months of a personal agent's memory it raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98.

papers.title: Boundary Representation-Driven Graph Transformer Modeling for Machining Operation Sequencing
papers.abstract: Machining process planning is inherently complex due to the interdependence between part geometry, machining operations, and evolving manufacturable states. Traditional approaches rely heavily on expert knowledge and rule-based systems, limiting scalability and automation. While recent machine learning methods have shown promise, most operate on simplified geometric representations, such as voxels or hand-crafted features, which fail to fully exploit the rich geometric and topological information encoded in Boundary Representation (B-Rep) models. In this work, we propose a graph transformer-based framework for geometry-to-sequence learning that directly predicts machining operation sequences from B-Rep design geometry. The proposed method constructs topology-aware graphs from B-Rep entities, where faces and their adjacencies are encoded as node and edge features capturing both geometric and relational information. A graph neural network encoder learns geometry-aware embeddings, which are then used to condition a dual-decoder transformer that autoregressively generates machining operation sequences. This formulation enables the model to capture both operation-type prediction and process-level ordering constraints directly from design geometry, without requiring intermediate feature extraction or machining-state representations. Experiments on a dataset of 2,991 synthetic machined parts demonstrate strong performance, achieving 95% accuracy for main operation prediction, 64% accuracy for sub-operation prediction, and 93% accuracy for sequence length prediction. Further analysis shows that the model effectively captures precedence relationships and geometry-dependent constraints inherent in machining processes. These results highlight the potential of B-Rep-driven graph learning for scalable and automated machining process planning.
papers.summary: Machining process planning has relied on expert rules or on learning from simplified geometry such as voxels, which discards the topology stored in Boundary Representation (B-Rep) models. The proposed framework builds a graph from B-Rep faces and their adjacencies, encodes it with a graph neural network, and conditions a dual-decoder transformer that autoregressively generates the machining operation sequence directly from design geometry. On a dataset of 2,991 synthetic machined parts it reaches **95% accuracy for main operation prediction**, 64% for sub-operation prediction and 93% for sequence length prediction.

papers.title: A Piecewise-Linear Activation Function for Implicit Neural Representations
papers.abstract: Coordinate networks with ReLU activations perform poorly on implicit neural representation tasks, and the activations that address this, such as sinusoids and Gabor wavelets, all leave the piecewise-linear function class, so it remains unclear which property of ReLU is at fault. We introduce JaSIN, a family of bounded piecewise-linear activations that interpolates between ReLU and a piecewise-linear sinusoid without any the use of transcendental operation. Our results show that a bounded range improves image reconstruction PSNR on average by 0.06 dB, a single bump 3.29 dB, and centering that bump a further 3.64 dB. The oscillation count improves 6.30 dB more, raising ReLU from 24.0 to 37.3 dB on Kodak images, placing third over eleven activations, within 1.3 dB of the state-of-the-art, though beyond four oscillations the reconstruction collapses. Because an INR is fit on the grid on which it is evaluated, a unit whose pre-activations never reach the support of its activation is certifiably inactive over the entire domain; deleting such units is lossless without fine-tuning, removing up to 84% of parameters at zero loss in performance (dB) and decoding 3.2 times faster. Reference code and demos are available at https://github.com/jeovafarias/jasin.
papers.summary: Coordinate networks with ReLU activations do poorly as implicit neural representations (INRs), and the usual fixes such as sinusoids leave the piecewise-linear function class, so it is unclear which property of ReLU is to blame. `JaSIN` is a family of bounded piecewise-linear activations that interpolates between ReLU and a piecewise-linear sinusoid, letting the authors attribute gains separately to boundedness, a single centered bump, and oscillation count. Together these changes **raise image reconstruction on `Kodak` from 24.0 to 37.3 dB**, third among eleven activations and within 1.3 dB of the best, though reconstruction collapses beyond four oscillations. Because units whose pre-activations never reach the activation's support are provably inactive on the evaluation grid, they can be deleted losslessly, removing up to 84% of parameters and decoding 3.2 times faster.

papers.title: Provenance Loss and Repair in Multilingual Compaction
papers.abstract: Conversational assistants compact older messages into short notes and evict the originals. When the note's language requires a distinction that English leaves open, such as Spanish adjective gender (agotado vs. agotada), messages that omit or explicitly state that attribute can yield the same note. After eviction, later turns cannot tell them apart: taking the inflected form literally asserts an attribute the user never gave, whereas discounting it as routine grammar discards one the user did give. We propose a training-free repair across writing, pre-eviction verification and reading. The writer marks unstated attributes with paired forms (e.g., agotado/a), a likelihood check before eviction rewrites unsupported single forms into paired ones, and the reader trusts remaining single forms as stated facts. On five Qwen3.5 and Gemma-4 models, eviction cuts recall of stated attributes from 90% to 34% in question answering (QA); our repair raises F1 (which penalizes both errors) on every model, by 9-53 points in QA and 12-40 points in agent handovers.
papers.summary: Conversational assistants compact old messages into short notes and evict the originals, and when the note's language forces a distinction the user may not have stated, such as Spanish adjective gender, stated and unstated attributes collapse into the same note. The proposed training-free repair has the writer mark unstated attributes with paired forms, runs a likelihood check before eviction that rewrites unsupported single forms into paired ones, and has the reader trust the remaining single forms as stated facts. On five `Qwen3.5` and `Gemma-4` models, eviction cuts recall of stated attributes from 90% to 34% in question answering (QA), and the repair **raises F1 on every model, by 9-53 points in QA and 12-40 points in agent handovers**.

papers.title: Neural Interoperability Protocols: Specifying Compatibility Before Training
papers.abstract: Neural networks are increasingly developed as reusable components, yet their intermediate representations remain difficult to exchange across independently trained models. Existing approaches can align representations or encourage compatible features, but successful transfer between particular models does not by itself define what future implementations must satisfy to interoperate. We introduce Neural Interoperability Protocols (NIPs), a specification-first framework that treats neural compatibility as a set of public interface obligations rather than a property inferred solely from model-pair performance. A NIP specifies an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations that recipients must support, independently of the architectures and training procedures implementing it. We investigate this distinction through controlled retrieval, vision, and continuous-memory experiments involving independently trained models, differing architectures and objectives, and later training cohorts. Matched-competence controls demonstrate that native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer in the evaluated settings. Withheld-information experiments show that recipient models can continue computations requiring information unavailable to donors at exchange time. Partial-contract experiments and packet interventions further establish that observed compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations, and recipient continuations being evaluated. Together, these results support public neural interface specifications as a framework for designing prospective component exchange and distinguishing demonstrated interoperability from stronger conformance claims.
papers.summary: Intermediate representations are hard to exchange between independently trained neural networks, and a successful transfer between two particular models does not say what future models must satisfy to interoperate. Neural Interoperability Protocols (`NIPs`) are a specification-first framework that defines an exchange boundary, the semantics and admissibility conditions of exchanged packets, and the downstream computations recipients must support, independent of architecture or training procedure. Controlled retrieval, vision and continuous-memory experiments show that **native task success does not ensure interoperability, while shared semantic supervision enables substantial direct transfer** in the evaluated settings. Further experiments show that compatibility is conditional on the semantics, packet populations and recipient computations being tested.

papers.title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.
papers.summary: Diffusion-based multimodal language models commit candidate tokens based on confidence, which cannot tell whether a token comes from image evidence or from the language prior. A paired forward ablation finds that **nearly nine in ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image**, and that degenerate and hallucinated samples show higher entropy in deep-layer attention. The proposed training-free decoding method, `CD-APC`, rescores candidates by visual evidence within a pool supported by the base model, gates commits on model acceptability and contrastive concentration, and adapts its window to step difficulty. It improves results consistently across two backbones and five benchmarks.

papers.title: Curvature-Equilibrated Policy Optimization for Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Gradient-based actor optimization is central to deep reinforcement learning. However, conventional first-order optimizers do not explicitly exploit the local curvature of neural actor losses. We propose EQUIP (Curvature-Equilibrated Gradients for Policy Search), a novel approach that seeks to balance local contraction and expansion of the actor parameter space by equilibrating positive and negative curvature. EQUIP constructs a trajectory-informed search subspace and uses the projected Hessian of actor loss to build a bounded local metric for curvature equilibration. First-order loss matching preserves the approximated first-order decrease in actor loss. Meanwhile, gradient mixing and curvature-based gradient selection adjust the gradient applied for actor optimization. We establish the geometric properties of curvature equilibration, derive bounds on gradient alignment and magnitude, and identify conditions for improved actor loss reduction and convergence toward stationarity under direct gradient updates. We integrate EQUIP into Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) without modifying its actor loss, critic learning, or replay mechanism. Experiments on 6 MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks show that the resulting EQUIP-SAC algorithm achieves higher mean sample efficiency than SAC and two second-order policy optimization baselines. Ablation studies further highlight the benefits of curvature equilibration and trajectory-informed geometry for policy training.
papers.summary: First-order optimizers used for actor updates in deep reinforcement learning do not exploit the local curvature of the actor loss. `EQUIP` builds a search subspace from the optimization trajectory, uses the projected Hessian of the actor loss to form a bounded local metric that balances positive and negative curvature, and adjusts the applied gradient while preserving the approximate first-order decrease in loss. The authors derive bounds on gradient alignment and magnitude and conditions for improved loss reduction. Integrated into Soft Actor-Critic (`SAC`) without changing its loss, critic or replay, the method **achieves higher mean sample efficiency than `SAC` and two second-order baselines on 6 `MuJoCo` continuous control benchmarks**.

papers.title: LimoBench: How Street Smart Are Large Language Models?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. But are LLMs truly location-aware, able to reliably interpret and precisely answer location queries involving real-world coordinates, points of interest (POIs), and geospatial distances? To answer this concretely, we present LimoBench, a street-level benchmark of 82 natural-language location queries over seven canonical spatial operations: geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, directionality, range search, $k$-nearest-neighbor search, and spatial join. The queries are grounded in real map data of West Lafayette, Indiana, and are graded by location and semantic complexity. They are designed to probe LLMs' street-level spatial awareness, from simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning. We also present Limo, an approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enhances the location awareness of LLMs. Limo grounds LLMs in PostGIS-backed spatial data through a compact set of tools. We find that ungrounded models mostly achieve single-digit accuracy (3.1% for GPT-6 Luna) across different spatial operations. In contrast, the same models achieve near-perfect accuracy (99.3% for GPT-6 Luna) when given access to Limo's spatial tools through MCP. Current LLMs thus have limited and unreliable street-level spatial knowledge, while grounding provides accurate answers at modest overhead (+0.2 s latency, 7.7$\times$ tokens, and 2.2$\times$ cost for GPT-6 Luna). We release the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code to encourage the community to evaluate their own location-aware LLM approaches.
papers.summary: `LimoBench` tests whether large language models can answer street-level location questions, using 82 natural-language queries over seven spatial operations such as geocoding, routing, range search and spatial join, grounded in real map data for West Lafayette, Indiana. The authors also present `Limo`, a compact set of tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that grounds models in a `PostGIS` spatial database. Ungrounded models mostly score in the single digits, and **`GPT-6 Luna` goes from 3.1% to 99.3% accuracy when given the spatial tools**. The grounding costs about 0.2 seconds of extra latency, 7.7x the tokens and 2.2x the cost for that model.

papers.title: CROSS-Calib: Selective Channel Calibration for Ultrasound Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging provides views of internal tissue in real time for medical diagnosis. However, ultrasound signals may be affected by interference, and correcting errors and removing transient interference while preserving valid echoes remains challenging. We propose CROSS-Calib, a channel recovery method that uses predictions from other channels as references for amplitude and phase calibration, while a gate using context selectively combines calibrated measurements with predicted echoes to retain usable samples and repair unreliable ones. On the in vivo test set, CROSS-Calib outperforms all baseline models under gain errors and transient interference, while phantom tests show that the model restores cyst contrast with echo widths of wire targets close to the clean reference. CROSS-Calib can perform channel calibration and selective repair before beamforming to improve echo usability and image quality.
papers.summary: Ultrasound channel signals can be corrupted by gain errors and transient interference, and repairing them without discarding valid echoes is difficult. `CROSS-Calib` uses predictions from other channels as references for amplitude and phase calibration, and a context-based gate selectively combines calibrated measurements with predicted echoes so that usable samples are kept and unreliable ones repaired before beamforming. It **outperforms all baseline models on the in vivo test set under gain errors and transient interference**, and phantom tests show restored cyst contrast with wire-target echo widths close to the clean reference.

papers.title: Right Destination, Wrong Journey: Synthetic Counseling Dialogues Miss Human Interactional Dynamics
papers.abstract: LLM-generated counseling dialogues are increasingly used for training and evaluating mental-health systems, yet existing evaluations focus largely on response quality and final outcomes rather than how support unfolds over time. We conduct a trajectory-centered evaluation of process fidelity across ten human, reconstructed, and synthetic counseling datasets. Our results show that synthetic dialogues often reach plausible endpoints but differ from human support in recovery dynamics and turn-by-turn responsiveness. While generation design can shift global properties such as recovery timing and trajectory structure, contingent patient--counselor responsiveness remains consistently lower in fidelity across models and generation paradigms. Our experiments on controlled synthetic datasets show that targeted generation interventions can narrow the gap with real data on several trajectory-level measures, but do not fully recover interactional fidelity, with turn-level responsiveness remaining limited. We release three controlled synthetic datasets comprising 2,050 dialogues, together with annotations and the evaluation framework.
papers.summary: Synthetic counseling dialogues generated by large language models are widely used to train and evaluate mental-health systems, but they are usually judged on response quality and final outcomes rather than on how support unfolds. A trajectory-centered evaluation across ten human, reconstructed and synthetic counseling datasets finds that **synthetic dialogues often reach plausible endpoints but differ from human support in recovery dynamics and turn-by-turn responsiveness**. Targeted generation interventions narrow the gap on several trajectory-level measures, yet turn-level patient-counselor responsiveness stays low across models and generation paradigms. The authors release three controlled synthetic datasets totaling 2,050 dialogues along with annotations and the evaluation framework.

papers.title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems.
