To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.
papers.summary: Statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization is studied in the setting where derivatives are unavailable or costly, where existing stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) methods either need gradients or are computationally expensive. The proposed sketched derivative-free method, `SDF-SSQP`, uses randomized sketching to **cut per-iteration cost to O((d+m)^2)** for d decision variables and m constraints, and a random-scaling approach that avoids estimating the asymptotic covariance matrix. The authors prove asymptotic normality of the averaged primal-dual iterates and construct an asymptotically pivotal self-normalized statistic, giving a fully online inference procedure with no matrix inversion. Numerical experiments support both the optimization performance and the accuracy of the inference.

papers.title: GRUN: Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network for Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Image restoration remains a fundamental challenge in low-level vision, requiring methods that handle diverse degradations while preserving scene structures and details. We revisit classical Retinex theory and propose a Generalized Retinex formulation that extends the illumination-reflectance decomposition into a Retinex-inspired content-environment factorization prior for image restoration. The key idea is to restore images using two learned factors: a content-dominant response (generalized reflectance) capturing scene properties and an environment-side response (generalized illumination) encoding task-dependent variations associated with the observed degradations. Based on this formulation, we develop GRUN (Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network), a MAP-guided deep unfolding framework that alternates reflectance restoration, illumination estimation, and progressive degradation inference across K stages with degradation-conditioned proximal operators. We further introduce a Degradation-aware Coupling Regularizer (DCR) that combines mutual information minimization, gradient decorrelation, and scale anchoring to promote complementary content-environment factor representations. Experiments on seven image restoration tasks, including denoising, dehazing, deraining, low-light enhancement, deblurring, underwater enhancement, and backlit enhancement, demonstrate competitive results on multiple benchmarks using the same architecture with task-specific weights. Moreover, the proposed Generalized Retinex design can be integrated into existing restoration methods, demonstrating its cross-architecture applicability. Code will be released.
papers.summary: Classical Retinex theory, which decomposes an image into illumination and reflectance, is generalized into a content-environment factorization prior for image restoration across many degradation types. `GRUN` is a deep unfolding network that alternates reflectance restoration, illumination estimation and progressive degradation inference over several stages, with a Degradation-aware Coupling Regularizer (DCR) that pushes the two factors toward complementary representations. Using one architecture with task-specific weights, it shows **competitive results on seven restoration tasks**, including denoising, dehazing, deraining, deblurring and low-light enhancement. The factorization can also be plugged into existing restoration methods.

papers.title: Rapid Exploratory Maps and their potential role in supporting evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes
papers.abstract: Producing useful evidence syntheses requires clearly formulated research questions linked to an understanding of their optimal scope. When policymakers (or other end users) commission or steer the production of systematic reviews or other evidence syntheses to fulfil a demand for evidence, these parameters are rarely specified sufficiently for production to proceed. Instead, these details are typically developed via a collaborative dialogic process involving evidence producers and users to ensure the resulting synthesis will meet users' needs. This process is informed by scoping and (more-or-less formally) mapping the existing evidence base, which can take many weeks or months, slowed by applying mostly manual processes to identify and characterise the evidence. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have opened up new opportunities for more rapid, iterative, and responsive mapping of relevant evidence to support such early-stage evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes. In this article, we outline and characterise this emerging approach, termed Rapid Exploratory Maps (REMs). We also present two illustrative case studies drawn from first-hand experiences within a programme of evidence reviews production to inform government policy in England. While this approach could be transformative for the mapping process, its broader potential is as yet largely unassessed, and it confers important challenges and likely risks, as well as benefits. Determining whether REMs could usefully support more efficient ways of working with end users when developing and designing evidence syntheses will require continued development and careful evaluation.
papers.summary: Scoping an evidence synthesis for policymakers normally involves weeks or months of largely manual mapping of the existing research before the review question can be settled. The article outlines Rapid Exploratory Maps (REMs), an approach that uses AI tools to map relevant evidence quickly and iteratively during early dialogue between evidence producers and users, and illustrates it with two case studies from a programme producing evidence reviews for government policy in England. The authors conclude that **the approach's broader potential is still largely unassessed** and that it carries risks as well as benefits, requiring further development and careful evaluation.

papers.title: CATWAY: Cost-sensitive agentic three-way robot decisions with calibrated language-model confidence
papers.abstract: A language-model robot agent must decide whether to execute, question or refuse an instruction, and an unsafe execution costs far more than an unneeded question. No prior robot gate derives all its thresholds from error costs or acts on calibrated probabilities, and none was fitted in one domain and evaluated unchanged in another. We propose CATWAY, a cost-sensitive three-way decision gate: a loss matrix over four instruction conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe) fixes execute, ask and refuse regions on the probability simplex, the question being the information-gathering step. Its probabilities fuse a ten-sample vote with graded scores of ambiguity, infeasibility and risk by logistic regression. Fitted on household instructions and frozen, CATWAY was tested on text-level decisions of three small models in-domain, in two new robot domains and on the external TRUST-NAV benchmark. At eleven generations per decision against one, it was significantly cheaper than a direct prompt, a cost-aware prompt and an unguarded agent in all 18 household comparisons (mean loss per item 0.28 against 0.57-0.83), in 9 of 18 in the new domains and in 10 of 18 on TRUST-NAV (Holm per set), and never significantly costlier. It executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions. On a unanimous vote, the minimum-expected-loss rule reduces calibration to one loss-derived threshold, so for two of six model configurations a gate on the vote alone never executed a clear instruction, costing 0.49 per item on TRUST-NAV against CATWAY's 0.13 and 0.09; the fused estimate avoided this on every set.
papers.summary: A robot agent driven by a language model must choose whether to execute, question or refuse an instruction, with unsafe execution costing far more than an unnecessary question. `CATWAY` derives execute, ask and refuse regions from a loss matrix over four instruction conditions (clear, ambiguous, infeasible, unsafe), with probabilities obtained by fusing a ten-sample vote with graded ambiguity, infeasibility and risk scores through logistic regression. Fitted on household instructions and then frozen, it was tested on three small models in-domain, in two new robot domains and on the `TRUST-NAV` benchmark, at eleven generations per decision instead of one. It was **significantly cheaper than direct prompting, cost-aware prompting and an unguarded agent in all 18 household comparisons**, in 9 of 18 in the new domains and 10 of 18 on `TRUST-NAV`, was never significantly costlier, and executed none of the 142 unsafe test instructions.

papers.title: FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World-Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation
papers.abstract: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/
papers.summary: Manipulating a moving object requires predicting the scene at the moment an action executes, but slow prediction lets the scene drift further. `FoveaWAM` is a 4D world-action model that splits prediction by role: the target's motion is modeled as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and static content is read from the current frame. It acts in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines. On the new `OnTimeBench` benchmark, where the scene keeps moving while the policy computes, it reaches **82.1% success, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline**, and it also leads on `DOMINO` and real-robot tasks.

papers.title: Stopping criteria in structural reliability analysis: An overview
papers.abstract: Stopping criteria have become a crucial component of probabilistic and statistical methods in structural reliability analysis, helping prevent structural defects and failures, as well as inaccurate evaluations of existing structures. Over time, these rules have evolved in both concept and application, whereas their treatment in the literature remains fragmented. They are often developed and presented in connection with specific models or analytical frameworks, obscuring their broader applicability across diverse models and methodologies. On this basis, the aim of this article is twofold. First, it overviews a wide range of stopping rules, drawing on concepts from applied probability and statistics. These strategies include classical methods based on error estimates or variance, and stability detection. While many of these ideas were developed in other fields, they have the potential to offer useful tools for structural reliability tasks like managing sampling, improving surrogate models, and checking for convergence. Second, this article introduces a structured framework to organize past and recent developments in this area. It brings together various stopping criteria, clarifies their conceptual roles, explains their theoretical foundations, and compares their practical strengths and limitations. By relating these methods to common modeling and methodological practices, and by incorporating a systematic comparison of performance aspects such as accuracy, computational cost, and robustness, we aim to identify dominant strategies, highlight shared challenges, and point to directions for further progress.
papers.summary: Rules for deciding when to stop sampling or refining a model in structural reliability analysis are scattered across the literature and usually tied to specific models. The overview collects stopping rules from applied probability and statistics, including classical criteria based on error estimates or variance and criteria based on stability detection. It then **organizes these criteria into a structured framework** that explains their conceptual roles and theoretical foundations and compares them on accuracy, computational cost, and robustness.

papers.title: PRETZEL: A Benchmark for Cyclic Peptide Structure Prediction
papers.abstract: Macrocyclic peptides are a growing therapeutic modality, and co-folding models are increasingly used to predict their structures. Yet published evaluations rely on small, loosely curated target sets that differ from paper to paper, so results are not comparable, and most report pose RMSD alone, without checking whether the predicted molecule is chemically correct. We introduce PRETZEL (Prediction of Ring-Enclosed Topology: Zero-shot Evaluation of cycLic peptides), a benchmark of 285 curated cyclic peptide-protein complexes spanning three cyclization chemistries, all post-dating the training cutoff of every model evaluated. PRETZEL has three components: PRETZEL-SET, an evaluation set annotated by cyclization chemistry and chemical novelty; PRETZEL-TWIST, a specification layer that compiles a single canonical macrocycle description into each engine's native input format and verifies the returned structure; and PRETZEL-SALT, an evaluation suite pairing standard pose metrics with validity checks for bond distances, bond angles, dihedrals, and ring closure. Using these, we evaluate AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, Protenix-v2, and HighFold3. Protenix-v2 achieves the best median RMSD at 9.05 A, with 19.3% of predictions under 2 A and 37.5% under 5 A. Accuracy varies by cyclization chemistry: models handle head-to-tail macrocycles relatively well but degrade on stapled targets. Chemical validity is weaker still: at most 8.1% of predictions have a fully valid set of inter-residue bonds, and no engine closes every macrocycle in more than 80.7% of its predictions, so pose accuracy alone is an insufficient criterion. These failures share a cause: co-folding models place macrocycles without representing them, treating cyclization and non-canonical chemistry as annotations layered onto a residue sequence rather than as first-class structure. PRETZEL is released with all inputs, predictions, and evaluation code.
papers.summary: Evaluations of co-folding models on macrocyclic peptides use small, inconsistent target sets and mostly report pose error without checking chemical correctness. `PRETZEL` is a benchmark of 285 curated cyclic peptide-protein complexes across three cyclization chemistries, all post-dating the training cutoffs of the evaluated models, with a layer that compiles one macrocycle description into each engine's input format and a suite of bond, angle, dihedral, and ring-closure validity checks. Among `AlphaFold3`, `Boltz-2`, `Protenix-v2`, and `HighFold3`, `Protenix-v2` has the best median RMSD at 9.05 angstroms, with 19.3% of predictions under 2 angstroms. Chemical validity is worse: **at most 8.1% of predictions have a fully valid set of inter-residue bonds**, and no engine closes every macrocycle in more than 80.7% of its predictions.

papers.title: EventSSM: Causal Spatial-State Modelling for Asynchronous Events Event-Depth Estimation
papers.abstract: Event cameras report asynchronous brightness changes, yet metric-depth supervision is typically available only at sparsely sampled reference timestamps. Aggregating events into frame-like representations simplifies learning but can obscure the fine-grained temporal structure of the original event stream. We introduce EventSSM, a causal spatial-state framework for event-associated metric-depth estimation using a recurrent memory updated by chronological event packets. To bridge asynchronous predictions and frame-time supervision, predicted event depths are geometrically transported using calibrated camera poses and differentiably rendered at reference timestamps. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate improvements over established event-depth methods across multiple depth-error measures. Controlled ablations further examine cross-modal initialization, temporal recurrence, individual state, readout, and supervision components, and packet subdivision. Together, these findings establish EventSSM as an effective framework for causal event-associated metric-depth estimation, combining persistent spatial context with physically timed state retention.
papers.summary: Event cameras emit asynchronous brightness changes, but metric-depth ground truth exists only at sparse reference timestamps, and aggregating events into frames hides fine temporal structure. `EventSSM` is a causal spatial-state framework that updates a recurrent memory with chronological event packets and predicts depth per event. To train against frame-time labels, **predicted event depths are geometrically transported using calibrated camera poses and differentiably rendered at the reference timestamps**. The authors report lower depth error than established event-depth methods on benchmark evaluations, with ablations over initialization, recurrence, and supervision components.

papers.title: fork() for Agents: Agent Kernel for Non-blocking LLM Orchestration
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents typically execute tool calls synchronously and discard completed work upon failure. Subgraph-selective recovery, re-executing only a failed node's transitive descendants, is a well-established pattern in distributed systems (Spark, Erlang/OTP, Dryad), and recent agent runtimes (Sherlock, AgentGit, Atomix) preserve completed work through verifiers, version control, or transactional tool boundaries. We present \textbf{Agent-Kernel}, a non-blocking runtime that ports this pattern to the LLM \emph{content plane}: its primitive, \textbf{Sub-Graph Recovery (SGR)}, fires on a raw exception with no trained verifier or planner, resets a failed node's descendants while preserving completed siblings, and composes each parent's text into its children's prompts (context inheritance), all on a durable substrate with a formal state-preservation guarantee. Across 14{,}434 runs on synthetic and standard benchmarks (tau-bench, Gaia2, AutomationBench, InterruptBench), SGR reaches full recovery within budget=3 where whole-trajectory replay exhausts (100\% vs.\ 55\%), and is roughly 10$\times$ faster than an adapted Sherlock rollback that also recovers. It matches ReAct-serial accuracy within noise on linear workloads while adding recovery and parallelism (up to 12.7$\times$ speedup) where structure permits. Ablation isolates SGR: removing it collapses success to 39.4\%.
papers.summary: LLM agents usually run tool calls synchronously and throw away completed work when a step fails. `Agent-Kernel` is a non-blocking runtime whose primitive, Sub-Graph Recovery (`SGR`), fires on a raw exception without a trained verifier or planner, resets only the failed node's descendants while keeping completed siblings, and passes each parent's text into its children's prompts. Across 14,434 runs on synthetic tasks and benchmarks including `tau-bench`, `Gaia2`, `AutomationBench`, and `InterruptBench`, **`SGR` reaches full recovery within a budget of 3 where whole-trajectory replay manages 55%**, and is roughly 10 times faster than an adapted `Sherlock` rollback. It matches serial `ReAct` accuracy on linear workloads and gives up to a 12.7x speedup where the task structure allows parallelism.

papers.title: Tokenization and Architecture Jointly Allocate Component Roles in Time Series Transformers
papers.abstract: Time series transformers have achieved strong forecasting performance, yet it remains unclear which of their components, attention or the feed-forward network (FFN), constructs temporal features, and how tokenization such as patching changes this. We propose a temporal probing framework that uses 15 token-level diagnostic tasks to measure feature construction as the gain in linear decodability of temporal properties from one sub-layer to the next (a matched MLP probe already saturates at the embedding). It targets models whose probed representations are read by a linear forecasting head. Applied to 5 supervised models trained on 8 long-term forecasting benchmarks, it finds that the constructing component is not fixed but allocated by the interaction of tokenization and architecture. Under patch tokenization (PatchTST), the FFN's gain exceeds attention's in probing on all 8 datasets, and its 8-dataset mean is 3.2x attention's. Without attention, the FFN alone reaches nearly the same total gain, both when attention is removed from a trained model and when PatchTST is trained without it, and the retrained model forecasts within a few percent of the full model. In probing, attention dominates under variate tokenization (iTransformer); in CATS, cross-attention is the only input path. In a controlled manipulation of PatchTST, single-scalar tokens (P=1) nearly eliminate the FFN's construction, while one more point per token (P=2) restores it. Our forecasting-side interventions (activation patching, knockout, and training without attention) establish component-level reliance and sufficiency. These results offer a representational reading of prior findings on the gains from patching, the competitiveness of self-attention-free models (TSMixer, PatchMLP), and the distinct role of cross-attention in CATS.
papers.summary: Which component of a time series transformer builds temporal features, attention or the feed-forward network (FFN), and how tokenization changes that, has been unclear. A probing framework with 15 token-level diagnostic tasks measures feature construction as the gain in linear decodability between sub-layers, applied to 5 supervised models on 8 long-term forecasting benchmarks. The constructing component turns out to depend on the interaction of tokenization and architecture: **under patch tokenization in `PatchTST`, the FFN's mean gain is 3.2x attention's**, and a version trained without attention forecasts within a few percent of the full model. Attention dominates instead under variate tokenization in `iTransformer`, and single-scalar tokens nearly eliminate the FFN's role in `PatchTST`.

papers.title: Geo-SMILE: Statistical Model-Agnostic Interpretability with Local Explanations for Geospatial Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Conventional post-hoc explanation methods were developed largely for non-spatial inputs and often provide limited explicit treatment of geographic context. We introduce Geo-SMILE, a model-agnostic framework that distinguishes substantive Feature explanation from geographic-position response through complementary perturbation branches. The Feature branch masks substantive predictors while retaining observed coordinates; the Geo branch relocates geographic units while holding substantive predictors fixed. Following the statistical-distance-weighted surrogate principle of SMILE, input-distribution Wasserstein distances determine coalition locality weights and weighted Ridge surrogates approximate expected black-box predictions. GeoSensitivity, signed in the keep orientation, quantifies fitted-model responses to geographic-player relocation under the specified design. Across crime prediction in Hull, housing-price prediction in Seattle and ride-hailing demand in Chicago, held-out weighted surrogate fidelity ranges from $R_w^2=0.910$ to $0.989$ in the Feature branch and from $0.842$ to $0.906$ in the Geo branch. The framework makes geographic position an explicit object of post-hoc explanation while requiring separate assessment of interpretation, stability and reference dependence.
papers.summary: Post-hoc explanation methods were built mostly for non-spatial inputs and handle geographic context poorly. `Geo-SMILE` is a model-agnostic framework with two perturbation branches: one masks substantive predictors while keeping coordinates, and the other relocates geographic units while holding predictors fixed. It weights perturbations by Wasserstein distance and fits weighted Ridge surrogates to the black-box predictions, following the earlier `SMILE` method. On crime prediction in Hull, housing prices in Seattle, and ride-hailing demand in Chicago, **held-out surrogate fidelity ranges from 0.910 to 0.989 in the feature branch and from 0.842 to 0.906 in the geographic branch**.

papers.title: MOSAIC: Memory-Organized Search with Anti-Imitation Crossover for Training-Free Microarchitecture Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search. In our adaptations of published search methods, generated code resembles established policies, with cosine similarities of 0.78-0.84. The wider comparison also shows held-out harmonic-mean instructions-per-cycle (IPC) losses of 1.0-2.4%. We present MOSAIC, a search controller that improves policies without updating language-model weights. It stores concise lessons from previous evaluations rather than repeatedly copying high-scoring code. When improvement stops, it selects two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ and asks the model to combine their mechanisms. Novelty prompts and model rotation support this search; controlled memory edits test how the stored lessons affect later proposals. We evaluate cache replacement using intervention-level cross-validation and a wider comparison on ten memory-intensive SPEC2006 workloads. MOSAIC reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the primary search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean in the intervention study. Removing crossover reduces these values by 7.8 and 21.8 percentage points, respectively, whereas the tested stronger model improves the held-out mean by 0.4 points. In the wider IPC comparison, MOSAIC has the smallest held-out gap (0.31%) and the highest held-out IPC among the evaluated LLM configurations. Adapting the same controller to data prefetching gives a 4.8% mean speedup over the LRU reference configuration. The accompanying corpus contains 10,687 generated policies with lineage and per-iteration prompt logs.
papers.summary: LLM-generated cache-replacement policies tend to resemble established policies and lose performance on workloads excluded from the search. `MOSAIC` is a search controller that leaves model weights untouched: it stores concise lessons from past evaluations instead of copying high-scoring code, and when progress stalls it asks the model to combine two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ. On ten memory-intensive `SPEC2006` workloads it reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean, and **removing crossover cuts the held-out mean by 21.8 percentage points** while a stronger model adds only 0.4. It also has the smallest held-out gap in instructions-per-cycle (IPC) among the evaluated LLM configurations, at 0.31%, and gives a 4.8% mean speedup when adapted to data prefetching.

papers.title: BEARING: Who Is Talking to Whom? Grounding Acoustic Direction in Vision for Online Multi-Party Conversation
papers.abstract: Understanding a group conversation means deciding, from video and audio, who is speaking and to whom. Leading systems treat these tasks offline on single-channel clips and align models with a self-evaluation reward. We propose BEARING, a geometry-first alternative built on one measured signal: the direction from which a microphone array beside the camera hears a sound. A label-free calibration learned from the stream registers this direction into the camera image, and an online registry of faces, voices and directions needs no enrollment. The registered direction serves as (i) a visual prompt for a vision-language model, a marker on the speaker or an arrow toward an off-screen source; (ii) one input of a reliability-weighted fusion with visual active-speaker detection, for speakers in the same direction from the array; and (iii) a verifiable reward for alignment: the named speaker must sit where the sound comes from, the confidence must match that check, and always answering "group" earns nothing. Every decision is online, with the lookahead as an explicit parameter. On 9,498 addressee-labelled utterances from three AMI sites and egocentric EasyCom, the direction prompt raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74%; addressee accuracy moves by about two points, because telling one addressee from the group depends on the words more than on where people are. For co-located speakers on AVDIAR, visual active-speaker detection holds 95% where direction alone falls to 59%. The verifiable reward beats self-evaluation under GRPO, reward-ranked fine-tuning and DPO; shrinking the lookahead from 5 s to 0.5 s costs 4.5 DER points on AMI, and learning the registration online costs a dip in the first two minutes before the system overtakes vision alone. Code and evaluation protocols will be released.
papers.summary: Deciding who is speaking and to whom in a group conversation is usually handled offline on single-channel clips. `BEARING` instead uses the direction from which a microphone array beside the camera hears a sound, registers it into the camera image with a label-free calibration, and uses it as a visual prompt for a vision-language model, as an input fused with visual active-speaker detection, and as a verifiable reward for alignment. On 9,498 addressee-labelled utterances from `AMI` and `EasyCom`, **the direction prompt raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74%**, while addressee accuracy moves by only about two points. For co-located speakers on `AVDIAR`, visual active-speaker detection holds 95% where direction alone falls to 59%, and the verifiable reward beats a self-evaluation reward across three fine-tuning methods.

papers.title: Reproducing History Is Not Enough: Intervention-Level Assurance for LLM-Generated Simulators
papers.abstract:
Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies. However, a program that reproduces recorded history can still give wrong answers to what-if questions; requested changes may be applied wrongly, or they may be applied to records other than the ones the question is about, or the program may stop being valid once its policy is revised. Current checks return a pass-or-fail verdict for the whole program, which says little about whether any single answer can be trusted. We propose Vouch, a library that judges whether an answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the change being asked about. Each what-if question is turned into a structured change, which is checked against the program and the current records. The library also keeps a record of the kinds of change each program has passed or failed, and repeats the relevant tests whenever the program is reused. We apply it to three program-generation platforms, with programs built by five language models, across four domains: manufacturing, IT operations, and pharmacy and loan-application workflows, using independently checked reference answers. Our baselines are the platforms' own checks where such checks exist, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a ReAct agent that can run the program. We measure how many correct answers are trusted, how many are wrongly rejected, how many wrong answers are accepted, and what the checking costs.
  On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, Vouch removes 97.6% of the wrong answers, while still trusting 80.1% of all answers. At equal coverage, it accepts fewer wrong answers than LLM judges built on Claude Haiku. We disclose code and results for reproducibility.
papers.summary: An LLM-written simulation program that reproduces recorded history can still answer what-if questions wrongly, and whole-program pass-or-fail checks say little about any single answer. `Vouch` is a library that turns each what-if question into a structured change, checks it against the program and current records, and tracks which kinds of change each program has passed or failed, rerunning relevant tests on reuse. It is evaluated on three program-generation platforms with programs from five language models across manufacturing, IT operations, pharmacy, and loan-application workflows, against platform checks, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a `ReAct` agent. On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, **`Vouch` removes 97.6% of the wrong answers while still trusting 80.1% of all answers**.

papers.title: GreenDynaMix: Thermal-Aware Dynamic Mixed-Precision MoE LLM Inference Systems
papers.abstract: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time frequency scaling, which inevitably comes at the cost of either throughput or accuracy. To address this tightly coupled challenge, we propose GreenDynaMix, the first runtime system to jointly integrate a DVFS-based thermal manager with a dynamic precision-tuning throughput compensator. A sensitivity-aware allocator leverages intrinsic importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to assign higher precision to critical experts, preserving accuracy. Experiments on server, desktop, and embedded platforms demonstrate that GreenDynaMix reduces the temperature-induced aging rate of GPUs during LLM inference by 25-33%. Without offline profiling or model retraining, it recovers throughput at a perplexity cost of 0.9-1.6% with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.
papers.summary: Sustained LLM inference heats GPUs and accelerates silicon aging, and throttling frequency to control temperature costs throughput or accuracy. `GreenDynaMix` is a runtime system that pairs a DVFS-based thermal manager with dynamic precision tuning to recover throughput, using importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to give critical experts higher precision. On server, desktop, and embedded platforms it **reduces the temperature-induced GPU aging rate by 25-33%**, with no offline profiling or retraining. The throughput recovery costs 0.9-1.6% in perplexity with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.

papers.title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
papers.abstract: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.
papers.summary: Classic interaction design assumes a user who is present in the loop, which no longer holds when users delegate an outcome to an agent that takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, the authors argue that **delegation opens two new gulfs: a gulf of specification and a gulf of oversight**. The first is the gap between what a user wants and can express, and the second is the gap between what an agent is doing and what the user can know, assess, and control. They argue both meet in the harness of tools, permissions, checks, and loop around the model, and call on human-computer interaction research to decide which parts should be user-owned, adjustable, or built in.

papers.title: FN-Prune: Training-Free Expert Pruning with Finite RMSNorm Perturbations
papers.abstract: Expert pruning reduces the memory footprint of mixture-of-experts language models, but retaining model quality depends on which experts are removed. Frequency- and magnitude-based scores measure the expert in isolation and overlook how normalization consumes its contribution: subtracting one expert changes both the direction of the residual stream and the scale applied to what remains. We propose FN-Prune, a training-free criterion that compares the next RMSNorm outputs before and after subtracting each router-weighted expert contribution, holding original routes and weights fixed. Squared differences are averaged over all calibration tokens in one pass; low-scoring experts are physically deleted at uniform per-layer ratios, and inference reroutes among survivors. At 50% expert removal, FN-Prune achieves lower WikiText-2 perplexity than the best published methods on Qwen3, ERNIE, and OLMoE, including a 32% reduction on OLMoE. At the same budget, GSM8K accuracy improves over the best published methods by 7.5 and 7.0 percentage points on Qwen3 and ERNIE, respectively, while multiple-choice gains remain task-dependent.
papers.summary: Pruning experts from mixture-of-experts language models saves memory, but common frequency- and magnitude-based scores ignore how normalization absorbs each expert's contribution. `FN-Prune` is a training-free criterion that compares the next RMSNorm output before and after subtracting each router-weighted expert contribution, averaged over calibration tokens in one pass, then deletes low-scoring experts at uniform per-layer ratios. At 50% expert removal it gets lower `WikiText-2` perplexity than the best published methods on `Qwen3`, `ERNIE`, and `OLMoE`, **including a 32% reduction on `OLMoE`**. `GSM8K` accuracy improves by 7.5 and 7.0 percentage points on `Qwen3` and `ERNIE`, while multiple-choice gains are task-dependent.

papers.title: RVLM-X: Towards a Universal VLM Harness
papers.abstract: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) have grown with the models' capabilities, notably for images far larger than those seen in training, where downscaling loses small details. Most of them wrap the VLM in a fixed procedure, such as a zoom tree, that decides in advance where it looks and how the evidence is combined. These procedures make up for the weaknesses of older models by keeping them on a task-specific path, but with frontier models that reliably plan and use tools, they can lower accuracy. We propose RVLM-X, a task-generalizable recursive VLM harness that runs unchanged across photographs, charts and maps. Following the recursive inference of Recursive Language Models, the VLM programmatically controls its own visual context in a code REPL that holds the full-resolution image and calls itself recursively on regions that it chooses. With a cost-efficient frontier model as the base of every method, RVLM-X is more accurate than a single call on all 7 public benchmarks and has the highest pooled accuracy. Because existing benchmarks mostly test whether a model finds one small detail, we also introduce MapGenBench, procedurally generated maps whose questions combine fine-detail perception with multi-step reasoning. There, RVLM-X answers 71.4% of held-out questions against 55.5% for the strongest baseline. Overall, our findings suggest that as VLMs plan and use tools more reliably, letting the model write its own visual search works better than fixing one in advance.
papers.summary: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) on very large images usually impose a fixed procedure such as a zoom tree, which can lower accuracy for frontier models that plan and use tools reliably. `RVLM-X` is a recursive harness in which the VLM controls its own visual context from a code REPL holding the full-resolution image and calls itself on regions it chooses, running unchanged across photographs, charts, and maps. With the same cost-efficient frontier model under every method, it beats a single call on all 7 public benchmarks and has the highest pooled accuracy. On the new `MapGenBench` of procedurally generated maps, **`RVLM-X` answers 71.4% of held-out questions against 55.5% for the strongest baseline**.

papers.title: TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents
papers.abstract: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.
papers.summary: Existing safety benchmarks for tool-use agents do not fully test agents that must refuse policy-violating requests while still finishing the legitimate work in the same conversation. `TACT-Bench` is a stateful benchmark of scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and escalation that adapts to responses, where each adversarial task targets an action the assistant's hidden policy prohibits and is paired with a benign counterpart. A variant, `TACT-TrustPrime`, places an unrelated benign task before the attack, and a new metric, Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), combines safe refusal with capability on matched benign tasks. Averaged over 6 assistant models, **the base tasks raise Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four attack baselines and the trust-priming variant adds a further 17.01%**, while two evaluated defenses cut AFR by only 8.35%-9.41%.

papers.title: Verified Proof Refactoring with Codex and Qwen
papers.abstract: We refactor existing Lean 4 proofs to reduce source length and checking cost while preserving theorem statements and compatibility across Lean versions. A locally served Qwen model uses the open-source Codex CLI to inspect source, retrieve declarations, and test proof replacements. The host keeps a replacement only if it improves the objective and Lean accepts it on every required version. A deterministic CPU pass then refines the verified proofs. On the 60 problems in Lean Refactor Arena, model search achieves a local mean combined score of 82.07, and cleanup raises it to 82.18. The final proofs pass all 127 required proof--version checks. Our system placed first in the open-source LLM track of Lean Refactor Arena at VeriCodeGen.
papers.summary: The goal is to refactor existing Lean 4 proofs so they are shorter and cheaper to check while keeping theorem statements intact and compatible across Lean versions. A locally served `Qwen` model drives the open-source `Codex CLI` to inspect source, retrieve declarations, and test proof replacements, and a replacement is kept only if it improves the objective and Lean accepts it on every required version; a deterministic CPU pass then refines the results. On the 60 problems of `Lean Refactor Arena`, **model search reaches a mean combined score of 82.07 and cleanup raises it to 82.18**, with all 127 required proof-version checks passing. The system placed first in the benchmark's open-source LLM track at VeriCodeGen.

papers.title: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset
papers.abstract: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.
papers.summary: Text-driven generation of hand motion is held back by datasets that treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are small. `RoMo Hands` is an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of **about 542K sequences (884 hours), an order of magnitude larger than prior work**, filtered to keep highly articulated bimanual movement. Each clip has five captions ranging from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, and the authors propose a 393-dimensional bimanual motion representation. Benchmarking diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators shows distinct trade-offs, including a divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility.
papers.highlight_summary:
Text-conditioned generation of pure hand motion has lagged body motion because text-paired hand datasets are small, so `RoMo Hands` assembles **~542K** in-the-wild bimanual sequences (**884 hours**, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) with five captions per clip at increasing detail. It also contributes a 393-D bimanual motion representation and a benchmark of body-motion generators retrained on hands.

- The pipeline reuses the `RoMo` web-video pool, recovers per-frame MANO hand poses with `WiLoR` anchored to the body's SMPL wrist trajectory, drops poorly visible or near-static clips with detection-ratio and dexterity filters (keeping ~884 of ~1,238 hours), and captions each clip at five levels (L0 headline to L4 full paragraph) with `Qwen3.5-27B`.
- The result is **10.6×** the duration of `CLUTCH` and **5.6×** the caption count of `HandX` (about 2.71M captions), and a 250-clip human audit rated action match at 4.16/5, caption–motion faithfulness at 3.79/5, and reconstruction quality at 3.53/5.
- The `R_hand` representation stacks a 9-D root frame built on a synthetic wrist-midpoint root and inter-wrist heading with positions, velocities, and 6D rotations for 32 joints, which lifts `MoMask` R@1 from 0.395 (raw MANO) to **0.547**, but helps `Kimodo M` only marginally (0.646 to 0.665), where the `CLUTCH` representation keeps the best FID.
- In the benchmark no generator wins on both metric families: `MoMask` and `Kimodo M` are effectively tied on retrieval (R@1 of 54.00% and 53.82% against 63.77% for ground truth), while `Kimodo M` has the best FID (0.087) and the cleanest physical profile overall, and `MoMask` shows intra-hand jerk about **18×** ground truth (265.2 vs 14.3 m/s³).
- Rankings are indicative only because the adaptations are uneven (`MDM` is prefix-conditioned with a 60-frame horizon, `MotionMillion` runs at 150M rather than 1B parameters, and `MoMask` Stage 2 had not converged), and pose quality is validated by Likert ratings rather than error against ground-truth 3D hands, with retrieval scored by a single `TMR` evaluator trained on the same dataset.

papers.title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
papers.abstract:
Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign.
  We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.
papers.summary: Processor architects can see where a design loses pipeline slots and which configuration scores best, but not why a design-space exploration (DSE) search stops improving. `DELTA` treats every parent-child edge in an exploration tree as a controlled single-knob intervention and stores it in a Design Memory, including failed edits, along with measured and predicted instructions-per-cycle (IPC) and a Top-Down breakdown from `StallLens`, a `gem5` implementation. Aligning two parents under which the same edit helps and hurts localizes the interaction responsible. On four `SPEC CPU2017` workloads, **the system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost** and predicts the IPC of its own proposals within 3.3%; a root-cause query also led to a throttled variant of the `Best-Offset` prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37%.

papers.title: SPARQL-Planned Single-Hop Traversal over a Live Knowledge Graph for Multi-Hop Question Answering
papers.abstract: Semantic retrieval struggles with multi-hop question answering on both recall and precision: gold passages are buried among distractors that degrade the reader's answer, and retrieving them requires reasoning over the query rather than matching it. GraphRAG techniques expand semantic retrieval by connecting passages to graph nodes and performing one or more hops of expansion after initial retrieval. This improves recall, but multi-hop expansion becomes expensive and brings additional noise into the retrieved set. We break this tradeoff by \emph{interleaving} dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal for complex multi-hop questions. Dense retrieval locates the first relevant regions of the search space at good recall, while traversal of a pre-existing external KG (Wikidata) restores precision and improves recall by confirming retrieved passages against a reasoning path through the KG. To keep traversal both question-adaptive and reliable, we have an LLM plan it as code generation task for graph traversal in SPARQL format but \emph{parse rather than execute} the query. On full 1{,}000-question splits under a shared corpus and reader, and with a single configuration applied identically to every dataset, we reach \textbf{62.5 / 75.1} EM/F1 on HotpotQA, \textbf{73.5 / 81.0} on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and \textbf{37.1 / 50.0} on MuSiQue, ahead of reproduced HippoRAG2, T\textsuperscript{2}RAG, and IRCoT on all three benchmarks. A second, token-matched setting stays ahead of T\textsuperscript{2}RAG on HotpotQA and 2Wiki while spending roughly its per-query budget. Executing the generated SPARQL instead of parsing it costs up to 11.4 EM, mostly because raw queries return empty results, not because of syntax errors.
papers.summary: Multi-hop question answering strains semantic retrieval, and graph-based expansion improves recall at the cost of expense and noise. The proposed method interleaves dense retrieval with traversal of an existing external knowledge graph (`Wikidata`), having an LLM plan the traversal as a SPARQL query that is parsed into single-hop steps instead of being executed. With one configuration across 1,000-question splits, it reaches **62.5 / 75.1 EM/F1 on `HotpotQA`**, 73.5 / 81.0 on `2WikiMultiHopQA`, and 37.1 / 50.0 on `MuSiQue`, ahead of reproduced `HippoRAG2`, `T2RAG`, and `IRCoT`. Executing the generated SPARQL directly costs up to 11.4 EM, mostly because raw queries return empty results.

papers.title: VISOR: A Vision-Language Selector for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Recent time-series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast a distribution over futures, and multimodal time-series (TS) forecasting further exploits other modalities to improve forecasting accuracy. However, existing works have two limitations: 1) TSFMs reduce the predictive distribution to its median or mean, flattening diverse futures into a calm line, and 2) multimodal TS forecasting models incorporate text into the forecaster through TS-language alignment, which is substantially weaker than vision-language alignment. To address these limitations, we propose the VIsion-language SelectOR (VISOR), a multimodal TS forecasting framework that selects one plausible future instead of averaging across candidates, leveraging the alignment capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to select the most suitable candidate based on textual information. VISOR consists of two components: 1) a text-free stochastic predictor that samples diverse candidate futures, and 2) a VLM selector that reads the candidates as a single chart image and selects one based on the text. To avoid overly calm forecasting paths, we train the selector with a shape-aware target that evaluates each candidate based on both point-wise error and path shape. Across three benchmarks covering ten datasets, VISOR achieves the best average ranking in both point and volatility errors compared with TSFMs and multimodal TS forecasting models. Code: https://github.com/seunghan96/VISOR.
papers.summary: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) predict a distribution over futures but typically collapse it to a mean or median, and multimodal forecasters rely on comparatively weak alignment between time series and text. `VISOR` pairs a text-free stochastic predictor that samples diverse candidate futures with a vision-language model (VLM) selector that views the candidates as a single chart image and picks one based on the accompanying text. The selector is trained with a shape-aware target that scores candidates on both point-wise error and path shape. Across three benchmarks covering ten datasets, it **achieves the best average ranking in both point and volatility errors** against TSFMs and multimodal forecasting models.

papers.title: SciFig2Data: A Workflow for Recovering Structured Data from Scientific Figures
papers.abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.
papers.summary: Measurements in scholarly articles are often locked inside compound figures rather than published as machine-readable data. `SciFig2Data` is an automated pipeline that chains document element detection, compound-figure decomposition, two-stage OCR filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided reconstruction by a multimodal large language model (MLLM), with batch execution, caching, and logging for large runs. On 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles, it **reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs respectively**, each linked to experimental metadata taken from the figure caption.

papers.title: Three-Dimensional Wake Reconstruction and Cross-Scale Transfer for Floating Offshore Wind Turbines via Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and transfer across turbine scales. Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers $St=fD/U_\infty$ of 0.2-0.6 (where $f$, $D$, and $U_\infty$ are the motion frequency, rotor diameter, and inflow velocity) for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW ($D=126$ m) and International Energy Agency 22 MW ($D=284$ m) turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator framework combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes. Trained on the 5 MW fixed and $St=0.2$-$0.5$ cases, the framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through $St=0.6$ (mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of $D$), while 10% planar sampling preserves near-dense accuracy (relative $L_2$ error 0.0689 versus 0.0684). Applying transfer learning from the 5 MW to the 22 MW turbine lowers the three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at $St=0.6$ by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics ($St$-$3St$). Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework shows potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.
papers.summary: Floating offshore wind turbines surge and pitch, producing unsteady wakes that are hard to reconstruct in three dimensions from sparse measurements or to transfer between turbine sizes. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator, regularized with continuity and momentum residuals and trained on large-eddy simulations of the `NREL 5 MW` turbine, reconstructs the full unsteady wake from two observation planes, with mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of rotor diameter. Transfer learning to the `IEA 22 MW` turbine **lowers streamwise-velocity error by 36% relative to zero-shot inference**, although fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped.

papers.title: Byte Patches versus BPE at Matched Data: A Matched-Twin Comparison at 350M Parameters
papers.abstract: We compare a MEGABYTE-style byte-patch Transformer with a 64-byte sliding local decoder (local64) to a matched byte-level 8k BPE decoder (BPE-8k) under identical raw bytes, document order, and approximately matched bytes per optimizer step: 350M parameters and 10 billion training bytes. Under matched-span document sliding (identical scored byte ranges), BPE-8k leads with relative gaps of -5.2%, -4.9%, -9.3% and -6.1% in bits per byte (overall, text, code, math; paired bootstrap). Downstream, CharBench equal fine-tuning favors local64 (53.7% vs 40.0%), fact200 favors BPE-8k (16.5% vs 7.0%), and PIQA (raw and length-normalized) and ARC-Easy length-normalized favor BPE-8k after Holm correction at alpha = 0.05; remaining tasks are ties. Evaluation pitfalls that changed conclusions include context-length extrapolation past the BPE training context, bits per token reported as bits per byte, and inconsistent byte denominators. Unlike controlled tokenizer studies that vary the subword tokenizer under a fixed token budget, or FLOP-controlled byte-model scaling studies, we hold the raw bytes, their order and the optimizer recipe fixed and ask whether a fixed-patch byte model can replace the tokenizer at all. Limits: one size, one seed, one 8k vocabulary fixed before the runs, and a known difference in embedding initialization between the twins.
papers.summary: Can a fixed-patch byte model replace a subword tokenizer when the raw bytes, document order, and optimizer recipe are all held fixed? A `MEGABYTE`-style byte-patch Transformer with a 64-byte sliding local decoder is compared against a matched 8k-vocabulary byte-pair-encoding model, both at 350M parameters and 10 billion training bytes. The tokenized model **leads by 5.2% in bits per byte overall** (9.3% on code), and wins on `fact200` and `PIQA`, while the byte model wins on `CharBench` (53.7% vs 40.0%). The authors also document evaluation pitfalls that changed conclusions, such as reporting bits per token as bits per byte, and note the study covers one size and one seed.

papers.title: SwarmLeak: Does Coordination Improve Privacy Attacks on LLM Agents?
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly collaborate in group chats while holding tool access to confidential records, which makes the shared chat an attack surface. It remains unclear whether several colluding attackers extract such information more effectively than one. We introduce SwarmLeak, a red-teaming dataset of 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, where attackers pose as colleagues to make a victim agent post protected fields despite an explicit confidentiality policy. With GLM 5.2 attacking five victim models through seven conversational strategies, we compare one attacker with a swarm of four sharing a private channel, matching scenarios, strategies, and a 200,000-token budget that also covers swarm coordination. Swarms show no advantage: a single attacker matches or exceeds them on every victim, and the share of runs leaking any field differs between conditions by at most 14.3 percentage points, whereas changing the victim shifts it from 0% to 99.4%. On the two most vulnerable models, nearly every run leaks under both conditions, but single attackers expose more of the record at first disclosure (85.4% vs. 68.1% of protected fields on Nemotron 3.5 Lightning). Four of the five victims leaked despite the policy. GLM 5.2 retrieved protected data in 64.3% of individual-attack runs and leaked in 0.6%: retrieval does not imply disclosure, but in high-stakes settings even one leaked field can identify a patient or client. At equal budgets, a larger red team is not automatically a stronger one; the victim model matters far more.
papers.summary: When LLM agents with access to confidential records collaborate in group chats, do several colluding attackers extract protected data more effectively than one? `SwarmLeak` is a red-teaming dataset of 24 synthetic group-chat scenarios across healthcare, law, finance, and software engineering, used to compare a single `GLM 5.2` attacker with a four-agent swarm sharing a private channel under the same 200,000-token budget. **Swarms show no advantage: a single attacker matches or exceeds them on every victim model**, and the leak rate differs by at most 14.3 percentage points between conditions, whereas changing the victim shifts it from 0% to 99.4%. Four of the five victim models leaked despite an explicit confidentiality policy.

papers.title: AGL-SKILL: Coding Harnesses as Agentic Optimizers
papers.abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used through harnesses as agents, with growing autonomy to do useful work. Agent performance can often be enhanced by the use of skills: reusable workflows, code, and prompts that provide task-related information or guide the behaviour of the model. Skills, being textual in nature, present themselves as another editable surface to be optimized; current methods have improved on handcrafting and one-shot generation by treating skill development as an iterative process, using score-driven search to tweak and improve performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficacy of the agents themselves as optimizers: across five benchmarks, a coding agent without guidance substantially improves every target and outperforms published skill-optimization methods. More broadly, this shows the capability of agents to do such work and to refine their own behaviour to provide task-specific context, as long as they are given a metric to measure against.
papers.summary: Agent skills (reusable workflows, code, and prompts that guide a model on a task) are usually handcrafted or tuned by score-driven search methods. `AGL-SKILL` instead hands the optimization to a coding agent itself, giving it a metric to measure against and no further guidance. Across five benchmarks, the authors report that the **unguided coding agent substantially improves every target and outperforms published skill-optimization methods**.

papers.title: Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.abstract: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. However, proposing a consistent macro causal model is difficult, because macro causal relations are almost never well-defined, since distinct micro-level interventions associated with the same apparent macro intervention can produce different effects. Our central insight is that causally consistent macro-level models can be obtained constructively: ill-defined macro interventions can be interpreted as missing variables on the macro level, and can be accounted for by introducing a complementary variable q that retains omitted causally relevant state. In the linear case, q has a unique form and we provide sufficient conditions for valid implementations to exist; in the nonlinear case, we provide an ODE-based algorithm for constructing implementations. We call this framework Constructive Causal Abstraction (CCA), and use CCA to formulate the difference between machine-learning model auditing and editing. With the Bias-in-Bios biographies dataset, we demonstrate that CCA allows practitioners to articulate assumptions when detecting the model's gender bias. Finally, CCA resolves a well-known paradox known as "interpretability illusion" which points to a mismatch between the subspace for editing and the one where the model implements a signal-to-output pathway.
papers.summary: Causal abstraction frameworks usually propose a high-level causal model and then check it against a low-level one, but consistent high-level models are hard to propose because different micro-level interventions behind the same macro intervention can have different effects. Constructive Causal Abstraction (`CCA`) builds consistent macro models directly by adding a complementary variable that retains the omitted causally relevant state, with a unique form in the linear case and an ODE-based construction algorithm in the nonlinear case. The framework is used to formalize the difference between auditing and editing a model, demonstrated on gender-bias detection with the `Bias-in-Bios` dataset, and the authors claim it **resolves the interpretability illusion, a mismatch between the subspace used for editing and the one the model actually uses**.

papers.title: A Generative AI Agent to Emulate Interactive Human-driven Vehicles for Automated Driving Testing in Urban Areas
papers.abstract: Realistic modeling of human-driven vehicle (HDV) interactions is essential for automated driving safety testing in urban areas. Existing methods struggle to reproduce realistic safety-critical interactions involving high collision risk for the following reasons: they often assume full observability, overlooking interactions arising from occlusion. Driving styles are mainly characterized by vehicle maneuvers, limiting the diversity of safety-critical interaction behaviors. Moreover, learning signals from safety-critical interactions can be diluted by non-critical driving behaviors. To address these issues, we propose a generative AI agent to emulate interactive HDVs. The agent incorporates field-of-view modeling to account for driver visibility under occlusion and characterizes the interaction process using five metrics spanning its initial, intermediate, and final stages. It automatically learns diverse interaction styles through a dynamic mixture-of-experts network. Through residual reinforcement learning, the agent further refines generated trajectories to match the real-world distributions of safety-critical interaction characteristics. Experiments on the INTERACTION dataset show that our method reduces Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) by 39.9\%--87.1\% across five interaction characteristics compared with a state-of-the-art baseline. Our method achieves greater improvements of up to 87.1\% in final-stage interaction metrics, suggesting that it can reduce error accumulation in long-horizon trajectory generation. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component, particularly highlighting the importance of residual refinement. Generalization experiments show that our method approaches the performance of full training on unseen intersections with only one epoch of fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Safety testing of automated driving needs realistic simulated human-driven vehicles (HDVs), but existing models assume full observability and dilute rare safety-critical interactions among ordinary driving. The proposed generative agent models driver field of view under occlusion, describes interactions with five metrics across their initial, intermediate, and final stages, learns interaction styles with a dynamic mixture-of-experts network, and refines trajectories through residual reinforcement learning. On the `INTERACTION` dataset it **reduces Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) by 39.9% to 87.1% across five interaction characteristics** against a state-of-the-art baseline, and approaches full-training performance on unseen intersections after one epoch of fine-tuning.

papers.title: Learning Compact State Abstractions for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.
papers.summary: LLM agents typically treat their entire interaction history as state, carrying forward observations and actions that may no longer matter. Here agent state is defined as a compact abstraction of history that preserves the task performance of a fixed reference agent, represented as a deterministic recursive program and found with an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. On `ALFWorld` and `ScienceWorld`, the learned abstractions keep near-reference task success while **reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%** respectively, and the resulting programs can be read directly to see what is retained, updated, and discarded.

papers.title: TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework for Brainprint Authentication
papers.abstract: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) based brainprint authentication relies on privacy-sensitive data, and existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes assume a trusted client. The authors show that a compromised client with plaintext query features and continuous scores can exactly recover a registered template in finitely many interactions. `TopoCryptoEEG` counters this by encrypting preprocessed EEG at the client and running feature extraction, matching, and scoring on ciphertexts under homomorphic encryption, using depth-limited encodings and packing schemes. On `HGD` and `BCICIV-2a`, homomorphic computation takes 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs, an **average speedup of over 18x against the `EER` baseline**.

papers.title: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib
papers.abstract: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has.
