We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.
papers.summary: As AI systems generate proofs faster than mathematicians can read them, it becomes necessary to tell whether two proofs of the same theorem contain different ideas. The authors define 19 dissimilarity measures in six families (syntactic, structural, dependency and resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) plus 10 desirable properties, and test them on five machine-checked proofs of the infinitude of primes in a Curry-Howard kernel and on 19 proofs of three theorems in `Lean 4`/`Mathlib`. **Dependency-closure measures track intuitive proof distance best**, while raw syntax cannot separate a rewrite from a new argument and semantic measures invert the intuitive ordering. They recommend reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile and release code and data.

papers.title: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings
papers.abstract:
Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it.
  We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost.
  We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.
papers.summary: Safe Rust interfaces that wrap unsafe code, such as C or C++ libraries, can let purely safe programs trigger undefined behavior if they encode the underlying rules too weakly. After defining a taxonomy of such defects, the authors measure how well LLM agents audit a real crate using `Claude Opus 5.5` and `DeepSeek V4.1 Flash`: findings are almost always real, but agents rarely confirm with a sanitizer and stop early, and the open model matches the closed one at a quarter of the cost. Their system `Crustify` then audited 16 widely used crates, including bindings to OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, libcurl, and V8, and found **225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts** at a median cost under $50 per audit. It found 15 more issues in the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, and maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 reported findings.

papers.title: Compressible Representations: Functional Spines in Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.
papers.summary: How much of a deep network's high-dimensional representation actually drives its behavior? Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over hidden representations, the authors rank directions at each layer by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, **a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance**, often with far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives, and the compressed representation is more robust to adversarial attacks crafted on the full network. The same decomposition separates shape-sensitive from texture-sensitive directions, improves gradient-projection continual learning, and shows higher inter-model alignment in task-sensitive directions at later layers.

papers.title: Exploring Multi-Player Social Games as Verifiable Training Grounds for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The training of socially intelligent language models often relies on large language model (LLM) judges, which are expensive, noisy, and vulnerable to reward hacking. Multi-player social games offer a natural alternative: they require open-ended communication to coordinate with teammates and infer hidden roles, while their rules provide an objective outcome which can serve as a verifiable reward for training. Using three social games, we explore how much social intelligence Qwen3 models can acquire through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Results show that against a much stronger Gemma-3-27B model, SFT and RLVR raise the win rate of Qwen3-4B from 33% to 81% on the three trained games, and from 39% to 54% on three additional held-out games. In contrast, in-context strategies such as prompting improve the win rate of Qwen3-4B by only about 6 pp across the same games we train and evaluate on. Furthermore, we show that the gains from SFT and RLVR hold across the model sizes 1.7B, 4B, and 32B. Qualitative analyses of agent behavior show signs of stronger social intelligence; for example, trained agents tend to share information more openly, check each other's claims against public evidence, and coordinate their votes. More broadly, our results demonstrate that training LLMs on verifiable outcomes in social games can cultivate generalizable social behaviors, which offers a scalable path for building socially intelligent agents.
papers.summary: Training socially capable language models usually depends on LLM judges, which are costly, noisy, and open to reward hacking. Multi-player social games are used here instead, since their rules give an objective outcome usable as a reward, and `Qwen3` models are trained on three games with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Against a stronger `Gemma-3-27B` opponent, the **win rate of `Qwen3-4B` rises from 33% to 81% on the trained games** and from 39% to 54% on three held-out games, while prompting strategies add only about 6 percentage points. The gains hold at 1.7B, 4B, and 32B model sizes, and trained agents share information more openly, check claims against public evidence, and coordinate votes.

papers.title: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures
papers.abstract: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.
papers.summary: Generating the hardest final problems of the Chinese Gaokao mathematics exam requires controlling the underlying mathematical idea and solution path, not just the listed skills. `GaokaoMathGen` extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and synthesizes new ones constrained by skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step, then estimates realized difficulty from logical-quality filtering, solver effort, and structural signals. Of 609 scored candidates, 78.0% pass the logical-quality filter, and in a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates **all were judged to reach finale or penultimate difficulty**, with one showing a severe logical issue.

papers.title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
papers.abstract: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.
papers.summary: Interpretation methods for AI models are often validated through isolated examples rather than graded by how much evidence supports their trustworthiness. `TRUST` is a tiered evaluation framework built on the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations, with five tiers running from task-aligned foundations through epistemic grounding, semantic understanding, scope transferability, and targeted prospective validation. In a case study, the **iterative Random Forest (`iRF`) family is taken through all tiers, while other LLM interpretation methods are shown to struggle at specific tiers**. The authors close with initial thoughts on extending the framework to autonomous agentic workflows.

papers.title: POISE: Curvature-Aware Critic Regularization for Smooth Actor-Critic Control
papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods achieve high returns in robotic control, yet trained actors exhibit high-frequency action oscillations. Most smoothness methods constrain the actor, whereas PAVE regularizes the critic by separately penalizing action-gradient variation and encouraging negative action curvature. The same gradient change, however, moves the critic's preferred action farther where the critic is flat, and separate penalties do not measure this motion. We characterize this motion through the greedy shift, which approximates greedy-action displacement across state transitions to first order under local concavity. Since displacement alone does not reflect its critic-value consequences, the analysis further shows that the shift's curvature-weighted energy approximates the value lost by retaining the previous greedy action to second order. Based on this relationship, POISE regularizes the curvature-weighted energy along temporal and spatial state displacements. It employs a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling while leaving the actor unchanged. On six continuous control tasks with TD3, POISE reduces the smoothness score on every task by $5.9\times$ on average ($4.5\times$ geometric mean), compared with $2.2\times$ ($1.9\times$) for the strongest baseline, and achieves the lowest score on five tasks. Paired return intervals include zero on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.
papers.summary: Actor-critic policies for robotic control reach high returns but tend to produce high-frequency action oscillations. `POISE` regularizes the critic rather than the actor, penalizing a curvature-weighted energy of the greedy shift, which is the displacement of the critic's preferred action across state transitions and which the authors show approximates the value lost by keeping the previous greedy action. On six continuous control tasks with `TD3`, it **reduces the smoothness score by 5.9x on average, versus 2.2x for the strongest baseline**, with the lowest score on five tasks. Returns are statistically unchanged on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.

papers.title: Gaze World Model
papers.abstract: Where a person looks indicates their focus of attention, and how their gaze shifts between targets reveals how that attention responds to a changing scene. Existing gaze target estimation methods largely operate frame by frame and do not model these shifts. Gaze shifts are often driven by dynamic changes in the scene, which is the kind of information world models are designed to encode. This relationship is subtle, however, since an event far across the frame may produce only a slight movement of the person's head or eyes. We therefore introduce the Gaze World Model (GWM), which co-trains latent scene prediction with person-conditioned gaze supervision on a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; in our ablations, the latent prediction objective improves both shift detection and gaze localization. Given a video clip and the person's head box, GWM estimates gaze locations and detects gaze shifts in the observed clip, and forecasts future gaze and shifts from predicted scene features. To train and evaluate these tasks, we augment VideoAttentionTarget and ChildPlay with event-level gaze-shift annotations. GWM achieves state-of-the-art shift detection on these benchmarks, about 10 points higher in four-class AP than the strongest baseline, while remaining comparable to the strongest image-based models in gaze target estimation, and outperforms the compared baselines on future gaze localization and shift forecasting.
papers.summary: Gaze target estimation methods mostly work frame by frame and do not model how a person's gaze shifts in response to changes in the scene. The Gaze World Model (`GWM`) co-trains latent scene prediction with person-conditioned gaze supervision on a frozen `V-JEPA 2.1` encoder, estimating gaze locations and shifts in an observed clip and forecasting future ones from predicted scene features. Using new event-level gaze-shift annotations added to `VideoAttentionTarget` and `ChildPlay`, it scores **about 10 points higher in four-class AP for shift detection than the strongest baseline**, while staying comparable to the strongest image-based models on gaze target estimation.

papers.title: Spec-Test Coverage Gap: Detecting Overspecified Tests in SWE-Bench-Style Benchmarks
papers.abstract: SWE-bench-style benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Verified (Verified) and SWE-bench Pro (Pro), evaluate coding agents with tests taken from the change that originally fixed each issue. However, these tests can enforce details the task never states, causing correct alternative fixes to fail. Such overspecified tests have so far been found mainly through expensive expert review. To address this, we define the Spec-Test Coverage Gap (STCG), a 1-4 scale measuring overspecification, and score it with two LLM judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, which are given the specification and the test patch. A task is flagged as overspecified when both judges score it 3 or higher. Our study has three parts. First, we validate the judges on 206 tasks that earlier human audits and agent results label as overspecified or fine. Second, we apply STCG to all 500 Verified and 731 public Pro tasks and compare the flags with the results of the top 30 Verified submissions. Third, we verify the flags by asking Claude Opus 5.5 to loosen the overspecified requirements of flagged tasks, and regrade 2,186 failed patches from those submissions. Our main findings are: (1) Overspecified tests are detectable: on the validation tasks, the judges correctly flag 89% of the tasks that human audits identify as overspecified and wrongly flag only 4% of the tasks known to be fine. (2) Overspecified tests are common: applied to whole benchmarks, the judges flag 23% of Verified and 35% of Pro tasks. (3) Flagged tasks are much harder for agents: the top 30 Verified submissions resolve only 31% of the flagged tasks on average, against 88% of the other tasks. (4) Overspecified tests change the leaderboard: relaxing the tests lets 61% of the 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass. Counting these patches as resolved would add 33 to 60 tasks to each top-30 submission, raising resolve rates by up to 12 percentage points.
papers.summary: Benchmarks in the style of `SWE-bench` grade coding agents with tests from the original fix, which can enforce details the task never states and so reject correct alternative patches. The Spec-Test Coverage Gap (STCG) is a 1-4 overspecification score assigned by two LLM judges, `Claude Opus 5.5` and `GPT-6.1 Sol`, which on 206 validation tasks flag 89% of the tasks human audits call overspecified and wrongly flag 4% of known-good ones. Applied to whole benchmarks, the judges flag **23% of `SWE-bench Verified` and 35% of `SWE-bench Pro` tasks**, and top-30 submissions resolve only 31% of flagged tasks against 88% of the rest. Relaxing the tests lets 61% of 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass, which would raise resolve rates by up to 12 percentage points.

papers.title: Faithful Persona Steering under Incongruity via Dual-Stream Refinement
papers.abstract: Standard LLM personalization typically frames identity as a static retrieval task, overlooking the inherent incongruity of human personas, where stable traits coexist with atypical, context-specific stances. Existing methods struggle to reconcile these dimensions: prompting succumbs to context drift over long sequences, while fine-tuning often suppresses idiosyncratic "quirks" in favor of generic distributional patterns. To bridge this gap, we present QuirkyMind, a framework that disentangles identity definition from its expression. First, Traits Anchoring constructs a dual-stream latent state, fusing a sentence-level summary for semantic stability with a token-level sequence for generative control. This state is stabilized via In-Context Narrative Refinement using an alternating objective: a discriminative InfoNCE loss anchors the persona in representation space to prevent drift, while a generative cross-entropy loss ensures faithful verbalization. Finally, Persona Steered Generalization transfers the refined state to downstream tasks via parameter-efficient adapters. Empirical evaluations on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference demonstrate that QuirkyMind mitigates drift, consolidating persona knowledge without erasing authentic incongruities.
papers.summary: LLM personalization tends to treat a persona as static, although real people combine stable traits with atypical, context-specific stances; prompting drifts over long contexts and fine-tuning smooths away such quirks. `QuirkyMind` builds a dual-stream latent state from a sentence-level summary and a token-level sequence, refines it by alternating a contrastive `InfoNCE` loss with a generative cross-entropy loss, and transfers it to downstream tasks through parameter-efficient adapters. On persona-steered question answering and narrative inference, the authors report that it **mitigates persona drift without erasing the persona's incongruities**.

papers.title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.
papers.summary: Joint-embedding predictive pretraining on chest computed tomography suffers from what the authors call the context shortcut: a masked finding such as a small nodule is not predictable from surrounding anatomy, so the loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. `JECT` uses the radiology report both as a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, as a target the encoder must predict from the unmasked scan, with a hierarchical 3D encoder that predicts at every stage. Ablations show the text target improves classification and localization while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, it **reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models** in classification, retrieval, and nodule malignancy.

papers.title: Two-Stage Post-Training for Flow-Based Embodied Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretraining provides embodied models with general capabilities, but reliable task execution still requires post training. In multitask settings, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) faces distribution mismatch between training and deployment, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) is limited by sparse rewards and uneven learning progress across tasks. Multi-teacher on policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates expert capabilities through dense supervision on the model's own trajectories, but achieving performance beyond the teachers remains challenging. We propose a two-stage post training framework for flow-based embodied models, constructing distillation objectives from the velocity regression formulation of conditional flow matching. Stage 1 efficiently consolidates expert capabilities through MOPD. Stage 2 combines RL with teacher distillation that weights velocity errors according to the sampling noise, where distillation is restricted to failed trajectories to supplement sparse rewards with dense guidance without directly constraining successful behaviors. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that the framework outperforms joint SFT and exceeds the corresponding teachers' aggregate success rates. Sample efficiency comparisons show higher success rates than direct RL with fewer environment interactions.
papers.summary: Post-training of pretrained embodied (robot) models in multitask settings is hampered by train-deployment mismatch under supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and by sparse rewards and uneven task progress under reinforcement learning (RL). The proposed two-stage framework for flow-based models first consolidates expert skills with multi-teacher on-policy distillation (`MOPD`), then combines RL with noise-weighted velocity distillation applied only to failed trajectories, so successful behaviors are not constrained. Across multiple models and benchmarks, it **outperforms joint SFT and exceeds the teachers' aggregate success rates**, while reaching higher success than direct RL with fewer environment interactions.

papers.title: Modeling Event-Conditioned Emotional Expression Response with LLM Agents in a Synthetic Social Simulation
papers.abstract: Emotions are central drivers of human behavior, yet most behavioral models fail to capture their role in shaping perception, decision-making, and collective action. Application areas such as emergency response and public health are especially constrained by the lack of emotion-aware modeling. While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into agent-based models (ABMs), little work has examined how to endow LLM agents with emotional reasoning or validated their ability to reproduce empirically observed emotional patterns. This study addresses this gap by introducing a hierarchical prompting framework that conditions LLM agents with demographic, psychological, and contextual cues to generate event-conditioned emotional responses to real-world events. We validate the resulting event-conditioned emotional responses against large-scale social media reaction data derived from the Social Science One Facebook URL Shares Dataset, complemented by demographic and personality benchmarks. Our simulation results reproduce both polarized and consensus-driven emotional patterns with significant fidelity, supporting the application of LLM agents for emotion-aware modeling in behavioral simulations. We also find, however, that systematic gaps in emotional expression of LLM agents and human populations exist, such as the underexpression of anger relative to human baselines. As such, these findings highlight the need for continued calibration if LLM agents are to serve as proxies for human populations in behavioral modeling. By quantifying their divergence from human populations in terms of emotional expression, we hope that our methods can aid in this effort.
papers.summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) built on large language models (LLMs) rarely model emotion or check whether agents reproduce observed human emotional patterns. A hierarchical prompting framework conditions LLM agents on demographic, psychological, and contextual cues to generate emotional reactions to real-world events, validated against reaction data from the `Social Science One Facebook URL Shares Dataset`. The simulations reproduce both polarized and consensus-driven emotional patterns, but show systematic gaps such as **underexpression of anger relative to human baselines**, indicating that further calibration is needed before agents can stand in for human populations.

papers.title: Explainable Deep Learning for Malaria Parasite Detection and Species Differentiation in Thick Blood Smear Images: A Pilot Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Species-level differentiation of Plasmodium falciparum (PF) and P. vivax (PV) determines treatment, yet deep learning detectors rarely test whether their explanations are reliable. In this pilot feasibility study of TRACE-Mal, a research prototype combining YOLOv8n-seg detection and a six-model soft-voting ensemble, we examined whether agreement among three post-hoc explanation methods (Grad-CAM, LIME and SHAP) is associated with the correctness of species calls. the study analysed 2,847 parasite crops from 250 thick smears within publicly available Lacuna Malaria Datasets. The model achieved an mAP50 score of 0.79 and the ensemble had a macro F1 of 0.84 (PF recall 0.86; PV recall 0.74). Unadjusted analyses of crops revealed that predictions explained by greather than or equal to 2 methods were more accurate (86.2% vs 78.9%; difference 7.3 percentage points; 95% CI 3.5-11.1) compared to those explained by less than 2 methods. As the number of explanatory methods increased so did prediction accuracy (from 73.8% for no methods to 89.5% for all three methods). When performing a cluster-bootstrap analysis of 60 test images, again there was a positive consensus difference (7.3 percentage points; 95% CI 2.9-11.8). Further, incorporating explanation information into a model's prediction confidence enhanced its error differentiation ability (AUROC 0.024; 95% CI 0.008-0.041). PF and PV parasite crops have distinct morphologies. Although based on one unvalidated public data source, these findings demonstrate proof-of-concept and should not be taken as a measure of diagnostic capability.
papers.summary: Deep learning malaria detectors rarely test whether their explanations are reliable, even though distinguishing Plasmodium falciparum from P. vivax determines treatment. This pilot study of `TRACE-Mal`, a prototype combining `YOLOv8n-seg` detection with a six-model soft-voting ensemble, asks whether agreement among `Grad-CAM`, `LIME`, and `SHAP` explanations tracks the correctness of species calls on 2,847 parasite crops from the `Lacuna Malaria Datasets`. Predictions supported by at least two explanation methods were **7.3 percentage points more accurate (86.2% vs 78.9%)**, and adding explanation information to prediction confidence improved error discrimination by 0.024 AUROC. The authors frame the results as proof-of-concept from a single unvalidated public data source, not as a measure of diagnostic capability.

papers.title: Start Where the Data Are: Statistical Priors for One-Step Generation on Manifolds
papers.abstract: Fast generation on manifolds is important for scientific applications such as protein design, yet existing one-step generators often produce spurious samples in low-density gaps between data modes. Our analysis highlights the mismatch between uniform noise and concentrated data, motivating a statistical prior that captures the data's coarse structure. We first estimate this prior by fitting mixtures of tangent-space Gaussians through geometry-aware moment matching. However, independent noise-data pairing can still connect different modes and weaken the benefit of the fitted prior. We therefore introduce posterior coupling, which samples a latent component conditioned on each data point and draws its paired noise from that component. To extend this approach to long torsion-angle chains, where full-covariance mixtures become costly, we use a hidden Markov prior to model sequential dependence with shared parameters. The resulting framework plugs into existing one-step training pipelines while retaining the generator architecture, training objective, and single network evaluation at inference. Experiments on spheres, tori, and SO(3) demonstrate substantial improvements across multiple generators, reducing distributional error by up to $125\times$ and the protein Ramachandran outlier rate from 12.1% to 0.55%.
papers.summary: One-step generators on manifolds, used in applications such as protein design, often produce spurious samples in low-density gaps between data modes because uniform noise is mismatched with concentrated data. The authors fit a statistical prior from mixtures of tangent-space Gaussians, add a posterior coupling that pairs each data point with noise drawn from its own latent component, and use a hidden Markov prior for long torsion-angle chains. The approach plugs into existing one-step training pipelines without changing the architecture, objective, or single-evaluation inference. On spheres, tori, and SO(3), it reduces distributional error by up to 125x and **cuts the protein Ramachandran outlier rate from 12.1% to 0.55%**.

papers.title: No Fixed Configuration Is Best: Context- and Cost-Aware Tuning of LLM Pipelines, with an Application to Schema Matching and Mapping
papers.abstract: The numeric settings of a multi-stage LLM pipeline (a compound AI system) are the usual target of tuning. We tuned all of them for an LLM pipeline for schema matching and mapping, with accuracy and cost as joint objectives, and we show what this buys, what it cannot buy, and where the remaining accuracy is. First, tuning buys cost and a little accuracy. On 35 tasks, with whole groups of tasks held out from tuning, one tuned configuration gains 2.9 points of top-1 accuracy (HR@1) over the default at 18% more cost, and another keeps the accuracy of the default at 32% lower cost. Second, the accuracy depends on a choice that numeric tuning cannot reach. Restricting the search for each source column to one assigned target table changes HR@1 by +30 points on a MIMIC-III to OMOP task and by -52 points on a task built from database views, more than numeric tuning gains on nine of ten test tasks. Neither setting is right for all tasks: on the larger set of 41 tasks used for the remaining results, mean HR@1 is 75.7% with the restriction (the default) and 83.1% without it. Third, choosing the setting per task is not enough either: even an oracle that picks the better setting for each task reaches only 87.8% on the 41 tasks, because the better setting differs between the columns of one task. The pipeline therefore runs both settings, and an LLM judge chooses among their candidate answers on the 26% of columns on which they disagree. This reaches 91.5% HR@1 on the 41 tasks, at 5.9 times the cost of the default, about one cent per column.
papers.summary: Tuning the numeric settings of a multi-stage large language model (LLM) pipeline for schema matching and mapping, with accuracy and cost as joint objectives, yields only modest returns: one tuned configuration gains 2.9 points of top-1 accuracy at 18% more cost, and another matches the default at 32% lower cost. A structural choice that numeric tuning cannot reach, restricting each source column's search to one assigned target table, shifts accuracy by +30 points on one task and -52 on another, and even a per-task oracle over that choice reaches only 87.8% on 41 tasks. Running both settings and letting an LLM judge pick among candidates on the 26% of columns where they disagree reaches **91.5% top-1 accuracy at 5.9 times the default cost**, about one cent per column.

papers.title: CALVIN-MAX: When Does a Mid-Execution Change Hurt a Robot Policy?
papers.abstract: Robots must often keep working after the world changes, as when a block moves or the camera shifts while the robot still acts on what it saw before. Recent work showed that one change during a task lowers success for every policy tested, but did not separate the effect of its timing from the cost of the changed world, or measure what it costs afterwards. We introduce CALVIN-MAX, a benchmark of 7,828 cases on CALVIN's five-instruction chains, each with one change to the objects, the camera, the robot, or the instruction. Each case compares three runs that are identical until the affected instruction begins: one without the change, one with it in place from that moment, and one in which it arrives while the robot is moving. The second run against the first gives the cost of the changed world, and the third against the second the effect of meeting it mid-motion. On 1,526 held-out cases per policy, with hypotheses fixed in advance, each of ten released policies loses 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction over the eight core changes. Whether timing matters depends on the change: one that alters what the robot sees costs 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start, whereas a change to the scene itself or to the robot shows no detectable effect. Rewinding the robot to the start of the instruction removes the benefit for every policy; the stricter test we fixed in advance, that the rewound run then matches the second run, passes for three. The cost also outlasts the affected instruction: the change stays in place, and a policy that still completes that instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.
papers.summary: `CALVIN-MAX` is a benchmark of 7,828 cases built on `CALVIN` five-instruction chains that separates the cost of a changed world from the effect of meeting that change mid-motion, by comparing three runs: no change, change in place from the start of an instruction, and change arriving while the robot moves. On 1,526 held-out cases per policy with pre-registered hypotheses, **each of ten released policies loses 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction**. Timing matters only for changes to what the robot sees, which cost 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start, while scene and robot changes show no detectable timing effect. The cost also persists: a policy that still completes the affected instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning Crosses Modalities
papers.abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.
papers.summary: Subliminal learning, where a trait such as an animal preference is passed from one language model to another through training on seemingly meaningless number sequences, is shown to carry over across modalities. A diffusion model that uses the trained student as its text encoder **generates the student's animal more often than with the original encoder**, though color and style traits do not transfer. Much of the shift is explained by a constant component of the student's change, which affects concepts that depend on the whole prompt but not ones encoded in a single token. The authors also introduce `weight lens`, a method that identifies the subliminal trait of nearly every student from the weights of a single trained model.

papers.title: RepoEviAgent: Scalable Synthesis of Evidence-Grounded Repository-Level Question Answering Tasks
papers.abstract: Real-world software engineering (SWE) tasks require agents to understand repository structures, cross-module dependencies, and runtime behaviors, posing significant challenges for constructing high-quality training and evaluation data. To address this, we propose RepoEviAgent, a scalable SWE data construction framework that integrates quality-aware data curation and role-specialized multi-agent task synthesis. Starting from 8,477 open-source repositories and approximately 2.48 million pull request records, we employ semantic alignment, complexity constraints, and multidimensional quality assessment to identify valuable SWE data. We further develop a sandbox-based multi-agent framework that integrates automated environment construction, execution validation, repository exploration, and evidence-grounded Q&A synthesis. Based on this framework, we construct RepoEviQA, a benchmark for Repository-Level Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, comprising 334 tasks across five programming languages and diverse SWE categories, with rigorous rubric-based evaluation. We evaluate five frontier coding models on RepoEviQA, revealing substantial performance differences across task categories and programming languages.
papers.summary: Building training and evaluation data for software engineering (SWE) agents is difficult because tasks depend on repository structure, cross-module dependencies, and runtime behavior. `RepoEviAgent` filters 8,477 open-source repositories and about 2.48 million pull request records by semantic alignment, complexity, and quality, then uses a sandboxed multi-agent pipeline for environment construction, execution validation, repository exploration, and evidence-grounded question-answer synthesis. The resulting benchmark, `RepoEviQA`, contains **334 repository-level question answering tasks across five programming languages** with rubric-based evaluation. Five frontier coding models evaluated on it show substantial performance differences across task categories and languages.

papers.title: EEG-Jev: A Unified Single-Pass Decision Model for EEG
papers.abstract: EEG analysis spans choosing alternatives, judging statements, and rating ordered attributes, requiring calibratable probabilities with explicit meaning. We present EEG-Jev, a unified single-pass decision model for EEG. Given an EEG window, a question and an answer specification, one forward pass returns a typed readout: CHOICE gives a candidate distribution, NOUL a proposition probability, and SCORE an ordered-level distribution and expectation. One checkpoint is trained jointly and evaluated once on held-out splits of 35 public sources. Core raw outputs reach 54.08% balanced accuracy on Stieger2021 motor imagery, 70.45% on Sleep-EDF-SC sleep staging, 72.11% per window at threshold 0.5 on CHB-MIT seizure detection with 0.825 AUROC, and 1.700 MAE on 0-10 ds005292 pain ratings. Prior correction and temperature scaling lower negative log-likelihood from 0.766 to 0.606 on Sleep-EDF-SC and 0.166 to 0.019 on CHB-MIT, while direct readout cuts batch-1 latency from 122.43 to 63.11 ms (1.94-fold) against a matched-backbone generative comparator. Interactive demonstration and aggregate results: https://neuroimglab.github.io/EEG-Jev/.
papers.summary: `EEG-Jev` is a single model for electroencephalography (EEG) analysis that takes an EEG window, a question, and an answer specification, and returns a typed probabilistic readout in one forward pass: a distribution over candidates, a proposition probability, or an ordered-level distribution with its expectation. One jointly trained checkpoint is evaluated on held-out splits of 35 public sources, reaching 54.08% balanced accuracy on `Stieger2021` motor imagery, 70.45% on `Sleep-EDF-SC` sleep staging, and 0.825 AUROC on `CHB-MIT` seizure detection. Prior correction and temperature scaling lower negative log-likelihood on the sleep and seizure tasks, and the direct readout **cuts batch-1 latency from 122.43 to 63.11 ms** against a generative comparator with a matched backbone.

papers.title: Multi Agent Reinforcement Learning enhanced Federated Learning for Predicting Remaining Useful Lifetime
papers.abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction is central to Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). The growth of industrial IoT has unlocked large multivariate sensor streams and enabled deep models - especially Transformers - for long-horizon sequence learning. However, transformers are parameter-heavy and data-hungry, while operational datasets are often siloed and privacy-sensitive. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this by training across clients without raw data sharing, but in practice many clients connect over lossy wireless links where UDP is preferred for low latency, making model exchange vulnerable to packet drops. We present a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework that adapts FL to lossy channels by selecting per-client layer subsets to transmit and capping retransmissions. This framework is trained with QMIX value-function factorization for scalability. We instantiate the approach with a Graph Convolution Position-Aware Transformer (GCPATr) for RUL forecasting. On the CMAPSS dataset, our MARL-enhanced FL (RL-FL) consistently improves mean square error over standard FL, with the largest gains at high packet loss (e.g., up to 18% improvement on FD003 at 50% loss). These results show that MARL is an effective countermeasure to wireless degradation in FL-based RUL prediction.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction lets industrial clients train without sharing raw sensor data, but model exchange over lossy wireless links using UDP is vulnerable to packet drops. A cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework, trained with `QMIX` value-function factorization, selects which layer subsets each client transmits and caps retransmissions, and is instantiated with a Graph Convolution Position-Aware Transformer (`GCPATr`) forecaster. On the `CMAPSS` dataset it consistently improves mean square error over standard FL, with the largest gains at high packet loss, **up to 18% on `FD003` at 50% loss**.

papers.title: Rethinking Video Agents: When and Why Video Harnesses Work
papers.abstract: Video understanding depends not only on how models reason about visual evidence, but also on which evidence they observe. Fixed observation policies determine this evidence in advance; agentic harnesses allow models to seek further observations as their understanding develops. This shift creates an opportunity to realize capabilities that fixed inputs leave untapped, yet the ability to request observations does not ensure their effective use. We investigate when and why video harnesses improve understanding, examining how task demands and models' capacity for interaction jointly shape their benefits. Using Video-Relook as an experimental framework, we let models adapt their temporal and spatial observations from a common default configuration, and analyze performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks. Adaptive observation yields substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2. Even under the same observation interface, gains differ substantially across models; interaction traces reveal corresponding differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision. The benefits also vary across tasks for the same model, ranging from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions. Together, these findings support an account in which harness effectiveness depends on the alignment between opportunities for informative observation and the model's ability to turn interaction into reliable revisions. They motivate video harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning, matching observational autonomy to task demands and model capabilities.
papers.summary: Agentic video harnesses let a model request further observations as its understanding develops instead of receiving a fixed set of frames, but the ability to ask for more evidence does not guarantee it is used well. Using `Video-Relook` as an experimental framework, the authors let models adapt temporal and spatial observations from a common default and analyze performance and interaction traces across models and tasks. Adaptive observation gives substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding and extends to `Video-MME-v2`, yet **gains vary widely across models and tasks, from large improvements to regressions**. The traces link these differences to how models seek evidence and how reliably they revise answers, supporting the view that a harness helps when informative observation opportunities align with the model's ability to turn interaction into correct revisions.

papers.title: HEAR, SEE, SPIKE ONCE: Highly Efficient NeuroAI Temporal Neural Networks for Low-Precision Multimodal Audio-Visual Classification and Online Learning
papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.
papers.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for audio-visual classification typically rely on deep encoders, full-precision weights, and backpropagation through time, without treating hardware efficiency as a primary goal. `NeuTNN-AV` instead builds on the NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (`NeuTNN`), in which neurons have multiple dendritic segments, each input spikes at most once, weights are 4-bit integers learned by a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule, and inference uses only comparisons and additions. It reaches **78.6% on `CREMA-D` with 2.34M synapses, against 77.14% for the 31M-parameter `MISNet-XL`**, and 98.82% on `UrbanSound8K-AV` with 1.38M synapses. Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower, and the model learns `CREMA-D` in a single pass at 73.8% accuracy.

papers.title: Cheap Memory Costs Future Compute: Co-Designing Persistent KV and GPU Execution for Efficient Streaming Video Diffusion
papers.abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
papers.summary: Block-causal video diffusion conditions each new block on a persistent key-value (KV) cache, and once denoising is made cheap, the extra noise-free pass that writes clean KV into the cache dominates runtime, while reusing stale KV corrupts later blocks and inflates their denoising steps. `SAMR` (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction) is a training-free method for frozen causal video diffusion transformers that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest by fusing motion-aligned historical KV with debiased in-flight KV, reserving true refreshes for tokens flagged by an error proxy. On 48-second `LongLive-1.3B` videos, it **reduces transformer latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates**, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB. The reconstruction also transfers zero-shot to frozen `Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B`.

papers.title: Loupe: Reinforcing Knowledge-Intensive Video Generation Agents
papers.abstract: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.
papers.summary: Prompts for knowledge-intensive video generation often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships needed for accurate output. `Loupe` is an agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to build evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images, trained with Rubric-Based Credit (`RBC`), which scores intermediate search and planning steps against prompt-specific requirements so that no videos need to be rendered during reinforcement learning. On the new 150-prompt `Search-VBench`, it improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, **raising the overall score of `MiniMax-H3` from 32.80 to 70.67**. Full `RBC` training beats standard supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level `GRPO` by 5.27 points.

papers.title: A General Framework for E-process Stopping Rules in Best-Arm Identification
papers.abstract: We propose an e-process stopping rule in the best-arm identification problem. The e-process stopping rule is different from the Chernoff stopping rule by its hypothesis structure on the stopping decision. The major benefit of an e-process stopping rule is the flexibility in stopping rule design and in fact, it recovers previously suggested Chernoff stopping rule on several bandit problems. Moreover, we analyze the asymptotic optimality of the $\delta$-PAC algorithm with the decomposition of e-processes. The decomposition separates optimality conditions into three parts; the sampling policy allocation convergence, the efficiency of e-process design, and the bandit problem's inherent stochastic behavior. Subsequently, we prove a sufficient condition for asymptotic optimality in bandit algorithms. For the application of an e-process stopping rule, we derived an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the generalized linear bandit problem.
papers.summary: Best-arm identification in bandits needs a rule for deciding when enough evidence has been gathered to stop sampling. The authors propose a stopping rule based on e-processes, which differs from the Chernoff stopping rule in its hypothesis structure and recovers previously proposed Chernoff rules on several bandit problems. A decomposition of the e-process splits asymptotic optimality into sampling allocation convergence, efficiency of the e-process design, and the problem's inherent stochastic behavior, yielding a sufficient condition for optimality. As an application, they derive **an asymptotically optimal algorithm for generalized linear bandits**.

papers.title: MIFLOW: Dynamic Recent-Behavior Priors for Reference-Calibrated Online Flow-Policy Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Flow-based policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. In online actor-critic learning, off-policy value estimates can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, where expressive policies may shift probability mass toward critic-favored actions. We propose MIFLOW, which calibrates online flow-policy learning with a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions. Inspired by canalization as a qualitative analogy for path-dependent stabilization, we use the prior as a moving density reference for value-guided policy improvement. MIFLOW uses the approximate recent-action log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets. This correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, MIFLOW achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks. In a Walker2d-v4 case study, MIFLOW shows a lower proportion of actions assigned low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. Prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and prior-defined diagnostics. These results support dynamic recent-behavior priors for reference calibration in the evaluated settings. The diagnostics measure how sampled actions align with the learned reference. True action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured in these experiments.
papers.summary: In online actor-critic learning with expressive flow-based policies, unreliable value estimates in poorly covered action regions can pull probability mass toward actions the critic favors. `MIFLOW` fits a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior to recently executed actions and uses its approximate log-density as a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets, raising the cost of low-density actions without excluding them. Across six `MuJoCo` tasks and five seeds, it achieves **competitive mean return curves and higher late-training returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks**. The authors note that their diagnostics measure only alignment with the learned reference, leaving true action support and critic extrapolation error unmeasured.

papers.title: OrangeTree: A Linear and Tree-based Time Series Forecasting Model Supporting Multiple Input and Output Lengths
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) models suffer from a critical rigidity: the inability to handle Multiple Input and Output Lengths (MIOL) within a single architecture. Current workarounds, such as padding or autoregression, often incur computational redundancy or suffer from error accumulation. We propose OrangeTree, a linear and tree-based architecture that decouples model parameters from sequence lengths. It employs a Segment Tree Encoder and an Inverse Tree Decoder to translate multi-length input history into multi-length output predictions within a unified framework. Crucially, a Range Weighter and a Feature Fuser bridge these components, dynamically selecting and fusing relevant ranges into optimal contexts for forecasting. Experiments on six benchmarks confirm OrangeTree achieves the SOTA performance. In MIOL settings, it matches the accuracy of length-fixed models without substantial accuracy degradation or a substantial increase in inference latency typical of heuristic methods. Code is available at https://github.com/Tang-Yiqi/OrangeTree.
papers.summary: Time series forecasting models usually cannot handle Multiple Input and Output Lengths (MIOL) in one architecture, and workarounds such as padding or autoregression add redundant computation or accumulate errors. `OrangeTree` is a linear, tree-based model that decouples parameters from sequence length, using a Segment Tree Encoder and an Inverse Tree Decoder connected by a Range Weighter and a Feature Fuser that select and fuse relevant ranges. On six benchmarks the authors report state-of-the-art performance, and in MIOL settings it **matches the accuracy of fixed-length models without a substantial increase in inference latency**.

papers.title: TQ-HQNet: A Trainability-Aware and Qubit-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for Cross-Domain Learning on Heterogeneous Data
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks are a promising direction for noisy intermediate-scale quantum computing, but their practical effectiveness is often limited by poor trainability, rigid circuit design, and weak robustness across heterogeneous real-world tasks. This paper proposes TQ-HQNet, a Trainability-Aware and Qubit-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for cross-domain learning on heterogeneous data. The proposed framework combines three mechanisms: 1) adaptive latent compression to map domain-specific features into qubit-compatible representations, 2) trainability-aware search over compact variational circuit candidates, and 3) hybrid fusion of multiple shallow quantum experts to improve robustness without increasing qubit cost excessively. TQ-HQNet is evaluated on four public datasets spanning neurological screening, phishing detection, financial direction prediction, and DNA sequence classification. Across all domains, the proposed model consistently improves over a fixed hybrid quantum baseline, with balanced-accuracy gains of +0.280, +0.170, +0.071, and +0.060, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity studies confirm that gains arise from trainability-aware compact circuit selection and expert fusion, not circuit scaling. Although classical baselines outperform on some tasks, fixed-split results show consistent improvements over the fixed hybrid reference. These analyses support the practical role of compact selection and fusion, with repeated-split and hardware-aware studies left for future work.
papers.summary: Hybrid quantum neural networks for noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware are often limited by poor trainability, rigid circuit design, and weak robustness across heterogeneous tasks. `TQ-HQNet` combines adaptive latent compression into qubit-compatible representations, a trainability-aware search over compact variational circuits, and fusion of multiple shallow quantum experts. On four public datasets covering neurological screening, phishing detection, financial direction prediction, and DNA sequence classification, it **improves balanced accuracy over a fixed hybrid quantum baseline by +0.280, +0.170, +0.071, and +0.060**. Classical baselines still outperform it on some tasks, and repeated-split and hardware-aware studies are left for future work.

papers.title: Your VLM Knows What to Inspect: Semantic Probe-Guided Adaptive Focusing for GUI Grounding
papers.abstract: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models (VLMs): even when their coordinate predictions are incorrect, they can describe visual evidence worth inspecting. We introduce \textbf{SPARK}, \textit{\textbf{S}emantic \textbf{P}robe-guided \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{R}egion see\textbf{K}ing}, a training-free framework that turns this semantic guidance into targeted visual observations. Exploration probes describe relevant context and distinguishing target details, while verification probes identify evidence needed to assess emerging hypotheses. Their spatial attention guides view placement, contextual responses determine crop extent, and observation history encourages complementary inspection. The resulting predictions are combined through uncertainty-weighted voting. On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and UI-TARS, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Consistent gains across four additional benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse interfaces and grounding tasks. These results establish semantic probing as an effective mechanism for turning a frozen VLM's understanding of what to inspect into more accurate GUI grounding.
papers.summary: Grounding instructions to locations in graphical user interfaces (GUIs) requires resolving fine visual detail in context, and vision-language models (VLMs) can often describe what evidence is worth inspecting even when their coordinate predictions are wrong. `SPARK` is a training-free framework that uses exploration and verification probes to turn this semantic guidance into targeted crops, with the model's spatial attention guiding view placement and the resulting predictions combined by uncertainty-weighted voting. On `ScreenSpot-Pro`, it **improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points** with `Qwen3-VL`, `Qwen2.5-VL`, and `UI-TARS`, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Gains hold across four additional benchmarks.

papers.title: ReJEPA: Bounded Predictive Regulation for Latent World Models
papers.abstract:
Latent world models learn representations by predicting future states in an abstract embedding space rather than reconstructing raw pixels. When training across multi-frame sequences, however, not all frames and spatial regions are equally informative or predictable. We argue that forcing a world model to minimize every prediction error may be unnecessary and harmful. Under standard $L_2$ loss, unbounded gradients force the encoder and predictor to overfit noisy or transient frames at the expense of core physical structure, while amplifying gradient conflict with representation regularizers. Conversely, $L_1$ loss bounds large gradients, but its constant gradient magnitude near zero disrupts the local smoothness required for planning. We resolve this tension with \textbf{ReJEPA}, a bounded predictive regulation principle that combines bounded gradients for large errors with smooth quadratic behavior near zero, instantiated simply via the element-wise $\log\cosh$ loss.
  As a drop-in training replacement across Temporal Straightening, LeWorldModel, and V-JEPA~2.1, $\log\cosh$ consistently outperforms $L_2$, a curvature-matched quadratic control, $L_1$, and Smooth-$L_1$ baselines without altering architectures or inference procedures. Notably, the gains grow with environmental complexity, scaling from simple navigation to contact-rich manipulation and real-world autonomous driving on NAVSIM. Probing and geometric analyses confirm that relaxing the penalty on extreme errors yields representations that better capture physical states and align with the true planning cost landscape.
papers.summary: Latent world models trained to predict future embeddings with an L2 loss receive unbounded gradients from noisy or unpredictable frames, while an L1 loss bounds those gradients but loses the smoothness near zero that planning relies on. `ReJEPA` combines bounded gradients for large errors with quadratic behavior near zero by using an element-wise log-cosh loss as a drop-in replacement during training. Across `Temporal Straightening`, `LeWorldModel`, and `V-JEPA 2.1`, it **consistently outperforms L2, L1, Smooth-L1, and a curvature-matched quadratic control** with no change to architecture or inference. The gains grow with environment complexity, from simple navigation to contact-rich manipulation and real-world driving on `NAVSIM`.

papers.title: Meta-Amortized Cognitive Modeling
papers.abstract: Cognitive modeling is highly iterative. Researchers repeatedly revise model structures, parameterizations, covariates, and experimental designs as theories evolve and data accumulates. Amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks provides rapid estimation for individual models, but every revision requires new simulations and training. Here, we introduce CogFormerV2, a meta-amortized framework that enables researchers to specify, revise, and fit cognitive models with a single network, carrying amortization across an entire space of models all at once. Trained once in about a day on a single GPU, it delivers accurate, well-calibrated posteriors across more than 14.6 billion model configurations spanning binary, multi-alternative, and continuous decisions, with varying parameter sets, covariate structures, trial counts, and contamination levels. It can fit empirical data from distinct behavioral tasks and extends to new models through continual learning and representation transfer. Released as an open-source interactive application, CogFormerV2 provides a reusable infrastructure for meta-amortized inference in cognitive modeling, while carrying the potential to accelerate computational modeling workflows at large.
papers.summary: Cognitive modelling involves repeatedly revising model structures, parameters, covariates, and experimental designs, and amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks normally needs new simulations and training after each revision. `CogFormerV2` is a meta-amortized framework in which a single network covers a whole space of models, spanning binary, multi-alternative, and continuous decisions with varying parameter sets, covariate structures, trial counts, and contamination levels. Trained once in about a day on a single GPU, it is reported to give accurate, well-calibrated posteriors across **more than 14.6 billion model configurations**. It also fits empirical data from distinct behavioural tasks, extends to new models through continual learning and representation transfer, and is released as an open-source interactive application.

papers.title: Machine learning enables full Bayesian inference for spinning extreme-mass-ratio inspirals
papers.abstract: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar-mass compact objects spiralling into massive black holes, promise to measure the masses and spins of the central black holes, reveal the strong-field environment around them and gauge cosmic distances via millihertz gravitational-wave observations. Yet most forecasts for the parameter inference of these systems assume known source parameters, and broad-prior analyses have addressed only simplified versions of the problem. The joint inversion of all 14 parameters of a spinning source from the complete prior has remained unsolved. Here we solve it for the augmented analytic kludge model: generative networks narrow the complete prior and reveal a ring of degenerate spin directions, and the exact detector likelihood determines the posterior. For a simulated one-year LISA-Taiji observation, within one ring sector we obtain, for the first time, a 14-parameter posterior of a spinning EMRI from the complete prior, the most precise yet obtained for such a source from broad priors. The redshifted mass and spin of the massive black hole are determined to two parts in $10^5$, the mass two orders of magnitude beyond any electromagnetic measurement. The compact object's redshifted mass is measured to one part in $10^4$, and its eccentric, retrograde orbit discriminates between capture channels. The 0.8% distance and sub-square-degree localization are sufficient for dark-siren cosmology. Year-long coherent analysis resolves the inspiral driven by radiation reaction itself.
papers.summary: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) are stellar-mass compact objects spiralling into massive black holes, and jointly inferring all 14 parameters of a spinning source from the complete prior had not previously been achieved. For the augmented analytic kludge waveform model, generative networks narrow the complete prior and reveal a ring of degenerate spin directions, after which the exact detector likelihood determines the posterior. For a simulated one-year `LISA`-`Taiji` observation, the authors obtain a full 14-parameter posterior within one ring sector, with the redshifted mass and spin of the massive black hole determined to **two parts in 100,000**. The compact object's redshifted mass is measured to one part in 10,000, and the 0.8% distance estimate and sub-square-degree localization are described as sufficient for dark-siren cosmology.

papers.title: Rethinking Universal Time Series Foundation Models from Unified Representations to Shared Dynamics (UniTFU)
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have attracted increasing attention in cross-domain forecasting. Existing works mainly rely on large-scale pre-training and general modeling paradigms. However, the former heavily relies on the diversity and domain coverage of pre-training data. Meanwhile, the latter learns unified representations across heterogeneous domains without explicitly identifying the temporal regularities shared among them, limiting robust cross-domain generalization. This work explores cross-domain generalization by characterizing commonalities in recurring local dynamics across domains, rather than relying solely on implicitly learned temporal representations. To capture such cross-domain commonalities, we propose Time Series Foundation Units (TFUs) as reusable building blocks discovered from multi-scale temporal segments, each characterizing a recurring local dynamic pattern shared across domains. Building on TFUs, we develop a unified time series foundation model (UniTFU) that explicitly reuses and composes shared temporal regularities across domains for forecasting.
