Experiments on seven public datasets show that UniTFU substantially outperforms existing TSFMs in cross-domain forecasting and can efficiently adapt to target-domain dynamics by updating its reusable components with limited target data. UniTFU also achieves strong forecasting performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.
papers.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically depend on large-scale pre-training and learn unified representations across domains without explicitly identifying the temporal regularities those domains share. The authors propose Time Series Foundation Units (`TFUs`), reusable building blocks discovered from multi-scale temporal segments that each capture a recurring local dynamic pattern, and build a forecasting model, `UniTFU`, that reuses and composes them. On seven public datasets, `UniTFU` is reported to **substantially outperform existing TSFMs in cross-domain forecasting**. It can also adapt to a target domain by updating its reusable components with limited target data.

papers.title: Scoring What Matters: Exact Feedback Reduction for Language Model Comparison
papers.abstract: Comparing language-model checkpoints requires estimating performance differences, yet evaluation pipelines can pay to score responses whose contributions cancel from those differences. We introduce Contrast-Aware Feedback Acquisition (CAFA), a sampler-agnostic method that identifies which scores a requested linear report needs before acquiring feedback. CAFA groups identical scoring inputs and aggregates their report coefficients, removing queries beyond ordinary caching while preserving the fully scored result. For a fixed response bank and an otherwise unrestricted scalar scorer, we characterize necessary and sufficient query sets for exact recovery of sample means, either alone or jointly with ordinary sample covariances. On controlled updates, CAFA removes 55.8% and 90.1% of the scoring inputs remaining after caching for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, respectively, averaged over four generation repetitions. Across three online group relative policy optimization (GRPO) trajectories, Independent Star sampling with CAFA achieves 46.1-51.3% lower recorded generation-plus-feedback cost than independent autoregressive sampling with caching at a common empirical precision threshold (RMS MCSE $\leq 0.04$). This is a post hoc comparison of completed runs on a fixed budget grid. All 504 evaluated report cells reproduce the fully scored means and covariances to numerical precision. We provide a modular implementation supporting existing response banks, versioned caches and external scorers.
papers.summary: Comparing language-model checkpoints means estimating performance differences, yet evaluation pipelines often pay to score responses whose contributions cancel out of those differences. Contrast-Aware Feedback Acquisition (`CAFA`) identifies which scores a requested linear report actually needs before any feedback is acquired, grouping identical scoring inputs and aggregating their coefficients, and the authors characterize necessary and sufficient query sets for exactly recovering sample means and covariances. On controlled updates it removes **55.8% and 90.1% of the scoring inputs remaining after caching** for `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct` and `SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct`, respectively. Across three group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) trajectories, a post hoc comparison shows 46.1-51.3% lower generation-plus-feedback cost than independent autoregressive sampling with caching, and all 504 evaluated report cells reproduce the fully scored results to numerical precision.

papers.title: Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation for LLM Unlearning
papers.abstract: Large language model unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data while preserving unrelated model capabilities. Existing likelihood-based methods commonly optimize against fixed forget sequences, providing only negative supervision on what the model should not generate and overlooking the states visited by the evolving unlearned policy. We introduce Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation (CPSD), a new unlearning framework that constructs an explicit knowledge-reduced target distribution and distills it along the model's own trajectories. Given a student rollout, a frozen reference model evaluates each token under a plain context and a privileged context containing the forget information. CPSD treats the resulting distributional shift as a knowledge-associated direction and reverses it to obtain a counterfactual unlearning target. The student is then trained to match this target at every rollout position while retaining its utility on unrelated data. We further introduce a privacy-enhanced variant that combines distributional unlearning with lightweight sequence-level suppression. Experiments under OpenUnlearning show that CPSD improves the forgetting-utility trade-off over NPO across TOFU forget-set sizes and Llama models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters. On MUSE-News, the privacy-enhanced variant improves all reported knowledge, memorization, privacy, and utility metrics over NPO.
papers.summary: Large language model unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data while keeping unrelated capabilities, but likelihood-based methods optimize against fixed forget sequences and ignore the states the evolving model actually visits. Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation (`CPSD`) has a frozen reference model score each token of a student rollout with and without the forget information in context, reverses the resulting distributional shift to form a knowledge-reduced target, and trains the student to match it at every rollout position. Under `OpenUnlearning`, `CPSD` **improves the forgetting-utility trade-off over `NPO`** across `TOFU` forget-set sizes and `Llama` models from 1B to 8B parameters. On `MUSE-News`, a privacy-enhanced variant with lightweight sequence-level suppression improves all reported knowledge, memorization, privacy, and utility metrics over `NPO`.

papers.title: CAPE: Coordinating Calibration and Search for Tool-Use Policies
papers.abstract: A tool call can fail even when the operation behind it is correct, because the receiving tool parses delimiters, dates or record layouts under a configuration the agent cannot inspect. Compiling a tool-use policy for such a tool requires both calibration, which evaluates candidate calls on candidate configurations, and search over the evaluated calls. The two share one compilation budget: calibrating everything first postpones any improved policy until the end, while re-solving every partially known model delays the next useful query. A call becomes usable as soon as its effects are known on the configurations that reach it. We present CAPE, a training-free compiler built on this observation. It maintains an executable policy at all times, directs calibration to the calls that can improve this policy, and tightens bounds only where doing so ends calibration early. Returned policies preserve every configuration the initial policy completes, and CAPE certifies optimality when its executable and optimistic values meet. On CSV and JSON workflows built from 64 requests, CAPE reaches the independently computed optimum in 502 of 504 compilations while taking 22.0% less compilation time than eager exact search. On larger CSV families it returns policies with higher completion at similar compilation time, and it raises completion by 15.38 to 34.66 percentage points over an LLM that revises its serialization from error feedback.
papers.summary: Tool calls can fail even when the underlying operation is correct, because the receiving tool parses delimiters, dates, or record layouts under a configuration the agent cannot inspect. `CAPE` is a training-free compiler for tool-use policies that shares one budget between calibration (evaluating candidate calls on candidate configurations) and search, keeping an executable policy at all times and directing calibration only to calls that could improve it. On CSV and JSON workflows built from 64 requests, it reaches the independently computed optimum in **502 of 504 compilations while taking 22.0% less compilation time** than eager exact search. It also raises completion by 15.38 to 34.66 percentage points over an LLM that revises its serialization from error feedback.

papers.title: Beyond the Last Loop: Reinforcement Learning with a Teacher Extrapolated from the Model Itself
papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop can be read out through the shared language-model head. Post-training them with verifiable rewards is hard: the outcome reward carries one bit per response, spreading it over loops trains intermediate loops on tokens sampled from the last loop, and distillation needs either a teacher that ignores the reward or an external, larger model. We observe that a looped model already contains a teacher stronger than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELGO (Extrapolated-Loop Group-relative Optimization) adds to GRPO a dense per-token distillation term towards this distribution. The teacher is computed from an anchor copy of the model, which stays frozen and is replaced by the current model once the student's KL to the teacher falls below a threshold, so the teacher improves with the student without chasing its own extrapolation. The outcome reward splits probability between correct and incorrect responses, and the teacher decides which tokens are preferred inside a response. Between refreshes the objective is KL-regularised RL anchored at the teacher, whose optimum tilts the teacher by the reward. On Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, ELGO raises the average avg@8 over five math benchmarks from 62.32 with GRPO to 64.20 and is the best compared method on every benchmark, while spreading the reward over loops falls below the base model.
papers.summary: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and post-training them with verifiable rewards is difficult because the outcome reward carries only one bit per response and spreading it across loops trains intermediate loops on tokens sampled from the last one. `ELGO` (Extrapolated-Loop Group-relative Optimization) adds to `GRPO` a dense per-token distillation term towards a teacher distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last, computed from a frozen anchor copy of the model that is refreshed once the student's KL divergence to the teacher falls below a threshold. On `Ouro-1.4B-Thinking`, it raises the average avg@8 over five math benchmarks from **62.32 with `GRPO` to 64.20** and is the best compared method on every benchmark. Spreading the reward over loops, by contrast, falls below the base model.

papers.title: MELODI: Similarity-Identity Decoupling for Lightweight Ranking
papers.abstract: For latency-constrained candidate ranking, we propose a similarity-identity decoupling framework that separates target-history compatibility from target-only information. We study two orders for computing pooled similarity, similarity-then-pool and pool-then-similarity, and identify linearity of the similarity operator in its history argument, for each fixed target, as sufficient for their equivalence, justifying the cheaper pool-then-similarity form. We instantiate the framework as multi-head efficient lightweight operator for decoupling identity and similarity (MELODI), whose similarity branch combines target-conditioned multi-head history pooling with a single residual-free cross layer that is linear in its pooled-history input and whose identity branch is problem-dependent. On public benchmark datasets, MELODI matches or surpasses the evaluated target-aware and target-agnostic baselines. On two large-scale industrial datasets, its area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), normalised discounted cumulative gain (NDCG), and recall values are equal to or higher than those of the evaluated target-aware baselines. Processor measurements show lower latency than the evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts, further reduced by request-local history reuse.
papers.summary: For latency-constrained candidate ranking, the authors separate target-history compatibility from target-only information in a similarity-identity decoupling framework. They show that linearity of the similarity operator in its history argument is sufficient for similarity-then-pool and pool-then-similarity to be equivalent, which justifies the cheaper pool-then-similarity form, and instantiate this as `MELODI`, combining target-conditioned multi-head history pooling with a single residual-free cross layer. `MELODI` **matches or surpasses the evaluated target-aware and target-agnostic baselines** on public benchmarks and matches or exceeds target-aware baselines on two large-scale industrial datasets. Processor measurements show lower latency than candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts.

papers.title: DUST: Directional Uncertainty-aware and Scale-invariant Transfer Learning
papers.abstract: Transfer learning seeks to improve efficiency in a target regression task by borrowing information from related external source dataset(s). Existing approaches achieve this by enforcing Euclidean proximity between the target and source regression parameters or, more recently, by encouraging their directional alignment through angle-based penalties. While such angle-based penalties mitigate the sensitivity of the transfer learning methods to the scale differences between source and target regression coefficients, they still rely on a point estimate of the source regression parameter and thus provide no direct mechanism to incorporate uncertainty in the source information. To that end, we propose a probabilistic framework for transfer learning that operates at the level of a \emph{scale-invariant directional distribution} of the source regression parameter estimate, rather than its point estimate, to enable robust, scale-invariant and uncertainty aware transfer under heterogeneous source information. Specifically, we project the sampling distribution of the source regression estimate onto the unit sphere, thereby extracting its scale-free directional distribution. Transfer from source to target is then induced through a novel \emph{angular cone prior} which shrinks the target regression parameter towards directions in which the source distribution assigns high probability, while allowing its magnitude to be learned exclusively from the target dataset. The proposed construction admits exact finite-sample characterizations of posterior angular concentration and posterior computation remains tractable via careful low-dimensional augmentation in the parameter space.
papers.summary: Transfer learning for regression usually pulls target parameters toward a point estimate of the source parameters, either by Euclidean proximity or by angular alignment, which gives no direct way to account for uncertainty in the source information. `DUST` projects the sampling distribution of the source regression estimate onto the unit sphere to obtain a scale-free directional distribution, then applies an angular cone prior that shrinks the target parameter toward directions the source distribution favours while its magnitude is learned only from target data. The construction **admits exact finite-sample characterizations of posterior angular concentration**. Posterior computation remains tractable through a low-dimensional augmentation of the parameter space.

papers.title: Beyond Rigid Hands: Deforming Skin into Contact-Consistent Hand Meshes
papers.abstract: Hands grasp objects with soft skin. A fingertip flattens against a mug, and a palm curves around a bottle. Yet hand-object datasets and estimators represent the hand as a rigid articulated mesh, which hovers above or penetrates the object where skin would press against it. Existing refiners keep the mesh rigid and adjust only the pose, trading pose accuracy for physical plausibility. We ask whether a rigid hand can instead touch the object as skin does while staying close to its original pose. We lift annotated or estimated rigid hands to contact-consistent meshes through an optimization that (i) slightly adjusts the joints and wrist to bring the fingers onto the object, (ii) deforms the skin so that penetrating regions settle onto the surface, and (iii) keeps this deformation consistent over time. Since deformation reaches only skin already near the object, we further train a lightweight head on the lifted annotations to predict where an estimated hand should touch and steer the deformation there. Unlike existing refiners, the lift more than doubles the skin lying on the object surface for three published estimators while barely changing the pose. Guidance from the learned head further improves grasp stability by closing contact gaps that the estimate leaves open. Existing hand-object datasets and estimators can thus adopt contact-consistent hands without changing the hand model or retraining the estimators.
papers.summary: Hand-object datasets and estimators represent the hand as a rigid articulated mesh, which hovers above or penetrates objects where real skin would press against them, and existing refiners fix this only by adjusting pose. The proposed optimization lifts rigid hands to contact-consistent meshes by slightly adjusting joints and wrist, deforming penetrating skin onto the object surface, and keeping the deformation consistent over time, with a lightweight learned head predicting where an estimated hand should touch. The lift **more than doubles the skin lying on the object surface** for three published estimators while barely changing the pose. Guidance from the learned head further improves grasp stability, and no change to the hand model or retraining of the estimators is required.

papers.title: Perception Is Enough, at the Right Scale: Scale-Adaptive Token Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $\tau$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $\tau$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting compute cost limits real-time robotic control. `TauPrune-VLA` is a training-free token pruning method that selects tokens from perceptual semantics rather than internal attention, controlling the scale of the retained representation with a single perception temperature that is updated online from semantic trends, robot-state changes, and action magnitude. Because semantics change little between consecutive frames, retention indices computed on one observation are applied at the next policy invocation, so selection runs asynchronously with inference. Across several VLA models and simulation benchmarks it achieves **up to a 1.86x inference speedup** with near-baseline task success, and it is also validated on two real-world robot platforms.

papers.title: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion
papers.abstract: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.
papers.summary: Bot defenses have mostly been evaluated against web agents that do not coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behaviour. `DarkAgent` is an autonomous web agent built as an adversarial stress test, pairing a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts with generative models for human-like mouse and keyboard traces, including a keyboard model that jointly generates key events and timings. It achieves an **89% page-access bypass rate** on a third-party stealth benchmark, 12 percentage points above the strongest published baseline, and released agent detectors accept its generated behaviour as human. On a new benchmark measuring fingerprints, behaviour, and network activity, browser and behavioural modifications are complementary, with only their combination evading all tested checks, and timing between actions remains a signal for defenders.

papers.title: Sounding the Black Box: Online Training of Embedded Neural Networks in Forward-Only Physical Simulators
papers.abstract: Hybrid physics-neural simulators embed neural networks in partial differential equation (PDE) solvers to model unresolved subgrid dynamics while preserving resolved physics and conservation laws. Because closure outputs feed back across time steps, single-step offline regression does not directly minimize multi-step rollout error, motivating online trajectory optimization. Solver backpropagation through time (BPTT) is the standard online solution when solver derivatives are available, yet many operational Fortran and C/C++ simulators expose only non-differentiable, forward-only interfaces. We introduce FORGE (Forward-Only Response and Gauss-Newton Estimation), an online framework that trains embedded networks from forward runs alone by decoupling exact network derivatives from black-box simulator dynamics. Stage I warms up the rollout via a low-dimensional Gauss-Newton step along output-orthonormal weight directions, canceling multi-layer feature drift via a final-layer correction. Stage II perturbs spatial output fields to fit a gain-bounded causal linear response operator across rollout steps, solves for regularized target outputs, and updates all weights via network backpropagation. Across five 2D and 3D benchmarks spanning phase separation, reaction-diffusion, fluid and MHD turbulence, and ocean circulation, FORGE outperforms gradient-free, reinforcement-learning, and emulator-based baselines, cutting coarse-solver test mean squared error (MSE) by 50%-96% in 2D and 70% in 3D, outperforming the strongest forward-only baseline by 16%-69%, and recovering 88%-98% of Solver BPTT's gains. Code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/FORGE.
papers.summary: Hybrid simulators embed neural networks in partial differential equation (PDE) solvers to model unresolved subgrid dynamics, but training them on multi-step rollouts normally requires solver backpropagation through time (BPTT), which many operational Fortran and C/C++ simulators cannot provide. `FORGE` (Forward-Only Response and Gauss-Newton Estimation) trains the embedded network from forward runs alone, first warming up with a low-dimensional Gauss-Newton step and then perturbing output fields to fit a linear response operator, solving for target outputs, and backpropagating only through the network. Across five 2D and 3D benchmarks covering phase separation, reaction-diffusion, fluid and magnetohydrodynamic turbulence, and ocean circulation, it cuts coarse-solver test mean squared error by 50%-96% in 2D and 70% in 3D. It beats the strongest forward-only baseline by 16%-69% and **recovers 88%-98% of the gains of solver BPTT**.

papers.title: On the Information Loss of Multi-Token Prediction: Origin and Solution
papers.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) accelerates autoregressive decoding through block-wise prediction, but remains vulnerable to error accumulation across sequentially generated blocks. To investigate this limitation, we analyze the distinction between block-wise and sequence-level cumulative information loss (CIL). Specifically, when the model generates using its own previous outputs without access to reference answers, the input-conditional gap equals the cross-block dependence of the reference targets. To improve prediction when these generated prefixes are imperfect, we propose Dual-MTP, which supervises shared prediction heads under full and randomly masked contexts. Together, complete-prefix supervision and context perturbations provide complementary training signals while retaining the MTP architecture. To characterize this training objective, we use the normalized dual loss to bound the divergence between the model's predictive distributions under full and masked contexts. Experiments across five backbones and six tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and GLUE understanding show that Dual-MTP achieves the highest average task score on four of five backbones, with gains of up to 2.46 points over MTP. On mathematical reasoning tasks, Dual-MTP also achieves 1.4 to 1.9 times the decoding throughput of the NTP reference. Together, these results show that dual-context supervision can improve prediction accuracy while retaining efficient multi-token decoding.
papers.summary: Multi-token prediction (MTP) speeds up autoregressive decoding by predicting blocks of tokens, but errors accumulate across sequentially generated blocks. The authors analyze the difference between block-wise and sequence-level cumulative information loss (CIL), showing that when the model conditions on its own outputs the gap equals the cross-block dependence of the reference targets, and propose `Dual-MTP`, which supervises shared prediction heads under both full and randomly masked contexts. Across five backbones and six tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and `GLUE` understanding, `Dual-MTP` achieves the highest average score on four of five backbones, with gains of up to 2.46 points over MTP. On mathematical reasoning it reaches **1.4 to 1.9 times the decoding throughput** of the `NTP` reference.

papers.title: DexOPD: Dual-Extrapolation On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Flow-based diffusion models have become a mainstream paradigm for text-to-image generation, where task-specific post-training produces specialist models with complementary strengths. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD) offers an efficient way to consolidate these specialists into a single unified student. Recent methods strengthen supervision through teacher extrapolation, constructing stronger proxy teachers that allow distilled students to surpass the original specialists. However, their extrapolation directions remain defined solely by frozen teacher and reference models, leaving the student's own training progress unexploited. To address this limitation, we introduce DexOPD, a dual-extrapolation on-policy distillation method for diffusion models. DexOPD retains extrapolated teacher supervision while leveraging a lagging historical student as the reference for student self-extrapolation. Sampling across multiple self-extrapolation gains from shared initial noise broadens exploration along the student's evolving trajectory, and task rewards convert pairwise differences in candidate quality into a normalized auxiliary regression direction. Empirically, we evaluate DexOPD on GenEval, OCR, and DrawBench. The resulting unified SD3.5-Medium student achieves a GenEval reward of 0.9736, an OCR score of 0.9515, and a DrawBench Aesthetic score of 6.4875, surpassing the corresponding specialist teachers as well as all evaluated OPD and multi-task reinforcement learning baselines across these three benchmarks while preserving standard single-model inference.
papers.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates specialist text-to-image diffusion models into one student, and recent methods extrapolate the teachers to build stronger proxy targets but ignore the student's own training progress. `DexOPD` keeps extrapolated teacher supervision and adds student self-extrapolation against a lagging historical copy of the student, sampling several extrapolation gains from shared initial noise and using task rewards to turn quality differences between candidates into an auxiliary regression direction. The resulting unified `SD3.5-Medium` student reaches a `GenEval` reward of 0.9736, an OCR score of 0.9515, and a `DrawBench` Aesthetic score of 6.4875. It **surpasses the corresponding specialist teachers and all evaluated OPD and multi-task reinforcement learning baselines** on these three benchmarks while keeping standard single-model inference.

papers.title: Predict Backbone, Graft Dynamics: A Decoupled Paradigm for Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Modern long-term forecasters are typically optimized for point-wise accuracy, which rewards dominant low-frequency backbones but often suppresses high-utility local dynamics such as abrupt variations, transient surges, and turning points. We propose Predict Backbone, Graft Dynamics, a decoupled forecasting paradigm that separates stable structural prediction from grounded dynamic restoration. We instantiate it as GRAFT, where a base forecaster predicts the reliable trajectory backbone, and a dedicated grafting path restores historically recurrent dynamics through retrieval-based evidence, phase-aware release, channel-wise control, and restoration-cooperative optimization. Unlike generic post-hoc revision methods that correct residual errors, GRAFT formulates the second stage as grounded dynamic grafting, where historical response evidence is calibrated into transferable dynamics and selectively grafted onto the backbone under phase-, channel-, and confidence-aware constraints. Across the full evaluation grid of seven benchmarks, two metrics, four horizons, and six backbones, GRAFT improves over the corresponding backbone in 87% of all comparisons, with average MSE/MAE reductions of 4.6%/3.9%. Dynamic-window analyses show that GRAFT restores local dynamics while preserving the stable backbone structure. These results suggest a new principle for high-utility forecasting: predict the backbone, then graft the dynamics.
papers.summary: Long-term forecasters optimized for point-wise accuracy capture dominant low-frequency structure but tend to suppress local dynamics such as abrupt variations, transient surges, and turning points. `GRAFT` decouples the two: a base forecaster predicts the stable trajectory backbone, and a separate grafting path restores historically recurrent dynamics using retrieval-based evidence under phase-, channel-, and confidence-aware constraints. Across seven benchmarks, two metrics, four horizons, and six backbones, it improves over the corresponding backbone in **87% of all comparisons**, with average MSE and MAE reductions of 4.6% and 3.9%. Dynamic-window analyses indicate that local dynamics are restored while the backbone structure is preserved.

papers.title: A Minimax Optimal Leave One Out Bound for Bounded Losses
papers.abstract: We study proper leave-one-out prediction with $M$ real-valued experts on $n$ fixed inputs. Each label is hidden in turn, and the learner uses the remaining labels to choose one of the experts' predictions at the held-out input. We determine how closely such a rule can match the average loss of the best single expert on the full sample. For any bounded loss that is a continuous nondecreasing function of absolute error and vanishes at zero, let $B$ denote its maximum value. Over classes of size $M$ and samples on which the best expert has average loss at most $r$, the minimax excess loss is of order $\min\{B, \sqrt{\frac{Br\log M}{n}}+\frac{B\log M}{n}\}$. For each class and loss, one deterministic rule attains this rate for every $r\in[0,B]$. The matching lower bound holds even for randomized proper rules given $r$.
papers.summary: The setting is proper leave-one-out prediction with M real-valued experts on n fixed inputs, where each label is hidden in turn and the learner must pick one expert's prediction at the held-out input using the remaining labels. For any bounded loss that is a continuous nondecreasing function of absolute error with maximum value B, and samples on which the best expert has average loss at most r, the authors determine the minimax excess loss: it is **of order the minimum of B and sqrt(B r log M / n) + B log M / n**. A single deterministic rule attains this rate for every r between 0 and B, and the matching lower bound holds even for randomized proper rules that are given r.

papers.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
papers.abstract: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.
papers.summary: Existing game benchmarks test language models as computer-use agents that query the model throughout play, which incurs repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, means acting while the environment keeps moving. `Coding4Games` instead evaluates whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to write standalone programs that play 15 modern games from visual observations and standard inputs, with a development phase in a sandbox followed by frozen, independent testing without any language-model inference. Evaluation covers game performance and reliability as well as how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. The best program per game **outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 of 15 games** and ties on one, while a human player still outscores all agents on 10 games.
papers.highlight_summary:
Existing game benchmarks either have a language model pick every action or hand bots a structured game API; `Coding4Games` instead asks coding agents to write a standalone program that plays modern games from screenshots and standard keyboard-and-mouse inputs. The selected program is then frozen and tested in a fresh environment with no language-model inference at all.

- The benchmark wraps **15 modern games** across five categories (combat, strategy, 3D sports, movement and timing, multi-step tasks) behind a gym-like game server, with agents developing in a persistent sandbox under per-game token and game-tic budgets while the host controls initialization and scoring.
- Across **12 coding agents**, the best program per game beats the strongest GUI-agent baseline on **13 of 15 games** and ties one, though this picks the best of twelve agents per game against only two GUI baselines.
- On average normalized score, `GPT-6-Astra` leads at **52.6** and `Claude-Opus-5.5` follows at **44.0**, against roughly **26–27** for the two GUI agents and **97.2** for the human player, who outscores every agent on **10 games**.
- Same-model comparisons are close to a coin flip, with `GPT-5.6-Sol`'s programs beating its own GUI agent on 8 games and losing on 7, and `Claude-Sonnet-5`'s winning 7, losing 6 and tying 2.
- Process analysis shows agents get relevant test feedback for **80–100%** of their fixes but resolve the targeted problems only **35.7–83.3%** of the time, and more elaborate control did not guarantee better play, as `Qwen3.8-flash`'s PID controller on Forza Horizon 5 scored 443.7 against 645.7 for `Claude-Sonnet-5`'s simpler route follower.
- Limitations include a single non-expert human reference, only three test episodes per entry, GUI baselines run with the game paused during inference, and scores min–max normalized within each game.

papers.title: Localizing Cross-Lingual Generalization in Parameter Space
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual transfer is uneven across tasks, succeeding for natural language understanding but often failing for mathematical reasoning. We argue that this asymmetry is governed by the geometry of parameter space. Specifically, cross-lingual generalization is determined by whether English and target-language LoRA adapters share a low-error basin. To test this, we use linear mode connectivity (LMC) between English and target-language adapters, evaluating on three tasks. We find that NLI and QA model-language pairs are mostly linearly connected, whereas mathematical reasoning (Math) pairs are not, indicating that basin geometry is task-dependent. Such disconnection in Math is ``local'' rather than global. A small target-language task sample, applied only to the English adapter's language encoding or semantic composition layers, is enough to repair it. Cross-lingual generalization is also factorizable into language-specific encoding and language-agnostic composition, each supplied separately from a cheaper signal. English task data routed to the composition layers and an unlabeled target-language corpus routed to the language encoding layers each alleviate it on their own for nearly every pair. Composition is the more influential of these, and it needs no target-language data. Together, these results suggest that cross-lingual generalization decomposes into language-specific and language-agnostic components in parameter space. This decomposition offers a practical route for low-resource cross-lingual adaptation.
papers.summary: Cross-lingual transfer works for natural language understanding but often fails for mathematical reasoning, and the authors attribute this to whether English and target-language `LoRA` adapters share a low-error basin in parameter space. Testing with linear mode connectivity (LMC), they find that NLI and QA model-language pairs are mostly linearly connected while mathematical reasoning pairs are not, and that the disconnection is local: a small target-language task sample applied only to the English adapter's language encoding or semantic composition layers repairs it. Generalization further factorizes into language-specific encoding and language-agnostic composition, each of which can be supplied from a cheaper signal such as an unlabeled target-language corpus or English task data. **Composition is the more influential component and needs no target-language data**, which the authors present as a route for low-resource cross-lingual adaptation.

papers.title: Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth
papers.abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.
papers.summary: Looped diffusion transformers, which reuse one block of shared weights along the network's depth, have so far been trained from scratch despite strong pretrained non-looped models being available. `Dooop` (Distill to Loop) distills a pretrained diffusion transformer into a looped student initialized from the teacher's blocks, treating distillation as a fixed-point iteration in which each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth, so one model can run any number of loops at test time and use higher-order solvers along depth. On `SD3-medium`, a student with **about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher** on average over `GenEval`, `ImageReward`, `PickScore`, and `HPSv2.1` with two to four loops, using about 58% of the teacher's compute at two loops. A loop guidance technique that contrasts outputs at different loop counts raises the four-metric average from 88.2 to 99.2 on a four-step `SD3-medium`.

papers.title: Reading, Writing and Repairing Game-Theoretic Policies in Weight Space
papers.abstract: Can a language model work in the weight space of a policy network for a repeated game? We put four questions to a mid-size open model, on recurrent networks of 1{,}218 weights with exactly checkable answers. Given a population of opponents described in English, write a policy that is optimal: its value is a finite computation over the agent's information state, so a submitted network has an exact gap from the optimum. Given a network's weights, report its action after each of fifteen opponent histories; recover the state machine it implements, judged on every opponent sequence to depth ten; or repair a network whose output was altered in one place and say which round first goes wrong. The model recovers the program in 62 of 66 replies, reports all fifteen behavioral entries correctly in 34 of 36, and attains the optimum in 20 of 20 when it states a policy the evaluator compiles. Repair is the exception: 4 of 18 repaired, 5 of 18 diagnosed, with a median patch covering one of the two entries needed.
papers.summary: Whether a language model can operate directly on the weights of a policy network is tested on recurrent networks of 1,218 weights that play a repeated game, where every answer can be checked exactly. A mid-size open model is asked to write an optimal policy for opponents described in English, report a network's actions after fifteen opponent histories, recover the state machine it implements, and repair a network altered in one place. The model recovers the program in 62 of 66 replies, gets all fifteen behavioral entries right in 34 of 36, and reaches the optimum in 20 of 20 compiled policies, but **repair succeeds in only 4 of 18 cases**, with 5 of 18 correctly diagnosed.

papers.title: Discovering Bandwidth-Efficient Prefetchers to Shrink the Cache Hierarchy
papers.abstract: Shared last-level caches (LLCs) increasingly dominate server processor die area, forcing architects to trade core counts for cache capacity. While intelligent data prefetching offers a pathway to reclaim this silicon, designing coordinated, multi-level prefetching policies for multi-core systems is bottlenecked by day-long, cycle-level simulations. This simulation wall limits even LLM-based microarchitecture discovery; the state-of-the-art ArchAgent system evolves one cache level at a time on single-core benchmarks, adds multi-core configurations only at the end, and trails the human champion under multi-core shared cache contention. We introduce DuoArchitect, an autonomous agentic framework for multi-fidelity, multi-core co-discovery of prefetchers. Agents jointly evolve evaluation proxies and coordinated prefetching policies across the L1D, L2, and LLC hierarchies, constructing simulation proxies 3-26x faster than cluster evaluation and hardware diagnostic oracles to guide the search. To study how much cache silicon a smarter prefetcher can replace, we evaluate and evolve prefetchers under reduced cache budgets, and find that evolving under our tightest cache constraint (with both the L2 and LLC halved) produced our strongest prefetcher overall at every cache size we tested: DuoArch-Nano. On the Fourth Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4) benchmarks with full-size caches, DuoArch-Nano delivers a 9.2% geomean IPC speedup (+10.5% on four-core mixes) while reducing four-core DRAM traffic by 11.4%, more than doubling the gains of the human champion BertiGO and the agentic ArchAgent v2. When the LLC is halved, DuoArch-Nano erases the baseline's 8.6% overall slowdown and edges out the full-LLC baseline overall (+0.88%), showing that agentic frameworks can generate prefetchers that reclaim megabytes of LLC SRAM per core with zero overall IPC penalty.
papers.summary: Shared last-level caches (LLCs) take up a growing share of server processor die area, and designing coordinated multi-level prefetchers that could replace some of that cache is slowed by day-long cycle-level simulations. `DuoArchitect` is an autonomous agentic framework in which agents jointly evolve fast simulation proxies (3-26x faster than cluster evaluation) and coordinated prefetching policies across the L1D, L2 and LLC levels on multi-core workloads. Its strongest prefetcher, `DuoArch-Nano`, was evolved under the tightest cache budget and delivers a **9.2% geomean IPC speedup** on the Fourth Data Prefetching Championship (`DPC4`) benchmarks while cutting four-core DRAM traffic by 11.4%, more than doubling the gains of the human champion `BertiGO` and the agentic `ArchAgent v2`. With the LLC halved, it erases the baseline's 8.6% slowdown and slightly exceeds the full-LLC baseline.

papers.title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
papers.abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models commit several tokens per step by sampling each from its own marginal, which loses the dependency between them; the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. The authors estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion models from two families and test how well decoders that see only per-position marginals can predict it. On three of the four models the best marginal-only predictor is **off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17)**, 1.8 to 3.7 times better than a baseline that knows only the bound, and pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. They also show that `Dream` and `LLaDA` place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and that reading the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times.

papers.title: Metric-Dependent Scaling Laws for Sketched Multiclass Softmax Regression
papers.abstract: We study scaling laws for full-batch gradient descent with general stable deterministic learning rates in sketched multiclass softmax regression. In a Gaussian teacher student model with power law feature and teacher spectra, the student observes a random feature sketch and reuses a finite labeled sample throughout optimization. Sketching generally makes the student misspecified, so the analysis must jointly account for approximation, nonlinear finite time learning, and the fixed empirical perturbation induced by data reuse. On an exponentially likely sketch event, we show that cross entropy excess and excess zero one risk share a common spectral scale, consisting of a resolution term and an effective learned dimension divided by sample size; teacher student decision disagreement follows the square root of that scale. The resulting balance gives rate optimal sketch and cumulative horizon choices, and synthetic experiments support the predicted regimes and metric dependent exponents.
papers.summary: Scaling laws are derived for full-batch gradient descent in sketched multiclass softmax regression, using a Gaussian teacher-student model with power-law feature and teacher spectra in which the student sees a random feature sketch and reuses a finite labeled sample. The analysis jointly handles the misspecification caused by sketching, nonlinear finite-time learning, and the perturbation from data reuse. The authors show that **cross-entropy excess and excess zero-one risk share a common spectral scale**, made of a resolution term plus an effective learned dimension divided by sample size, while teacher-student decision disagreement follows the square root of that scale. This yields rate-optimal choices of sketch size and training horizon, which synthetic experiments support.

papers.title: ADE: A Zero-Training Unlearning Method for Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Latent world models learn compact recurrent dynamics from offline trajectories, yet deployed simulators can retain backdoor triggers or stale transitions from outdated physical regimes. Existing unlearning methods fail in autoregressive physics: gradient updates distort latent manifolds and compound rollout drift, naive output zeroing suppresses valid control responses on trigger onset, and single-step deletion leaves corruption inside recurrent hidden states. We propose Analytical Dynamics Excision (ADE), a deterministic, zero-training closed-form unlearning algorithm for latent world models. Using only cached pretraining moments, ADE recovers retain covariances via single-pass matrix downdating without raw retain data and cascades closed-form edits across the input bottleneck, hidden states, and downstream heads. Pairing orthogonal excision with whitened recurrent damping and mean-preserving affine calibration neutralizes out-of-manifold backdoors and realigns in-manifold shifts without variance collapse. Across four regimes on three MuJoCo benchmarks, ADE outperforms seven tuned baselines on DreamerV1, eliminating HalfCheetah and Hopper velocity-flip triggers $4.4\times$ faster than fine-tuning, and transfers zero-shot to DreamerV3.
papers.summary: Latent world models trained on offline trajectories can retain backdoor triggers or stale transitions, and existing unlearning methods distort latent dynamics or leave corruption inside recurrent hidden states. Analytical Dynamics Excision (`ADE`) is a deterministic, closed-form unlearning algorithm that needs no training: it uses cached pretraining moments to recover retain-set covariances without the raw data, then cascades edits across the input bottleneck, hidden states and downstream heads. Across four regimes on three `MuJoCo` benchmarks it outperforms seven tuned baselines on `DreamerV1`, removing `HalfCheetah` and `Hopper` velocity-flip triggers **4.4x faster than fine-tuning**, and it transfers zero-shot to `DreamerV3`.

papers.title: Grounding Language Models in Revealed Audience Behavior
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to simulate how an audience will respond to a headline or a post, and such simulators are validated against what people say. We validate them against what people do. We call a model grounded in revealed audience behavior when it is fine-tuned on records of what audiences actually clicked, liked or watched, and we ask not only whether asking a model falls short of grounding it, as prior work found, but why and where. Why: the gap is a property of the training signal, not mainly of model size or prompting. The same 8B model is right about half the time when asked which headline readers will click and 86.5% of the time when grounded in the clicks; the strongest prompting we tried only matches a text classifier; a grounded 0.6B model beats every prompted frontier model in our runs; and whether the clicks are fitted as counts or as shares makes no detectable difference in a pre-registered test. The asked 8B model also reproduces stated-preference cues, favoring question headlines that in fact lower clicks. Where: across four behaviors, grounding wins where the text carries the signal (short-video likes, +20 points on 200 pre-registered videos), only ties an asked model given the reader's history (news clicks), and nothing text-only gets far from chance on watch time. Code, adapters and run outputs will be released.
papers.summary: Language models used to simulate audience reactions are usually validated against what people say; here they are validated against what people actually clicked, liked or watched. The authors compare prompting a model with fine-tuning it on behavioral records and find the gap comes from the training signal, not model size or prompting: the same 8B model is right about half the time when asked which headline readers will click and **86.5% of the time when fine-tuned on the clicks**, and a fine-tuned 0.6B model beats every prompted frontier model tested. The prompted model also reproduces stated-preference cues, favoring question headlines that in fact lower clicks. Across four behaviors, fine-tuning wins where the text carries the signal (short-video likes), only ties a prompted model given reader history on news clicks, and no text-only method gets far from chance on watch time.

papers.title: TableRouter: Query-Aware Evidence Construction for Long-Table Question Answering
papers.abstract: LLMs can reason over tables, but when tables outgrow the context budget, retrieving relevant rows is only part of the solution. A retrieved subset may omit information required for an exact aggregate; even complete evidence may remain difficult for an LLM to use. We introduce TableRouter, a training-free framework that analyzes each query, then chooses between two routes: a computation route, which derives question-conditioned statistics from the full table, and a coverage route, which retrieves relevant rows and column summaries. The chosen context is passed to a frozen LLM in one call. Across three LLMs and three large-table benchmarks, TableRouter outperforms the strongest of six single-call baselines in all nine settings by 1.2-18.3 accuracy points, using 77-95% fewer estimated FLOPs than truncated-table prompting, with indexing amortized across questions. The gains extend to long tables from databases not used in earlier experiments, where TableRouter achieves 35.8% with Qwen2.5-7B, versus 16.4% for the strongest external baseline. A controlled experiment shows that explicitly providing computed statistics improves accuracy by up to 40.0 points, even when all answer-determining rows are available. These results distinguish evidence access from evidence use: long-table reasoning depends on how information is represented, not only on which rows are retrieved.
papers.summary: When a table is too large for a language model's context, retrieving relevant rows can miss information needed for exact aggregates, and even complete evidence may be hard for the model to use. `TableRouter` is a training-free framework that analyzes each query and picks between a computation route, which derives question-specific statistics from the full table, and a coverage route, which retrieves relevant rows and column summaries, before passing the result to a frozen model in a single call. Across three models and three large-table benchmarks it beats the strongest of six single-call baselines in all nine settings by 1.2-18.3 accuracy points while using 77-95% fewer estimated FLOPs than truncated-table prompting. A controlled experiment shows that **supplying computed statistics improves accuracy by up to 40.0 points** even when every answer-determining row is already available.

papers.title: LIBRA: Runtime Co-Tuning of Batch Size and Parallelism for Time-Efficient LLM Training
papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) requires choosing both a batch size and a parallel configuration. Existing systems make these decisions in isolation, tuning parallelism for throughput and batch size for convergence, but neither objective alone determines training efficiency. We present LIBRA, a lightweight runtime framework that co-tunes batch size and parallel configuration to minimize end-to-end time. LIBRA treats throughput and convergence as two noisy objectives and searches their joint space using parallel noisy expected hypervolume improvement (qNEHVI). To make this runtime search efficient, we propose hierarchical pruning, which removes infeasible and low-throughput parallel configurations through system-level performance estimation and then narrows batch-size candidates through critical-batch-size-aware convergence monitoring. We further design acquisition-guided parallel evaluation (AGPE), which evaluates surviving candidates concurrently across GPU groups in order of their acquisition values. On clusters of up to 256 GPUs, LIBRA reduces time-to-convergence by 31.1% on average over state-of-the-art methods, while runtime tuning accounts for only 0.3-3.5% of overall time.
papers.summary: Training large language models requires choosing both a batch size and a parallel configuration, which existing systems tune separately for convergence and throughput. `LIBRA` is a lightweight runtime framework that co-tunes the two to minimize end-to-end training time, treating throughput and convergence as noisy objectives searched with parallel noisy expected hypervolume improvement (`qNEHVI`). It prunes infeasible or slow parallel configurations and narrows batch-size candidates hierarchically, then evaluates the survivors concurrently across GPU groups using acquisition-guided parallel evaluation (AGPE). On clusters of up to 256 GPUs it **reduces time-to-convergence by 31.1% on average** over state-of-the-art methods, with tuning taking 0.3-3.5% of overall time.

papers.title: Calm Agent: Reframing Agent Interaction around Intermittent Human Attention
papers.abstract: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention: tasks should continue between interactions, and users should be able to return with little effort to understand and control them. We develop this position as Calm Agent. It connects three on-demand interaction modes: Delegate, Adjust, and Check, through a persistent task representation. Generative interaction provides controls and feedback suited to open-ended goals, while existing controls support routine actions. We illustrate these principles with Orvlet, a desktop prototype for background execution and compact task interfaces. We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.
papers.summary: AI agents can run auxiliary tasks while a user focuses on other work, but the user still needs to understand task state, make changes and respond when help is needed. This position piece argues that such agents should be **designed around intermittent human attention**, so that tasks continue between interactions and users can return to them with little effort. The proposed `Calm Agent` design connects three on-demand interaction modes, Delegate, Adjust and Check, through a persistent task representation, and is illustrated with `Orvlet`, a desktop prototype for background execution with compact task interfaces. The authors list open challenges including preserving continuity as interfaces adapt, coordinating attention across tasks, and learning user habits over time.

papers.title: Marketing-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Models and Agents on Real-World Marketing Capabilities
papers.abstract: As frontier AI models and agents are deployed more broadly in the real world, marketing is emerging as one of their largest applications. Marketing teams use AI models to produce brand assets like website copy and social media posts, while consumers' agents autonomously discover products, research purchases, and navigate websites. However, evaluating marketing capability is difficult because unlike areas like software development, customer support, or legal review where ground truth is more objectively defined, marketing is subjective, and output quality is judged based on taste and brand. We introduce Marketing-Bench, the first open-source marketing benchmark, which pairs discriminative tasks (detecting brand anomalies) with generative tasks (remediation), while keeping answers verifiable. Marketing-Bench tests five key pillars: factuality, consistency, coherence, structure, and brand voice, all crucial elements for good brand content on the web. We find that frontier models are far from solving the benchmark: the average model corrects only about half of the introduced issues (53.1%), whereas a marketing expert corrects nearly all of them. Even the strongest, GPT-6 Astra, reaches only 74.8%, with Claude Opus and Fable, Gemini Argon, and GPT-6 Sol falling well short. These findings suggest that marketing capabilities are less mature than adoption implies, and that principled evaluation should precede further scaling of usage. Marketing-Bench is a first step toward "frontier marketing models" with superhuman marketing performance.
papers.summary: Marketing output is judged on taste and brand, which makes model capability in this area hard to evaluate objectively. `Marketing-Bench` is an open-source benchmark that pairs discriminative tasks (detecting brand anomalies) with generative ones (fixing them) while keeping answers verifiable, covering factuality, consistency, coherence, structure and brand voice. The average frontier model **corrects only 53.1% of the introduced issues**, whereas a marketing expert corrects nearly all of them. The strongest model, `GPT-6 Astra`, reaches 74.8%, with `Claude Opus` and `Fable`, `Gemini Argon` and `GPT-6 Sol` falling well short.

papers.title: To Critic Or Not To Critic
papers.abstract: As large language models tackle longer and more complex tasks, understanding when a critic improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes increasingly important. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains a critic to reduce variance and provide fine-grained credit assignment, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) drops the critic and avoids the bias of bootstrapping from the critic's value estimates. Although recent critic-based methods have reported strong performance relative to GRPO, it remains unclear when each approach is preferable. We argue that there is no universal answer; instead, the choice depends on several interacting factors, including batch size, critic reliance, and task complexity. We study the bias-variance tradeoff in terms of gradient direction, measuring how closely each method's gradient estimates align with the true policy gradient as batch size grows. Under a shared actor objective, we compare GRPO with PPO in control tasks, short-horizon math, and long-horizon terminal agents. Across more than 1,200 training runs, including 96 with LLMs, we find that PPO generally leads at small batch sizes, while GRPO often overtakes heavily bootstrapped PPO and reaches parity with lightly bootstrapped PPO at larger batches. At longer horizons and in more complex domains, GRPO needs larger batches to catch up to PPO's performance. Accounting for training compute, critics pay off at small budgets, but their returns diminish at larger budgets.
papers.summary: Whether a learned critic helps reinforcement learning for language models is examined by comparing Proximal Policy Optimization (`PPO`), which trains a critic for variance reduction and credit assignment, with Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`), which drops the critic to avoid bootstrapping bias. Using a shared actor objective, the authors measure how closely each method's gradient estimates align with the true policy gradient as batch size grows, across control tasks, short-horizon math and long-horizon terminal agents. Over more than 1,200 training runs, including 96 with language models, **`PPO` generally leads at small batch sizes while `GRPO` catches up or overtakes at larger ones**, needing bigger batches to do so at longer horizons and in more complex domains. Accounting for training compute, critics pay off at small budgets with diminishing returns at larger ones.

papers.title: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls in Resilience4j
papers.abstract: Circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings in Java microservices are tuned once and frozen, although the best setting depends on the fault a dependency is currently showing. We study whether an online learner can pick these settings at runtime. AdaptR4j swaps Resilience4j policies atomically in Spring Boot 3 and lets a contextual bandit choose among complete CircuitBreaker/Retry/Bulkhead configurations from Prometheus signals. Our first, naive design scored worse than keeping the default policy in three of four winnable fault scenarios under the reward it optimised: exploring a menu that contained aggressive circuit breakers rejected most traffic while the learner was still learning. Two safeguards fix this: a safe policy menu (no breaker stricter than the latency SLO) and safe exploration with a bounded reward. With them, AdaptR4j beats the production default in every winnable scenario (p < 0.001, three runs each, run-to-run SD <= 0.03), beats the best fixed policy when the fault changes over time, and cuts user-visible failures up to 3.7x compared with the naive design. A context-free bandit on the same safe menu performs statistically indistinguishably, so the safeguards - not the learner - carry most of the benefit. We also report how an earlier version of our harness produced convincing but wrong results: a unit mismatch made every circuit breaker 100x too strict and rejected calls were invisible to the metrics, so 94% of user requests failed while latency and error metrics looked excellent.
papers.summary: Circuit breaker, retry and bulkhead settings in Java microservices are typically tuned once, even though the best setting depends on the fault a dependency is currently showing. `AdaptR4j` swaps `Resilience4j` policies atomically in Spring Boot 3 and lets a contextual bandit choose among complete configurations using Prometheus signals. A naive first design did worse than the default policy in three of four winnable fault scenarios because exploring aggressive circuit breakers rejected most traffic; restricting the policy menu and adding safe exploration with a bounded reward lets it beat the production default in every winnable scenario, and since a context-free bandit performs indistinguishably, **the safeguards rather than the learner carry most of the benefit**. The authors also describe an earlier harness in which a unit mismatch made every breaker 100x too strict and rejected calls were invisible to the metrics, so 94% of user requests failed while latency and error metrics looked excellent.

papers.title: Structure-Aware Transformers for Hierarchical Authorization in Personal AI Agents
papers.abstract: Personal AI agents can carry out complex, multi-step tasks on users' behalf, but doing so often involves numerous permission requests. Manually reviewing each request is time-consuming, while indiscriminate approval poses privacy and security risks. Predicting users' authorization preferences offers a way to reduce this burden while preserving user control. However, authorization prediction is challenging because permission requests are often hierarchical and observed user decisions are sparse and potentially correlated. To address these challenges, We propose the Parent-gated Authorization Transformer for Hierarchies (PATH) to predict users' authorization preferences for personal AI agents. PATH is a novel neural network architecture that combines hierarchy-aware attention masks with a parent-gated probability formulation to ensure hierarchy-consistent predictions. Hierarchy-level embeddings further support learning from sparse observations and patterns shared within each authorization level. We establish finite-sample risk bounds and provide sufficient conditions for consistent authorization probability estimation and algorithmic convergence. Experiments on simulated data, AI-generated user profiles, and real user authorization data demonstrate strong predictive performance with zero hierarchy violations.
papers.summary: Personal AI agents generate many permission requests, and reviewing each one by hand is slow while blanket approval creates privacy and security risks. The Parent-gated Authorization Transformer for Hierarchies (`PATH`) predicts a user's authorization preferences by combining hierarchy-aware attention masks with a parent-gated probability formulation, so predictions stay consistent with the permission hierarchy, and uses hierarchy-level embeddings to learn from sparse observations. The authors give finite-sample risk bounds and sufficient conditions for consistent probability estimation and convergence. Experiments on simulated data, AI-generated user profiles and real user authorization data show strong predictive performance with **zero hierarchy violations**.

papers.title: PFedHASNet: A Personalized Federated Hybrid Analog-Spike Network for Multi-Subject Motor Imagery EEG Decoding
papers.abstract: Motor imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) data are often collected and stored separately across subjects or institutions, and EEG acquisition and annotation remain costly. Training models solely on individual subject data limits the use of information from other subjects, whereas centralizing raw EEG recordings raises privacy and data governance concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw EEG data, providing a practical approach to leveraging information from multiple subjects. Accordingly, we propose PFedHASNet, a personalized federated hybrid analog-spike network for MI-EEG decoding. The shared encoder integrates continuous-valued temporal features, leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) spike responses, and channel-wise log-variance statistics through learnable fusion weights. Client-private residual adapters and classifiers perform subject-specific feature refinement and personalized prediction, respectively. Experiments on held-out trials from participating subjects across four public MI-EEG datasets show that PFedHASNet achieves the highest mean client macro-F1 among 18 model configurations in cross-model comparisons, while maintaining competitive decoding performance with a compact client-side model in comparisons using the same backbone. Ablation studies further examine the contributions of hybrid representations and personalization components to decoding performance.
papers.summary: Motor imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) data are costly to collect and usually siloed by subject or institution, and pooling raw recordings raises privacy concerns. `PFedHASNet` is a personalized federated learning model whose shared encoder fuses continuous-valued temporal features, leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) spike responses and channel-wise log-variance statistics through learnable weights, while each client keeps private residual adapters and a private classifier. On held-out trials from participating subjects across four public MI-EEG datasets it achieves the **highest mean client macro-F1 among 18 model configurations**, with a compact client-side model.

papers.title: HuluOPD: Unifying Heterogeneous Medical Specialists into One Lightweight Model with Unlabeled Prompts
papers.abstract: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their specialties but hard to unify: their training data are often private, and independently developed specialists cannot be assumed to share an architecture. Deploying these large models separately is costly. We present HuluOPD, an on-policy distillation recipe that unifies heterogeneous specialists into one lightweight VLM using only unlabeled prompts, without requiring reference answers or the specialists' training data. The lightweight model answers each prompt, and the specialist of the prompt's modality supervises its response; a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss makes this possible even when they differ in architecture and tokenizer. We apply HuluOPD to five specialists, for ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography, and dental imaging. To distill and evaluate them, we build HuluOPDCorpus, 914k unlabeled prompts, and HuluOPDBench, 47k held-out test items, from over 90 public datasets, and score all models under one protocol on 132k test items, including third-party benchmarks. A single model with 10% of the five specialists' combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance, and one with 2% retains 89%. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of unifying heterogeneous medical specialist VLMs without requiring their training data or a shared architecture.
papers.summary: Specialist medical vision-language models (VLMs) are strong within their own specialty but costly to deploy separately and hard to merge, since their training data are often private and their architectures differ. `HuluOPD` is an on-policy distillation recipe in which a lightweight model answers unlabeled prompts and the specialist for that imaging modality supervises its response, with a continuation-aligned cross-tokenizer loss bridging different architectures and tokenizers. Applied to five specialists covering ultrasound, pathology, optical coherence tomography, fundus photography and dental imaging, a single model with **10% of their combined parameters retains 94% of their question-answering performance**, and one with 2% retains 89%. The authors also build `HuluOPDCorpus` (914k unlabeled prompts) and `HuluOPDBench` (47k held-out test items) from over 90 public datasets.

papers.title: Beyond Before-and-After Images: Evaluating Temporal Grounding in a Lightweight VLM for Disaster Assessment
papers.abstract: Bi-temporal satellite imagery is central to disaster assessment: deciding what was damaged requires comparing a pre-event scene with its post-event counterpart. A vision-language model (VLM) can nonetheless appear to answer change questions while relying mainly on the post-event image or on the prompt's temporal framing. We present a controlled diagnostic of temporal grounding and apply it to one lightweight VLM, InternVL3-2B, on DisasterM3: 1,659 optical and SAR image pairs from 41 events and nine disaster types, in event-disjoint partitions, with 9,031 reasoning questions.
