We compare post-only input, the true pre/post pair, the post image repeated twice, reversed image order, and an unrelated pre-event image. The true pair scores $+0.5$ accuracy points above the repeated-post control (95\% paired bootstrap CI $[-0.2, +1.2]$), and reversing the order changes accuracy by $-0.2$ points ($[-0.8, +0.5]$). Under this protocol we therefore find no measurable benefit from the content of the true pre-event image and little sensitivity to temporal order. The model is not blind to the first image, however: the true pair scores $2.5$ points above a pair whose pre-event image comes from another event ($[+1.6, +3.4]$). State-transition and multi-hop questions remain hard, and optical and SAR inputs show different profiles. We outline temporal scene graphs as a testable next step, not a validated solution, and argue that temporal benchmarks for Earth observation should report whether answers depend on the intended evidence, not only how often they are right.
papers.summary: A vision-language model (VLM) asked about change between pre- and post-disaster satellite images may answer from the post-event image or the prompt's framing alone. The authors run a controlled diagnostic on one lightweight model, `InternVL3-2B`, using `DisasterM3` (1,659 optical and SAR image pairs with 9,031 reasoning questions), comparing the true pair against post-only input, a repeated post image, reversed order and an unrelated pre-event image. The true pair scores only **+0.5 accuracy points above the repeated-post control** (95% confidence interval -0.2 to +1.2) and reversing the order changes accuracy by -0.2 points, so no measurable benefit from the true pre-event image content is found. The model is not blind to the first image, though, since the true pair scores 2.5 points above a pair whose pre-event image comes from another event.

papers.title: IncrementDET: Continual AI-Generated Music Detection via Enrollment
papers.abstract: AI-generated music has become common on music streaming platforms, and listeners often cannot distinguish it from music made by humans. AI-music detection is therefore needed, but detectors trained on a fixed set of generators often fail on unseen generators. As new generators emerge frequently, updating a universal detector, a single model for all generators, typically requires substantial training data and computation, while risking performance degradation on previously learned generators. We therefore introduce IncrementDET, a detector that learns each new generator by a process called enrollment. For each generator, IncrementDET trains one linear classifier, which we call a needle, to separate samples of that generator from a fixed set of human reference tracks. Enrolling a new generator adds one needle while the previously constructed needles remain unchanged. A Sidak correction keeps the overall false-positive rate at its target as needles are added. To compare detectors under these conditions, we define the task of continual AI-generated music detection and introduce a benchmark in which generators arrive one at a time. The benchmark measures the accuracy of a detector before and after each update and the cost of each update. For this benchmark, we also construct EvoMusicFake-17K, a dataset of instrumental music from six recent generators and four human music platforms. Compared with SpecTTTra, a state-of-the-art universal detector, IncrementDET learns a new generator more accurately from only a few samples, generalizes better to unseen generators and better preserves detection performance on previously learned generators, at a substantially lower update cost. The structure of IncrementDET can also be applied to the detection of generated images and video, where new generators are released just as frequently.
papers.summary: Detectors of AI-generated music trained on a fixed set of generators often fail on new ones, and retraining a single universal detector is expensive and risks degrading performance on generators already learned. `IncrementDET` instead enrolls each new generator by training one linear classifier, called a needle, that separates its samples from a fixed set of human reference tracks, leaving earlier needles untouched and using a Sidak correction to hold the overall false-positive rate at its target. The authors define a continual detection benchmark in which generators arrive one at a time and build `EvoMusicFake-17K`, a dataset of instrumental music from six recent generators and four human music platforms. Compared with the universal detector `SpecTTTra`, it **learns a new generator more accurately from only a few samples**, generalizes better to unseen generators and better preserves earlier performance, at a substantially lower update cost.

papers.title: Do Occupancy World Models Really Follow Actions?
papers.abstract: Occupancy world models predict future 3D scenes conditioned on ego actions, yet their predictions may not faithfully follow the specified trajectory under counterfactual actions. Because driving datasets provide sparse coverage of alternative trajectories for each scene, existing models learn the spatial effect of ego motion implicitly from observed scene--trajectory combinations, which may entangle action effects with scene--trajectory correlations. We propose ReCast, an ego-trajectory-guided transformer that grounds future prediction in action-induced geometric correspondence across ego-centric frames. ReCast decouples historical encoding from future decoding and aligns deformable interactions using relative ego transformations, while retaining flexibility for non-rigid scene evolution. We also introduce a counterfactual action-faithfulness benchmark covering in-distribution, tail, and out-of-distribution trajectories. On Occ3D-nuScenes, ReCast achieves competitive standard forecasting performance while improving counterfactual forecasting, with particularly clear gains under out-of-distribution trajectories.
papers.summary: Occupancy world models predict future 3D driving scenes conditioned on ego actions, but because datasets rarely cover alternative trajectories for the same scene, their predictions may not follow a counterfactual action faithfully. `ReCast` is an ego-trajectory-guided transformer that grounds prediction in the geometric correspondence an action induces across ego-centric frames, decoupling historical encoding from future decoding and aligning deformable interactions with relative ego transformations. The authors also introduce a counterfactual action-faithfulness benchmark covering in-distribution, tail and out-of-distribution trajectories. On `Occ3D-nuScenes`, `ReCast` is competitive on standard forecasting and improves counterfactual forecasting, with the **clearest gains under out-of-distribution trajectories**.

papers.title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination
papers.abstract: Real-world applications of modern AI systems require generalization to both unseen environments and novel human users. The field of zero-shot coordination (ZSC) has focused primarily on deploying AI to cooperate with novel partners in otherwise familiar environments. Popular population-based methods achieve this by partnering the agent with a diversity of simulated human users during training in a fixed environment, but does not consider the more realistic scenario where both the users and the environment are unseen during training. Recently, training across environments has been explored in training a single self-play agent, which shows better generalization on both novel human users and unseen environments. In this work, we ask whether jointly modeling partner diversity and environment diversity yields stronger coordination with novel partners in novel environments. We introduce Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across a distribution of procedurally generated environments, and then trains a cooperator policy against this partner population. To further couple social and environmental reasoning, we add a next-state prediction module that encourages representations to encode both partner behavior and task structure. We evaluate CECP on both a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task, and the popular ZSC benchmark Overcooked, under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions. CECP achieves the strongest performance among the compared baselines and attains state-of-the-art results under our evaluation protocol for human-AI collaboration. We analyze the model's latent representation encoded by the next-state prediction module, showing it can not only improve the performance of the cooperative AI, but also provide more interpretable latents, demonstrated by the inference of partner skill levels.
papers.summary: Zero-shot coordination (ZSC) research mostly trains agents to cooperate with new partners in a familiar environment, leaving open the case where both the partner and the environment are unseen. Cross Environment Co-Play (`CECP`) is a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across procedurally generated environments and then trains a cooperator policy against that population, with a next-state prediction module encouraging representations that encode both partner behavior and task structure. Evaluated on a cooperative foraging task and on `Overcooked` with held-out partners and held-out environments, it achieves the **strongest performance among the compared baselines**. The latent representations learned by the prediction module are also more interpretable, allowing partner skill levels to be inferred.

papers.title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes
papers.abstract:
Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement.
  Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. All benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion as well as multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.
papers.summary: Agreement among language models is not independent evidence for changing production infrastructure, because models share pretraining priors and conform to each other during deliberation. Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (`PIEQ`) is a certification layer that keeps every language model outside the trusted computing base: it certifies diagnostic preconditions from physically separate failure domains, admits a proposed change only if it is safe under every fault hypothesis not yet ruled out (falling back to read-only probes when ambiguous), and binds each approval to the exact execution through snapshot, revision and authorization-freshness checks. Across formal guarantees, automated `etcd` fault suites, software benchmarks and live model runs, it achieves **zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits**, turning agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks. The authors note that all benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and physical failover promotion and multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.

papers.title: Scale-Robust and Global-Aware Representation Learning for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) is an essential task for identifying abnormal system behaviors and supporting reliable operations across diverse real-world applications. Despite substantial advances in MTSAD, two key challenges in representation learning remain underexplored: (C1) how to learn scale-robust temporal representations that capture anomalies across different temporal scales and (C2) how to learn global-aware relational representations that capture inter-series dependencies by incorporating series-level global characteristics beyond local windows. To address these challenges, we propose STAGER, a novel method that jointly learns two complementary representations: scale-robust temporal and global-aware relational representations. Specifically, STAGER employs (1) a scale-robust temporal encoder that constructs a multi-scale temporal directed acyclic graph (DAG) to learn scale-robust temporal representations and (2) a global-aware relational encoder that incorporates learnable series-level global embeddings into the temporal representations and models inter-series relationships through graph neural networks. Two complementary auxiliary objectives further enhance the distinctiveness of the global embeddings. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that STAGER achieves the best average rank among ten evaluated MTSAD methods across three evaluation metrics. Ablation and sensitivity analyses validate the effectiveness of the proposed components and auxiliary objectives, while efficiency evaluations demonstrate that STAGER achieves a favorable trade-off between detection performance and inference time compared with existing methods.
papers.summary: Multivariate time series anomaly detection (MTSAD) methods struggle to capture anomalies at different temporal scales and to model dependencies between series beyond a local window. `STAGER` pairs a temporal encoder built on a multi-scale directed acyclic graph with a relational encoder that adds learnable series-level global embeddings and models inter-series relationships with graph neural networks, plus two auxiliary objectives that keep the global embeddings distinct. On three real-world benchmark datasets it achieves **the best average rank among ten MTSAD methods across three evaluation metrics**, with a reported favorable trade-off between detection performance and inference time.

papers.title: Online Environment Repair for Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Programmatic verifiers provide scalable reward signals for training coding agents with reinforcement learning, yet subtle harness defects and incomplete unit tests allow policies to earn full credit without solving the intended task. Existing training-time defenses intervene either by penalizing suspicious outputs or by filtering flagged tasks and rollouts. However, output penalties leave the underlying verifier exploitable, driving policies to disguise shortcuts under reasoning monitors or zeroing out valid solutions under detector false positives, whereas task and rollout filtering discards or mutes the hardest problems where shortcuts emerge earliest. Pre-training verifier hardening repairs the environment directly, but misses vulnerability classes that surface only as the policy improves during reinforcement learning. In this paper, we propose online environment repair, which leaves triggering rollout rewards unchanged to remove hiding incentives and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training. Candidate repairs triggered by execution invariants or differential fuzzing are deployed only after passing three automated validation gates that block the exploit while preserving valid solutions, canceling detector false positives and enabling structural propagation across repositories without scaffold labels or reference solutions. Across 20 controlled GRPO experiments on heterogeneous software-engineering repositories, online environment repair reduces cumulative reward hacking from 36.9% to 0.06% and improves held-out Pass@8 from 21.7% to 46.7%, consistently outperforming reward-penalty, rollout-filtering, and static-hardening baselines while eliminating zero-shot exploitation on unseen loophole classes.
papers.summary: Coding agents trained with reinforcement learning can earn full reward by exploiting defective test harnesses or incomplete unit tests, and existing defenses either penalize suspicious outputs, which encourages hiding, or filter out the hardest tasks. The proposed online environment repair leaves the reward of the triggering rollout unchanged and asynchronously patches exploited environments during training, deploying candidate repairs found via execution invariants or differential fuzzing only after three automated validation gates confirm they block the exploit while preserving valid solutions. Across 20 controlled `GRPO` experiments on software-engineering repositories, it **cuts cumulative reward hacking from 36.9% to 0.06% and raises held-out Pass@8 from 21.7% to 46.7%**, outperforming reward-penalty, rollout-filtering, and static-hardening baselines.

papers.title: FlashQLA: Efficient Context Parallelism for Gated DeltaNet
papers.abstract: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) achieves linear computational complexity through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism, particularly for long-context workloads with small batch sizes or limited head-level parallelism per GPU. We present FlashQLA, a context-parallel execution framework for GDN that exposes additional sequence-level parallelism while reducing boundary-state preprocessing overhead. FlashQLA reduces boundary-state preprocessing overhead through decay-aware preparation and extends sequence parallelism across GPUs with Dual CP, which shares summary computation across parallelism levels. Workload-adaptive Auto CP and CP-aware kernel co-design further improve execution efficiency. FlashQLA achieves $1.7\times$-$3.1\times$ forward speedup and up to $4.4\times$ backward speedup over Flash Linear Attention (FLA) on a single GPU. On eight GPUs with context lengths up to 1M tokens, Dual CP achieves up to $4.8\times$ forward speedup and $4.4\times$ speedup for combined forward and backward execution over FLA KCP.
papers.summary: Gated DeltaNet (`GDN`) runs in linear time through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism on long contexts with small batch sizes. `FlashQLA` is a context-parallel execution framework that reduces boundary-state preprocessing through decay-aware preparation, extends sequence parallelism across GPUs with `Dual CP`, and adds workload-adaptive `Auto CP` with co-designed kernels. It reports **1.7x-3.1x forward and up to 4.4x backward speedup over `Flash Linear Attention` on a single GPU**, and up to 4.8x forward speedup on eight GPUs with contexts up to 1M tokens.

papers.title: Spec-CoFrGeNet: Reparametrizing Continued Fraction Networks for Stable and Accurate Training
papers.abstract: Continued fractions have been shown to be a function class capable of constructing expressive yet parameter-efficient neural networks. These neural networks are not only effective for supervised learning, but also for training LLMs. However, the rational form of this function class introduces poles when the denominator approaches zero, which prior work has avoided by enforcing a small positive (non-smooth) lower bound. We show that performance and training stability can be highly sensitive to the choice of this lower bound. In this work, we introduce a novel transformation of the partial denominators, inspired by its connection to the Green's function in physics, that mitigates the above issue elegantly by constraining the spectra of the constructed tridiagonal Hamiltonian. Our approach further eliminates the need for incremental training used by previous works for stability, thus avoiding involved modifications to standard pre-training procedures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our reparameterization by replacing FFNs with a previously proposed continued fraction architecture for both language and image generative modeling. Across diverse models, such as GPT-2 XL, (nano) Llama-MoE, and Granite, we show that our proposed method achieves performance comparable to the original (FFN-based) architectures while maintaining ~30%-50% parameter savings as before, and in most cases even outperforms the more complicated incremental training baseline. We further demonstrate, for the first time for continued fraction networks, that their effectiveness also carries over to image generative modeling, that utilize diffusion objectives. On a state-of-the-art Diffusion Transformer, we show that our approach again achieves performance comparable to the original FFN-based models with ~30% parameter savings and significantly outperforms the previous incremental training approach.
papers.summary: Continued fraction networks are parameter-efficient but their rational form produces poles when denominators approach zero, which earlier work handled with a non-smooth lower bound that the authors show strongly affects performance and training stability. `Spec-CoFrGeNet` reparametrizes the partial denominators, drawing on a connection to the Green's function in physics, to constrain the spectrum of a constructed tridiagonal Hamiltonian, which also removes the need for incremental training. Replacing feed-forward layers in `GPT-2 XL`, a nano `Llama-MoE`, `Granite`, and a Diffusion Transformer, the method reaches **performance comparable to the original architectures with roughly 30%-50% fewer parameters**, and in most cases outperforms the incremental training baseline.

papers.title: From Rule-based to Agentic: LLM Agent based Real-time Control of Urban Drainage Systems for Flooding and Sewer Overflow Mitigation
papers.abstract: Real-time control (RTC) for urban drainage systems (UDS) remains hampered by sparse in-network sensing. While heterogeneous multi-modal meteorological early warnings often contain decision-critical information for UDS RTC, none of the existing approaches can exploit such externally-sourced information within the control workflow. Here we introduce AgenticAI-Control, an agentic artificial intelligence framework able to assimilate multi-source meteorological early warnings in RTC. Two coupled large language model agents are integrated to generate control strategies by retrieving meteorological early-warnings and fusing them with domain engineering expertise. Validated via simulation studies of a combined sewer catchment in eastern China across 10 real-world rainfall events, the AgenticAI-Control achieved 69.1-90.6% reduction in aggregated flood and overflow volumes compared to the rule-based baseline control. Rigorously standardized prompt engineering and modular workflow constraints substantially compress performance disparities among four distinct LLMs. Our work establishes AgenticAI as a viable tool to unify multi-source meteorological monitoring and practitioner domain knowledge, surmounting longstanding monitoring limitations of UDS RTC and delivering cost-efficient, robust intelligent control solutions for sensor-sparse sewer infrastructures.
papers.summary: Real-time control (RTC) of urban drainage systems (UDS) is limited by sparse in-network sensors and cannot currently use meteorological early warnings from external sources. `AgenticAI-Control` couples two large language model agents that retrieve multi-source weather warnings and combine them with domain engineering expertise to generate control strategies. In simulations of a combined sewer catchment in eastern China over 10 real rainfall events, it **reduced aggregated flood and overflow volumes by 69.1-90.6% compared with rule-based control**, and standardized prompts and modular workflow constraints narrowed the performance differences among four LLMs.

papers.title: Do Clinician-Scored Examples Help LLMs Code ADOS-2 from Hour-Long Transcripts?
papers.abstract: Large language models can apply a written rubric to a transcript, making automated coding of the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2) look within reach. A common way to align such a rater with clinicians is to show it expert-scored examples, but whether correct labels improve agreement is rarely tested. We test this for eight speech-based items of hour-long ADOS-2 Module 3 sessions from 48 children, with one local model and a pre-registered, placebo-controlled design. We compare few-shot scoring, an anchored comparison in which the model only judges a child better, similar or worse than scored anchors and a fixed rule gives the score, post-hoc calibration, protocol-based evidence routing and direct scoring of the full transcript. On 40 held-out children, agreement with clinicians was modest, with quadratic weighted kappa between 0.22 and 0.30. Replacing every example's label with a wrong one changed about a third of the few-shot predictions, more often towards the corrupted labels than chance, but did not lower agreement, 0.25 with correct and 0.23 with wrong labels. A larger second model did the same. The anchored comparison did not improve on few-shot scoring, its cross-child judgements were no more accurate than those implied by absolute scores, and routing did not help. Among the registered, uncalibrated arms, direct scoring of the full transcript agreed best at 0.30. Exploratory follow-up analyses found that the model's graded judgements ranked children better than its final scores, that existing batch calibration raised agreement to 0.46 on the same children, and that in controlled synthetic sessions scoring episodes separately did not beat calibrated whole-transcript scoring. Expert-scored examples do not by themselves calibrate model-based clinical raters, and claims of calibration or added pipeline complexity need corrupted-label controls and strong baselines.
papers.summary: A pre-registered, placebo-controlled study tests whether showing a large language model clinician-scored examples improves its agreement with clinicians when coding eight speech-based items of the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (`ADOS-2`) from hour-long transcripts of 48 children. Using a local model, it compares few-shot scoring, anchored comparison against scored examples, post-hoc calibration, evidence routing, and direct scoring of the full transcript. Agreement on 40 held-out children was modest, and **replacing every example's label with a wrong one did not lower agreement (quadratic weighted kappa 0.25 with correct labels versus 0.23 with wrong ones)**, a result repeated with a larger second model. Direct full-transcript scoring was the best uncalibrated arm at 0.30, and an exploratory batch calibration raised agreement to 0.46.

papers.title: EffectWAM: Learning Action-Grounded Effects for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: World-action models connect visual prediction with executable robot control. We present EffectWAM, which develops this connection through three complementary components: Effect, camera positional encoding (CaPE), and Action Grounding. Effect represents visual change as the difference between independently encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor. CaPE conditions endpoint pooling on relative camera pose when reliable extrinsics are available, while sharing the same learned parameters with pose-free pooling for uncalibrated trajectories. Action Grounding trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. An exponential moving average of the observation encoder supplies Effect targets. A shared generation expert learns to jointly predict Effect and an executable action chunk through flow matching, and reuses the sampled pair to generate future video on demand. This allows the controller to execute actions without waiting for video synthesis. We train on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, excluding unused chain-of-thought data, and accommodate dataset-specific joint, end-effector, and hand-pose representations. Our evaluation uses the Small (8B) configuration on all five benchmarks and additionally evaluates the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. Experiments examine closed-loop manipulation across complementary benchmarks, and comparisons across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from Action Grounding.
papers.summary: `EffectWAM` is a world-action model for robot manipulation that represents visual change as the difference between encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor, called Effect. It adds camera positional encoding (`CaPE`) that conditions on relative camera pose when extrinsics are available, and an Action Grounding objective that trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. A shared flow-matching expert jointly predicts Effect and an action chunk so the controller can act without waiting for video synthesis, and the model is trained on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data. Across five benchmarks, including `RoboDojo`, comparisons against multiple baseline policies show **consistent improvements from Action Grounding**.

papers.title: More Powerful, Less Verifiable? Mitigating Hard-to-Verify Hallucinations in MLLM's Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) strengthens model capabilities through feedback from humans and environments. However, emerging evidence suggests that reward optimization can produce outputs whose errors are harder for humans to detect. To address this issue, we construct ITHV (the Image-Text Hallucination Verifiability Dataset), comprising 2,728 visually grounded instances that distinguish between obvious hallucinations, which humans readily detect, and elusive hallucinations, which humans struggle to identify. We then propose DAPO-V, an extension of DAPO that maximizes correctness subject to a budget on verifiability-aware risk. Specifically, DAPO-V combines a verifiability-aware reward with adaptive dual control, where larger penalties are assigned to incorrect responses on questions with lower human verification accuracy. An adaptive multiplier further adjusts the penalty strength according to risk-budget violations. Across three MLLM base models, DAPO-V improves overall accuracy while substantially improving accuracy on elusive hallucination questions by 5.78--9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO. We further test DAPO-V with a blinded human study, which shows that hallucinations are more readily detected in DAPO-V than those of the base model.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can produce errors that are harder for humans to detect. The authors build `ITHV`, the Image-Text Hallucination Verifiability Dataset, with 2,728 visually grounded instances that separate obvious hallucinations from elusive ones humans struggle to identify, and propose `DAPO-V`, an extension of `DAPO` that penalizes incorrect answers more heavily on questions with low human verification accuracy and adjusts the penalty with an adaptive multiplier tied to a risk budget. Across three base models, `DAPO-V` improves overall accuracy and **raises accuracy on elusive hallucination questions by 5.78-9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only `DAPO`**, and a blinded human study found its hallucinations easier to detect than the base model's.

papers.title: Integral DeltaNet: Improved Linear Attention with Adaptive Memory Integration
papers.abstract: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a linear formulation, enabling linear-time computation with a fixed-size recurrent state instead of a growing key-value cache. These computational and memory advantages have attracted growing interest in linear attention for long-context language modeling. However, compressing past information into a fixed-size state causes memory collisions that hinder long-context understanding. Although DeltaNet mitigates memory collisions through delta-rule updates and Gated DeltaNet extends this approach with gating, these mechanisms may also discard information relevant to future predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce Integral DeltaNet, which maintains two complementary recurrent states: a fast-updating delta state that captures current key-value associations and an integral state that preserves a weighted history of the delta state. At readout, the model adaptively combines these states to access information across different timescales. We further derive a chunkwise parallel formulation that enables hardware-efficient training. We evaluate Integral DeltaNet using 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B FineWeb-Edu tokens, respectively. Comparisons with strong recurrent baselines show improved overall performance in language modeling, commonsense reasoning, real-world and synthetic retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation. We also compare training throughput and activation memory, as well as decoding latency and memory.
papers.summary: Linear attention compresses past context into a fixed-size recurrent state, which causes memory collisions, and the delta-rule updates and gating used by `DeltaNet` and `Gated DeltaNet` can discard information needed later. `Integral DeltaNet` maintains two states, a fast-updating delta state for current key-value associations and an integral state holding a weighted history of the delta state, and adaptively combines them at readout, with a chunkwise parallel formulation for training. With 340M and 1.3B parameter models trained from scratch on 15B and 100B `FineWeb-Edu` tokens, it shows **improved overall performance over strong recurrent baselines across language modeling, retrieval, long-context understanding, and length extrapolation**.

papers.title: Fix How It Acts, Not How It Thinks: Surgical Fine-Tuning of Frontier LLMs
papers.abstract: Open-weight LLMs are competent software engineers, but they sometimes fail at tasks they are otherwise able to do. Often it is not a failure of reasoning. It is a few small missteps over a long trajectory (repeating a step that has already failed, or declaring the task done while a requirement is still unmet) that make the difference. Correcting this calls for a surgical weight update that steers the model toward the right actions without interfering with its reasoning. Such updates, typically learned with LoRA adapters, are often too small to survive merging into a released checkpoint. In our BF16 release, the median weight change is only 1.5% of a single rounding step, and merging loses roughly two thirds of the update's norm. When the same adapter is merged into the mixed FP8/NVFP4 release of the same model, 93% of the update disappears. Instead of increasing the size of the update, we directly train on the surviving part. We introduce merge-aware fine-tuning. Standard LoRA rounds the merged weights to the storage format only at export, so the loss never sees the rounded weights. We instead round the sum of base weights and adapter update to the release format at every training step, keeping the vendor's quantization scales, and compute the loss on these weights. The forward pass matches the serving engine numerics, and the gradient passes straight through the rounding, so the model we train is the model we ship. The loss optimizes only the model's actions and keeps its reasoning close to the base model. Applied to Nemotron-3.5, the recipe improves agentic coding in both the BF16 and the NVFP4 release, by up to 8.4 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and we publicly release both models.
papers.summary: Small LoRA updates meant to correct behavioral missteps in agentic coding, such as repeating a failed step or declaring a task done prematurely, largely vanish when merged into a released checkpoint: the authors measure about two thirds of the update's norm lost in a BF16 release and 93% lost in a mixed FP8/NVFP4 release. Their merge-aware fine-tuning rounds the sum of base weights and adapter to the release format at every training step, keeping the vendor's quantization scales and passing gradients straight through the rounding, while the loss targets only the model's actions and keeps its reasoning close to the base model. Applied to `Nemotron-3.5`, the recipe improves agentic coding in both the BF16 and NVFP4 releases by **up to 8.4 points on `Terminal-Bench 2.1`**, and both models are publicly released.

papers.title: KKT Atlas: Learning Low-Dimensional Local Scenario Models for Contextual Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: In contextual stochastic optimization, integrated learning trains conditional models on operational loss, but repeatedly solving stochastic programs with many scenarios is costly. We propose KKT Atlas, which partitions contexts into local charts and identifies a low-dimensional subspace per chart from decision gradients of the scenario cost. It generates shared scenarios by jointly fitting subspace coordinates and context-dependent probabilities. We show that one more scenario than the subspace dimension suffices to approximate the conditional Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality condition under regularity conditions, yielding decision and risk bounds under local strong convexity, with generalization error scaling with the compact parameter dimension. On three synthetic problems, Atlas uses 4-18 scenarios per decision versus 500 for direct-solve full-support integrated learning. It attains comparable or lower risk with about $4$-$23\times$ construction and $13$-$61\times$ batch deployment speedups. Atlas also achieves lower risk than clustering-based reduction at matched support budgets. In real-world European grid reserve commitment, Atlas compresses 728 scenarios to 8-9, cutting construction and deployment times by factors of about 4 and 3 relative to full-support integrated learning. Its loss is lowest over 11 quarters and, over 17 later quarters with fixed settings, slightly higher than with full-support integrated learning and significantly lower than with the remaining benchmarks.
papers.summary: Integrated learning for contextual stochastic optimization trains conditional models on operational loss but requires repeatedly solving stochastic programs with many scenarios. `KKT Atlas` partitions contexts into local charts, finds a low-dimensional subspace per chart from decision gradients of the scenario cost, and generates a small shared scenario set with context-dependent probabilities; the authors show that one more scenario than the subspace dimension suffices to approximate the conditional Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) optimality condition under regularity conditions. On three synthetic problems it uses **4-18 scenarios per decision instead of 500 at comparable or lower risk**, with roughly 4-23x construction and 13-61x batch deployment speedups, and in a European grid reserve commitment task it compresses 728 scenarios to 8-9.

papers.title: The algorithmic behavioral sink: Modeling the transition to irreversible demographic collapse
papers.abstract: In 2025, the vast majority of major global economies reported a Total Fertility Rate below the replacement level of 2.1. This synchronized collapse has persisted despite extensive pro-natalist financial interventions, revealing a structural limitation in conventional linear demographic models. This paper proposes that the ubiquity of mobile internet and Artificial Intelligence acts as a synthetic mating disruptor, precipitating a non-linear phase transition in human pair-bonding dynamics. Treating the marriage market as a complex system governed by thermodynamic constraints, we present a Fermi-Dirac selection model, using national income distributions as the input spectrum and fitted with Japanese longitudinal data to illustrate how digital hyper-reality generates an increasingly prohibitive Marriage Energy Barrier. Our model quantifies a Tech Factor that decouples female mating expectations from local economic realities during initial courtship, a distortion we predict will be severely exacerbated as AI evolves into an emotional substitute. Projections indicate that this substitution effect is accelerating; without intervention, the world post 2040 risks entering an irreversible demographic contraction, as the sudden surge in TFR required for recovery is biologically impossible. Ultimately, this framework explains why traditional financial subsidies fail to reverse falling birth rates and suggests that digital convenience may represent a behavioral Great Filter that erodes the imperative for species persistence.
papers.summary: The authors propose that mobile internet and AI disrupt human pair-bonding and help explain why fertility rates remain below replacement despite financial incentives. They model the marriage market with a Fermi-Dirac selection model that takes national income distributions as input and is fitted to Japanese longitudinal data, defining a Marriage Energy Barrier and a Tech Factor that they say decouples mating expectations from local economic conditions. Their projections claim that, **without intervention, the world after 2040 risks an irreversible demographic contraction**, with the effect accelerating as AI becomes an emotional substitute.

papers.title: ExpGuard: Guarding Long-Horizon LLM Agents against Corrupted Experience
papers.abstract: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences. Misleading or adversarial guidance in source trajectories can corrupt these experiences, allowing harmful instructions to persist across tasks and influence future agent actions. Assessing the risks of potentially corrupted experiences poses three challenges: (1) modeling provenance and execution dependencies before experience reuse, (2) learning task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and (3) repairing risky experiences at online inference. To address these challenges, we present ExpGuard, a framework for retrieval-triggered experience risk assessment and online repair. Specifically, to tackle challenge (1), ExpGuard integrates experience semantics with provenance and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risks before experience reuse. To enable task-conditioned risk supervision and tackle challenge (2), we conduct matched counterfactual replays of each original experience and its minimally neutralized counterpart from the same task and environment checkpoint, deriving separate risk labels from differences in attack success and legitimate task completion. To tackle challenge (3) at inference time, ExpGuard repairs candidate experiences flagged as high-risk by the graph-based predictor at retrieval and re-predicts their risks before they enter the agent's active experience context. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpGuard in identifying risky experiences and defending agents against experience corruption.
papers.summary: Long-horizon LLM agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences, and misleading or adversarial content in those trajectories can persist and steer future actions. `ExpGuard` represents experience semantics, provenance, and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risk before an experience is reused, with risk labels derived from matched counterfactual replays of each experience and a minimally neutralized version from the same task and environment checkpoint. At inference, experiences flagged as high-risk at retrieval are repaired and re-scored before entering the agent's context, and experiments indicate the framework **identifies risky experiences and defends agents against experience corruption**.

papers.title: From Memory Access to Evidence Sufficiency: Diagnosing and Addressing Demand--Evidence Misalignment
papers.abstract: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence misalignment through MemPath, an interventional framework that diagnoses failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose BiDE-Mem, which represents questions as typed demands and uses them to guide retrieval and evidence organization. We formalize demand--evidence support; in the evaluated compact path, it is conveyed through provenance-aware evidence organization and Reader guidance rather than a separate generative four-state verification step. On LoCoMo, BiDE-Mem improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis; on LongMemEval, it achieves 91.80%, with strong multi-hop and temporal performance. Supplementary Qwen-Reader evaluations place it first among seven systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S under two judging protocols. Ablations and evidence-level analyses show that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute to answer quality.
papers.summary: Long-term memory retrieval for LLM systems often returns records that are relevant to the query but do not jointly satisfy a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. `MemPath` is an interventional framework that separates failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization, and `BiDE-Mem` builds on that diagnosis by representing questions as typed demands that guide retrieval and provenance-aware evidence organization. `BiDE-Mem` improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over `Mnemis` on `LoCoMo` and reaches **91.80% on `LongMemEval`**, with ablations showing that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute.

papers.title: A Fused Gaussian Process Bandit Framework for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used to maximize expensive black-box functions when direct evaluation is costly. In many real-world applications, the high-fidelity objective can be approximated by a series of lower-fidelity models that provide partial but informative signals at substantially reduced cost. Multi-fidelity BO (MFBO) algorithms aim to strategically combine these information sources to achieve an optimal trade-off between accuracy and evaluation cost. However, existing MFBO methods often oversimplify the complex dependencies between fidelity levels or rely on heuristic acquisition functions that lack theoretical performance guarantees. To address these limitations, we introduce a new formulation of the MFBO problem as a fused Gaussian Process bandit and develop a corresponding Fused Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (FGP-UCB) algorithm. Our approach accurately predicts the high-fidelity function by fusing multi-fidelity observations through an autoregressive Gaussian Process model and explicitly quantifies the uncertainty arising from parameter estimation across fidelity levels. The proposed method also provides theoretical simple-regret guarantees, overcoming a key limitation of existing MFBO algorithms that lack provable performance bounds. Effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated via both theoretical analysis and empirical studies.
papers.summary: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) combines cheap low-fidelity approximations with expensive high-fidelity evaluations, but existing methods often oversimplify dependencies between fidelity levels or use heuristic acquisition functions without guarantees. The authors recast the problem as a fused Gaussian process bandit and develop `FGP-UCB`, a Fused Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound algorithm that predicts the high-fidelity function through an autoregressive Gaussian process model and explicitly quantifies uncertainty from parameter estimation across fidelity levels. The method comes with **provable simple-regret guarantees**, supported by empirical studies.

papers.title: MARGIN: A Risk-Aware Agent for Robot Program Refinement
papers.abstract: Robot-programming agents improve executable control policies through repeated testing and repair, yet binary success saturates while execution risk persists across unseen scenes. We introduce MARGIN, a risk-aware agent that converts successful robot rollouts into actionable evidence for program refinement. Its near-miss margin measures the fraction of the execution budget remaining in the slowest successful development rollout. The agent uses this signal to prioritize fragile programs, guide targeted repairs, and select revisions that preserve development success while increasing execution headroom. An exact safe-racing rule accelerates success-based candidate evaluation. We evaluate MARGIN across LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-90, and Robosuite. In our 80-task LIBERO-Pro reproduction, 78 programs attain perfect development success while accounting for substantial failures on unseen seeds. The near-miss margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774, and low-margin programs exhibit 2.97 times higher failure risk. Across two independent evaluation rounds spanning 37 unique LIBERO-Pro tasks, MARGIN reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0%, with reductions of 18.0-20.0% on LIBERO-90 and Robosuite. Safe racing reduces fixed-sequence candidate-evaluation episodes by 53.5% while retaining identical selections, and paired execution probes improve acceptance decisions by identifying hidden regressions. Together, these results establish near-miss evidence as an effective basis for risk-aware, budget-efficient robot program refinement.
papers.summary: Robot-programming agents refine executable control programs through testing and repair, but binary success saturates on development scenes while failures persist on unseen ones. `MARGIN` uses a near-miss margin, the fraction of the execution budget remaining in the slowest successful development rollout, to prioritize fragile programs, guide repairs, and select revisions, together with an exact safe-racing rule that speeds up candidate evaluation. In an 80-task `LIBERO-Pro` reproduction, **the margin predicts held-out failures with an AUC of 0.774 and low-margin programs show 2.97 times higher failure risk**. `MARGIN` reduces executed control steps by 10.7% and 15.0% on `LIBERO-Pro` and by 18.0-20.0% on `LIBERO-90` and `Robosuite`, while safe racing cuts evaluation episodes by 53.5% with identical selections.

papers.title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments
papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.
papers.summary: `Clinical3D-Bench` is a simulated benchmark of 3,368 questions in eight types over egocentric walkthrough videos of 373 hospital-room layouts, testing spatial skills such as tracking look-alike equipment, patient-relative directions, and passage widths. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), **the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset**. Fine-tuning on the 44,750-question `Clinical3D-45K` set lifts two models 16-20 points above the best proprietary model, yet 3D maps supplied as input go largely unused. The proposed `GeoJeV` instead reconstructs a scene memory from each video and runs selected 3D operations whose evidence is added to the option scores, achieving the highest accuracy of all evaluated models.
papers.highlight_summary:
Hospital assistants need spatial judgments that general benchmarks barely test, such as which bed a piece of equipment belongs to, what lies on the patient's left, and whether a transport bed fits through a gap. `Clinical3D-Bench` measures these from egocentric video, and `GeoJeV` improves on fine-tuning by letting the model call 3D computations instead of receiving 3D maps as input.

- The benchmark has **3,368 multiple-choice questions** of eight types on photorealistic walkthroughs of **373 simulated hospital-room layouts**, with answers computed from the 3D scene, paired scene states that change the correct answer, and layouts screened by ten physicians.
- Across 35 zero-shot models, the best open and proprietary models reach **45.7%** and **53.6%** macro accuracy, against 40.8% for a test-fitted answer prior and **79.0%** for physicians on a 400-question subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions.
- Fine-tuning on the 44,750-question `Clinical3D-45K` lifts `VideoJev-4B` from 45.5% to **73.9%** and its patient-frame accuracy from 17.0% to 93.7%, yet 3D maps fed as input go largely unused, since swapping in another clip's map (even a ground-truth one) changes accuracy by at most 0.5 points.
- `GeoJeV` reconstructs a scene memory per clip, uses linear heads on the frozen model's question state to pick one of three 3D primitives and its arguments, and adds the resulting evidence to the option scores, reaching **75.7%** and dropping to 70.4% when given another layout's memory.
- The gain over plain fine-tuning is a modest **+1.8 points**, route planning (59.5%) and passability (69.8%) remain the weakest tasks, and the scenes are simulated with training and test layouts drawn from the same generator.

papers.title: PreferenceScene: Personalized Indoor Scene Synthesis from Feedback
papers.abstract: Text-to-scene methods turn a short instruction into a furnished 3D room, but the room that a particular person wants rarely comes across fully in words: many preferences surface only when the person sees a concrete room and can point to what they like and dislike in it. We therefore study personalized indoor scene synthesis under hidden user preferences: over several turns, a system shows a 3D scene, and the user, who sees only rendered images of the scene, replies with brief free-form feedback and a satisfaction score. The system must therefore bring the whole room toward the user's preferences from feedback that comments on only part of it at a time. It must also be able to change every part of the room, because a preference concerns not only single objects but the look and atmosphere that surfaces, lighting, textiles, furniture and their arrangement create together. We present PreferenceScene, in which a large language model keeps an explicit estimate of the user's preferences for every design attribute of the room and, after each turn, infers the taste behind the feedback and revises the whole estimate, including the parts that the feedback does not mention. A scene instantiation module builds every estimated value as its own part of the room, so that each of these parts can follow the user's preferences. We evaluate on the test set of a benchmark with 320 instances in ten room types, with a simulated user and a render-based evaluator. PreferenceScene matches the hidden preferences better than five published text-to-scene baselines adapted to the same interaction, and its match rises with every turn. It even surpasses them when they are given the preferences directly, and a vision-language model rates its scenes as the most realistic and functional.
papers.summary: Text-to-scene systems generate a furnished 3D room from a short instruction, but many user preferences emerge only once a person sees a concrete room. `PreferenceScene` addresses multi-turn scene synthesis under hidden preferences: a large language model maintains an explicit estimate of the user's preference for every design attribute, revises the whole estimate after each round of free-form feedback and a satisfaction score, and a scene instantiation module builds each estimated value as its own part of the room. On a benchmark of 320 instances across ten room types with a simulated user, it **matches hidden preferences better than five text-to-scene baselines, even when those baselines are given the preferences directly**, and its match rises with every turn.

papers.title: EEGJev: A System One Decision Model and Benchmark for Multi-Task EEG Question Answering
papers.abstract: A single electroencephalographic (EEG) recording can support multiple decoding tasks. Fixed-label tests cannot show how EEG foundation models handle changing questions or options. We introduce EEGJev, a fast decision model that scores candidate answers in one pass. Our benchmark, EEGJev-Bench, covers six question types across 19 public EEG sources. We held the recording and options fixed while switching between questions about attributes paired during training, such as facial expression and the hand participants were asked to use. Across 13 test sources, EEGJev selected a label for the requested attribute with 99.70% accuracy (49.20% under uniform choice). Balanced accuracy for the specific answer was 62.04%. Its 95th-percentile response time was shorter than NeuroLM's on matched validation questions answered individually. EEGJev lets users switch decoding targets by changing the question. With EEGJev-Bench, researchers can test whether new decoders follow the question more reliably, identify the correct answer more often, or both.
papers.summary: Fixed-label evaluations do not show how electroencephalographic (EEG) foundation models respond when the question or answer options change. `EEGJev` is a fast decision model that scores candidate answers in a single pass, and `EEGJev-Bench` covers six question types across 19 public EEG sources. When the recording and options are held fixed and only the question changes, `EEGJev` selects a label for the requested attribute with **99.70% accuracy across 13 test sources (49.20% under uniform choice)**, while balanced accuracy for the specific answer is 62.04%. Its 95th-percentile response time is shorter than `NeuroLM`'s on matched validation questions.
papers.highlight_summary:
Fixed-label benchmarks cannot show whether an EEG decoder follows a change in the question, because the answer options usually give away which attribute is being asked about. `EEGJev` is a question-guided decision model that scores every offered answer in one pass, and `EEGJev-Bench` tests it by holding the recording and option list fixed while the question changes.

- A `CBraMod` encoder (fine-tuned, then frozen) and a frozen `MPNet` text encoder feed a two-layer bidirectional transformer that scores each candidate at a marker position, with a separately trained head deciding whether to refuse.
- The benchmark covers six question types across 19 public EEG sources with participant-disjoint splits, and on 13 test sources the model picked a label belonging to the requested attribute **99.70%** of the time (49.20% under uniform choice), though balanced accuracy for the correct answer was only **62.04%**.
- On single-attribute questions it reaches **63.8%** balanced accuracy, statistically level with a per-task `EEGNet` at 64.5% and ahead of instruction-tuned `NeuroLM` at 58.6%, while `METIS` and `LEAF` with released weights sit at 43.5–45.0%, near the no-EEG controls.
- It locates events in long windows at **68.31%** against 58.62% for readouts trained on the same labels (a lead whose interval spans zero once sources are resampled), and its 95th-percentile response time is **9.60 ms** on GPU against 24.99 ms for `NeuroLM-B`, but per-task `EEGNet` still wins on paired questions (44.2% vs 39.3% joint) and two-window comparisons (80.8% vs 77.7%).
- Limitations are substantial: replacing candidate names with letter codes drops accuracy to the no-EEG level of 43.5%, refusal scores only 59.2% against a 50% baseline, the model stays at chance on two unseen motor-imagery datasets, many sources have one to three test participants, and the benchmark questions and labels remain private.

papers.title: Duo: Towards Spatiotemporal Action Coordination in Bimanual Policies
papers.abstract: Bimanual manipulation requires each arm to perform distinct motions while coordinating with the other. Common flow-based robotic policies combine both arms' actions into one token per future timestep, giving attention distinct positions across time but not across arms. We introduce Duo, a simple but effective design that models spatial and temporal dependencies within one shared action head. Specifically, Duo separates both arms into two action tokens per timestep, allowing each arm's motion to interact via cross-arm attention during flow matching. On RoboTwin 2.0, Duo improves the overall success of all four base policies, from 0.45B to 3.62B parameters, with gains of 12.55 and 9.02 percentage points for FLOWER (0.89B) and $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.62B), respectively. Despite its compact size, FLOWER-Duo achieves the best randomized-generalization, precision, and memory scores on RoboDojo. In real-world tasks, it outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in both success rate and execution speed, while scaling effectively with increasing training data. To provide deeper insight into the design of Duo, we conduct systematic ablations on inter-arm coordination, action grouping, and token granularity, confirming that cross-arm attention drives the improvement while arm-wise interaction offers the best accuracy-compute trade-off.
papers.summary: Flow-based bimanual robot policies typically pack both arms' actions into one token per future timestep, so attention distinguishes positions across time but not across arms. `Duo` splits the arms into two action tokens per timestep within one shared action head, letting each arm's motion interact through cross-arm attention during flow matching. On `RoboTwin 2.0` it improves overall success for all four base policies from 0.45B to 3.62B parameters, with **gains of 12.55 and 9.02 percentage points for `FLOWER` and `pi0.5`**. The compact `FLOWER-Duo` posts the best randomized-generalization, precision, and memory scores on `RoboDojo` and outperforms `pi0.5` in real-world success rate and execution speed.

papers.title: PhysRF-WorldJEPA: Transforming Heterogeneous Large Language Models into Manifold-Decoupled Millimeter-Wave Radar World Models
papers.abstract: Adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar enables privacy-preserving, all-weather physical scene understanding across darkness, smoke, and walls. However, standard instruction tuning treats continuous radar streams as static text-like tokens, causing near-random global radar-to-text retrieval and severe physical drift under sensor blackouts. Conversely, coupling pairwise contrastive losses (e.g., SigLIP) directly into the shared backbone improves retrieval but injects $O(B^2)$ repulsive gradients that fracture continuous coordinate manifolds ($R^2 < 0$). We present PhysRF-WorldJEPA, a manifold-decoupled Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) that separates continuous electromagnetic state prediction from cross-modal language alignment. An unattenuated 1.0x clock anchor and parallel dual-scale RF encoder feed a lean ~3% LoRA LLM trained with two-step state-space EMA-JEPA (Denoise -> Rollout) and sample-axis Batch-VICReg to predict +3.0 s physical states; a stop-gradient alignment head then maps frozen prompt states onto the text hypersphere with false-negative masking. On a 4,541-window tri-domain suite (77/60.25/60 GHz) against 10 baselines, freezing the physical backbone and training only the decoupled head lifts R->T R@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% and improves MedRank from 107.0 to 60.0 while preserving identical physical readout: 3.37 deg ($R^2=+0.961$) blackout +3.0 s torso tilt, 1.89 m ($R^2=+0.679$; 1.19 m/+0.863 at the RF front-end) cluttered UAV altitude, 2.04 m ($R^2=+0.461$) behind-wall NLOS range, 0.9976 virtual-RIS invariance, and 100% fall recall. Across five 0.5B-1.8B LLM families (15 zero-overhead models), World-JEPA improves retrieval and 75%-drop completion in 10/10 runs and blackout tilt in 4/5 (Span-Euc), 2/5 (Scatter), and 5/5 (per-family best) over SFT.
papers.summary: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar by plain instruction tuning gives near-random radar-to-text retrieval and physical drift during sensor blackouts, while adding contrastive losses to the shared backbone damages the continuous coordinate representations. `PhysRF-WorldJEPA` is a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) that separates the two jobs: a LoRA-adapted LLM predicts physical states 3 seconds ahead, and a separate stop-gradient head aligns frozen states with text. On a 4,541-window suite spanning three radar bands and 10 baselines, training only the decoupled head **raises radar-to-text recall@10 from 5.95% to 15.01% while leaving physical readout unchanged**, including 3.37 degrees of torso-tilt error under blackout and 100% fall recall. Across five LLM families of 0.5B to 1.8B parameters, the approach improved retrieval over supervised fine-tuning in all 10 runs.

papers.title: An Automated Framework Integrating Deep Learning and Anatomical Reasoning for Cardiac Phenotyping From CCTA
papers.abstract: Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) depicts coronary anatomy and cardiac fat, but segmentation alone does not ensure anatomically consistent measurements. We propose an automated framework that combines deep learning with anatomical reasoning for quantitative cardiac phenotyping. Its anatomical measurement module uses graph geometry, branch identity, and surrounding structures to define vessel-specific pericoronary adipose tissue (PCAT) sampling and a surrogate epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) compartment. The latter also generates training targets without requiring expert pericardium contours. A companion module quantifies coronary calcium on non-contrast CT. Component-wise benchmarking was conducted on five public datasets: ImageCAS, ImageCAS-X, COCA, Visual Lab, and MultiD4CAD. On ImageCAS-X Test-160, lumen segmentation with validation-selected post-processing achieved a Dice score of 0.9133 and a clDice score of 0.940, exceeding the corresponding published CAS-Net point estimates. In the four-split ImageCAS evaluation, the four-member ensemble outperformed the single ResEnc-L model. Analysis of 800 paired scans showed that PCAT attenuation measurements differed between whole-vessel and lumen references. External EAT evaluation showed strong volume correlation and good spatial overlap. Explicit anatomical rules make the resulting measurements interpretable and inspectable. In practice, the framework provides a standardized pipeline for processing cardiac CT cohorts and quantifying coronary calcium, PCAT, and EAT for population-level analysis and comparison across studies. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/HarryTRAN207/CardiacCT-Research
papers.summary: Segmentation of coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) scans does not by itself guarantee anatomically consistent measurements of vessels and cardiac fat. The proposed framework pairs deep-learning segmentation with explicit anatomical rules based on graph geometry, branch identity, and surrounding structures to define vessel-specific pericoronary adipose tissue (PCAT) sampling and a surrogate epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) compartment, plus a companion module for coronary calcium on non-contrast CT. Benchmarked component by component on five public datasets, lumen segmentation on `ImageCAS-X` reached **a Dice score of 0.9133 and a clDice of 0.940**, above the published `CAS-Net` point estimates. An analysis of 800 paired scans also found that PCAT attenuation values differ depending on whether the whole vessel or the lumen is used as the reference.

papers.title: Monte Carlo Tree Search for Classifier Chains
papers.abstract: Multi-label classification continues to be relevant to a variety of modern tasks. Among other challenges, modern data sets are increasingly large with respect to the number of labels, and these labels may be noisy or missing in the training sets. Label-wise scores and ranking-based metrics have been popular, but optimising exact multi-label evaluation (where a predicted set of labels should match the true set exactly) is particularly relevant for many domains, e.g., in medicine; alongside some measure of confidence. This requires an estimation of joint probability across labels (a model of label dependence; conditioned on each input instance). A family of methods known as probabilistic classifier chains provides such inference. However, these existing varieties either do not scale to a large number of labels or do so by approximating joint via marginal distributions in a way that compromises the estimation of uncertainty for exact match accuracy. We overcome this issue by proposing TSCC; leveraging a Monte Carlo Tree Search methodology to enhance chain inference via an efficient balance between the exploration of label space and the exploration of promising label-set predictions. Results are promising both in terms of predictive and computational performance.
papers.summary: Exact-match multi-label classification requires estimating the joint probability over all labels, and existing probabilistic classifier chains either fail to scale to many labels or approximate the joint with marginals in a way that weakens uncertainty estimates. `TSCC` applies Monte Carlo Tree Search to chain inference, balancing exploration of the label space against exploitation of promising label-set predictions. The authors report that the method is **promising in both predictive and computational performance**, without giving headline numbers in the abstract.

papers.title: CoverMem: Coverage-Constrained Visual Memory for Budgeted Embodied Question Answering
papers.abstract: Episodic-memory embodied question answering enables agents to answer questions based on previously recorded visual observations of the surrounding scenes. However, growing observation histories, varying observation quality across viewpoints, and limited computational resources make it challenging to construct and maintain compact visual memories while retrieving sufficient evidence for question answering. To address these challenges, we introduce CoverMem, which incorporates three key components: (1) a coverage-constrained memory construction method that selects a compact set of informative full frames satisfying object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements; (2) a coverage-preserving incremental maintenance strategy that locally reselects only the affected frames to satisfy updated coverage requirements as observations arrive; and (3) a budgeted complementary frame selection method that balances question relevance, additional support for question requirements, and redundancy with selected frames within a fixed budget. Experimental results on three benchmarks covering diverse environments and question types demonstrate that CoverMem improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets.
papers.summary: Embodied agents that answer questions from previously recorded observations face growing histories, uneven view quality, and limited compute for storing and retrieving visual evidence. `CoverMem` builds a compact memory of full frames chosen to satisfy object-quality and scene-coverage requirements, updates it incrementally by reselecting only the frames affected by new observations, and at question time picks frames under a fixed budget by weighing relevance, added support, and redundancy. On three benchmarks covering varied environments and question types, the authors report that it **improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets**.

papers.title: EnSurv: Deep Generative Survival Modeling with Application to Kidney Graft Outcomes
papers.abstract: Kidney transplantation is the optimal treatment for life-threatening end-stage renal disease, providing significant survival advantages over dialysis. Given the severe shortage of donor organs, accurately predicting the time to premature graft failure is an essential clinical task for optimizing organ allocation and tailoring individualized immunosuppressive therapies. This study is motivated by a comprehensive United Network of Organ Sharing (UNOS) dataset containing 243,443 kidney transplant records with complex multi-region structures and high right-censoring rates. We propose EnSurv (survival engression), a deep generative survival framework designed to capture complex, non-linear clinical covariate interactions for modeling time to graft failure. Within a pre-additive noise model (pre-ANM) family, EnSurv optimizes an energy score augmented with pooled Kaplan-Meier tail completion to handle right-censoring. We identify the pooled-completion target of the objective, establish consistency for its best approximation within the pre-ANM family, and give conditions and error bounds for its relation to true conditional graft survival. EnSurv also provides global explainability through summaries of fitted feature weights and incorporates domain constraints through established clinical directions using a soft gradient penalty. Extensive simulation experiments were conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed method in comparison with existing methods. Application to the UNOS cohort demonstrates that EnSurv effectively models individual and region-level effects, consistently outperforming baselines across evaluation metrics encompassing discrimination, calibration, and accuracy.
papers.summary: Predicting time to premature kidney graft failure matters for organ allocation and for tailoring immunosuppression, but the data are heavily right-censored and structured across regions. `EnSurv` is a deep generative survival model that optimizes an energy score, uses pooled Kaplan-Meier tail completion to handle censoring, and adds a soft gradient penalty to encode known clinical directions; the authors also prove consistency and give error bounds relating its target to true conditional survival. Applied to **243,443 transplant records** from the United Network of Organ Sharing (`UNOS`), it is reported to outperform baselines on discrimination, calibration, and accuracy.

papers.title: Bit-Flip Attacks on Quantized Neural Networks without Knowledge of Model Parameters
papers.abstract: We show that quantization asymmetry concentrates bit-flip vulnerability in small tensors retained at high precision. CoarseHammer targets these tensors and accepts flips at any bit, without parameter values, gradients, or data. It remains effective under continued fine-tuning. Under ideal placement, CoarseHammer reaches chance accuracy in at least 81.5% of runs on each of ten evaluated models, including four large language models, with median successful runs requiring at most 24 flips. On simulated DRAM with 0.01 flippable bits per million, it outperforms three prior attacks on every evaluated convolutional network, succeeding in up to 83.6% of runs while they never succeed. On a real system, CoarseHammer steers heap-allocated tensors onto vulnerable frames despite address space layout randomization, without accessing the model file. With 16 templated frames, median accuracy reaches chance for all four language models and approximately chance for four convolutional networks.
papers.summary: Bit-flip attacks on neural networks normally need knowledge of the model's weights, gradients, or data. `CoarseHammer` exploits the fact that quantized models keep a few small tensors at high precision, which concentrates vulnerability there, so flipping any bit in those tensors is damaging without knowing parameter values. Under ideal placement it **drives accuracy to chance in at least 81.5% of runs on each of ten models, including four large language models, with a median of at most 24 flips**. On a real system it steers heap-allocated tensors onto vulnerable memory frames despite address space layout randomization, and on simulated DRAM with very few flippable bits it succeeds in up to 83.6% of runs where three prior attacks never succeed.

papers.title: Rethinking Reasoning Effort Training in Large Language Models: On-Policy Distillation or Reinforcement Learning?
papers.abstract: Large language models have shown strong capabilities on complex tasks, yet how to control their reasoning effort remains a significant challenge for practical deployment. This paper provides a systematic investigation of reasoning-effort training, contrasting reinforcement learning (RL) with on-policy distillation (OPD). We find that compressing reasoning and separating effort tiers are governed by different signals. Length-penalized RL reliably compresses a single policy, reducing thinking on AIME25 by 70\% without accuracy loss, but collapses the tiers when they are trained jointly. Multi-teacher OPD separates them: across 33 benchmarks, low and medium use 58\% and 43\% fewer thinking tokens than high, while high improves on the reference policy by 3.1 points. We trace this difference to the training signal. A sequence-level reward cannot tell tier-specific behavior from shared behavior, whereas OPD supplies a tier-specific target at every visited state, including the decision to stop.
