Building on this analysis, we show that a single token-level KL anchor on the high tier is sufficient to learn separated tiers within one RL stage, and that natural-language effort instructions make this separation emerge from the start of training, yielding a policy competitive with multi-teacher OPD at matched thinking length. Finally, the separation built by dense targets holds only on the states seen in training: it does not carry over to unseen agentic tasks, where effort acts mainly through the number of interaction turns, whereas the compression induced by sequence-level rewards does.
papers.summary: Controlling how much a language model thinks at low, medium, and high effort settings is studied by comparing reinforcement learning (RL) with on-policy distillation (OPD). Length-penalized RL compresses a single policy well, cutting thinking on `AIME25` by 70% without accuracy loss, but collapses the tiers when they are trained together, because a sequence-level reward cannot distinguish tier-specific from shared behavior. Multi-teacher OPD does separate them: across 33 benchmarks, **low and medium effort use 58% and 43% fewer thinking tokens than high**, and a single token-level KL anchor on the high tier is enough to get the same separation inside one RL stage. The separation does not carry over to unseen agentic tasks, where effort mostly shows up as the number of interaction turns, whereas the compression from sequence-level rewards does.

papers.title: Interpretable Orthogonal Latent Diffusion with Scale-Selective Uncertainty for Medical Image Super-Resolution
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly used for medical image reconstruction and super-resolution, but their samples may contain plausible fine-scale hallucinations that are difficult to identify from the reconstructed image alone. We propose Med-PODiff, a patch-wise proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) diffusion framework for brain MRI super-resolution that performs generative reconstruction in compact and interpretable local coefficient spaces. Unlike pixel-space or learned-latent diffusion models, Med-PODiff uses the POD structure to separate low-rank anatomical variation from fine-detail residual variation, enabling predictive uncertainty to be decomposed into total, coarse, and fine components. Building on this decomposition, we define a pixel-wise hallucination-risk score, $H_p$, that emphasizes regions where fine-detail uncertainty dominates coarse structural uncertainty. On brain MRI, Med-PODiff outperforms representative diffusion baselines in reconstruction quality while producing well-calibrated predictive intervals, with total uncertainty detecting high-error regions at AUROC 0.954. More importantly, the decomposed uncertainty is scale-selective: coarse and fine uncertainty preferentially predict errors at the corresponding scales, with $H_p$ localizing fine error at AUROC $0.906$. Controlled injections and retrospective Cartesian $k$-space undersampling further support fine-detail localization and degradation robustness. The discarded POD tail is only $3.8\%$ of the retained fine-error magnitude, and Med-PODiff improves downstream segmentation consistency while requiring substantially less inference time than pixel-space diffusion.
papers.summary: Diffusion models used for medical image super-resolution can invent plausible fine details that are hard to spot in the output. `Med-PODiff` runs diffusion in patch-wise proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) coefficient spaces, which separates low-rank anatomical variation from fine-detail residuals and lets uncertainty be split into coarse and fine parts, from which a per-pixel hallucination-risk score is derived. On brain MRI it outperforms diffusion baselines in reconstruction quality, total uncertainty flags high-error regions at an AUROC of 0.954, and **the hallucination-risk score localizes fine-scale errors at an AUROC of 0.906**. Inference is also substantially faster than pixel-space diffusion.

papers.title: VIDE : Training-Free Video Anomaly Detection via Visual Intrinsic Distribution Estimation
papers.abstract: In embedding-based video anomaly detection (VAD), normal clips can have high similarity to anomalous descriptions, an anomaly bias that leads to false positives. Methods such as PRISM mitigate this bias by measuring deviations from a normality reference along anomaly directions. Both the normality reference and the anomaly directions are derived from text and shared across videos, although normal activity and the appearance of anomalies vary across scenes. The resulting scores are also sensitive to prompt selection. To address these limitations, we propose Visual Intrinsic Distribution Estimation (VIDE), a training-free framework that adapts text-derived scoring to each test video using frozen clip embeddings. VIDE estimates normal scene content from clips with low initial anomaly scores and uses this estimate to partially correct the textual reference. It then rescales category responses, penalizes clips with strong responses across categories, and refines the anomaly directions using high-scoring clips. VIDE averages scores across prompt views to reduce sensitivity to prompt selection and fuses scores from two frozen encoders. With both encoders, VIDE improves AUC over the best PRISM result by $1.5$, $1.9$, and $3.5$ points on UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, and MSAD, respectively, and AP by $6.5$ points on XD-Violence and $9.3$ points on MSAD. VIDE yields the highest AUC among the compared training-free methods on all three benchmarks and the highest reported AUC among all compared methods on XD-Violence and MSAD. Our code is included in the supplementary material and will be made publicly available.
papers.summary: Embedding-based video anomaly detection (VAD) suffers from false positives because normal clips can resemble anomaly descriptions, and existing fixes such as `PRISM` use text-derived references shared across all videos. Visual Intrinsic Distribution Estimation (`VIDE`) is a training-free method that adapts scoring to each test video: it estimates normal scene content from low-scoring clips, corrects the textual reference, rescales category responses, refines anomaly directions with high-scoring clips, and averages over prompt variants and two frozen encoders. It **improves AUC over the best `PRISM` result by 1.5, 1.9, and 3.5 points on `UCF-Crime`, `XD-Violence`, and `MSAD`**, and has the highest AUC among compared training-free methods on all three.

papers.title: Calibrated Reading of Latent Reasoning and Communication
papers.abstract: Latent reasoning and key-value communication store intermediate information in continuous representations, limiting direct inspection of model behavior. Existing activation readers trade the low cost of task-specific probes against the flexibility of language-model decoders. We propose the Calibrated Latent Reader, CLR, a compact transformer that predicts reasoning outcomes and message content through task-conditioned interactions between states and candidate answers. Source adapters support transfer across models, while conformal calibration provides coverage and false-alarm guarantees under exchangeability. On two CODI models, CLR improves accuracy over MLP and attention probes by 4-18 percentage points for final-answer prediction and reference-value membership. On CODI-GPT-2, it achieves accuracy comparable to a 1.7B LatentQA-based verbalizer using 437-648 times fewer inference FLOPs. On synthetic Qwen3-4B communications, comparing decoded facts with public commitments detects 93.1% of message substitutions at a nominal 5% false-positive rate.
papers.summary: Models that reason or communicate in continuous latent representations are hard to inspect, and existing activation readers are either cheap but task-specific probes or flexible but expensive language-model decoders. The Calibrated Latent Reader (`CLR`) is a compact transformer that predicts reasoning outcomes and message content from latent states, with adapters for transfer across source models and conformal calibration for coverage and false-alarm guarantees. On two `CODI` models it beats MLP and attention probes by 4 to 18 percentage points, and matches a 1.7B `LatentQA`-based verbalizer with 437 to 648 times fewer inference FLOPs. On synthetic `Qwen3-4B` communications, comparing decoded facts with public commitments **detects 93.1% of message substitutions at a nominal 5% false-positive rate**.

papers.title: ARS-VLM: Visually Aligned Augmented Random Search for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.
papers.summary: Post-training vision-language models with gradient-based reinforcement learning such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) carries heavy memory overhead, while forward-only methods like Evolution Strategies and Augmented Random Search (ARS) overfit to patch-grid artifacts and cause forgetting when applied directly. `ARS-VLM` concentrates weight perturbations on visual signals shared across paired views, anchors shallow visual-fusion layers while leaving deep layers free, and discards perturbation directions that are fragile across views. On `Qwen3-VL-8B` it reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for `GRPO`, and **scores 75.41% across seven out-of-distribution vision reasoning benchmarks against 75.31% for full-parameter `GRPO`, without backpropagation**.

papers.title: RetraQ: Manifold-Constrained Critic Guidance for Flow Policies in RL
papers.abstract: A learned critic can improve a pretrained flow-matching policy by steering sampled actions toward higher predicted value. However, even a critic that fits the behavior data well can provide misleading action gradients. Gradient components pointing away from the data-supported region are weakly constrained by behavior data and can lead guidance to exploit critic extrapolation errors. We introduce RetraQ (Retraction-based Q-guidance), which uses geometry encoded by the pretrained flow to constrain both the direction and the destination of critic guidance. A single velocity evaluation of the frozen flow defines a denoising map. RetraQ filters the critic gradient with the map's Jacobian and applies the map itself to correct the updated action. Our analysis characterizes when these operations approximate tangent filtering and retraction onto the behavior manifold. The same update guides actions at test time and provides targets for policy distillation and online reinforcement learning. In controlled studies, RetraQ improves true return while keeping refined actions close to the data-supported region, and its distillation targets remain more stable than those of raw critic ascent. In offline-to-online training on LIBERO and OGBench, RetraQ achieves higher mean final success than the evaluated critic-guidance baselines. On a real-world plug-insertion task, test-time RetraQ improves the success rate of a behavior-cloned $\pi_{0.5}$ policy from 55.0% to 76.7%. Online training further increases success to 98.3% in only 30 minutes and 100% within one hour. Project page: https://2027ICLR.github.io/retraq/
papers.summary: Steering a pretrained flow-matching policy with a learned critic's gradients can push actions outside the region supported by the data, where the critic's estimates are unreliable. `RetraQ` uses the frozen flow's own denoising map to filter the critic gradient through the map's Jacobian and then project the updated action back toward the behavior data, and the same update serves test-time guidance, policy distillation, and online reinforcement learning. It achieves higher mean final success than the evaluated critic-guidance baselines in offline-to-online training on `LIBERO` and `OGBench`. On a real plug-insertion task it **raises a behavior-cloned `π0.5` policy from 55.0% to 76.7% success at test time, and online training reaches 98.3% in 30 minutes**.

papers.title: Breaking the Binary-Lifting Barrier for DNA Minimizer Density: Exact Optimization of a Native 4-ary Order at (w, k) = (12, 5)
papers.abstract: Minimizer schemes sample at least one $k$-mer from every window of $w$ consecutive $k$-mers via a total order $\pi$ on $\Sigma^k$. For DNA ($\sigma = 4$), state-of-the-art lookup schemes such as GreedyMini and OptMini optimize a binary order ($2^k$ ranks) and lift it to $\Sigma^k$ by ranking one bit-plane primarily and breaking $2^k$-way ties lexicographically on the other bit-plane. At $(w, k) = (12, 5)$, this projection locks sets of $32$ DNA $5$-mers into contiguous blocks and restricts the active universal hitting set (UHS) prefix to $448$ of $1024$ $5$-mers, giving exact expected DNA density $2246214544 / 2^{34} \approx 0.1307468945$ for OptMini (k5-w12-13.txt) and $2248978620 / 2^{34} \approx 0.1309077849$ for GreedyMini (w12_k5.gm). We bypass binary lifting and optimize directly over native $4$-ary permutations ($|\Sigma^k| = 1024$) from scratch via: (i) an exact de Bruijn endpoint transfer-matrix dynamic program over $B(4, 4)$ ($256$ states), (ii) a weighted set-cover ratio initializer (SetCover4) producing a compact $U = 314$ UHS prefix, (iii) bitmask-sparse simulated annealing preserving the zero-cost $w$-walk-free tail invariant, and (iv) two-pass $O(N)$ exact best-insertion sweeps with large-neighborhood ruin-and-recreate search. The resulting explicit $4$-ary order achieves exact expected DNA density $2234289615 / 2^{34} \approx 0.130052772292$ (density factor $1.690686$), cutting charged windows by $11924929$ contexts ($-0.530890\%$ relative) below OrensteinLab/Minimizers and $14689005$ ($-0.653141\%$) below w12_k5.gm at $8200$-byte lookup storage ($1280$ bytes bit-packed). Warm-start relaxation stalls at $U = 379$ ($0.1301728789$), whereas native $4$-ary initialization breaks $32/32$ high-bit blocks across all $2+2$ nucleotide partitions.
papers.summary: Minimizer schemes for DNA sequence sampling are usually built by optimizing an order over binary strings and lifting it to the four-letter alphabet, which locks groups of 32 DNA 5-mers into contiguous blocks. For window size 12 and k-mer length 5, the authors instead optimize directly over orderings of all 1,024 DNA 5-mers, using an exact dynamic program for density, a set-cover initializer, simulated annealing, and large-neighborhood search. The resulting order has **an exact expected density of about 0.13005, roughly 0.53% and 0.65% below `OptMini` and `GreedyMini` respectively**, at the same lookup-table storage cost.

papers.title: Making Evaluation Explicit Is Not Enough: Supervising the Evaluation Process in Generative Reward Models
papers.abstract: Generative reward models (GRMs) make language-model evaluation more explicit by generating critiques, rubrics, or intermediate analyses before predicting a final preference. However, explicit evaluation does not necessarily imply a reliable evaluation process: under outcome-only supervision, a model may reach the correct final preference while producing weak or unsupported intermediate judgments, turning the evaluation into a post-hoc rationalization. We introduce STEP-GRM, a framework that directly supervises the intermediate evaluation process of rubric-based GRMs. In addition to conventional preference supervision, STEP-GRM provides structural guidance for rubric construction and local supervision for criterion-level judgments, encouraging the model to learn not only the correct final preference but also a more reliable process for reaching it. Extensive experiments show that STEP-GRM achieves strong performance on standard reward-modeling benchmarks while improving the consistency and correctness of intermediate evaluations. Moreover, reward signals produced by STEP-GRM lead to better downstream policy optimization, demonstrating that more reliable evaluation processes can translate into practical gains beyond reward-model accuracy.
papers.summary: Generative reward models (GRMs) write out critiques or rubrics before giving a preference, but when trained only on the final outcome they can reach the right answer through weak or unsupported intermediate judgments. `STEP-GRM` adds supervision on the evaluation process itself, with structural guidance for building rubrics and local supervision of each criterion-level judgment alongside the usual preference labels. The authors report strong results on standard reward-modeling benchmarks, more consistent and correct intermediate evaluations, and that **its reward signals lead to better downstream policy optimization**.

papers.title: RightDiff: Learning Generative Reward Models to Judge by the Right Differences
papers.abstract: Generative reward models typically rely on generic query-level rubrics or unconstrained rationales, overlooking the fact that pairwise preference is driven by response-specific differences. Moreover, optimizing solely for outcome correctness encourages models to exploit superficial shortcuts such as verbosity and formatting, triggering rationale drift. To address this, we propose RightDiff, which structures pairwise evaluation into an evidence-grounded evaluation trajectory executed in a single autoregressive generation. RightDiff explicitly discovers contrastive differences between candidates, categorizes them into material or immaterial factors, and induces pair-specific rubrics before final adjudication. To train this process without post-hoc rationalization, we synthesize demonstration data via response-isolated prompts and optimize the reward model with a difference-alignment reward regularized by budget-constrained one-to-one matching and multiplicative gating. RightDiff achieves state-of-the-art preference modeling performance on RewardBench and RM-Bench, surpassing all open-source reward models and leading proprietary LLM judges. Downstream, it provides reliable supervision for direct preference optimization on Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval while effectively resisting length shortcuts.
papers.summary: Generative reward models that compare two responses tend to rely on generic rubrics or free-form rationales, and training only for the correct outcome lets them lean on shortcuts such as length and formatting. `RightDiff` has the model, in a single generation, list the concrete differences between the two candidates, label each as material or immaterial, derive a pair-specific rubric, and then decide; it is trained with a reward that checks whether the identified differences align with reference ones. It is reported to **surpass all open-source reward models and leading proprietary LLM judges on `RewardBench` and `RM-Bench`**, and to give reliable supervision for direct preference optimization on `Arena-Hard` and `AlpacaEval` while resisting length shortcuts.

papers.title: Benchmarking Protein Structure Tokenizers as Generation Targets for Language Models
papers.abstract: Discrete structure tokenizers are the standard way to give a language model access to protein three-dimensional structure, yet they are selected on how accurately they can be read, their reconstruction fidelity, while the property that governs generation is how well a model can write them. We measure this property, writability, directly: holding the base model, data, recipe and compute fixed, we swap only the tokenizer and train the same 9B model to emit structure tokens residue by residue, over eight tokenizers, four compute budgets and three evaluation sets (96 cells). At 2B tokens final writability runs from TM 0.662 down to 0.378 under identical conditions, with five of the eight arms clearing the TM 0.5 mark at which a fold is usually called correct and three falling short of it. Neither codebook size nor reconstruction ceiling explains where an arm lands; the best and worst both use 8192 codewords. What does explain the spread is local structure preservation of the code space. In DPLM-2 a one-bit codeword error costs 0.019 TM where a random codeword costs 0.347, and the trained model's own errors are correspondingly local, at 0.51 of the random Hamming expectation; FoldToken4 fails both tests at the same codebook size and is 0.13 TM less writable. Three controls discipline how such a benchmark may be read. A same-recipe rerun puts the noise floor at $\sigma=0.0067$ TM, which collapses an apparent six-way ranking into four tiers. A reference-free geometry panel turns out to be nearly orthogonal to TM (Pearson $-0.58$), with the worst arm by TM producing the most physically valid backbones. And two pre-registered interventions are null for a reason the mechanism measurements reveal: the quantity they target saturates at 1.5B tokens while TM is still rising. All 131 evaluation cells, including raw generated token streams, are released.
papers.summary: Discrete tokenizers for protein 3D structure are usually chosen by how accurately they reconstruct structures, not by how well a language model can learn to generate their tokens. Holding model, data, and compute fixed, the authors train the same 9B model with eight different tokenizers and measure this writability directly. At 2B training tokens, **generation quality ranges from a TM-score of 0.662 down to 0.378 under identical conditions**, and neither codebook size nor reconstruction ceiling explains the spread; what does is whether nearby codewords correspond to similar structures, as in `DPLM-2`, where a one-bit codeword error costs 0.019 TM versus 0.347 for a random codeword. A same-recipe rerun sets the noise floor at 0.0067 TM, which collapses an apparent six-way ranking into four tiers.

papers.title: Multi-view Random-set Learning
papers.abstract:
Trusted multi-view learning aims to integrate heterogeneous views for accurate and reliable predictions. However, multi-view data often exhibit the view degradation phenomenon: individual views contain only partial discriminative information and cannot independently determine the instance-level label. Requiring such views to produce unambiguous class evidence can distort evidence learning and mislead subsequent fusion. Existing methods addressing this problem have at least one of the following drawbacks: (1) assigning evidence to individual classes without explicitly representing unresolved class groups; (2) projecting composite beliefs onto individual classes before fusion, preventing direct refinement of candidate groups through cross-view set intersections.
  To address these limitations, we propose a new Multi-view Random-Set Learning (MRSL) paradigm, which preserves view-specific support for candidate class sets and refines candidate classes through cross-view fusion. Specifically, we quantify class overlap to select a compact collection of sets for each view, avoiding the exponential cost of modeling all class subsets. We then perform set-level fusion by assigning joint support to set intersections, allowing complementary views to narrow the candidate classes before probability conversion. Experiments on synthetic and eight real-world datasets validate the proposed overlap measure and demonstrate that MRSL achieves the highest accuracy on all eight datasets. Compared with the strongest baselines, MRSL improves average accuracy by 4.71% and reduces average expected calibration error by 6.33%. All datasets and code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
papers.summary: In multi-view learning, a single view often carries only partial information and cannot pin down the label alone, yet existing trusted-fusion methods force each view to assign evidence to individual classes. Multi-view Random-Set Learning (`MRSL`) lets each view assign support to sets of candidate classes, chosen compactly using a class-overlap measure, and fuses views by assigning joint support to set intersections so that complementary views narrow the candidates before converting to probabilities. It attains the highest accuracy on all eight real-world datasets tested, **improving average accuracy by 4.71% and reducing average expected calibration error by 6.33%** over the strongest baselines.

papers.title: Mind the Band: The Hidden Frequency Variable in Geometric RoPE
papers.abstract: Geometric rotary position encodings (RoPE) incorporate 3D camera geometry into multi-view attention by rotating token features according to viewing rays, depths, and reprojected image coordinates. Each coordinate is rotated across a progression of frequencies--its frequency band--yet existing implementations leave this band to inherited defaults, either retaining standard 2D RoPE's top frequency or letting the frequency span grow exponentially with the attention head dimension. We show that this unstandardized setting can reverse benchmark rankings. In novel view synthesis on RealEstate10K, RayRoPE matches the strongest baseline in the 47M model (144-channel heads), yet trails by 1.2 dB in the 25M model (48-channel heads), and exhibits the same reversal when varying head size alone at fixed model width. Populating a 243x range with four frequencies instead of the 3x default at 48 channels recovers 0.9 dB of that gap. Across view synthesis and two-view depth estimation, overly narrow bands consistently blur correspondence, whereas all three projection-based encodings perform reliably when their top frequency lies within 0.3--3 rotations per 8-pixel patch (10--90 rotations across 256x256 RealEstate10K). At the opposite extreme, overly wide bands degrade RayRoPE through a forward-backward asymmetry: averaging rotations over a predicted depth interval damps high frequencies in the forward pass, yet leaves their gradients with respect to predicted depth undamped. Blocking only those high-frequency depth gradients recovers 90--93% of the lost PSNR, showing that forward smoothing does not guarantee backward stability. Guided by this analysis, we distill practical guidelines--setting bands in image coordinates, populating spans in small heads, and avoiding unconditional same-view damping--and advocate reporting and matching frequency bands in future multi-view benchmarks.
papers.summary: Geometric rotary position encodings (RoPE) inject 3D camera geometry into multi-view attention by rotating token features across a band of frequencies, but implementations leave that band to inherited defaults. The authors show the choice can reverse benchmark rankings: on `RealEstate10K` novel view synthesis, `RayRoPE` matches the strongest baseline with 144-channel attention heads but **trails by 1.2 dB with 48-channel heads, and widening the frequency span recovers 0.9 dB of that gap**. Bands that are too narrow blur correspondence, while bands that are too wide hurt through undamped high-frequency depth gradients, and blocking those gradients recovers 90 to 93% of the lost quality. The authors give guidelines for setting bands and recommend reporting and matching them in multi-view benchmarks.

papers.title: A Unified Control Framework for Gradient Inversion Defense in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Gradient perturbations are widely recognized as an effective defense against gradient inversion attacks in federated learning, but they are equally known to impair optimization, creating a persistent tension between privacy and utility. In this paper, we show that existing gradient perturbation defenses, despite their different formulations, can be unified under a controlled dynamics framework, providing a cohesive understanding of their optimization behavior and enabling the derivation of universal convergence and safety conditions without relying on case-specific analyses. Leveraging this observation, we propose ``Near Orthogonal Gradient Projection (NODE)'', which injects perturbations only along directions orthogonal to the original gradient so that the defended gradient maintains a fixed cosine similarity with the true gradient. By preserving the first-order descent direction, NODE substantially reduces the optimization cost of strong perturbations while maintaining effective protection against gradient inversion attacks. We theoretically establish convergence guarantees under standard optimization assumptions and further show that, under mild conditions on the gradient distribution, NODE remains effective in preventing inversion attacks. Comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and Chest X-ray, together with a variety of gradient inversion attacks, demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves an improved privacy--utility trade-off over existing defenses across a broad range of training settings.
papers.summary: Perturbing gradients defends federated learning against gradient inversion attacks, which reconstruct training data from shared gradients, but it also degrades optimization. The authors show that existing perturbation defenses fit a single controlled-dynamics framework that yields general convergence and safety conditions, and from it derive Near Orthogonal Gradient Projection (`NODE`), which **adds perturbation only in directions orthogonal to the true gradient so the defended gradient keeps a fixed cosine similarity with it**. They prove convergence under standard assumptions and report a better privacy-utility trade-off than existing defenses on `CIFAR-10`, `ImageNet`, and chest X-ray data across several attacks.

papers.title: DocPristine: Content-Aware Document Appearance Enhancement under Real-World Mixed Degradations
papers.abstract: Camera-captured documents often exhibit mixed degradations, such as highlights, shadows, and blur, that distort backgrounds and obscure text details. Document appearance enhancement (DAE) aims to mitigate these degradations and improve readability. Existing document appearance enhancement methods rely either on input-derived visual cues that can become unreliable under severe degradation or on LLM-based degradation diagnosis that lacks spatial guidance. Notably, we find that pretrained document visual encoders continue to attend to text regions in degraded documents, providing content-aware guidance. Based on this insight, we propose DocPristine, which adaptively fuses multi-layer features from a frozen document visual encoder and injects them into a pixel restoration network. To integrate these features into a pixel restoration network, DocPristine combines Adaptive Multi-Layer Feature Fusion (AMFF), Hierarchical Gated Conditioning (HGC), and Shifted-Window Cross-Attention (SWCA). Specifically, SWCA draws on structural cues from neighboring locations across window boundaries to recover fine text details.We also introduce DocACE, with a synthetic mixed-degradation training set (DocACE-Synthetic) and a real-world test set (DocACE-Real) containing manually restored ground-truth images and document parsing annotations. Comprehensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that DocPristine achieves state-of-the-art appearance enhancement quality and consistently improves downstream document parsing. Code, models, and data will be publicly available.
papers.summary: Photographed documents often combine highlights, shadows, and blur, and existing enhancement methods rely on visual cues that fail under severe degradation or on language-model diagnoses with no spatial guidance. Building on the observation that pretrained document visual encoders still attend to text regions in degraded images, `DocPristine` fuses multi-layer features from a frozen document encoder and injects them into a pixel restoration network, using a shifted-window cross-attention to recover fine text detail. The authors also introduce `DocACE`, with a synthetic training set and a real-world test set with manually restored ground truth and parsing annotations. Across three benchmarks they report **state-of-the-art enhancement quality and consistent gains in downstream document parsing**.

papers.title: ThinkMorph-SSL: Scaling Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning with Pretext Tasks
papers.abstract: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.
papers.summary: Interleaved multimodal reasoning, in which a model generates intermediate images to guide its own reasoning, usually depends on task-specific demonstrations that are hard to collect. `ThinkMorph-SSL` is a two-stage recipe that first turns visual pretext tasks such as colorization and denoising into instruction-free interleaved traces where the model describes a corrupted image, generates a restored one, and interprets the result, then applies question-driven instruction tuning on automatically constructed demonstrations. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models with the pretext stage beat those trained with instruction tuning alone, and the full recipe improves on the base model by **an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Training unified models to reason by generating intermediate images normally depends on task-specific demonstration pipelines that are hard to scale. `ThinkMorph-SSL` adds a self-supervised stage before that: classical visual pretext tasks are recast as instruction-free text–image–text traces, so unlabeled images teach the model to produce and read visual states before it is tuned on question-driven examples.

- Stage 1 trains on `Pretext-270K`, where seven corruptions (jigsaw, colorization, super-resolution, inpainting, rotation/flip, denoising, deformation) are presented with no instruction and the model must describe the corrupted image, generate the restored one, and interpret it; Stage 2 then tunes on `Instruct-180K`, built from nine automatic pipelines spanning perception, static spatial understanding, and mental world modeling.
- On `BAGEL-7B-MoT`, the full recipe gains an average of **11.33 points** across twelve benchmarks over the base model with 4k-token text reasoning, with the largest gain on mental world modeling (**+17.92**, including **+30.72** on `MindCube`) and **+9.87** on the nine out-of-domain benchmarks.
- At a matched instruction-tuning budget, the pretext stage alone adds **6.49 points** on three representative benchmarks, staged training beats mixing the two corpora on `MindCube` (**66.6%** vs about 57%), and instruction-free pretext traces beat instructed ones by about 2.7 points.
- The headline gains are measured against a baseline that collapses on mental world modeling (25.40 vs 36.42 for the same model answering directly), and the model still trails `GPT-5` on all three level averages and `SenseNova-U1-8B` on both spatial levels.
- Answers depend on the generated images, so defective ones track errors (67.8% vs 47.4% error rate on `MMSI`), and inference is costly even though `TeaCache` cuts FLOPs by **77%**; the authors also report no scaling study over pretext data, compute, or model size, and cannot rule out overlap with the backbone's non-public pretraining data.

papers.title: Blaming the Machine, Billing the Victim? How Mock Jurors Reassign Fault from Generative AI Systems and Respond to Liability Cliffs in Tort
papers.abstract: Generative AI complicates tort liability attribution when people blame a generative AI system that cannot itself bear legally relevant fault. We investigate where this blame goes when fault must be allocated among legal persons, and whether American discontinuous apportionment doctrines influence mock jurors' factual findings of fault. Such doctrines include Contributory negligence, Joint and several liability, and their 50% or 51% variations, all of which have a fault-percentage threshold or a "cliff" where the victim-entitled compensation (or a defendant's liability) jumps to zero (or to all compensatory damages). Our pre-registered human subjects experiment (N=199 Prolific participants) shows that as many U.S. mock jurors (36%) blame the AI system itself, the AI blame often "leaks" to the victim or to the AI user (in 27% to 73% of our AI-blaming records, depending on how leakage is calculated). Although mock jurors rarely change their blame assignment from one side of the liability cliff to the other, these participants do not acknowledge the legal doctrine or its monetary consequence when explaining their changes. Our empirical results illustrate how a narrow doctrinal exception in tort, carving out "joint and several liability" for those deploying or using Generative AI without reasonable care, might mitigate the impact of blame leakage on victims' deserved compensation without introducing significant jury nullification risks.
papers.summary: When people blame a generative AI system that cannot legally bear fault, that blame has to be reallocated among legal persons, and the authors ask where it goes and whether threshold-based apportionment doctrines in American tort law change jurors' findings. In a pre-registered experiment with 199 Prolific participants acting as mock jurors, **36% blamed the AI system itself**, and that blame then shifted onto the victim or the AI user in 27% to 73% of AI-blaming records, depending on how the shift is measured. Participants rarely moved their fault assignment across a liability threshold, and those who did made no mention of the doctrine or its monetary consequence when explaining the change. The authors argue that a narrow exception imposing joint and several liability on those who deploy or use generative AI without reasonable care could limit the effect on victims' compensation.

papers.title: SolarFilNet-V4: Multi-Scale Transformer Vision with Physics-Informed Adaptive Post-Processing for Solar Filament Segmentation
papers.abstract: Solar filaments are cool, dense chromospheric plasma structures held by magnetic field lines above polarity inversion lines. Their destabilization triggers coronal mass ejections and severe space weather hazards. Segmenting individual filaments from ground-based GONG H-alpha observations (2048 x 2048 pixels) is challenging due to low contrast, turbulent fibrils, delicate barb structures, and annotator boundary variance. In this technical report, we describe SolarFilNet-V4, a targeted segmentation framework developed for the MAGFiLO 1.0 benchmark (Solar Filament Segmentation Challenge 2026). Our method couples a lightweight Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT-v2-B1) backbone with anisotropic curvilinear strip convolutions (k=15) and dual-frequency feed-forward blocks (DFFN) to follow extended flux ropes while capturing thin central spines. A shallow full-resolution convolutional branch operating at 1024 x 1024 preserves high-frequency edge details and mitigates transformer downsampling. We train the network using multi-task supervision over masks, centerline spines, barb boundaries, and pixel-contrastive representations. At test time, we apply 8-fold dihedral test-time augmentation (D4), bilinearly upscale predictions to the native 2048 x 2048 grid, and apply an activity-adaptive post-processing routine that calibrates morphological joining parameters for quiet versus active solar disks. On the official benchmark, SolarFilNet-V4 achieves an out-of-fold validation Panoptic Quality of 0.4340 and a Public Leaderboard score of 0.380. The model contains 15.46M parameters and requires 224.34 GFLOPs per forward pass, reducing parameter count by 36.8% compared to standard ResNet-34 U-Net baselines.
papers.summary: Segmenting individual solar filaments in 2048 x 2048 ground-based H-alpha images is difficult because of low contrast, turbulent fibrils, thin barb structures, and inconsistent annotation boundaries. This technical report describes `SolarFilNet-V4`, an entry for the `MAGFiLO 1.0` benchmark that pairs a lightweight `PVT-v2-B1` Pyramid Vision Transformer backbone with long strip convolutions, a full-resolution convolutional branch, and multi-task supervision over masks, centerlines, barb boundaries, and pixel-contrastive representations, followed by test-time augmentation and post-processing tuned separately for quiet and active solar disks. It reaches **an out-of-fold validation Panoptic Quality of 0.4340** and a public leaderboard score of 0.380, using 15.46M parameters, which is 36.8% fewer than standard `ResNet-34` `U-Net` baselines.

papers.title: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction
papers.abstract: Request-derived authorizers such as Progent protect LLM agents from prompt injection by deriving what an agent may do from the user's request. Their guarantee rests on attribution: the request is taken to be what the user said. Compaction breaks it. At every automatic compaction we observed, Claude Code and Codex placed a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user message, so the compactor's quotation of the user, documents and injected text reads as the user speaking. Because a policy frozen at the first request lets the agent finish few later tasks, we let Progent derive its policy for each request, and find that what it grants then follows what the compactor wrote. Even a payee the user stated is not safe: when an attacker's notice states another account as plain data and the user asks to pay the rent, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary admits the notice's account in 91% of cases, and the one derived from the user's own words in none. The cause is general: we prove that an authorizer that cannot see who wrote which bytes cannot treat a forged record differently from the legitimate one it imitates by more than the two are distinguishable, and that the bound is tight. Frontier compactors bear this out: they mark injected instructions, which have no legitimate twin, but rarely injected data, which does. What a compactor keeps, and how it marks it, is a security parameter. The fix follows from attribution: the authorizer credits only what the user said, authenticated on arrival and carried verbatim across the boundary, while the agent still reads the summary. We prove that it then receives exactly that text or nothing, so an attacker can block the policy but cannot shape it, and adaptive attacks on our implementation confirm it. In 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes re-run with the fix, no attacker action completes while the agent reads the summary.
papers.summary: Authorizers such as `Progent` defend large language model (LLM) agents against prompt injection by deriving what the agent may do from the user's request, which assumes the request really is what the user said. The authors observe that `Claude Code` and `Codex` insert a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user message at every automatic compaction they examined, so text quoted from documents or injected content is read as the user speaking. In a rent-payment scenario where an attacker's notice states a different account as plain data, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary **admits the attacker's account in 91% of cases**, against none when the policy is derived from the user's own words. They prove a tight bound on what an authorizer can do without knowing who wrote which bytes, and propose carrying authenticated user text verbatim across the compaction boundary, under which no attacker action completed in 40 attacked `AgentDojo` episodes.

papers.title: When Answering Is Administering: Permission Replies That Rewrite Coding-Agent Policy
papers.abstract:
Coding agents let plugins and remote services answer permission prompts, and Claude Code documents that such an answer cannot override the operator's deny rules. However, we show that this guarantee, checked one decision at a time, fails over a whole run, because an answer to one permission prompt can rewrite the policy that every later answer is checked against. For example, a remote service with no access to the operator's files approves an unrelated command and attaches an update that deletes the deny rule protecting the project's secrets. The agent then reads the secrets in that session and the next, even inside the vendor's strict sandbox. The root cause is that Claude Code checks only updates that add or replace allow rules. Relays that forward such deletions already exist, including the vendor's own Remote Control. In effect, the right to answer a prompt has become the right to administer the policy. Worse, the deletion leaves the same records as a local edit by the operator, so Claude Code cannot tell who wrote a rule.
  More generally, what a runtime records decides what it can safely delegate. A runtime that cannot tell who wrote a rule can accept only updates that keep every currently denied call denied, whereas, to protect every party's restrictions, a runtime that records who wrote each rule can let each party remove only the restrictions proven to be its own. We prove that these two bounds are tight. They correctly predict whether the operator's restrictions survive in all thirteen permission designs across ten agent systems, including predictions we wrote down before running Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode, and Goose. Enforcing the bounds at the shared update step blocks the attack. A survey of 2,227 fetched marketplace plugins finds only two that send policy updates.
papers.summary: Coding agents let plugins and remote services answer permission prompts, and `Claude Code` documents that such answers cannot override the operator's deny rules. The authors show that this guarantee fails across a whole run because a reply to one prompt can carry a policy update, and `Claude Code` checks only updates that add or replace allow rules, so **a remote service can delete the deny rule protecting a project's secrets** and the agent then reads them in that session and the next. They prove two tight bounds on what a runtime can safely delegate, depending on whether it records who wrote each rule, and these bounds correctly predict whether operator restrictions survive in all thirteen permission designs across ten agent systems, including `Codex`, `Gemini CLI`, `opencode`, and `Goose`. Enforcing the bounds at the shared update step blocks the attack, and a survey of 2,227 marketplace plugins finds only two that send policy updates.

papers.title: Steerable by Design: Conditional Pretraining for Robust Control of Language Models
papers.abstract: Our goal is to build language models that are steerable by design. Today's language models are pretrained with next-token prediction, which relegates alignment and control to the final 1% of training tokens or inference-time interventions. These models repurpose a single input channel for both instructions and data, leading to common failure modes where the model mistakenly treats data as instructions such as intentional jailbreaks and unintentional in-context alignment drift. To correct this, we propose a pretraining method and architecture that separates the two from the very start, producing Mancelle-3B. An encoder processes high-level semantic features of upcoming text with cross-attention that prevents the token stream from writing back into this control channel. During pretraining, the model learns to rely on these features to predict the next token, turning the channel into an effective handle for steering the model. Mancelle-3B steers more strongly than prompt- and activation-based methods on comparable open models while maintaining fluency, and it withstands adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering that defeats those baselines. We reproduce this against a more controlled baseline with Mancelle-400M. Our results show that robust control can be built into language models if we do so early and intentionally.
papers.summary: Language models pretrained purely on next-token prediction use one input channel for both instructions and data, which leads to failures such as jailbreaks and drift in behavior over a long context. The authors propose a pretraining method and architecture that separates the two from the start: an encoder processes high-level semantic features of the upcoming text, and cross-attention keeps the token stream from writing back into this control channel, so the model learns to rely on it during pretraining. The resulting `Mancelle-3B` steers more strongly than prompt-based and activation-based methods on comparable open models while staying fluent, and it **withstands adversarial black-box and soft-prompt counter-steering that defeats those baselines**. The result is reproduced against a more controlled baseline with `Mancelle-400M`.

papers.title: Who gets the information? An $\alpha$-fair label-coverage framework for multi-label feature selection
papers.abstract: Recent information-theoretic filters for multi-label feature selection disagree on how to distribute relevance over labels: some amplify features that inform a few labels, others balance what every label receives. We show these choices are implicit social welfare functions. Treating labels as agents whose utility is the information they receive, we propose FLIC, which greedily maximises the $\alpha$-fair welfare of per-label information coverage. A single parameter $\alpha$ moves from utilitarian ($\alpha=0$) through proportionally fair ($\alpha=1$) to max-min selection ($\alpha\to\infty$), and a dozen published relevance terms lie on this axis, most as special cases, first-order approximations or limits. The objective is monotone submodular for every $\alpha\ge0$ whenever each label's information is, so greedy selection is a $(1-1/e)$-approximation; this fails for $\alpha<0$, and the max-min limit is inapproximable. Fano's and the Hellman-Raviv inequalities tie raw coverage to the Bayes Hamming loss and normalised coverage to per-label relative error. FLIC uses bias-corrected, label-wise conditional information and has no relevance-redundancy trade-off parameter. On 22 data sets, FLIC is the best of 14 information-theoretic filters on seven of nine metrics, winning 86 of 117 pairwise comparisons significantly and losing none significantly. Among 17 methods it ranks first on ranking loss, coverage and macro-AUC with two classifiers and has the best mean rank (narrowly with ML-kNN), while three embedded methods lead on Hamming loss, one-error and micro-F1.
papers.summary: Information-theoretic filters for multi-label feature selection disagree on how to spread relevance across labels, and the authors show that these choices amount to implicit social welfare functions over labels treated as agents. Their method `FLIC` greedily maximises an alpha-fair welfare of per-label information coverage, where one parameter moves from utilitarian through proportionally fair to max-min selection and a dozen published relevance terms fall on the same axis. The objective is monotone submodular for every non-negative alpha, which gives greedy selection a (1-1/e) approximation guarantee. On 22 data sets `FLIC` is the best of 14 information-theoretic filters on seven of nine metrics, **winning 86 of 117 pairwise comparisons significantly and losing none significantly**, although three embedded methods lead on Hamming loss, one-error, and micro-F1.

papers.title: OmniEVIE: Evidence-Vector-Informed Embedding for Multi-modal Retrieval
papers.abstract: Multimodal retrieval must match dense pages, fine-grained entities, ordered video, and agent tools and memory. Single-vector embeddings lose local evidence, cross-encoders reread every recalled item online, and uncompressed late interaction is too large to serve. We present OmniEVIE, a 4.5B multi-vector embedding model covering text, images, visual documents, video, and tools with one compressed index and a three-stage retriever. Each record stores at most 128 int8 vectors of dimension 64 (9,472 bytes, or 8.82 GiB per million records), providing a mean vector, 1-bit signs, and int8 multi-vectors for coarse, middle, and final search while localizing each hit to a page region or video interval. Training, merging, indexing, and retrieval are co-designed: all tasks share one retrieval format, a three-grade evidence check removes false negatives, dynamic sampling follows the baseline-teacher gap, candidates are compressed with ST-HAC during training to match the index, stage-wise and specialist models are merged by parameter block, and a saliency gate with a noise floor refines query scoring. Trained on public datasets, OmniEVIE scores 60.68 (full d=2048 sequence) and 60.06 (K128 x d64 int8 index) on MMEB-V3 (190 tasks), 77.96 on MMEB-V2 (78 tasks), and 62.96 on ViDoRe V3 (48 tasks). On 1M and 5M records, a single-thread query takes 54.2 ms and 120.2 ms (11.1x and 25.3x faster than exact 4096-d single-vector search; 236x and 532x faster than full int8 MaxSim). Video is encoded directly from frames without a parsing model: on QVHighlights (1,083 queries), the peak falls inside the labeled segment for 78.0% of queries and the returned span (18% of video length) intersects it for 94.3% vs. 44.9% random. Weights and code: https://huggingface.co/tencent/OmniEVIE-4B and https://github.com/Tencent/OmniEVIE.
papers.summary: Multimodal retrieval faces a trade-off in which single-vector embeddings lose local evidence, cross-encoders must reread every candidate at query time, and uncompressed late interaction is too large to serve. `OmniEVIE` is a 4.5B-parameter multi-vector embedding model for text, images, visual documents, video, and agent tools that stores at most 128 int8 vectors of dimension 64 per record, about 9.5 kilobytes, and searches them in three stages from coarse to fine. Trained on public datasets, it scores **60.06 on `MMEB-V3` with the compressed index, against 60.68 with the full uncompressed sequence**, along with 77.96 on `MMEB-V2` and 62.96 on `ViDoRe V3`. A single-thread query over one million records takes 54.2 ms, which is 11.1x faster than exact 4096-dimensional single-vector search, and weights and code are released.

papers.title: XMind: Thinking Twice via Cross-Memory Reasoning for LLM-Based Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Memory-augmented large language model (LLM) driving agents can reuse past experience, yet previously learned corrections often fail to transfer when traffic conditions change. A key limitation is that existing memories mainly record observed outcomes, providing little evidence about alternative actions. We introduce XMind, a training-free framework that enables LLM-based driving to "Think Twice" through cross-memory reasoning. XMind integrates working memory of recent traffic states with episodic memory of critical risk events. The agent first makes an initial decision from the current context and then cross-checks it against retrieved historical experience. If a conflict arises, it makes a second decision guided by the retrieved evidence. To construct reliable episodic memory, XMind evaluates alternative actions through counterfactual rollouts under perturbed traffic conditions and stores the verified outcomes as structured risk capsules. These capsules are retrieved by jointly matching spatial risk patterns and scenario semantics. Across closed-loop highway simulations, XMind achieves success rates of 83.3-93.3%, exceeding the strong baseline by 6.6 percentage points on average. Evaluation on K-Risk further demonstrates lower decision risk on unseen real-world high-risk interactions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of working memory, risk-text retrieval, and counterfactual verification. Code is available at https://github.com/xiangxiangliuwo/XMind
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) driving agents that keep a memory of past experience often fail to transfer learned corrections when traffic conditions change, partly because their memories record only observed outcomes and say little about alternative actions. `XMind` is a training-free framework in which the agent makes an initial decision, cross-checks it against retrieved episodic memories of critical risk events, and makes a second decision if the two conflict. Those memories are built by evaluating alternative actions through counterfactual rollouts under perturbed traffic conditions and storing the verified outcomes. In closed-loop highway simulations it achieves success rates of 83.3 to 93.3%, **exceeding the strong baseline by 6.6 percentage points on average**, and it shows lower decision risk on the real-world high-risk interactions in `K-Risk`.

papers.title: ArEssays: Towards Robust Arabic Handwritten Text Understanding in Educational Settings
papers.abstract:
Automated understanding of handwritten Arabic student essays remains challenging due to script complexity and high variability
  in children's writing. We introduce ArEssays, a large-scale dataset of authentic essays from primary to secondary students
  across Egypt, with both verbatim transcriptions and linguistically corrected versions. We benchmark 34 vision-language and OCR
  models, including fine-tuned systems, and find large performance gaps on real student handwriting. We release the dataset,
  training pipelines, and results to support research in Arabic OCR, document understanding, and educational NLP.
papers.summary: Handwritten Arabic essays by school students are hard to read automatically because of the script's complexity and the variability of children's writing. `ArEssays` is a large-scale dataset of authentic essays from primary to secondary students across Egypt, with both verbatim transcriptions and linguistically corrected versions. A benchmark of 34 vision-language and optical character recognition models, including fine-tuned systems, finds **large performance gaps on real student handwriting**. The dataset, training pipelines, and results are released.

papers.title: PoseVLN: Learning Geometric State Evolution for Vision-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to relate past experience, current spatial state, and future motion while following natural-language instructions. Recent approaches improve these capabilities through long-horizon memory, state-aware reasoning, and future prediction, yet these components are often modeled separately, leaving navigation state evolution insufficiently connected across time. We argue that camera pose provides a natural geometric representation for bridging past, present, and future states. Based on this insight, we propose PoseVLN, a pose-aware VLN framework that jointly learns navigation decisions and geometric state evolution. PoseVLN organizes visual memory and the current observation in an episode-relative coordinate frame, and jointly predicts the next K navigation actions together with a local $\Delta$Pose over the same horizon. The predicted $\Delta$Pose is composed with the current trajectory-level pose to obtain the future pose state, which is recursively propagated throughout navigation, forming a continuous geometric state evolution from past memory to future motion. Experiments on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE Val-Unseen splits demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly modeling geometric state evolution, with PoseVLN outperforming the strongest compared baselines by 2.6 and 2.9 percentage points in success rate, respectively, using only single RGB observations.
papers.summary: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to connect past experience, its current spatial state, and future motion while following natural-language instructions, but memory, state reasoning, and future prediction are often modeled separately. `PoseVLN` uses camera pose as a shared geometric representation: it organizes visual memory and the current observation in an episode-relative coordinate frame and jointly predicts the next several actions together with the pose change over the same horizon, which is then propagated recursively through the episode. On the `R2R-CE` and `RxR-CE` Val-Unseen splits it **outperforms the strongest compared baselines by 2.6 and 2.9 percentage points in success rate**, using only single RGB observations.

papers.title: Beyond Autoregression: Diffusion Language Model is All Analog In-Memory Computing Need
papers.abstract: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) enables energy-efficient language-model inference, but hardware non-idealities perturb matrix--vector multiplications and degrade generation quality. Autoregressive (AR) models are especially vulnerable: each token is committed to the causal context at birth, so perturbation-induced errors cascade. We study diffusion language models (DLMs), which iteratively refine a masked sequence, as an alternative paradigm. Across scale-matched model pairs and open checkpoints, DLMs degrade more gracefully than AR counterparts under persistent weight perturbations. Controlled analyses rule out cross-round noise averaging and support delayed token commitment and progressive context resolution as the mechanism. A larger denoising-step budget further shrinks the clean--noisy gap, a DLM-specific latency--robustness knob. We perform large-scale simulation tests across diverse datasets and models using a noise model calibrated from real silicon measurements. Furthermore, on a 16-chip 28nm eFlash AIMC cluster, hybrid on-board measurements show DLMs tolerate $1.4$--$3\times$ larger weight noise, making diffusion-based generation a promising paradigm for noise-resilient AIMC inference.
papers.summary: Analog in-memory computing (AIMC) offers energy-efficient language-model inference, but hardware imperfections perturb matrix-vector multiplications, and autoregressive models are especially exposed because each token is committed to the context as soon as it is generated, so errors cascade. The authors study diffusion language models (DLMs), which iteratively refine a masked sequence, and find across scale-matched model pairs and open checkpoints that they degrade more gracefully under persistent weight perturbations. Controlled analyses attribute this to delayed token commitment and progressive context resolution, not to noise averaging across rounds, and more denoising steps further narrow the gap between clean and noisy output. Measurements on a 16-chip 28nm eFlash AIMC cluster show that DLMs **tolerate 1.4 to 3 times larger weight noise**.

papers.title: Joint Classification and Generation on Tabular Data: an Empirical Study
papers.abstract: Many applications of machine learning on tabular data need both a classifier and a generator of realistic records. The default is to train two separate models, whereas a single joint model promises both from one set of weights. Several families of tabular deep learning models can be turned into such a joint model, which raises the question of which joint model is preferable at which computational budget. In this empirical study, we introduce and compare joint models based on four state-of-the-art tabular data modeling families (energy-based models, probabilistic circuits, tabular foundation models and tabular diffusion models) against measured FLOPs and wall-clock time, on 29 classification datasets. Methods are evaluated based on two defined aggregate scores that take into account different aspects of prediction and generation. We then also compare these joint models with every pair of a separate classifier and generator at different computational budgets, to see when a joint model may be a defendible choice against the regular practice of keeping a separate classifier and generator. We find that the best joint model is a probabilistic circuit at the smallest budgets and, beyond that, a tabular foundation model that generates column by column using a regressor (TabICL). Compared with pairs of separate models, this study finds a joint model is rarely preferable but often very close to the best pair, without the hassle of training and maintaining two separate models.
papers.summary: Many tabular applications need both a classifier and a generator of realistic records, and the usual practice is to train two separate models even though a single joint model could provide both. This empirical study builds joint models from four families, namely energy-based models, probabilistic circuits, tabular foundation models, and tabular diffusion models, and compares them on 29 classification datasets against measured compute and wall-clock time, including against every pairing of a separate classifier and generator. The best joint model is a probabilistic circuit at the smallest budgets and, beyond that, a tabular foundation model based on `TabICL` that generates records column by column. A joint model is **rarely preferable to the best separate pair but often very close to it**.

papers.title: Relational Bottleneck Models
papers.abstract: Achieving both interpretable and high-performance inference is a key challenge in deep learning. While Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) provide inherent interpretability, they are constrained by task-specific training and rely on isolated visual concepts that fail to capture higher-order visual semantic relationships. Conversely, Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate zero-shot capabilities through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. However, standard CoT lacks a strict causal dependency between the generated rationale and the final output, compromising faithfulness. To bridge this gap, we propose Relational Bottleneck Models (RBMs), a novel training-free framework that transforms any off-the-shelf LVLMs into inherently interpretable models in a plug-and-play manner. RBMs consist of two stages: (i) Structured Rationale Generation (SRG), which explicitly models semantic interactions between visual concepts as subject-predicate-object triplets, and (ii) Rationale-Grounded Decoding (RGD), which enforces a strict causal dependency between the rationales and the final output. RGD aggregates rationale-conditional next-token distributions via an importance-weighted product-of-experts strategy, strictly excluding the image inputs from the decoding context. Extensive zero-shot evaluations across diverse benchmarks and LVLM backbones demonstrate that RBMs achieve superior interpretability while improving task performance over CBM baselines, entirely without task-specific fine-tuning.
papers.summary: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) are interpretable but need task-specific training and rely on isolated visual concepts, while Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) using Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning give no guarantee that the final answer actually depends on the stated rationale. Relational Bottleneck Models (`RBMs`) are a training-free framework that first has an off-the-shelf LVLM generate rationales as subject-predicate-object triplets describing relations between visual concepts, then decodes the answer from those rationales alone by combining rationale-conditional next-token distributions with an importance-weighted product of experts, with the image excluded from the decoding context. In zero-shot evaluations across several benchmarks and LVLM backbones, the method **improves both interpretability and task performance over CBM baselines without any task-specific fine-tuning**.

papers.title: MYSTIQUE: Few-Shot Facial Identity Transfer with Performance Preservation
papers.abstract: In visual effects, identity transfer replaces the identity in a driving image with that of a target person, while preserving the expression, lighting, pose and scene of that image. Paired ground truth is rarely available, so many methods are trained by self-reconstruction, where the model can learn a shortcut by copying identity cues from the driving image. This shortcut causes identity leakage at inference, where the driving image shows a different person. Our key observation is that leakage can enter through any input that reads the driving image. We therefore present MYSTIQUE, a diffusion-based identity transfer method that takes identity from a set of the target's photos and reads expression, lighting and scene through separate streams. It learns to disentangle identity from the other streams through multi-stage training, with disentanglement strategies at their inputs: a random block mask whose boundaries do not follow the face outline, self-augmentation, which randomly changes the face shape in the expression input and keeps its expression, and face randomization, which replaces the person in the expression and lighting inputs while the ground truth stays the driving image. At inference, we also warp the lighting input onto the face shape of a first pass, which reduces face-shape leakage through the lighting stream. Since face-recognition scores and human judgments each have limits, we evaluate identity with both, together with face-shape metrics on rendered faces of known shape. In a user study, raters judge MYSTIQUE's results more like the target than those of each compared method. Among these methods, MYSTIQUE also recovers the target's face shape most accurately, and its recognition score gains the most as more photos of the target are given.
papers.summary: Identity transfer for visual effects replaces the person in a driving image with a target person while keeping expression, lighting, pose, and scene, but methods trained by self-reconstruction tend to copy identity cues from the driving image and leak them at inference. `MYSTIQUE` is a diffusion-based method that takes identity from a set of the target's photos and reads expression, lighting, and scene through separate streams, with multi-stage training and input-level strategies such as random block masking, face-shape augmentation, and face randomization to keep identity out of those streams. In a user study, **raters judge its results more like the target than those of each compared method**. It also recovers the target's face shape most accurately among the compared methods, and its face-recognition score gains the most as more photos of the target are provided.

papers.title: Roboclock: A Unified Benchmark for Time-Aware Robotic Intelligence
papers.abstract: Time is a fundamental dimension of robotic intelligence: a robot may fail despite physically correct actions if it acts outside a valid time window, responds too slowly to an event, or fails to meet required throughput. Yet existing robotic benchmarks primarily emphasize spatial correctness and logical task completion, largely overlooking the temporal constraints of real-world applications. We present RoboClock, a unified benchmark for time-aware robotic manipulation featuring 60 tasks across five application domains. Mirroring these failure modes, RoboClock structures tasks around three types of temporal constraints: Temporal Window, Event-Reactive, and Throughput. Furthermore, RoboClock incorporates a Latency-Aligned evaluation protocol that continuously advances environment time during model inference and control-interface delays, paired with time-sensitive metrics. Evaluating over 30 methods, we find that the best-performing approach is the trained VLA, yet it achieves only 8.3% temporal success even on Easy-level tasks, with persistent challenges in generalization and transfer. These findings reveal fundamental limitations in current robotic systems and highlight the need to jointly optimize physical competence, temporal reasoning, and execution latency.
papers.summary: Robot benchmarks mostly score spatial correctness and logical task completion, although a robot can also fail by acting outside a valid time window, reacting too slowly to an event, or missing a required throughput. `RoboClock` is a manipulation benchmark of 60 tasks across five application domains built around those three kinds of temporal constraint, with an evaluation protocol that keeps environment time advancing during model inference and control-interface delays. Across more than 30 evaluated methods, the best performer is a trained VLA model, yet it reaches **only 8.3% temporal success even on Easy-level tasks**, with persistent difficulties in generalization and transfer.

papers.title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.
papers.summary: Robot systems in which a multimodal agent orchestrates learned visuomotor policies often fail at the handoff, because a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states and the agent may invoke it outside that region. `Boundary-Aware Policy Learning` first fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses so that this region is wide and can be described to the agent through a simple protocol, then retrains on curated successful rollouts so the agent can hand over earlier with fewer language-model calls. Across `RoboTwin 2.0` and `RoboDojo` the system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching **98.4% success in randomized `RoboTwin 2.0` scenes** while cutting API cost by 41.3% and execution time by 37.5%.

papers.title: SkillCore: Internalizing Generalizable Skills via Scaffolding-Removed Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Runtime skills can improve agents' problem-solving capabilities by providing procedural guidance for tasks such as code review and debugging. However, these benefits reach only a minority of users, as most do not proactively invoke skills in practice. We argue that such generalizable procedures should become part of the model's capabilities rather than remain optional external add-ons, making them directly available without explicit skill loading. To this end, we present SkillCore, a data pipeline and supervised fine-tuning recipe for internalizing generalizable skills. We transform real agent trajectories by removing skill-loading scaffolding while preserving the task context and subsequent agent actions, thereby supervising direct execution without external skill content. To preserve access to task-specific skills that provide genuinely external information, we mix these scaffold-removed trajectories with a small proportion of skill-native trajectories that preserve supervision for skill invocation. On a held-out skill-free evaluation, SkillCore improves task completion quality over the base Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-72B models by 54.4% and 24.8%, respectively, while preserving task-specific skill invocation on a separate probe and general coding performance on SWE-bench Verified.
papers.summary: Runtime skills give agents procedural guidance for tasks such as code review and debugging, but most users never invoke them. `SkillCore` is a data pipeline and supervised fine-tuning recipe that takes real agent trajectories, strips out the skill-loading step while keeping the task context and subsequent actions, and trains the model to execute the procedure directly, mixed with a small share of unmodified trajectories so the model can still invoke skills that carry external, task-specific information. On a held-out evaluation without skills, it **improves task completion quality over the base `Qwen3-8B` and `Qwen2.5-72B` models by 54.4% and 24.8%**, respectively. Task-specific skill invocation on a separate probe and general coding performance on `SWE-bench Verified` are preserved.

papers.title: Refining and Aligning Clinical Reasoning with Health Guidelines via Formal Constraints
papers.abstract: Clinical reasoning from incomplete or conflicting patient evidence must account for low-probability but high-risk concerns while remaining grounded in health guidelines.
