We introduce VerClin, an explainable framework that extracts guideline conditions, exclusions, recommendations, and priorities into executable knowledge and represents patient conversations as scoped cases. A deterministic four-valued reasoner produces traceable guideline matches while preserving uncertainty and enforcing exclusions. Multiple specialty agents then screen matched guidelines for case applicability, and a consultation model synthesizes accepted guidance through specialty recommendations and a sentence-preserving formal-constraint channel. We present accepted guidance in ascending order of the sum of its priority and trigger-strength ranks, which can surface high-risk guidance with weaker triggers. VerClin outperforms direct generation and Top-5 RAG on HealthBench Hard and HealthBench Professional. On the LLMEval-Med subset, it outperforms direct generation and ties Top-5 RAG. Component analyses further examine semantic closure, example-guided refinement, specialty screening, and constraint-conditioned delivery.
papers.summary: Clinical reasoning from incomplete or conflicting patient evidence has to account for unlikely but high-risk concerns while staying grounded in health guidelines. `VerClin` extracts guideline conditions, exclusions, recommendations, and priorities into executable knowledge, matches them to patient conversations with a deterministic four-valued reasoner that preserves uncertainty and enforces exclusions, and then has multiple specialty agents screen the matches before a consultation model synthesizes the accepted guidance. It **outperforms direct generation and Top-5 retrieval-augmented generation on `HealthBench Hard` and `HealthBench Professional`**, and on the `LLMEval-Med` subset it beats direct generation and ties the retrieval baseline.

papers.title: Seldon TFM family: Seldon-Mini, Seldon and Seldon+
papers.abstract: We introduce Seldon, a family of tabular foundation models. Our classifier Seldon+ ranks first among 15 models on TabBench, our benchmark of 124 classification datasets, and on its variant with missing values. In our own runs of public benchmarks, it also ranks first on BeyondArena IID classification and TabBench-Bio, and second on TabArena classification. The open-weight models Seldon-Mini (27M parameters) and Seldon (213M parameters) both lie on the TabArena Pareto front of Elo against inference time: no entry is both more accurate and faster. On TabArena, Seldon ranks fourth and Seldon-Mini seventh among 109 leaderboard entries, and on the IID track of BeyondArena, Seldon ranks second among 42 entries. Seldon-Mini and Seldon handle both classification and regression, use an architecture similar to those of Kumo-Tabular, TabFM and TabPFN-3.5, and are trained on synthetic tables only.
papers.summary: `Seldon` is a family of tabular foundation models trained only on synthetic tables, comprising the open-weight `Seldon-Mini` (27M parameters) and `Seldon` (213M parameters), which handle classification and regression, and the classifier `Seldon+`. `Seldon+` **ranks first among 15 models on `TabBench`**, the authors' own benchmark of 124 classification datasets, and in their runs of public benchmarks it ranks first on `BeyondArena` IID classification and `TabBench-Bio` and second on `TabArena` classification. Both open-weight models sit on the `TabArena` Pareto front of Elo against inference time, where `Seldon` ranks fourth and `Seldon-Mini` seventh among 109 leaderboard entries.

papers.title: Unjamming Deferrals: Supporting Students Through JAMN Bot, a Mobile RAG-Grounded Policy Assistant
papers.abstract: In some educational institutions, workflows such as the exam deferral process can be slow, inconvenient, and inconsistent, which creates the need to implement novel digital systems. This paper presents Schedulater, a mobile app for managing university exam deferrals. JAMN Bot is a Large Language Model (LLM)-powered chatbot integrated into Schedulater that provides context-aware support to help users understand the deferral process. The system features a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Ollama (Llama 3.2 3B) for self-hosted inference which enables policy-grounded responses without sacrificing privacy. We evaluate the system using a 43-item benchmark spanning Exam Deferral, Privacy, Scheduling, Cross-Policy, and Adversarial & Out-of-Scope questions, and report inter-rater agreement among our human evaluators alongside retrieval hit-rate metrics. Subsequently, we utilize an LLM-as-a-judge approach with GPT-5.4, revealing slight-to-moderate alignment with our raters that improves with answer quality, and check the ranking against a panel including Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5 397B. The results of our study display trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models, as well as LLM-human evaluation alignment with answer quality. Schedulater demonstrates the feasibility of integrating lightweight LLMs into university administrative workflows with structured retrieval.
papers.summary: University exam deferral workflows can be slow and inconsistent, so the authors built `Schedulater`, a mobile app for managing deferrals, with an embedded Large Language Model (LLM) chatbot called `JAMN Bot` that explains the process. The bot uses a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline over policy documents with self-hosted inference through `Ollama` running `Llama 3.2 3B`, keeping student data private. On a 43-item benchmark covering deferral, privacy, scheduling, cross-policy, and adversarial or out-of-scope questions, human raters and an LLM-as-a-judge setup with `GPT-5.4` showed **only slight-to-moderate agreement, which improved as answer quality rose**. The evaluation also reports retrieval hit rates and trade-offs between open-weight and frontier models.

papers.title: Pando: Noise-Coupled Parallel Draft Trees for Efficient Edge Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract:
Autoregressive (AR) decoding emits one token per forward pass, reloading the full model each time, so LLM inference on edge devices is memory-bound while the compute units sit idle. Speculative decoding puts that idle compute to work by verifying several drafted tokens in a single pass. State-of-the-art parallel drafters such as DFlash and DSpark propose an entire block of draft tokens in one forward pass, which makes drafting compute-efficient. However, they are deployed with draft chains whose length is capped by the block size they are trained for, leaving most of the computational budget for verification unused.
  To tackle this problem, we propose Pando, which builds dynamic draft trees on top of a parallel drafter and thereby removes this cap. Pando employs noise-coupled pruning, which draws the target model's sampling noise before drafting and ranks candidate branches under that noise, so the tree retains the branches the target will actually sample. Noise coupling is lossless and requires no retraining or additional model pass, yet increases acceptance length by up to $8.4\%$ on Qwen3-8B. To optimize and evaluate Pando configurations across hardware, we normalize an operator-level roofline to AR decoding, reducing every platform to its ridge point. On a representative edge device, a 16-node Pando tree attains $5.3\times$ speedup and $4.2\times$ energy reduction over AR decoding: $25\%$ faster than DSpark's released chain, and $27\%$ faster and $72\%$ more energy-efficient than an EAGLE-3 tree. The best configurations remain memory-bound on every edge device we model, so added compute capacity does not reduce their latency.
papers.summary: LLM inference on edge devices is memory-bound, and parallel drafters for speculative decoding such as `DFlash` and `DSpark` are deployed with draft chains capped at their trained block size, leaving verification budget unused. `Pando` builds dynamic draft trees on top of a parallel drafter and prunes them with noise coupling: it draws the target model's sampling noise before drafting and ranks branches under that noise, which is lossless, needs no retraining, and raises acceptance length by up to 8.4% on `Qwen3-8B`. On a representative edge device, a 16-node tree reaches **5.3× speedup and 4.2× energy reduction over autoregressive (AR) decoding**, 25% faster than `DSpark`'s released chain and 27% faster than an `EAGLE-3` tree. The best configurations stay memory-bound on every modeled edge device, so extra compute capacity does not lower their latency.

papers.title: CoMNO: Commutator Memory Neural Operators for Long-Horizon PDE Prediction
papers.abstract: Solving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) over long time horizons is computationally expensive using traditional numerical methods. While neural operators provide an efficient alternative, they suffer from the accumulation of approximation errors along the predicted trajectory, typically caused by the failure to capture fine-scale details. In this work, we design a Commutator Memory Neural Operator that identifies fine-scale dynamical details by commuting two operations and leverages these details to enhance the neural operator's capability in capturing fine-scale features over long time horizons. Specifically, we identify a performance gap between two operations: downsampling the high-resolution field before rollout prediction versus performing rollout prediction before downsampling. We observe that fine-scale dynamical details are often encoded in this gap. By commuting these two operations, the fine-scale details removed during downsampling can be captured. Furthermore, we employ a memory module to store these fine-scale features along the trajectory and retrieve them during rollout, generating spatially adaptive corrections that enhance long-horizon fidelity. Empirical results across five systems demonstrate that CoMNO improves prediction accuracy and long-horizon rollout stability.
papers.summary: Neural operators that predict nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) dynamics accumulate errors over long rollouts, largely because they miss fine-scale detail. `CoMNO` exploits the gap between two orderings of the same operations, downsampling a high-resolution field before rollout versus rolling out before downsampling, on the observation that this commutator encodes the fine-scale dynamics lost to downsampling. A memory module stores these features along the trajectory and retrieves them during rollout to produce spatially adaptive corrections. Across five systems, the authors report **improved prediction accuracy and long-horizon rollout stability**.

papers.title: Reproducing the Speech Labels of Qwen3-Omni's Talker: Mimi in bf16, and a Last-Frame Pitfall
papers.abstract: Qwen3-Omni speaks through a Talker predicting 16 codebooks of a 12.5 Hz audio codec, but the encoder that made its training labels was not released, so new voices cannot be trained on matching labels. We identify this encoder from the released model's behavior. White-box regression shows that the codebook embeddings of the Talker, its multi-token predictor and the Code2Wav decoder match the first 16 codebooks of kyutai's Mimi layer by layer. A decoder-based test looks convincing but fails calibration: decoders trained on known labels cannot tell them apart. Teacher-forced Talker likelihoods, calibrated with 13 code language models trained on known labels, do tell implementations apart: the Talker prefers labels from kyutai's moshi package with bf16 weights over every other variant we tried. Loudness normalization and band-limiting of 20% or more of the data are ruled out. Separately, transformers' MimiModel encodes the last frame differently from kyutai's encoder unless the input length is a multiple of 1920 samples. After LoRA fine-tuning on its labels, 44--55% of generated sentences end in a noise burst, and the same frame costs the Mimi-based CSM-1B 119 nats; padding the input removes both. We release the encoding recipe, a label checker and a Talker fine-tuning toolkit.
papers.summary: `Qwen3-Omni` generates speech through a Talker that predicts 16 codebooks of a 12.5 Hz audio codec, but the encoder used to make its training labels was never released, which blocks training new voices on matching labels. Regression on the released weights shows the codebook embeddings match the first 16 codebooks of kyutai's `Mimi`, and teacher-forced Talker likelihoods, calibrated against 13 code language models trained on known labels, single out kyutai's `moshi` package with bf16 weights as the preferred variant. The authors also find that the `MimiModel` in `transformers` encodes the last frame differently unless input length is a multiple of 1920 samples; after LoRA fine-tuning on those labels, **44–55% of generated sentences end in a noise burst, which padding the input removes**. An encoding recipe, a label checker, and a Talker fine-tuning toolkit are released.

papers.title: $\epsilon$-Seg++: Ensembling Across Hierarchy and Training Time for Label-Efficient EM Segmentation
papers.abstract: Semantic segmentation of electron microscopy (EM) volumes is a central step in quantitative cell biology, but dense voxel-wise annotation is prohibitively expensive. $\epsilon$-Seg showed that a hierarchical variational autoencoder trained on sparsely annotated voxels can yield competitive segmentations, but it classifies from its topmost latent level only and operates exclusively on 2D patches. We introduce $\epsilon$-Seg++, which places a semantic expert at every level of the hierarchy and consolidates their predictions with a parameter-free product of experts. We further enable 3D inputs through a leakage-free sub-volume splitting protocol, which allows 2D and 3D models to be compared under identical sparse supervision. Because validation labels are just as scarce as training labels, we treat checkpoint selection as part of the method and average the top-ranked checkpoints, a second ensemble, this time across training time. On the BetaSeg FIB-SEM dataset, the multi-level experts improve 2D mean Dice by about 0.1 at 2,500 training labels. With up to 600 training labels, the 2D model matches or exceeds 3D $\epsilon$-Seg at about one eleventh of its prediction cost. Above roughly a thousand labels, 3D inputs dominate, and at matched annotation cost 3D $\epsilon$-Seg++ reaches a mean Dice of 0.905 versus 0.880 for D3PM, while predicting between 5.4 and 27 times faster (with our checkpoint ensemble or a single model, respectively). Checkpoint ensembling matches single-best selection on average and markedly improves the worst case when the validation set is small.
papers.summary: Dense voxel annotation for semantic segmentation of electron microscopy (EM) volumes is very expensive, and the earlier `ε-Seg` hierarchical variational autoencoder classified only from its top latent level on 2D patches. `ε-Seg++` puts a semantic expert at every hierarchy level and merges them with a parameter-free product of experts, adds 3D inputs through a leakage-free sub-volume splitting protocol, and averages top-ranked checkpoints because validation labels are scarce too. On the `BetaSeg` FIB-SEM dataset, at matched annotation cost the 3D model reaches **a mean Dice of 0.905 versus 0.880 for `D3PM`** while predicting 5.4 to 27 times faster. With up to 600 training labels the 2D model matches or exceeds 3D `ε-Seg` at about one eleventh of the prediction cost, while 3D inputs dominate above roughly a thousand labels.

papers.title: VC-OPD: Learning to See What Matters via Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Visual On-Policy Distillation (OPD) commonly uses cropped or zoomed-in image regions as teacher-side privileged information to improve fine-grained perception in small Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, local pixel-level cues are insufficient for complex visual reasoning that requires global structure, spatial relationships, and high-level semantics. We propose Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation (VC-OPD), which extends teacher-side privileged information beyond local image regions to question-conditioned visual cues. Advanced MLLMs generate cues capturing key visual details, structural relationships, and semantic evidence needed to answer each question. A multi-stage quality filtering process selects reliable cues, which are provided only to the teacher during training. This enables informative token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, helping the student learn to identify and reason over critical evidence directly from the original image. No additional information is required at inference time. Since advanced MLLMs are used only for visual cue generation, VC-OPD is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary black-box models. Experiments on STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements across model scales over reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation baselines. Notably, a 4B model trained with VC-OPD outperforms many baselines with 8B or more parameters, demonstrating effective capability transfer through question-conditioned visual cues.
papers.summary: Visual On-Policy Distillation (OPD) for small Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) usually gives the teacher cropped or zoomed image regions as privileged information, which does not help with reasoning that depends on global structure, spatial relationships, or high-level semantics. `VC-OPD` instead has advanced MLLMs generate question-conditioned visual cues, filters them through a multi-stage quality process, and shows them only to the teacher during training, so the student receives token-level supervision along its own generated trajectories and needs nothing extra at inference. On STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks it improves over reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation baselines across model scales, and **a 4B model trained this way outperforms many baselines with 8B or more parameters**.

papers.title: DAiSy: Online Data Selection by Adaptive Utility Estimation for LLM Pretraining
papers.abstract: Model-aware online data selection prioritizes the training documents that contribute the most given the model's current state. Existing online selectors rank candidates upon gradient-based data utility scores, which requires the full forward-backward pass of the main model on every candidate document. Scoring each document therefore pays as much as training on it, yet only a small fraction is used for the real model update. We introduce DAiSy, a lightweight linear auxiliary model that learns to predict data utility scores from frozen document embeddings, which eliminates the computation overhead and infrastructure burdens. The linear estimator is updated alongside the main language model, fitting to the exact gradient-based utility scores obtained from the backward pass of regular training steps. Consequently, scoring a candidate requires only a linear transformation, bypassing the costly gradient-alignment computation. We demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency for LLM pretraining in English and multilingual scenarios, with various steering target designs. The improvements from DAiSy can consistently survive the instruction-tuning phase.
papers.summary: Model-aware online data selection for LLM pretraining ranks candidate documents by gradient-based utility scores, which costs a full forward-backward pass per candidate even though only a small fraction is used for the actual update. `DAiSy` trains a lightweight linear auxiliary model to predict those utility scores from frozen document embeddings, fitting it to the exact scores that fall out of the backward pass of regular training steps, so **scoring a candidate requires only a linear transformation**. The authors report effectiveness and efficiency gains in English and multilingual pretraining under several steering-target designs, with improvements that persist after instruction tuning.

papers.title: Query-Guided Visual Minimization for Selective Disclosure to Cloud VLMs
papers.abstract: Cloud-hosted vision-language models (VLMs) require sending images beyond the user's local trust boundary, potentially exposing sensitive information the query does not need. We study query-guided visual minimization: a trusted local transformation preserves query-relevant visual content and reduces unnecessary disclosure before transmission. Unlike query-agnostic anonymization, it preserves the same sensitive content when the query requires it and suppresses it otherwise. We introduce QGVM, a framework that combines query grounding with an independent sensitive-item inventory, determines disclosure necessity at the type, instance, and text-content levels, and renders a minimized image for a black-box downstream VLM. We evaluate QGVM on complementary benchmarks measuring task utility, directly recoverable sensitive information, and inferential geolocation leakage. With OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol, QGVM achieves 85.3% DoxBench answer correctness versus 77.5% for PGP, while a separately prompted Sol geolocation attacker succeeds within 1 km on 5.8% of QGVM images versus 25.7% of unprotected images. On Scene-Privacy, QGVM reduces face re-identification from 27.7% (PGP) to 4.5%. On held-out BIV-Priv-Seg, unnecessary private-text recovery falls from 33.9% (PGP) to 15.3%. To verify that disclosure is query-dependent, we evaluate paired queries that either require or do not require the same sensitive information. QGVM achieves 69.6% correct disclosure switching, compared with 29.1% for grounding-only cropping. These findings highlight the value of distinguishing visual relevance from disclosure necessity, while revealing the privacy-utility trade-offs of selective visual disclosure.
papers.summary: Sending images to cloud-hosted vision-language models (VLMs) can expose sensitive content that the user's question does not need. `QGVM` is a trusted local transformation that combines query grounding with an independent inventory of sensitive items, decides at the type, instance, and text-content levels what must be disclosed, and renders a minimized image for a black-box downstream VLM. With `GPT-6.1 Sol` it reaches 85.3% answer correctness on `DoxBench` versus 77.5% for `PGP`, while **a geolocation attacker succeeds within 1 km on 5.8% of minimized images versus 25.7% of unprotected ones**; face re-identification on `Scene-Privacy` falls from 27.7% to 4.5%. On paired queries that do or do not require the same sensitive information, it switches disclosure correctly 69.6% of the time, compared with 29.1% for grounding-only cropping.

papers.title: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction
papers.abstract: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. ArabFake demonstrates robust performance, achieving an F1 score of 94.12% for fake news detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment, highlighting its reliability and effectiveness across multiple tasks. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.
papers.summary: Arabic fake news detection is usually treated as binary classification; `ArabFake` is a multitask framework built on `MARBERTv2` that jointly performs fake news detection, content categorization, and risk-level assessment through shared representations. The authors also introduce the `ArabFake Dataset` of 2,495 manually labelled news items with expert-verified category and risk labels. The model reports **F1 scores of 94.12% for detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk assessment**, and adds valence scoring to highlight misleading linguistic cues for interpretability.

papers.title: Sparse Poison, Strong Hijack: Efficient Trajectory-Level Backdoors in Vision-Language-Action Models with Only 1\% Poisoning
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models advance robotic manipulation, but their reliance on demonstrations exposes them to backdoor threats. Among these threats, trajectory-level targeted backdoors are particularly challenging and may pose greater safety risks than behavior-disrupting attacks: rather than merely causing task failures or local action deviations, they must sustain closed-loop redirection to complete an attacker-specified multi-step task. To reliably induce such behaviors, existing methods typically rely on high poisoning rates to obtain sufficient target-trajectory supervision. However, high poisoning rates may compromise clean-task performance, whereas low rates leave target-trajectory supervision scarce and backdoor learning vulnerable to interference from dominant clean-task updates. To resolve this trade-off at low poisoning rates, we propose a two-stage co-optimization framework guided by vision, language, and action. Stage I freezes the policy and uses differentiable rendering and multimodal supervision to optimize a 3D trigger's texture, translation, and scale, strengthening trigger-target associations from limited poisoned demonstrations. Building on the optimized trigger, Stage II applies source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation to decouple clean and backdoor updates and mitigate their interference, followed by learned column-wise calibration and analytic fusion into a unified policy. Experiments on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, $\pi_0$, and $\pi_{0.5}$ across four LIBERO suites show consistent gains over all evaluated attack baselines. With only 1% poisoned data, our method achieves 86.4% target success and 95.2% clean-task success on OpenVLA-OFT in LIBERO-Spatial. Real-robot trials also demonstrate trajectory-level hijacking.
papers.summary: Trajectory-level backdoors in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) robot policies must sustain closed-loop redirection toward an attacker-chosen multi-step task, and existing attacks need high poisoning rates that can hurt clean-task performance. The proposed two-stage framework first freezes the policy and optimizes a 3D trigger's texture, translation, and scale through differentiable rendering and multimodal supervision, then uses source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation to separate clean and backdoor updates before calibrating and fusing them into one policy. Tested on `OpenVLA`, `OpenVLA-OFT`, `π0`, and `π0.5` across four `LIBERO` suites, it beats all evaluated attack baselines, reaching **86.4% target success and 95.2% clean-task success with only 1% poisoned data** on `OpenVLA-OFT` in `LIBERO-Spatial`. Real-robot trials also show trajectory-level hijacking.

papers.title: ASTERISM: Do Multimodal LLMs Actually Look at All the Images?
papers.abstract: Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.
papers.summary: Multi-image benchmarks are meant to test whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) combine evidence across images, but an audit of about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks finds that **one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them**, and models take this single-image shortcut even where one image is insufficient. The authors build `ASTERISM`, 18.7k audited items that require more than one image, along with `ASTERISM-Train` and a manually verified hard subset, `ASTERISM-Lite`, on which the strongest proprietary model scores 68%. They argue that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) rewards the same shortcut, and propose cross-image credit assignment (`CICA`), which shifts credit toward tokens that need multiple images. On three open-source MLLMs, `CICA` raises the `ASTERISM` score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of other RL objectives trained on the same data.

papers.title: SPRUNN: Structural Proximity for Pruning in Deep Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have demonstrated significant accuracy across various machine learning tasks. However, these networks suffer from a huge number of parameters and computations, which leads to time-consuming processes. Consequently, parameter pruning approaches have been proposed to compress DNNs and efficiently implement them. The main challenge in pruning is selecting the appropriate parameters for pruning without significantly damaging the accuracy. In this paper, we propose SPRUNN, an algorithmic pruning approach based on the structural proximity criterion for filter pruning in convolutional layers of deep neural networks. Structural Proximity (SP) calculates filter similarity by considering all filters and comparing each one with the others, effectively identifying less important filters for pruning in the convolutional layers. Furthermore, we integrate this approach with fine-grained pruning in Fully Connected(FC)layerstocompresstheDNNsthatinclude both convolutional and FC layers.Toenhancetheaccuracyoftheprunedmodel,weproposealearning rate refinement strategy during the retraining phase. Experimental results demonstrate that SPRUNN achieves significant compression with high accuracy across diverse architectures and datasets.
papers.summary: Pruning deep neural networks requires choosing which parameters to remove without badly hurting accuracy. `SPRUNN` prunes convolutional filters using a structural proximity criterion that compares every filter with all others to identify the least important ones, pairs this with fine-grained pruning of fully connected layers, and adds a learning-rate refinement strategy during retraining. The authors report **significant compression with high accuracy across diverse architectures and datasets**, without giving specific figures in the abstract.

papers.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning via Monadic Continuations
papers.abstract: Alpha-beta pruning is a fundamental technique in game-playing AI, enabling efficient minimax search by avoiding the exploration of branches that cannot affect the optimal decision. We present a monadic formulation of alpha-beta pruning based on the combination of the continuation monad and the reader monad. Unlike previous approaches that encode alpha-beta bounds into the types of available moves, our construction records these bounds within monadic outcomes, leaving the move types unchanged. We further show that the ordinary continuation monad suffices to compute not only optimal outcomes but also optimal plays, by extending the outcome type to include the corresponding sequences of moves. This provides an alternative to generalisations of the continuation monad proposed to address the inefficiencies associated with the selection monad in alpha-beta search. We illustrate our approach with an implementation of Tic-Tac-Toe, observing a 39-fold reduction in the number of plays evaluated, compared with exhaustive search, in computing an optimal play. Finally, we formally establish the correctness of our construction by proving that the monadic alpha-beta search computes the same optimal outcomes and plays as exhaustive minimax search. Our results demonstrate how a foundational algorithm in AI can be expressed and verified using standard monadic abstractions, providing a basis for further development of compositional approaches to adversarial search.
papers.summary: Alpha-beta pruning for minimax game search is reformulated using a combination of the continuation monad and the reader monad, recording the alpha-beta bounds inside monadic outcomes rather than encoding them in the types of moves as earlier approaches did. Extending the outcome type to carry move sequences lets the ordinary continuation monad compute optimal plays as well as optimal outcomes, offering an alternative to generalised continuation monads proposed to fix inefficiencies of the selection monad. A Tic-Tac-Toe implementation evaluates **39 times fewer plays than exhaustive search** when computing an optimal play, and the authors prove the monadic search returns the same optimal outcomes and plays as exhaustive minimax.

papers.title: FigmaEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents in Professional UI Design
papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI agents have enabled autonomous UI design using professional tools such as Figma, yet evaluating their design capabilities remains challenging due to the open-ended nature of design tasks and the absence of unique ground truths. We introduce FigmaEval, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on professional UI design tasks, comprising 84 tasks and 783 screens derived from real-world Figma design files. FigmaEval adopts a constrained-specification, open-solution paradigm, standardizing task requirements and design resources while allowing agents to independently determine layouts, visual hierarchies, component composition, and visual presentation. To assess design quality beyond reference similarity, we develop 22 expert-grounded evaluation rubrics across six dimensions and introduce a human evaluation arena where professional designers compare agent-generated designs through blinded pairwise judgments. Evaluating eleven models under a unified Figma agent setup, we find substantial agreement between rubric-based assessments and human preferences, alongside distinct differences in design practices and quality--efficiency trade-offs. FigmaEval provides a framework for systematically assessing professional UI design capabilities and understanding the strengths and limitations of current AI agents.
papers.summary: Evaluating AI agents that design user interfaces in professional tools is difficult because design tasks are open-ended and have no single correct answer. `FigmaEval` comprises 84 tasks and 783 screens derived from real-world Figma files, fixing requirements and design resources while leaving layout, visual hierarchy, component composition, and presentation up to the agent. Quality is scored with 22 expert-grounded rubrics across six dimensions and with a human arena in which professional designers make blinded pairwise comparisons. Across eleven models in a unified Figma agent setup, **rubric-based scores agree substantially with human preferences**, and models differ in design practices and quality-efficiency trade-offs.

papers.title: When Exact Token Importance Is Not Enough: Limits of Top-K Selection in LLM Attention
papers.abstract: Long-context language models often retain only a limited set of past token positions for an attention query. A common strategy scores positions individually and keeps the highest-ranked K. Yet attention weights are renormalized over the chosen set: two individually important positions need not form the best pair. We ask whether independent ranking suffices even when each importance score measures the exact downstream change in next-token predictions caused by deleting that position alone. It does not. A four-position construction makes the ranked pair incur 133.2 times the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of the optimal pair, and a parametric family proves that this multiplicative gap is unbounded. An exact exchange identity and preference reversals for every K >= 2 explain the interaction. In exhaustive frozen-model audits of SmolLM2, Gemma, and Qwen, exact-singleton Top-4 leaves at least 10% relative improvement within a fully enumerated 24-position candidate pool in 55/60, 49/60, and 60/60 cases, respectively. SwapCert, a same-budget one-swap audit, detects 157/164 such cases and returns directly checkable improving supports. A KL-margin certificate relates support fidelity to next-token stability; larger-budget, multi-layer cached-decoding experiments measure predictive fidelity at K = 128 and 256. These results establish joint support quality as an essential object of analysis for sparse attention and motivate downstream-aware support selection under inference constraints.
papers.summary: Sparse attention schemes for long-context language models often score past token positions individually and keep the top K, but attention weights are renormalized over the kept set, so individually important positions need not form the best set. The authors show independent ranking fails even when each score is the exact downstream effect of deleting that position alone: a four-position construction makes the ranked pair incur 133.2 times the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of the optimal pair, and a parametric family proves the gap is unbounded. In exhaustive audits of frozen `SmolLM2`, `Gemma`, and `Qwen` models, **exact-singleton Top-4 leaves at least 10% relative improvement on the table in 55/60, 49/60, and 60/60 cases**. A one-swap audit called `SwapCert` detects 157 of 164 such cases and returns directly checkable improved supports.

papers.title: A recursive self-improvement framework for electron microscopy analysis
papers.abstract: Resolving local atomic structures such as defects and interfaces from electron microscopy contrast relies heavily on researcher judgement, leading to low efficiency and subjective standards. Here we present PhyEvo-Mic-RSI, a physics-guided and expert-informed recursive self-improvement framework that turns one-off human corrections into reusable, verifiable capabilities by updating executable operators, parameters and routing rules with versioned inheritance. Given researcher-defined tasks, the system selects analysis paths from image features without expert labels, while testing and inheriting code updates under fixed budgets. Combining physical priors with expert feedback improves atomic point-defect detection over larger models and raises cross-material interface coverage from 5.13% to 72.11% within a 10% area budget. Adapting the framework to micrographs from unseen studies further separates touching nanoparticles by aligning optimization with particle-level measurements. This work moves computational microscopy beyond standalone models and static scripts towards self-evolving platforms that accumulate human scientific expertise
papers.summary: Identifying local atomic structures such as defects and interfaces in electron microscopy images depends heavily on researcher judgement, which is slow and subjective. `PhyEvo-Mic-RSI` is a physics-guided, expert-informed recursive self-improvement framework that converts one-off human corrections into reusable capabilities by updating executable operators, parameters, and routing rules with versioned inheritance, testing code updates under fixed budgets. It improves atomic point-defect detection over larger models and **raises cross-material interface coverage from 5.13% to 72.11% within a 10% area budget**. Adapted to micrographs from unseen studies, it also separates touching nanoparticles.

papers.title: Part-Set Prototypes for Explainable Mountain Gazelles Sex Classification
papers.abstract: Self-explainable visual models for fine-grained recognition are often hindered by rigid geometric constraints that cannot capture diverse semantic shapes in unconstrained "in-the-wild" imagery. Real-world camera-trap data introduces challenges, including non-optimal poses, lighting variations, occlusions, animal camouflage, and environmental shortcuts. To address this, we introduce set prototypes, a general architecture where both part cardinality and unconstrained spatial layouts are mined directly from data. Our joint-matching formulation places parts simultaneously on a frozen DINOv3 token grid via truncated Sinkhorn competition, allowing unsupported parts to abstain without spatial collapse. We evaluate our approach on Mountain Gazelle sex classification, a camera-trap benchmark, where our model achieves 0.878 macro-F1--outperforming prior architectures and at par with an unconstrained linear probe. The strongest prototypes localize to distinctive biological areas such as horns, neck and body, allowing ecologists to visually verify decisions before trusting the metric. This formulation generalizes naturally to diverse ecological monitoring challenges beyond a single species.
papers.summary: Self-explainable prototype models for fine-grained recognition often impose rigid geometric constraints that fit poorly with camera-trap imagery, where poses, lighting, occlusion, and camouflage vary widely. The authors introduce set prototypes, in which the number of parts and their spatial layout are learned from data and parts are placed jointly on a frozen `DINOv3` token grid through truncated Sinkhorn competition, letting unsupported parts abstain. On a Mountain Gazelle sex classification benchmark the model achieves **0.878 macro-F1, outperforming prior architectures and matching an unconstrained linear probe**. The strongest prototypes localize to horns, neck, and body, which lets ecologists visually check decisions.

papers.title: DiCT: Teaching X-ray Vision-Language Models to Reason via Imagining CT
papers.abstract: Diagnosing with X-rays often requires reasoning about the 3D locations of abnormalities and their spatial relationships to surrounding anatomical structures, yet such reasoning remains challenging due to the loss of spatial information in 2D projections. To address this challenge, we propose Dreaming in CT (DiCT), a three-stage progressive CT-to-X-ray reasoning transfer framework that leverages a CT vision-language model (VLM) to guide an X-ray VLM. Through this CT-guided transfer, the student acquires CT-informed 3D reasoning capabilities, enabling it to reason directly from 2D X-rays without explicit CT reconstruction at inference time. The framework begins with instruct the dreamer, which equips the X-ray student with initial CT-oriented reasoning capabilities and establishes a structured interface that distinguishes X-ray observations from CT imagination. Building on this structure, visualize the dream introduces CT-guided on-policy distillation (OPD), where the CT teacher selectively guides the X-ray student's reasoning trajectories to transfer 3D anatomical knowledge. Finally, manifest the dream adapts the acquired reasoning capabilities from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) to real clinical X-rays. Experiments across two VLM backbones on 3D-RAD and ReXVQA demonstrate DiCT's effectiveness across radiological reasoning tasks, achieving a 1.66 percentage point improvement over a CT reconstruction-based baseline on 3D-RAD Abnormality Identification with 12.77$\times$ lower inference computation. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongYep/DiCT.
papers.summary: X-ray diagnosis often requires reasoning about the 3D location of abnormalities, information lost in a 2D projection. `DiCT` (Dreaming in CT) is a three-stage framework in which a CT vision-language model (VLM) teaches an X-ray VLM: the student first learns a structured format separating X-ray observations from imagined CT content, then receives CT-guided on-policy distillation (OPD) along its own reasoning trajectories, and finally adapts from digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) to real clinical X-rays. On `3D-RAD` Abnormality Identification it gains **1.66 percentage points over a CT reconstruction-based baseline with 12.77× lower inference computation**, with experiments spanning two VLM backbones on `3D-RAD` and `ReXVQA`.

papers.title: Beyond Hard Tokens: Predictive Memory for Multimodal Protein Generation
papers.abstract: Multimodal protein language models unify sequence and discrete structural tokens via iterative masked decoding, offering a promising paradigm for joint protein design. However, standard decoders rely on a memoryless mask reset at each iteration: only a sparse subset of newly committed hard tokens is carried forward, while all remaining unresolved sites are reset to an identical [MASK] embedding. In open-ended co-generation where neither modality provides a fixed external anchor, this stateless transition limits single-step refinement depth and deprives both tracks of stable cross-step soft anchors, leading to slow convergence or degenerative repetitive collapse. Observing that uncommitted predictions evolve with pronounced temporal coherence rather than erratic noise, we introduce Predictive Memory (PredMem), a training-free self-conditioning recurrence that carries these soft beliefs across steps. At each step, PredMem summarizes raw logits into a probability-weighted Top-$k$ expectation embedding at every residue and affinely interpolates it into eligible masked inputs on the next step at zero extra denoiser cost. Across DPLM-2, DPLM-2.1, and ESM3, PredMem raises unconditional sequence-structure co-generation success by 3.6, 17.7, and 48.7 percentage points, respectively, while improving the quality-diversity trade-off and suppressing repetitive mode collapse. Controlled diagnostics show that these gains stem primarily from early trajectory stabilization in unanchored cross-modal co-evolution rather than extra compute or simple entropy reduction, establishing PredMem as an efficient inference mechanism for multimodal discrete generation.
papers.summary: Multimodal protein language models co-generate sequence and structure tokens by iterative masked decoding, but each step carries forward only newly committed tokens and resets every unresolved site to the same mask embedding, which slows convergence and can cause repetitive collapse. `PredMem` (Predictive Memory) is a training-free self-conditioning mechanism that summarizes each residue's logits into a probability-weighted Top-k expectation embedding and interpolates it into the masked inputs of the next step at no extra denoiser cost. It raises unconditional sequence-structure co-generation success by **3.6, 17.7, and 48.7 percentage points on `DPLM-2`, `DPLM-2.1`, and `ESM3`**, respectively. Diagnostics attribute the gains mainly to early trajectory stabilization rather than extra compute or entropy reduction.

papers.title: CriticJEPA: World Models Are Better Critics Than Optimizers
papers.abstract: Visual world models enable goal-directed planning by predicting action outcomes. Gradient-based planners optimize actions to lower predicted goal cost, but continued optimization can exploit prediction errors after execution stops improving. Comparing plans requires informative relative scores; improving them also requires reliable update directions. Exact-state execution reveals that a frozen hierarchical world model ranks goal-conditioned proposals even when its rankings among outputs of prolonged gradient search are uninformative. Effective planning pairs goal-directed candidates with predictions that distinguish their outcomes. We introduce CriticJEPA, which learns goal-conditioned flow proposals from reward-free trajectories and uses frozen rollouts to select among them at every hierarchy level. Forward selection forms a complete planner; short anchored updates refine candidates before selection. Across visual navigation and manipulation, CriticJEPA increases success at a fraction of the planning compute, transferring shared settings across independently trained models, hierarchy depths, and unseen tasks while keeping every world-model weight fixed.
papers.summary: Gradient-based planners that optimize actions against a visual world model's predicted goal cost can end up exploiting prediction errors once real execution stops improving. Experiments with exact-state execution show that **a frozen hierarchical world model reliably ranks goal-conditioned proposals even when its rankings among the outputs of prolonged gradient search are uninformative**. `CriticJEPA` therefore learns goal-conditioned flow proposals from reward-free trajectories and uses frozen world-model rollouts to select among them at every hierarchy level, with optional short anchored updates before selection. Across visual navigation and manipulation it increases success at a fraction of the planning compute and transfers across independently trained models, hierarchy depths, and unseen tasks without changing any world-model weights.

papers.title: Implementation of Machine Translation for the Uzbek Language Based on Transformer Models
papers.abstract: This research focuses on building a machine translation system for the Uzbek language using transformer models such as T5 and mT5. Because of the limited data and the complexity of the Uzbek language, we collect, preprocess and augment data to create a strong Uzbek-English parallel corpus of about 3 million sentence pairs. The models are fine-tuned for optimal translation performance, and we use the BLEU score to evaluate the results. This study shows that our approach significantly improves upon older methods and helps promote the Uzbek language in the digital world.
papers.summary: Uzbek is a low-resource language with limited parallel data for machine translation. The authors collect, preprocess and augment data into an Uzbek-English parallel corpus of **about 3 million sentence pairs**, then fine-tune the transformer models `T5` and `mT5` on it. Translation quality is evaluated with the `BLEU` score, and the authors claim an improvement over older methods without giving figures in the abstract.

papers.title: The Control-Flow Tax: Specialized Decision Routing for LLM Agent Workflows
papers.abstract: An agent can spend almost as much deciding what to do as doing it. In our documentation workflow, control-flow routing accounts for 42.5% of baseline reference cost on the initial task. Lower token prices alone do not solve this control-flow tax: inexpensive general-purpose routers can trigger additional calls to the expensive generator. We evaluate a heterogeneous architecture in which Jev, a specialized System 1 decision model, controls finite actions while Sol generates documents. Across four software tasks, 480 valid runs comprise 470 completions and ten request-limit endpoints. Jev full routing achieves the lowest mean cost and elapsed time on every task, completing all 40 specialist-controlled runs along the shortest trajectory. On the initial task, mean cost falls by 49.6% (95% paired-bootstrap interval: 42.9% to 56.3%) and elapsed time by 33.2% (19.6% to 46.7%). Across three further tasks, cost reductions are 40.5% to 42.9% and concurrent elapsed-time reductions are 12.9% to 14.4%. Existence-only specialization saves just 1.8% on the initial task. Separately, Sol and Jev each select accepted actions on 100/100 reviewed retail states, with Jev using 97.88% less reference cost and 72.30% less mean request time. The results identify two requirements for efficient agent control: inexpensive decisions and trajectories that preserve those savings.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents spend a large share of their budget deciding what to do next: in the authors' documentation workflow, control-flow routing accounts for 42.5% of baseline cost. The study evaluates a heterogeneous architecture in which `Jev`, a specialized decision model, selects among finite actions while `Sol` generates the documents, across four software tasks and 480 valid runs. Full routing through `Jev` gave the lowest mean cost and elapsed time on every task, **cutting mean cost by 49.6% and elapsed time by 33.2% on the initial task** and by 40.5% to 42.9% in cost on the other three. Cheap general-purpose routers did not deliver the same savings because they can trigger extra calls to the expensive generator, and specializing only existence checks saved just 1.8%.

papers.title: Decision Models: An Introduction and Capability Evaluation
papers.abstract: Applications such as ticket routing and incident triage need decisions that software can act on. Decision models provide these outputs through explicit types for choices, binary judgments, and policy scores. We evaluate the accuracy, output validity, and request latency of eleven configurations on 1,000 English and Chinese cases across nine task suites. StartLux Instant achieves 95.3% overall accuracy, returns valid outputs on all 1,000 cases, and has a median request latency of 0.084 s. It reaches 99.4% on classification and routing and selects the correct response on all 100 tool-selection cases. The highest overall accuracy among the evaluated configurations is 97.1%. These results show how a typed decision service can support fast, programmatic decisions and why its suitability depends on task-specific errors and latency requirements.
papers.summary: Applications such as ticket routing and incident triage need model outputs that software can act on directly. Decision models address this by returning explicitly typed outputs for choices, binary judgments and policy scores, and the authors evaluate eleven configurations on 1,000 English and Chinese cases across nine task suites for accuracy, output validity and latency. `StartLux Instant` reaches **95.3% overall accuracy with valid outputs on all 1,000 cases and a median request latency of 0.084 s**, including 99.4% on classification and routing and all 100 tool-selection cases correct. The best configuration overall reaches 97.1%, and the authors note that suitability depends on task-specific errors and latency requirements.

papers.title: A Description-Derived Drug-Drug Interaction Benchmark Reveals Split-Dependent Molecular Representation Rankings
papers.abstract: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction is clinically important and poses a distinct challenge for molecular representation learning. Unlike single-molecule property prediction, DDI requires a predictor to compose two molecular representations into a relational outcome. DrugBank provides curator-authored DDI descriptions rather than ready-made categorical labels, so a categorical prediction target must first be derived from the text. We construct a dataset of DDI pairs by mapping processed descriptions to six text-derived categories and define a benchmark with four holdout regimes that restrict train-test chemical overlap from random pairs to scaffold-disjoint evaluation. We then use this benchmark to compare molecular fingerprints, pretrained sequence representations, and graph-derived features across five seeds and multiple classifier heads. Molecular fingerprints lead the high- overlap random split, whereas graph-derived representations lead the drug- and scaffold-holdout regimes, with the gap increasing as molecular overlap is restricted. Changing the classifier head affects absolute performance but not the relative representation ranking. These results show that representation rankings change with test-set novelty under a fixed description-derived label space.
papers.summary: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction requires composing two molecular representations into a relational outcome, and `DrugBank` supplies free-text interaction descriptions rather than categorical labels. The authors map those descriptions to six text-derived categories and define a benchmark with four holdout regimes, ranging from random pairs to scaffold-disjoint evaluation, then compare molecular fingerprints, pretrained sequence representations and graph-derived features across five seeds and several classifier heads. **Fingerprints lead on the high-overlap random split, while graph-derived representations lead on the drug- and scaffold-holdout splits**, with the gap growing as chemical overlap is restricted. Changing the classifier head shifts absolute performance but not the ranking of representations.

papers.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
papers.abstract: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.
papers.summary: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models, the standard statistical models of pharmacometrics, require maximizing an intractable marginal likelihood, which variational autoencoders (VAEs) approximate with an amortized neural encoder. A convergence analysis of the `VAE-NLME` algorithm is given in two parts. The version targeting the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to stationary points of the ELBO without assuming the encoder is trained exactly. The final algorithm, which uses the encoder as a proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics, is proven to **converge almost surely to stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood with no assumption on encoder training**.

papers.title: Metamorphic Testing of Learned Spatial Surrogates for Transit Accessibility
papers.abstract: Transit-network design requires evaluating many candidates, but detailed accessibility calculations are too slow to repeat inside an optimization loop. We therefore train a neural surrogate to approximate them. Given a candidate bus network and fixed information about rail service and nearby opportunities, it predicts the calculated spatial change in accessibility. We compare its predictions with routing-derived targets in geographically held-out regions and test specified qualitative relations under controlled input changes. Reference calculations on constructed networks assess the applicability of relations that have a routing-level counterpart. Models with positive predictive skill can still fail basic connectivity tests. One targeted intervention substantially increases pass rates for two connectivity relations while predictive skill also improves. Average prediction error is therefore insufficient when a learned model becomes an optimization objective. Predictive agreement and controlled behavioral tests should be reported separately.
papers.summary: Detailed transit accessibility calculations are too slow to run inside a network-design optimization loop, so a neural surrogate is trained to predict the spatial change in accessibility for a candidate bus network. Beyond comparing predictions with routing-derived targets in geographically held-out regions, the authors apply metamorphic tests that check whether specified qualitative relations hold under controlled input changes. **Models with positive predictive skill can still fail basic connectivity tests**, and one targeted intervention substantially raises pass rates on two connectivity relations while also improving predictive skill. The authors conclude that predictive agreement and behavioral tests should be reported separately when a learned model serves as an optimization objective.

papers.title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.
papers.summary: Validation of specifications generated by large language models (LLMs) has received less attention than validation of generated code, even though flawed requirements propagate into design and implementation. The authors describe a working prototype that generates acceptance criteria for user stories with several LLMs, optionally using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and lets a reviewer compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and edit or regenerate before submitting a final version. Model outputs, retrieval settings, user interventions and final criteria are all logged as a decision record. The work **explicitly does not claim improved generation accuracy**; its contribution is making validation an inspectable, accountable process.

papers.title: The Activity Geometry of Discrete Generative Sampling
papers.abstract: Iterative refinement is a key capability of diffusion-based generation and has motivated growing efforts to bring similar behavior to discrete diffusion and flow models. A growing line of work enables such refinement by allowing previously generated tokens to be revised during sampling, thereby shaping the coupling between successive sampling states. Despite its growing role in sampler design, this coupling freedom remains insufficiently characterized. We introduce Activity Geometry to study these finite-step couplings through expected transition cost, which we call activity. We show that activity decomposes into the minimum required by the induced marginal transport and an excess term arising from the coupling. Using this minimum as a reference, we propose Minimal-Activity Finite-Time Coupling (MAFTC) to realize prescribed marginals with minimum activity without retraining or additional model evaluations. In the continuous-time limit, the minimum activity per unit time converges to the minimum expected jump rate compatible with the prescribed path. For metric-induced Gibbs paths, we further show that the activity of the kinetic-optimal flux admits a geometric decomposition. We find that total activity alone can obscure coupling excess: a sampler may approach the minimum activity required by the prescribed marginal transport while still retaining substantial coupling excess. In language generation, as the number of model evaluations increases, refinement-based samplers accumulate additional trajectory activity with limited diversity gains, whereas MAFTC reduces trajectory activity while maintaining comparable generation quality and higher lexical diversity.
papers.summary: Discrete diffusion and flow samplers that revise previously generated tokens have freedom in how successive sampling states are coupled, and that freedom has been poorly characterized. The authors introduce `Activity Geometry`, which measures expected transition cost (activity) and decomposes it into the minimum required by the marginal transport plus an excess from the coupling. From this they derive Minimal-Activity Finite-Time Coupling (`MAFTC`), which realizes prescribed marginals at minimum activity without retraining or extra model evaluations. In language generation, refinement-based samplers accumulate trajectory activity with limited diversity gains as evaluations increase, whereas **`MAFTC` reduces activity while keeping comparable quality and higher lexical diversity**.

papers.title: Does Research-Paper Context Improve LLM-Generated Quadruped Navigation? An Exploratory Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Large language models can write competent robot navigation code, but not only does the research on the topic advance, a model may also, due to the volume of findings, fail to recall relevant findings and apply them to the task at hand. In this work, we test whether providing particular research papers as context improves the LLM-written navigation code for the Go2 quadruped, with the LLM (Claude Opus 5) and locomotion policy frozen. Specifically, we compare the navigation controllers the LLM writes when provided with and without particular papers across three settings: behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, 2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This difference appears only under physics: in an idealized kinematic simulator, the controllers written with and without the paper are indistinguishable. We hypothesize that an LLM provided research papers as context tends to overweight both their content and their goals -- in this case, the efficiency of incremental replanning -- negatively affecting the fulfillment of the main task and leading to less robust code.
papers.summary: The study tests whether giving a large language model (LLM) specific research papers as context improves the navigation code it writes for the `Go2` quadruped robot, holding the LLM (`Claude Opus 5`) and the locomotion policy fixed. Controllers written with and without papers are compared across behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, **only 2 of 8 controllers written with an incremental-replanning paper completed all four trips under `Isaac Sim` physics, against 7 of 8 without it** (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041), while the two groups were indistinguishable in an idealized kinematic simulator. The authors hypothesize that the LLM overweights the content and goals of supplied papers at the expense of robustness on the main task.

papers.title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
papers.abstract: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.
papers.summary: Architecture search driven by large language models (LLMs) usually reduces evaluation to a scalar score and discards information about why designs fail. The authors build a loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, form falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen `nnU-Net` pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into trigger-to-action design rules for 3D medical image segmentation. Eight search waves yield two principles, shifting computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder and a support-confined region contrast for nested anatomical compartments, which produce `LeanNeXt` (0.78 of the compute of `nnU-Net` and +1.63 Dice points on `KiTS23`). The trigger-routed `LeanNeXt+` **improves on `nnU-Net` in all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings** and beats the larger `ResEnc-M` on 12 of 15 at 0.30 of its parameter count.

papers.title: Evolve to Learn: Gradient-aligned experience evolution for model self-improvement
papers.abstract: Self-evolving language models can continuously acquire useful experience through test-time interaction, reflection, and prompt optimization, yet turning such experience into model itself to ensure self improvement remains challenging. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides a natural mechanism for internalizing test-time information into model parameters, yet it largely assumes that the gener- ated experience is worth learning. We show that this assumption does not always hold: experiences that improve test-time performance may provide limited or even harmful training signals. To better characterize which experience should be inter- nalized, we systematically analyze diverse mutated experiences across multiple tasks and reflection models, and find that gradient-based alignment is a more reli- able indicator of downstream distillation gains than immediate test-time improve- ment. Based on this finding, we propose E2L, a self-evolution framework that iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their esti- mated training utility. E2L closes the loop between experience generation and parameter learning, enabling agents to autonomously produce experience suitable for self-improvement.
papers.summary: Self-evolving language models gather useful experience at test time through interaction, reflection and prompt optimization, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) can internalize that experience into model weights, but it assumes the experience is worth learning. The authors show this assumption can fail: experience that improves test-time performance may give limited or even harmful training signal. Analyzing mutated experiences across tasks and reflection models, they find that **gradient-based alignment predicts downstream distillation gains more reliably than immediate test-time improvement**. They build `E2L` on this, a framework that iteratively generates, evaluates and distills experiences according to estimated training utility.

papers.title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories
papers.abstract: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.
papers.summary: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories must cope with high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times and subject-level variation, and existing methods either stay interpretable but do not scale or scale but lose structure. The Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (`LCMM-VAE`) is a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so each subject's latent trajectory splits into a class mean and a subject-specific deviation. A variational EM algorithm with closed-form updates is derived, along with identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. On simulated and real cohorts the model **returns a partition, reconstructions of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class dynamics together while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines**.

papers.title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics
papers.abstract: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. Across magnifications zeta in [10^0, 10^8], C^1 Fourier and lattice-noise bases collapse to post-standardization rank ~2.25 and SHA-256 PRNG exhibits avalanche discontinuity (rho ~ 0.019, 50.6% micro-step retention), whereas dM uniquely sustains both rank (~10.0) and local continuity (rho in [0.81, 0.97], 89.2% retention). Under leak-free 10-fold CV across four zero-scaler-byte non-linear benchmarks, FNS with an INT8 readout surpasses 0-hidden Linear-INT8 by +3.6 to +10.8 pp while delivering 10.7x-129x total Flash reduction (725x-2,773x hidden reduction) relative to converged Float32 MLPs (90.30% Ionosphere in 285 B; 97.22% Optical Digits in 2,598 B; 97.90% PenDigits in 2,598 B; 87.00% Satimage in 1,570 B).
papers.summary: Stored neural network weights take Flash memory proportional to parameter count, which is a constraint on edge microcontrollers. Fractal Neural Synthesis (`FNS`) replaces hidden-layer weight matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed near the boundary of the Mandelbrot set, from which weights are derived procedurally using a smooth escape-time kernel and several geometric sampling patterns. The authors report that this boundary sustains both high rank and local continuity across magnifications, unlike Fourier, lattice-noise or `SHA-256` pseudo-random bases. In 10-fold cross-validation on four benchmarks, `FNS` with an 8-bit integer readout beats a linear 8-bit baseline by 3.6 to 10.8 percentage points and achieves a **10.7x to 129x reduction in total Flash** relative to 32-bit float multilayer perceptrons, for example 97.22% on `Optical Digits` in 2,598 bytes.

papers.title: Not All Pairs Align: Caption-Guided Audio-Visual Contrastive Learning
papers.abstract: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal.
