We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.
papers.summary: Audio-visual contrastive learning assumes that co-occurring audio and video carry the same information, which fails when, for example, sounds come from off-screen sources. Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (`CGAAL`) is a model-agnostic objective that uses modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between the audio and video of each pair and weights positive pairs accordingly. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding introduce the weighting progressively during training. Applied to three contrastive baselines, it **consistently improves audio-visual retrieval performance**.

papers.title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.
papers.summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) agents struggle to recover after deviating from the instructed route. The authors trace this to what they call progress hallucination, where **agents read off-route observations as evidence of progress, so their internal instruction progress runs ahead of the actual task stage**. Their test-time framework `PHAR` (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery) uses a verifier that inspects residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) for cross-modal mismatch, with split conformal calibration to control false alarms, and a contextual bandit that chooses how far to rewind instruction progress. Experiments on `R2R-CE` and `RxR-CE` are reported to improve the reliability of several existing navigation methods.

papers.title: Optimal Transport Meets t-SNE: Integrated Visualization without Batch Effects in OT-tSNE
papers.abstract: Visual exploration is an integral step in understanding the structure of datasets. However, systematic variation between datasets collected under different conditions, known as batch effects, can obscure shared structure and complicate their joint visualization. Existing methods often rely on cross-batch nearest-neighbor relations to integrate the batches. Yet, these local correspondences can be unreliable for challenging cross-batch geometries. We propose optimal-transport t-SNE (OT-tSNE), which replaces nearest-neighbor-based matching with globally coupled affinities derived from entropic optimal transport. Controlled synthetic experiments demonstrated that nearest-neighbor-based methods can deteriorate, while optimal-transport affinities and OT-tSNE embeddings remain robust. Across seven real single-cell datasets, we benchmarked OT-tSNE against a broad range of integration and visualization methods and found that it achieves a Pareto-efficient trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation, and integrates batches particularly well.
papers.summary: Batch effects, the systematic variation between datasets collected under different conditions, can obscure shared structure in joint visualizations, and existing integration methods rely on cross-batch nearest neighbors that can be unreliable. `OT-tSNE` replaces nearest-neighbor matching in `t-SNE` with globally coupled affinities derived from entropic optimal transport. In controlled synthetic experiments nearest-neighbor methods deteriorate while the optimal-transport affinities stay robust. Across seven real single-cell datasets, the method **achieves a Pareto-efficient trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation**.

papers.title: A Framework for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification under Dataset Shift
papers.abstract: Graph node quantification is the supervised learning task of estimating the prevalence of different classes within an arbitrary sample of unlabelled nodes from a graph, subject to some form of dataset shift. Existing approaches to graph node quantification typically follow the standard aggregative paradigm, i.e., they use labelled nodes from the graph to train an intermediate node classifier, and obtain an estimated class distribution for the sample by aggregating the classifier's predictions for the individual nodes and then correcting the result via some adjustment strategy that accounts for dataset shift. In this work we propose a framework for graph node quantification that does away with both node-level supervision, since its training phase only requires node samples labelled by their class distribution, and node-level predictions, since it estimates class prevalence values directly, without the need of any intermediate node classifier. The framework thus allows symmetric quantification, since (unlike in standard ``asymmetric'' quantification methods) the labelled items used for training and the unlabelled items on which predictions must be issued are of the same type (i.e., node samples). This framework (that we dub GSQ, for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification) allows building pipelines consisting of a node encoder, an embedding pooler, a prevalence predictor, and an optional post-hoc scaling step. These components can be instantiated by choosing from different trainable and reservoir-based encoders, different pooling operators, and different prediction objectives. We evaluate the GSQ framework on binary and multi-class datasets with different levels of homophily, under prior probability shift and under structural covariate shift.
papers.summary: Graph node quantification estimates the prevalence of each class in a sample of unlabelled graph nodes under dataset shift, and is usually done by training a node classifier and correcting its aggregated predictions. The proposed framework, Graph Node Symmetric Quantification (`GSQ`), **needs neither node-level labels nor node-level predictions**: it trains on node samples labelled only by their class distribution and predicts prevalence directly. Pipelines combine a node encoder (trainable or reservoir-based), an embedding pooler, a prevalence predictor and an optional post-hoc scaling step. Evaluation covers binary and multi-class datasets with varying homophily under prior probability shift and structural covariate shift; the abstract reports no headline results.

papers.title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
papers.abstract: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) now pass more than 90% of `VerilogEval`, leaving little headroom to measure progress in hardware description language (HDL) generation. `CPU-Eval` is a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems built from six real CPU designs, from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores, written in `SystemVerilog`, `Chisel` and `SpinalHDL`. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, **mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower than on `VerilogEval v2` Spec-to-RTL**. Pass rates drop for submodules with more lines of source and for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, which the authors take as support for fine-grained modular design and for checking a model's proficiency in the target HDL.

papers.title: BEACON: Learning Observation-Conditioned Starting Points for Guided Conditional Flow Matching in Microscopy
papers.abstract: Fluorescence microscopy drives much of modern life science, but accessible imaging setups often yield images degraded by out-of-focus light, limited resolution, and strong signal-dependent noise. Computational restoration can recover high-quality images from such data, enabling cheaper and faster imaging at lower light dose, provided biologically meaningful structures are preserved. Guided conditional flow matching has recently shown strong results for microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution by learning distributions of plausible restorations. However, it pairs each clean target with an independent standard Gaussian sample, so the starting point of every training path does not leverage the degraded observation. This arbitrary noise--target coupling can produce conflicting velocity targets and makes the conditional velocity field harder to learn. We present BEACON, a $BE$st-of-$K$ $A$daptive learned coupling for guided $CON$ditional flow matching, which learns an observation-conditioned base distribution. During training, a lightweight conditional noise model proposes $K$ starting points for each degraded input, and the candidate with the lowest flow-matching loss supervises both networks, while a KL term keeps the proposal close to the Gaussian prior. At inference, a single draw from the learned proposal is transported along the velocity field, requiring neither candidate selection nor the target. We evaluate BEACON on ten datasets spanning microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution against 13 baseline families. BEACON achieves the best median perception--distortion rank for every pairing of a fidelity metric (PSNR, MicroMS-SSIM) with a perceptual metric (LPIPS, FID). Code and pretrained models will be released under a permissive license.
papers.summary: Guided conditional flow matching for restoring degraded fluorescence microscopy images pairs each clean target with an independent Gaussian noise sample, ignoring the degraded observation and producing conflicting velocity targets. `BEACON` learns an observation-conditioned starting distribution: during training a lightweight noise model proposes K candidate starting points, the one with the lowest flow-matching loss supervises both networks, and a KL term keeps proposals near the Gaussian prior. Inference needs only a single draw from the learned proposal. Across ten dehazing and super-resolution datasets and 13 baseline families, it **achieves the best median perception-distortion rank for every pairing of fidelity and perceptual metrics**.

papers.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
papers.abstract: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $\beta\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\ge\beta$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.
papers.summary: Several analyses fit survival models to AI agents' time-horizon curves, which plot task success probability against human completion time, and conclude that the hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The author shows that **the curve alone cannot identify within-task hazard**: any log-logistic curve with slope at most 1 is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a frailty model many within-task Weibull shapes produce the same curve. Repeated runs of the same task restore identification, because the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted along the log time axis by an amount that reveals the Weibull shape. Applied to `METR` public run-level data under assumptions the data cannot verify, no model's interval supports a declining hazard, and for the five frontier models in the `TH1.0` release the intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard.

papers.title: On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/Recurrent-DLLM/
papers.summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked token sequences, but they normally discard the continuous hidden states computed at each step and keep only token-level information. An analysis of those hidden states finds layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation when transformer blocks are removed, and strong final-state alignment between consecutive denoising steps. Building on this, the authors propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (`CSRR`), which **carries hidden-state information across denoising steps and improves text generation quality** in their experiments.

papers.title: Factorized Context Attention: From Emulated to Native Grid Probing
papers.abstract: Models read a book, an hour of video, or an image in one forward pass. As the context grows, this pass slows down, loses accuracy, and stops at the context window. Sparse attention is efficient, but keeps the other two limitations. Grid probing, a recent training-free method, recovers the accuracy and extends the reach by asking a frozen model the same question about short local and strided spans of the input, but every question repeats the whole computation, since each span is encoded again. Our insight is that grid probing is emulated attention, an attention pattern reproduced from outside the model through prompts, since each probe only restricts which part of the input the question can see. We introduce Factorized Context Attention (FCA), a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern natively, as the attention of the model itself. FCA encodes the input once into a KV cache, reads all spans as masked sequences in one batched forward, and uses a stair position schedule to keep every span inside the trained position range. Across long video understanding, long-context text inference and image grounding, FCA matches the accuracy and the reach of grid probing at a fraction of its cost. It gains about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels, finds needles in videos of over a thousand frames and in texts four times the length of the window, and answers a later question about the same input in as little as a tenth of the time of grid probing. Native attention thus keeps what emulated attention gains without its cost, all with existing frozen language and vision-language models.
papers.summary: Long inputs slow down a single forward pass, reduce accuracy, and eventually exceed the context window; grid probing fixes accuracy and reach by asking a frozen model the same question over short local and strided spans, but re-encodes every span. Factorized Context Attention (`FCA`) is a training-free block-sparse attention that runs the same pattern inside the model: the input is encoded once into a key-value cache, all spans are read as masked sequences in one batched forward pass, and a stair position schedule keeps spans inside the trained position range. On long video, long-text inference, and image grounding with frozen language and vision-language models, it matches grid probing's accuracy at a fraction of the cost, gaining **about 10 points over the single pass on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels**. It also finds needles in texts four times the window length and answers follow-up questions about the same input in as little as a tenth of grid probing's time.

papers.title: NRG-Twins: Pixel-Level Ground Truth for Rigidity Violations in Generated Videos
papers.abstract: Video generators now produce realistic clips of scenes and objects, which makes generated video an attractive source of 3D content. Yet generated video is not 3D consistent: static content slowly deforms or slides, 3D reconstruction degrades, and the errors are too subtle to label by hand. To make generators 3D consistent, or to build rewards and guidance that push them there, we need data that say where and by how much a generated video breaks rigidity, and these data must come from generated video itself. We obtain per-pixel ground-truth labels from real-generated twins: a real clip paired with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator. After inserting real keyframes so that the twin camera roughly follows the real one, we measure per pixel, in degrees, how far the twin departs from a rigid scene seen along its own camera path. We release Non-Rigidly Generated Twins (NRG-Twins), 871 twins, the code that builds them for new generators, and a benchmark with an official test split. A detector trained on these data, the Non-Rigidly Generated Pixel Detector (NRG-PD), predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. It separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with AUROC 0.85, against 0.40-0.74 for seven existing consistency and motion-segmentation methods, and its predictions improve 3DGS of video that contains generated content.
papers.summary: Generated videos are not 3D consistent, with static content slowly deforming or sliding in ways too subtle to label by hand. The authors obtain per-pixel ground truth from real-generated twins, pairing a real clip with its re-creation by a keyframe-conditioned video generator and measuring, in degrees, how far each pixel departs from a rigid scene along the twin's camera path. They release `NRG-Twins` (Non-Rigidly Generated Twins) with 871 twins, the construction code, and a benchmark, and train a detector, `NRG-PD`, that predicts the per-pixel angle from RGB alone. The detector separates inconsistent from consistent pixels with **AUROC 0.85 versus 0.40-0.74 for seven existing methods**, and its predictions improve `3DGS` reconstruction of video containing generated content.

papers.title: See the Answer, Learn to Embed: Learning Universal Multimodal Embeddings from Hindsight
papers.abstract: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.
papers.summary: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models that use intermediate reasoning to add context pay extra computation at inference time. Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (`HEME`) instead lets a teacher see the matched candidate during training, using a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to keep the query representation from leaking candidate-specific information or collapsing onto the candidate embedding. The frozen teacher's representation and similarity distribution are then distilled into a student that **encodes queries and candidates independently at inference, with no candidate conditioning or teacher**. Experiments on `MMEB-V2` and the agent and text tasks of `MMEB-V3` report improved effectiveness and more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.

papers.title: When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents When Ink Meets Pixel: Intent-Aware OCR with VLMs for Human-Corrected Financial Documents
papers.abstract: Human annotations on documents (such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions) express corrective intent yet existing OCR and document understanding systems treat these marks as visual noise rather than semantic edit operations. We introduce intent-aware OCR, the task of generating corrected transcriptions by jointly reasoning over original document content and visual intent cues (handwritten or digital) that convey edit intent. To support this setting, we present DocIntent, a multimodal dataset of 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated visual intent cues, each paired with layout-aware, intent-resolved OCR targets. We further introduce IntentBench, a 216-document benchmark designed to evaluate model robustness under diverse real-world annotation conditions. Leveraging DocIntent, we fine-tune DocIntentOCR, a suite of 3B and 7B parameter vision-language models, under direct intent supervision on corrected transcriptions. On IntentBench, the fine-tuned 3B and 7B models achieve F1-scores of 0.81 and 0.83, respectively, substantially outperforming commercial closed-source (e.g., GPT-4.1 (0.626)), and open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B (0.50)) demonstrating that intent-aware supervision enables compact domain-specific models to outperform substantially larger general-purpose systems on this task. This work establishes intent-aware OCR as a novel human-in-the-loop document understanding task and provides foundational resources (dataset, benchmark, models) to advance research in interactive document processing.
papers.summary: Handwritten or digital marks on documents, such as arrows, carets, strikethroughs, and insertions, express corrections that existing OCR systems treat as visual noise. The authors define intent-aware OCR, where the model outputs the corrected transcription, and release `DocIntent`, 1,600 financial documents with over 5,700 annotated intent cues, plus the 216-document benchmark `IntentBench`. Their fine-tuned `DocIntentOCR` vision-language models at 3B and 7B parameters reach **F1 scores of 0.81 and 0.83 on `IntentBench`, compared with 0.626 for `GPT-4.1`** and 0.50 for `LLaMA-3.2-Vision-90B`.

papers.title: The Teacher Is Already Inside: Self-Distilling Looped Language Models Beyond Their Last Loop
papers.abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop is readable through the shared language-model head. Post-training them is hard. Reward-only reinforcement learning needs a verifier and learns from one sparse signal per response; spreading the reward over loops collapses the entropy of every loop; and cross-loop self-distillation, as in LoopOPD, can only teach intermediate loops, because the last loop cannot learn from its own frozen copy: the loss is zero at initialisation. We observe that a looped model already contains a policy that decodes better than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELPSD (Extrapolated-Loop Policy Self-Distillation) turns this distribution into a self-distillation target: a frozen copy of the model computes it, and the model's own last loop is distilled towards it on its own rollouts, using the exact reverse KL at every visited prefix. Teacher and student are the same model, so ELPSD needs no reward, no external teacher and no privileged context, and it leaves rollouts and decoding unchanged. We show that the objective pulls the last loop towards the base model's last loop with weight 1+w and away from the base model's first loop with weight w, and that the teacher must stay frozen, since an idealised teacher recomputed from the current model extrapolates without bound. We evaluate ELPSD on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking across five math benchmarks against the base model, GRPO, RLTT and OPSD. Without any reward, ELPSD raises the average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69 and is the best method on all five benchmarks, ahead of GRPO (62.32), which uses a verifier, and the self-distillation method OPSD (61.77), which needs reference solutions.
papers.summary: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and existing post-training methods either need a verifier and sparse rewards or, like cross-loop self-distillation, cannot teach the last loop because its loss against its own frozen copy is zero. Extrapolated-Loop Policy Self-Distillation (`ELPSD`) uses as a target the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last, computed by a frozen copy of the model, and distills the model's last loop toward it on its own rollouts with exact reverse KL. The authors show the teacher must stay frozen, since a teacher recomputed from the current model extrapolates without bound. On `Ouro-1.4B-Thinking` across five math benchmarks, and without any reward, it raises **average avg@8 from 61.15 to 63.69**, ahead of `GRPO` (62.32) and `OPSD` (61.77).

papers.title: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
papers.abstract:
Parameter-efficient adaptation of a speech foundation model to dysarthric speech requires a rarely justified choice: which encoder layers to adapt. A recently proposed strategy is to probe the encoder, find where phonetic information becomes most decodable, and put the adapters there. We test that inference across two ASR models (Qwen3-ASR, Whisper-small) and two dysarthric corpora (Mandarin CDSD, English UASpeech), holding recipe and seed discipline constant.
  The inference fails. Measured under one pipeline rather than inherited from published figures, all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, each model's minimising layer moving no further between corpora than between probe seeds. The best adaptation band is not similarly constant: none of three natural mappings from the curve to a band -- steepest improvement, lowest band-mean error, or knee location -- recovers the best tested configuration. We do not claim no statistic of the curve could work, only that these three do not.
  Placement still matters, but is model- and corpus-specific. On CDSD the models disagree -- Qwen3-ASR prefers its upper third (29.88% CER, three-seed mean), Whisper-small all-block LoRA (53.56%) -- while on UASpeech neither favours the upper band. At three seeds, upper-versus-all is resolved (-1.31 pp, CI [-2.16, -0.25]) but upper-versus-middle is not (-0.83 pp, CI [-2.06, +1.86]). The two models' preferences differ as a directly tested interaction (-4.71 pp, CI [-6.17, -2.89]); we designate this the primary claim, and record that the designation was made post hoc. On Qwen3-ASR x UASpeech, adapting near the input is reliably worse than not adapting at all (+9.90 pp CER). We recommend choosing the band by a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand, not by reading it off a probe.
papers.summary: A recently proposed way to choose which encoder layers receive `LoRA` adapters for dysarthric speech recognition is to probe where phonetic information is most decodable and adapt there. Testing this on `Qwen3-ASR` and `Whisper-small` with the Mandarin `CDSD` and English `UASpeech` corpora, the authors find all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, yet **none of three natural mappings from the probe curve to an adaptation band recovers the best tested configuration**; they note other statistics of the curve might still work. Placement still matters but is model- and corpus-specific, and on `Qwen3-ASR` with `UASpeech` adapting near the input is worse than not adapting at all. They recommend a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand instead of reading the band off a probe.

papers.title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
papers.abstract: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.
papers.summary: Multi-reference image generation must preserve the appearance of chosen subjects while arranging them as instructed, and planned spatial relationships are rarely made explicit enough to inspect before synthesis. `MAGPIE` represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable `Blender` program, which a coding agent writes, checks against the instruction through geometry and a rendered view, and revises. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for an image generator trained on `MAGPIE-Instruct-3K` to follow the plan while taking each subject's appearance from its reference. With `FLUX`, overall success on `DreamOmni2` rises by **28.21 percentage points over the original backbone**, and the method also improves `Qwen` and achieves the highest overall score among evaluated models on `SconeEval`.
papers.highlight_summary:
Multi-reference image generators can preserve each subject's appearance yet still miscompose the scene, and the error only becomes visible in the final image. `MAGPIE` has a coding agent first build the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene in an executable Blender program, verify and revise it, and then pass the proxy rendering to the generator as a visual plan alongside the original references.

- The agent writes an instance-level scene specification that binds each entity to its reference, generates a Blender program from a library of parameterized components, and runs up to **six refinement rounds** that combine geometric checks (visibility, camera-relative ordering, surface contact) with a multimodal reviewer's feedback.
- Because pretrained generators do not reliably read proxy renderings as layout constraints, the authors build `MAGPIE-Instruct-3K` (**3,187** examples of references, instruction, Blender program, proxy rendering and target image) and train rank-32 LoRA adapters on `Qwen-Image-Edit-2511` and `FLUX.2-klein-base-9B`.
- On `DreamOmni2`, overall success rises from 38.87% to **67.08%** with FLUX (**+28.21 points**) and from 42.01% to **64.26%** with Qwen (**+22.25 points**), ahead of the open-weight `DreamOmni2` model (58.31%) and `Gemini-2.5-Flash-Image` (61.44%) but still below `Seedream-4.0` (68.97%); on `SconeEval`, the FLUX variant reaches **9.05** overall, the highest among the models compared (`GPT-4o` scores 8.94).
- Ablations show the gain is not just from extra data, since `MAGPIE` beats ordinary fine-tuning on the same reference–target pairs by **19.43** (Qwen) and **18.18** (FLUX) points, while the 3D proxy beats text and 2D bounding-box plans on generation by 12.28 and 8.77 points, and refinement lifts the FLUX overall score from 53.61% at zero rounds to 67.08% at six.
- Supplying the proxy without adaptation is unreliable (it drops Qwen to 29.47%), concrete-subject generation scores do not move on either backbone so the gains come from abstract-attribute and editing cases, and the training set is filtered to compositions expressible in coarse geometry, with all benchmark scores assigned by LLM judges.

papers.title: Describe, Don't Ask: Caption-Driven On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Visual Perception
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often recognize fine-grained details more accurately in a relevant crop than in the full image. Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) methods exploit this by transferring the advantage of a crop-view teacher to a full-image student. However, their supervision relies on region-specific questions curated through an elaborate synthesis pipeline, which brings three weaknesses: (1) every region needs a question--answer pair written exclusively for it, locking training into costly QA curation that is hard to scale to unlabeled images; (2) all rollouts of a region answer the same question, so the teacher supervises only the details it asks about, leaving other visual elements in the region unsupervised; and (3) every question presupposes that its target exists, so the student becomes prone to answering even when the target is absent. In this paper, we study how to turn unlabeled images into broad visual supervision through multi-aspect self-description and privileged-view distillation, and propose CaptionOPD, which replaces tailored questions with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts, ranging from general descriptions to focused captions of parts, colors, counts, text, and layout. The rollouts of a region receive different prompts, so the teacher supervises various aspects of the region. Moreover, because caption prompts mask the model to describe what is visible instead of querying a specific target, they avoid presupposing what the region contains. Using the model itself as the crop-view teacher, CaptionOPD requires no questions, no answers, and no larger model annotations: only images and region boxes. Experiments show that, trained on the same images and regions, CaptionOPD outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks.
papers.summary: Vision-language models often recognize fine details better in a crop than in the full image, and multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers that crop-view advantage to a full-image student, but existing methods depend on region-specific question-answer pairs that are costly to curate, supervise only what is asked, and presuppose the target exists. `CaptionOPD` replaces these questions with a fixed set of image-agnostic caption prompts covering general descriptions, parts, colors, counts, text, and layout, so different rollouts of a region supervise different aspects. The model serves as its own crop-view teacher, so training needs only images and region boxes. Trained on the same images and regions, it **outperforms prior OPD methods across multiple fine-grained and general perception benchmarks**.

papers.title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
papers.abstract: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.
papers.summary: A survey of **28 adult participants** examines how players perceive AI-driven user modeling and gamification in games and gamified applications. Respondents expressed strong concern about the collection and use of personal data while reporting low awareness and little sense of control over it. They rated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating, but rated retention mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative, citing fear of missing out and resemblance to gambling. Participants also supported regulation that limits exploitative design and protects vulnerable users.

papers.title: BCP: A Lightweight Boundary-Controlled Framework for Online Sign Language Recognition and Translation
papers.abstract: Online sign language recognition (SLR) and translation (SLT) incrementally produce gloss sequences or natural language text from sign video as it arrives, a capability essential for real-time communication and live captioning. However, powerful pretrained offline models cannot be directly deployed in this setting, while existing online methods typically retrain the entire model on simulated streaming prefixes constructed from offline videos, incurring high costs. To address this challenge, we propose Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (BCP), a unified lightweight framework that converts pretrained offline methods into online counterparts for sign-to-gloss (S2G), sign-to-text (S2T), and sign-to-gloss-to-text (S2G2T). Specifically, BCP freezes the pretrained model and introduces a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained SLR model, without any human annotation. At inference, a Boundary-Controlled Wait-K Output Policy then decides what to commit via prefix voting, yielding adaptive burst commits while preserving the output progress of the base Wait-K schedule. Experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily across four offline methods show that BCP, with less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per offline method, achieves a strong quality-latency trade-off on S2T and remains competitive on S2G and S2G2T.
papers.summary: Online sign language recognition and translation must emit glosses or text as video arrives, but pretrained offline models cannot be deployed directly and existing online methods retrain the whole model on simulated streaming prefixes. Boundary-Controlled Prefix Commit (`BCP`) freezes the offline model and adds a lightweight boundary adapter that decides when to commit output, supervised by Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) alignments from a pretrained recognition model with no human annotation. At inference, a boundary-controlled Wait-K policy chooses what to commit through prefix voting. On `PHOENIX-2014T` and `CSL-Daily` across four offline methods, it uses **less than 0.1% additional trainable parameters per method** while achieving a strong quality-latency trade-off on sign-to-text and remaining competitive on sign-to-gloss and sign-to-gloss-to-text.

papers.title: STAR: Counterfactual Dual-World Rollouts and Spatial Target Adaptive Reconstruction for Visual On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Vision-language models often rely on global context and language priors while overlooking answer-determining local details. Privileged visual on-policy self-distillation supervises full-image student rollouts using a frozen teacher that views high-resolution evidence crops. Yet our cross-scale diagnostics show that models retain over half of their full-image accuracy when local evidence is completely masked, indicating that single-image correctness does not guarantee reliance on local evidence, while the need for visual correction also varies across tokens with their spatial attention states. We propose STAR, a visual on-policy self-distillation framework combining independent counterfactual dual-world rollouts with spatial-attention-guided target reconstruction. Local image editing constructs paired worlds with identical questions and backgrounds but distinct answer-determining facts, where a shared student samples trajectories independently to expose contextual shortcuts under image-consistent prefixes. Within each world, the teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to determine the visual correction direction, while the divergence between student image attention and a teacher-centroid spatial reference adaptively controls token-wise target log-probability reconstruction. Without auxiliary attention losses or test-time tool overhead, STAR improves Qwen3.5 across scales by up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy over initialization across six fine-grained benchmarks, reaches OPSD's final accuracy $4.7\times$ faster, and generalizes to out-of-domain reasoning tasks.
papers.summary: Vision-language models often answer from global context and language priors instead of the local details that determine the answer; the authors' diagnostics show models keep over half of their full-image accuracy when the local evidence is fully masked. `STAR` is a visual on-policy self-distillation framework that uses local image editing to build paired worlds with the same question and background but different answer-determining facts, with a shared student sampling trajectories independently in each. A frozen teacher contrasts real and mean-color crops to set the correction direction, and the divergence between student image attention and a teacher spatial reference controls token-wise target reconstruction. It improves `Qwen3.5` by **up to 8.04 percentage points in average accuracy across six fine-grained benchmarks** and reaches the final accuracy of `OPSD` 4.7x faster.

papers.title: Progressive Reliable Supervision for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract: Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation (B$^2$-UniDA) aims to adapt a target model to an unlabeled target domain under arbitrary label-space relationships, while neither source data nor source-model parameters are accessible during adaptation. Under such restrictive information access, reliable target supervision is unavailable, while predictions from the black-box source model can be unreliable due to source bias and domain shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Progressive Reliable Supervision (PReS), which progressively establishes and refines reliable target supervision by coordinating complementary knowledge from the black-box source model, foundation models, and the evolving target model. PReS first identifies reliable known samples by exploiting semantic consistency under diffusion-based perturbations and cross-model consensus between the black-box source model and CLIP. It then estimates the sample-wise reliability of the two predictors and adaptively integrates their complementary predictions to construct reliable pseudo labels. The resulting supervision is exploited asymmetrically to encourage confident and discriminative predictions for reliable known samples while maintaining uncertain yet locally consistent predictions for potential unknown samples. As adaptation proceeds, the emerging target-domain knowledge is further leveraged to refine both the pseudo labels and the known/unknown sample partition, forming a closed-loop process in which supervision construction and target adaptation mutually reinforce each other. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under diverse label-space relationships demonstrate that PReS achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance under the restrictive B$^2$-UniDA setting.
papers.summary: Black-box universal domain adaptation adapts a model to an unlabeled target domain under arbitrary label-space relationships when neither source data nor source-model parameters are accessible, leaving only unreliable predictions from the source model. Progressive Reliable Supervision (`PReS`) identifies reliable known-class samples through semantic consistency under diffusion-based perturbations and agreement between the black-box source model and `CLIP`, then weights the two predictors by estimated per-sample reliability to build pseudo labels. Training treats reliable known samples and potential unknown samples asymmetrically, and the evolving target model is used to refine both the pseudo labels and the known/unknown partition in a closed loop. Across multiple benchmarks and label-space settings, it reports **state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance**.

papers.title: VISE: Verifier-Independent Skill Self-Evolution with Feedback from Tool Implementations
papers.abstract: Agent skills provide reusable workflows that guide LLM agents in using tools. Refining these workflows requires feedback on missing or incorrect instructions, but task-specific verifiers are not always available. We propose VISE (Verifier-Independent Skill Evolution), a scripts-first approach that uses tool implementations to guide skill revision. It extracts tool capabilities, input requirements, usage conditions, and output formats from source code. Using the task request and execution trace, it compares this information with current workflow instructions to identify missing or conflicting steps. It then recommends specific edits to SKILL.md, linking each change to the relevant implementation and usage conditions. We evaluate VISE as an additional revision stage for four evolution methods on SkillsBench and SkillLearnBench. Compared with the corresponding No-verifier conditions, it improves overall average task success by 9.14-13.35 percentage points. The proportion of tasks solved in all three runs increases by 12.36-18.29 points. A case study shows how revised instructions connect tool outputs to later steps. These results support tool implementations as a practical feedback source for skill self-evolution.
papers.summary: Agent skills are reusable workflows that guide LLM agents in using tools, and refining them normally needs feedback from task-specific verifiers that are not always available. `VISE` (Verifier-Independent Skill Evolution) instead extracts tool capabilities, input requirements, usage conditions, and output formats from tool source code, compares them with the current workflow instructions using the task request and execution trace, and recommends specific edits to `SKILL.md` linked to the relevant implementation. Added as an extra revision stage to four evolution methods on `SkillsBench` and `SkillLearnBench`, it raises **average task success by 9.14-13.35 percentage points over the corresponding no-verifier conditions**. The share of tasks solved in all three runs increases by 12.36-18.29 points.

papers.title: CodeWAM: A Code World Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Driving world models anticipate action consequences through representations of how the world evolves. For autonomous driving, these representations must capture both the surrounding scene and the ego vehicle's motion under a candidate plan. We propose CodeWAM, a driving world model that incorporates executable code as part of its world representation. Code represents ego dynamics by expressing how the vehicle state evolves under plan execution, while a learned visual model captures scene-dependent consequences. Executing the code produces a candidate-conditioned motion sequence, which is evaluated relative to the prior plan and recorded motion history. The resulting execution consequences and learned scene outcomes jointly represent the candidate's future, enabling the planner to assess both what a plan may lead to and how the vehicle transitions into that future. The selected plan becomes part of the next decision's execution context, linking successive choices within the model. CodeWAM achieves 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD. Further experiments demonstrate improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training, supporting executable code as a complementary representation for driving world models.
papers.summary: Driving world models need to represent both how the surrounding scene evolves and how the ego vehicle moves under a candidate plan. `CodeWAM` adds executable code to the world representation: code expresses how the vehicle state evolves when a plan is executed, while a learned visual model captures scene-dependent consequences, and the planner evaluates candidates using both. It reaches **93.6 PDMS on `NAVSIM` v1 navtest**, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on `NAVHARD`. Further experiments show improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on `Hydra-MDP` and `DrivoR` without additional training.

papers.title: When Knowledge-Tracing Rankings Depend on Available History: A Source-Correction and Matched-Information Audit on ASSISTments 2009 and 2015
papers.abstract: Knowledge-tracing benchmarks often compare models that have different access to a learner's previous responses. We examine how data provenance, history length, and representation affect those comparisons. First, we compare a pinned ASSISTments 2009 sequence mirror against the corrected official release. Of 4,148 learners represented in both, 817 have different ordered skill-response sequences; the mirror also contains fewer labeled events. Second, we retain earlier learner-disjoint model evaluations on the 2009 and 2015 datasets, distinguishing exploratory results from a corrective 2015 replication. Finally, we evaluate a new, nonoverlapping sample of 4,000 ASSISTments 2015 learners using three models constrained to the same one-event or 20-event prior-response window. On 20,592 test responses from 582 learners, the 20-event Brier scores were 0.17667 for count-based logistic regression, 0.17389 for an order-aware logistic model, and 0.17514 for a GRU. The GRU-minus-order-aware difference was 0.00125 (95% learner-cluster bootstrap interval [0.00008, 0.00243]); at one prior event, the corresponding difference was 0.00212 [0.00120, 0.00301]. Earlier comparisons had favored the GRU against simpler history summaries. The newer analysis instead favors a logistic comparator that represents order using the same permitted event stream. These results concern predictive performance on particular historical cohorts and model settings. They neither isolate an architectural effect nor establish generalization to contemporary classrooms.
papers.summary: Knowledge-tracing benchmarks often compare models that see different amounts of a learner's response history, and this audit examines how data provenance, history length, and representation affect such comparisons. Comparing a pinned `ASSISTments 2009` mirror against the corrected official release, 817 of 4,148 shared learners have different ordered skill-response sequences. On a new sample of 4,000 `ASSISTments 2015` learners with all models limited to the same 20-event window, **an order-aware logistic model scored a Brier of 0.17389 against 0.17514 for a `GRU`** and 0.17667 for count-based logistic regression, reversing earlier comparisons that favored the `GRU`. The authors state that the results apply to these cohorts and settings and do not isolate an architectural effect.

papers.title: Assessing Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.abstract: As the use of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes more widespread in cyber-physical systems, it becomes increasingly important to design RL agents that are able to adapt to changes in their environments in order to maintain safety and reliability. This paper addresses the question of whether different classes of RL algorithm are more robust against forgetting previously learned behaviours, a critical issue in continual learning, in non-stationary environments. We evaluate the robustness of representative examples of three important classes of RL algorithm in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment. These are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which is a model-free on-policy algorithm, Soft-Actor-Critic (SAC), which is a model-free off-policy algorithm, and Drama, which is a model-based algorithm. The agents must learn to successfully park in four different scenarios, which are presented successively, with parking spaces oriented at varying angles. We find off-policy algorithms appear to be more robust compared to on-policy algorithms due to their use of replay, while model-based algorithms do not appear to offer any direct advantage over model-free algorithms. These experiments also highlight the additional challenges of finding robust abstractions of the environment, and oversensitivity to hyperparameters.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning agents in cyber-physical systems must adapt to changing environments without forgetting earlier behaviours. The study compares Proximal Policy Optimization (`PPO`, model-free on-policy), Soft-Actor-Critic (`SAC`, model-free off-policy), and the model-based `Drama` in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment where four scenarios with differently angled spaces are presented in succession. The authors find that **off-policy algorithms appear more robust to forgetting than on-policy ones because of replay, while model-based algorithms show no direct advantage** over model-free ones. The experiments also point to difficulty finding robust environment abstractions and to oversensitivity to hyperparameters.

papers.title: InducedTFMs: A Family of Sub-Quadratic Tabular Foundation Models Using Induced Attention
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a serious competitor to gradient-boosted trees, predicting on a new table in a single forward pass by in-context learning. However, their attention is quadratic in the number of samples and features, which caps pretraining at small synthetic tables and forces inference on large ones to rely on chunking or subsampling. Row-compression models reduce the feature-wise cost, but only by discarding the cell-level representation, and remain quadratic in the number of samples. We introduce InducedTFM, which replaces both attention stages of a bidimensional TFM with the induced attention of the Set Transformer, preserving cell-level representations while making its cost linear in both samples and features. Under a training budget matched to a full-attention TabICLv2 reimplementation, InducedTFM matches its accuracy on TabArena and on a benchmark of larger datasets, and clearly outperforms a kernel linear-attention baseline of the same asymptotic cost. It overtakes TabICLv2 in inference time on narrow tables, reaching a 30x speed-up at 640K rows, although row compression remains preferable on wide tables.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict on a new table in one forward pass through in-context learning, but their attention is quadratic in samples and features, which limits pretraining table size and forces chunking or subsampling on large tables. `InducedTFM` replaces both attention stages of a bidimensional TFM with the induced attention of the `Set Transformer`, keeping cell-level representations while making cost linear in both samples and features. Under a training budget matched to a full-attention `TabICLv2` reimplementation, it matches that model's accuracy on `TabArena` and on a benchmark of larger datasets and outperforms a kernel linear-attention baseline. On narrow tables it reaches a **30x inference speed-up at 640K rows**, though row compression remains preferable on wide tables.

papers.title: RecurSciBench: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement in Data-Driven Scientific Research
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are advancing the automation of data-driven scientific research. Recent advances in recursive self-improvement (RSI) offer the potential for these agents to continuously improve through experience, but evaluating transfer across scientific tasks requires executable, scientifically verifiable tasks and independent assessment of self-improvement gains. We introduce RecurSciBench, a scalable benchmark for evaluating RSI in data-driven scientific research. Its RecurSciPipe framework automatically constructs scientific modeling and data analysis tasks from raw datasets, with execution-based verification and scientific validity checks. RecurSciBench spans four scientific domains, multiple data modalities, and varied scientific objectives. We evaluate four RSI systems by comparing their initial and evolved states on independent tasks after evolution on source tasks, covering within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain transfer. Experiments show that the benefits of self-improvement vary across agent systems and scientific domains. Positive overall gains can coexist with regressions on individual tasks. Experience can transfer across task types and benefit other domains even without measurable gains in the source domain.
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) could let LLM-based research agents improve through experience, but measuring whether gains transfer requires executable, scientifically verifiable tasks and independent assessment. `RecurSciBench` uses the `RecurSciPipe` framework to construct scientific modeling and data analysis tasks automatically from raw datasets, with execution-based verification and validity checks, spanning four scientific domains and multiple data modalities. Four RSI systems are evaluated by comparing initial and evolved states on independent tasks under within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain transfer. The results show that **self-improvement benefits vary across agent systems and domains, and overall gains can coexist with regressions on individual tasks**; experience can also help other domains even without measurable gains in the source domain.

papers.title: Analysis of Federated Graph Neural Networks for Predicting Nuclear Core Properties
papers.abstract: Federated learning has grown in popularity owing to the increasing data privacy and safety concerns. It allows multiple parties to collaboratively train a model without exchanging their raw data. As an example of highly sensitive infrastructure of national importance, nuclear reactors benefit from this approach, where---while pooling multiple large datasets from different institutions could improve machine learning solutions---the confidentiality of the datasets is paramount. In this paper, we demonstrate that a graph neural network (GNN) outperforms the convolutional neural network (CNN) baseline in a federated setting for a use case concerning nuclear reactor core optimization. The GNN architecture is better suited for the nuclear reactor geometry as, unlike the CNN, it does not require padding the cylindrical core and does not assume translation invariance. The key finding of this work is that input representation is more important than model size and complexity. More sophisticated federated algorithms were employed, but the improvements derived were of lower magnitude. Experimenting with training corpus volume led to the discovery that greater fuel inventory variance is more beneficial than arrangements of existing cases, which is a direct consequence of data heterogeneity. Going forward, focus will remain on enhancing the input and readout representation.
papers.summary: Federated learning lets institutions train a shared model without exchanging confidential data, which the authors apply to nuclear reactor core optimization. A graph neural network outperforms a convolutional baseline in the federated setting, since it needs no padding of the cylindrical core and does not assume translation invariance. The main finding is that **input representation matters more than model size and complexity**, with more sophisticated federated algorithms yielding smaller improvements. Experiments on training data volume also indicate that greater fuel inventory variance helps more than additional arrangements of existing cases.

papers.title: Branch and Consolidate: A Unified Recipe for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Specialists post-trained from a shared checkpoint acquire complementary capabilities, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) can consolidate them into a single model. However, we find that existing consolidation methods, from weight merging to MOPD, fall short when specialists diverge substantially from the shared checkpoint, whereas prior studies mostly examine specialists that remain close to it. We present a unified recipe for multimodal MOPD that consolidates such specialists back into the single student they branched from. The recipe specifies initialization, data selection, balanced supervision across teachers, and preservation of existing capabilities for consolidation, together with a targeted refinement stage for capabilities that still lag behind their specialists. In an industrial setting with six specialists, the student closely approaches each specialist in its own domain and surpasses the perception specialist. It recovers 97.0% of their average gain, compared with 79.8% for IM-MOPD. In the fully open five-domain setting with Qwen3-4B, our method recovers 95.7% of the specialists' average gain after consolidation and 97.5% after refinement, compared with 94.1% for IM-MOPD. We further analyze the full pipeline through mechanism ablations and training dynamics, providing practical guidance for diagnosing incomplete consolidation. Code will be released.
papers.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) aims to fold several specialist models, post-trained from one shared checkpoint, back into a single student, but the authors find that existing methods from weight merging to MOPD fall short when the specialists have drifted far from that checkpoint. They propose a recipe for multimodal MOPD covering initialization, data selection, balanced supervision across teachers, and preservation of existing capabilities, followed by a targeted refinement stage for capabilities that still lag. In an industrial setting with six specialists the student recovers **97.0% of the specialists' average gain, versus 79.8% for `IM-MOPD`**, and in an open five-domain setting with `Qwen3-4B` it recovers 95.7% after consolidation and 97.5% after refinement, against 94.1% for `IM-MOPD`.

papers.title: Wi-Fi Enabled Edge Intelligence Framework for Smart City Traffic Monitoring using Low-Power IoT Cameras
papers.abstract: Real-time traffic monitoring in smart cities demands ultra-low latency processing to support time-critical decisions such as incident detection and congestion management. While cloud-based solutions offer robust computation, their inherent latency limits their applicability for such tasks. This work proposes a localized edge AI framework that connects low-power IoT camera sensors to a client, or applies offloading of inference to an NVIDIA Jetson Nano (GPU). Networking is achieved via Wi-Fi, enabling image classification without relying on wide-area infrastructure such as 5G, or wired networks. We evaluate two processing strategies: local inference on camera nodes and GPU-accelerated offloading to the Jetson Nano.We show that local processing is only feasible for lightweight models and low frame rates, whereas offloading enables near-realtime performance even for more complex models. These results demonstrate the viability of cost-effective, Wi-Fi-based edge AI deployments for latency-critical urban monitoring.
papers.summary: Real-time traffic monitoring needs lower latency than cloud processing can offer, so the authors build a localized edge framework in which low-power Internet-of-Things camera nodes connect over Wi-Fi and either classify images themselves or offload inference to an `NVIDIA Jetson Nano` GPU. Comparing the two strategies, they find that **on-camera inference is only feasible for lightweight models at low frame rates, while offloading reaches near-real-time performance even for more complex models**. They conclude that Wi-Fi-based edge deployments can work for latency-critical urban monitoring without 5G or wired networks.

papers.title: What If Chinese Were Latinized? A Counterfactual Study of Input Representation, Tokenization, and Language Modeling
papers.abstract: If Chinese had been Latinized, as the Latinxua Sin Wenz movement proposed, what would it have meant for Chinese NLP? Homophones and tone marking complicate the answer. We convert Chinese corpora to syllable-separated Pinyin and train superBPE tokenizers from scratch. The resulting Pinyin vocabularies not only exhibit expected homophone collisions, but also show approximately 10% higher fertility than characters. An alternative BPE configuration changes the relative fertility of the two representations. We further pretrain Llama-style models on Chinese characters and Pinyin. The Pinyin models perform worse on per-character perplexity, homophone disambiguation, and overall ZhoBLiMP minimal-pair accuracy. An exploratory phonological probe yields near-chance performance for both representations. The broader implication is that written input representations are not merely neutral encodings. Choices for representations affect language modeling and their downstream performances. Latinization never actually happened for Chinese, but other languages did, such as Hangul and Latin script replaced character in Korean and Vietnamese; the cost we measure is a guide to where modeling effort for those languages should concentrate.
papers.summary: Asking what Chinese natural language processing would look like had the script been Latinized, the authors convert Chinese corpora to syllable-separated Pinyin, train `superBPE` tokenizers from scratch, and pretrain `Llama`-style models on both characters and Pinyin. The Pinyin vocabularies show homophone collisions and roughly 10% higher fertility than characters, although an alternative byte-pair-encoding configuration changes the relative fertility. **The Pinyin models perform worse on per-character perplexity, homophone disambiguation, and overall `ZhoBLiMP` minimal-pair accuracy**, while a phonological probe is near chance for both representations. The authors read this as evidence that written input representation is not a neutral encoding, with relevance for languages such as Korean and Vietnamese that did change scripts.

papers.title: ContinualDrive: A Deployment-Anchored, Multi-Axis Benchmark for Continual Updates of Learned Driving Planners
papers.abstract: Learned driving planners keep being updated after deployment as new logs arrive, yet continual learning evaluations rarely ask whether an update improves on the deployed model, and their verdicts rest on unstated evaluation choices. We present ContinualDrive, a deployment-anchored benchmark for post-deployment continual learning of driving planners. It updates a deployed planner on real-world nuPlan logs one scenario-type group at a time, evaluates the same checkpoints in open and closed loop, makes four measurement axes explicit (evaluation loop, reference checkpoint, temporal aggregation and stream protocol), and anchors a three-valued release verdict to the deployed checkpoint. We study two planners (PlanTF and Diffusion Planner) under full fine-tuning and adapter or LoRA updates, with and without replay or gradient projection, in three task orders. Verdicts can reverse or vanish when one axis changes: open-loop ADE ranks the final PlanTF model above the deployed one in half of its core-suite runs, whereas every closed-loop score ranks it below; backward transfer misses this loss, which on average is already present when each group has just been learned; and regime rankings vary far less across training seeds than across task orders. In the core suite of full and adapter updates, no regime measurably improved on the deployed planner in closed loop; on a panel more than ten times larger every evaluated final checkpoint trails it, and joint training on all groups recovers much of the loss without exceeding its nuPlan closed-loop score. We distill these findings into a reporting contract and will release the code and all checkpoints.
papers.summary: Learned driving planners are repeatedly updated after deployment, yet continual learning evaluations rarely check whether an update actually beats the deployed model. `ContinualDrive` updates a deployed planner on real-world `nuPlan` logs one scenario-type group at a time, evaluates the same checkpoints in open and closed loop, makes four measurement axes explicit, and ties a three-valued release verdict to the deployed checkpoint, covering `PlanTF` and `Diffusion Planner` under full fine-tuning and adapter or `LoRA` updates with and without replay or gradient projection. Verdicts can flip when one axis changes: open-loop error ranks the final `PlanTF` model above the deployed one in half of the core runs while every closed-loop score ranks it below. In the core suite, **no update regime measurably improved on the deployed planner in closed loop**, and joint training on all groups recovers much of the loss without exceeding the deployed score.

papers.title: Next-Manip: On-Demand Agent-Policy Collaboration for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: General-purpose robotic manipulation requires task reasoning, failure recovery, and precise control, yet limited manipulation data make these abilities difficult to obtain from a single policy. Recent multimodal agents show promise in task reasoning and recovery but lack reliable fine-grained control and incur high inference cost, whereas learned policies provide efficient fine-grained execution but struggle beyond their learned skills. Although their complementary strengths suggest combining the two, doing so requires repeatedly deciding which executor should act as task demands change. Instead of relying on the agent for each decision, we present Next-Manip, an on-demand agent--policy collaboration framework that decouples executor allocation from costly agent inference. We propose an Agent Invocation Controller (AIC) that allocates control between the policy and the agent through a lightweight classifier of current execution demands. We further introduce Task Dynamics Context (TDC), which packages informative manipulation changes from in-context examples into compact task references to support both agent reasoning and executor allocation. Across two simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments, Next-Manip achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing agent inference costs.
papers.summary: Multimodal agents handle task reasoning and failure recovery in robotic manipulation but are costly and imprecise, while learned policies give efficient fine-grained control but struggle outside their trained skills. `Next-Manip` combines the two with an Agent Invocation Controller (AIC), a lightweight classifier of current execution demands that decides which executor acts **without invoking the costly agent for each allocation decision**. A second component, Task Dynamics Context (TDC), packages informative manipulation changes from in-context examples into compact task references used for both agent reasoning and allocation. The authors report state-of-the-art results on two simulation benchmarks and in real-world experiments, with reduced agent inference cost.

papers.title: Advanced Synthetic Image Detection Using Hybrid Feature Extraction
papers.abstract: In the realm of generative AI, models such as GANs, MidJourney, DALL-E, and others have been continuously evolving to generate increasingly lifelike images. This rapid advancement has created an urgent need for robust methods to distinguish between real and AI-generated images. This paper proposes a novel approach for the detection of synthetic images by employing deep learning techniques for feature analysis. The proposed architecture classifies images by identifying variations that generative models struggle to replicate, particularly fine-grained textures and complex object features. Deformations in complexes are examined with the help of the CBAM architecture along with ResNet50. We have performed a selective patch-based analysis using Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) scoring, extracting the regions with the most and least complexity for further processing with an SRM Module and ResNet50 module. Experimental results show that our approach achieves high accuracy in classifying real-world images from synthetic ones, contributing to the development of more reliable detection frameworks.
papers.summary: To distinguish real photographs from AI-generated images, the authors propose a detector that looks for fine-grained textures and complex object features that generative models struggle to reproduce. One branch combines the `CBAM` attention architecture with `ResNet50`, while another scores image patches with the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), selects the most and least complex regions, and processes them with an `SRM` module and `ResNet50`. The authors claim **high accuracy in separating real from synthetic images**, though the abstract gives no figures.

papers.title: Avalon-M1: Reinforcement Learning from Collective Rewards
papers.abstract: We introduce reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR), a recipe for jointly training language models to act as agent organisations under latency constraints. A CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, co-ordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The deadline makes parallel work valuable when it increases the return earned before the cap. We train Avalon-M1-Mini (120B) across 147 environments. For the trained model, eight-hire organisational execution raises IMO-ProofBench-Advanced scores from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations achieve similar average scores at approximately one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution and just over half that of eight independent attempts followed by selection.
