The trained model also outperforms Nemotron 3 Super, post-trained from the same base model, across all evaluations when comparing each model's best tested configuration. On EdgeBench, organisations overtake the single agent after approximately 0.4 derived hours. Over the course of training, organisations develop hierarchies to manage communication costs, invest more in peer review, and alter how work is divided. Safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios. These results establish a shared-advantage baseline for studying organisational learning, performance-latency trade-offs, and collective oversight.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning from collective rewards (RLCR) jointly trains a language model to act as an agent organisation under a deadline: a CEO and up to eight specialists share one policy, coordinate through a message board and workspace, and are trained with a common outcome-derived advantage. The authors train `Avalon-M1-Mini` (120B) across 147 environments and find that eight-hire organisational execution raises `IMO-ProofBench-Advanced` scores **from 23.8% to 39.0% relative to single-agent execution**. Across 12 benchmarks, organisations reach similar average scores at about one-third the derived latency of token-matched single-agent execution, and the model outperforms `Nemotron 3 Super`, post-trained from the same base. Over training the organisations develop hierarchies and invest more in peer review, while safety evaluations find near-universal refusal of harmful actions but sustained declines in external reporting in two of three oversight scenarios.

papers.title: Beyond Robust Algorithmic Recourse: Sharing the Burden of Validity through Model Multiplicity
papers.abstract: Algorithmic recourse provides actionable recommendations that enable individuals to achieve favourable outcomes. Implementing recourse for individuals requires significant time and effort, thus emphasizing robust recourse: recommendations that remain valid even under future model updates. While robustness preserves validity, we show it introduces systematic harms by constraining feasible recommendations to regions that disproportionately reflect majority behavior, reducing individual flexibility and amplifying disparities. Thus, non-robust recourse risks invalidation, whereas robust recourse creates a preference for high-density regions in the data that induces unfairness. However, this trade-off is driven by an implicit assumption that individuals alone should bear the burden of validity. We challenge this narrative and show that strategic model selection can help maintain validity while relaxing robustness requirements for individuals. By leveraging multiplicity, the existence of equally good yet competing models, system owners can share this burden with individuals, thus resolving the tension between validity and unfairness.
papers.summary: Algorithmic recourse gives people actionable recommendations for obtaining a favourable model decision, and robust recourse keeps those recommendations valid after future model updates. The authors show that robustness constrains feasible recommendations to high-density regions reflecting majority behaviour, which reduces individual flexibility and amplifies disparities. They argue this trade-off rests on the assumption that individuals alone must bear the burden of validity, and show that **strategic model selection among equally good competing models can maintain validity while relaxing the robustness demanded of individuals**.

papers.title: Contact Geometry for Generative Models: An Unbalanced Optimal Transport Formulation
papers.abstract: Real-world generative problems in biology, medical imaging, or robotics, rarely come with perfectly paired source and target distributions. While unbalanced Optimal Transport (uOT) provides a robust framework to bridge unpaired datasets via minimum-length paths in probability space, existing formulations based on the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry introduce a structural bias toward high density regions, often triggering mode collapse. We introduce Contact unbalanced Optimal Transport (CuOT), a novel uOT formulation grounded in contact geometry that decouples density transport direction from mass growth to eliminate structural bias. This allows CuOT to adapt sampling steps to the local data structure, naturally reducing step sizes in high-density regions to prevent overshooting and ensuring stable convergence. The result is a stable, scalable path-length minimization solver that consistently outperforms WFR-based methods on biological dynamics reconstruction, unpaired image-to-image translation, and video generation.
papers.summary: Unbalanced optimal transport (uOT) bridges unpaired source and target distributions, but existing formulations built on the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geometry are biased toward high-density regions and often trigger mode collapse. Contact unbalanced Optimal Transport (`CuOT`) reformulates the problem in contact geometry, **decoupling the direction of density transport from mass growth to remove that structural bias**. This lets the sampler shrink its step size in high-density regions to avoid overshooting. The authors report that the resulting path-length minimization solver consistently outperforms WFR-based methods on biological dynamics reconstruction, unpaired image-to-image translation, and video generation.

papers.title: MXI-MemICL: Towards In-Context Robot Manipulation through Self-Retrieved Interaction Memory
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) offers robots a way to acquire new skills from a single demonstration without parameter updates. However, existing robotic ICL methods either rely on large-scale pretraining constrained by scarce, costly robot interaction data or require additional annotations yet struggle to generalize across tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose MXI-MemICL, a framework for memory-guided ICL in vision-language-action (VLA) models. By treating demonstrations as retrievable memory, MXI-MemICL enables in-context manipulation without additional large-scale pretraining or specialized annotations. Specifically, a visual-action causal encoder turns actions and their observed effects in demonstrations and completed interactions into reusable memory to guide execution. To retrieve experience suited to upcoming execution, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent and uses it to query memory. The retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through experience-token prefixes and gated cross-attention, guiding action generation with a learned gate that regulates its influence. MXI-MemICL improves success over the baseline by +8.2% and +14.4% on RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0. Real-robot experiments show a +9.0% gain, with demonstrations adding +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks. The code will be made publicly available.
papers.summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets a robot pick up a skill from a single demonstration without parameter updates, but existing methods need large-scale pretraining or extra annotations. `MXI-MemICL` treats demonstrations and completed interactions as retrievable memory for vision-language-action (VLA) models: a visual-action causal encoder stores actions with their observed effects, an intention predictor forecasts the next stage's intent to query that memory, and retrieved experience conditions the language backbone through prefix tokens and gated cross-attention. Success improves over the baseline by +8.2% on `RoboCasa365` and **+14.4% on `RoboTwin 2.0`**, with a +9.0% gain in real-robot experiments, where demonstrations add +5.0% on seen and +16.7% on unseen tasks.

papers.title: Evaluating Latent Knowledge Stability in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Changes in image viewpoint and question formulation can alter latent knowledge representations in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, output correctness and overall representational drift provide limited insight into how these changes affect model decisions. We therefore evaluate latent knowledge stability across visual and linguistic elicitation conditions from two complementary perspectives: answer preference and internal support. Specifically, we devise the margin retention score (MRS), which measures the first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin over competing options across conditions and assesses how changes in latent knowledge representations affect this margin. We also present latent knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which evaluates reference-correct items by comparing internal support profiles constructed using the margin gradient under the reference condition, which jointly reflects changes in how internal support is distributed and changes in total support magnitude. We further construct MMStableBench, comprising 19,452 knowledge items (facts), each probing the same latent knowledge across varied image viewpoints, semantically equivalent question formulations, and answer-option permutations. Experiments across 15 MLLMs show that MRS and KSS reveal latent knowledge instability not captured by accuracy, while an MRS-inspired regularizer further improves the generalization of edited latent knowledge.
papers.summary: Changing an image's viewpoint or rewording a question can shift what a multimodal large language model (MLLM) internally represents, in ways that output accuracy alone does not reveal. The authors define a margin retention score (MRS), measuring first-order projected degradation of the initial answer's logit margin across conditions, and knowledge support-structure stability (KSS), which compares internal support profiles built from the margin gradient. They also build `MMStableBench`, with 19,452 knowledge items each probed across varied viewpoints, equivalent question phrasings, and answer-option permutations. Across 15 MLLMs, **MRS and KSS expose latent knowledge instability that accuracy misses**, and a regularizer inspired by MRS improves the generalization of edited knowledge.

papers.title: Representation and Model Contributions on Small Molecular Benchmarks: Controlled Comparisons and External Evaluation
papers.abstract: Improvements in molecular property prediction are usually attributed to the model, although part of the gain may come from the molecular representation. New models are commonly benchmarked against a random forest (RF) trained on a molecular fingerprint, a comparison that changes the model and the representation at the same time. We separate the two contributions with a two-by-two factorial design in which the RF and a second model (CatBoost or the tabular foundation models TabPFN and TabFM) are each trained on a fingerprint and on RDKit descriptors, and each effect is tested with a paired scaffold bootstrap. Seven small MoleculeNet datasets (3 regression, 4 classification) are evaluated on the published split of a recent graph transformer (DGT), on 10 additional scaffold splits and on external datasets. For solubility and lipophilicity, the representation effect exceeds the model effect in every main factorial design, in all three evaluations. For hydration free energy, the result depends on the starting fingerprint: from ECFP4 the representation effect is larger, and from MACCS neither effect is significantly larger. On the classification datasets, only one main factorial design has a significant difference between the two effects. Although the model effect is smaller on solubility and lipophilicity, TabFM outperforms the RF on all 7 datasets when both use RDKit descriptors. With RDKit descriptors in place of a fingerprint, the RF baseline reported for DGT surpasses the transformer's published solubility score. We recommend that model comparisons evaluate classical baselines on more than one representation and report the representation and model effects separately.
papers.summary: Gains in molecular property prediction are usually credited to the model, even though new models are typically compared with a random forest (RF) on a molecular fingerprint, which changes model and representation together. The authors separate the two with a two-by-two factorial design, training the RF and a second model (`CatBoost`, `TabPFN`, or `TabFM`) on both a fingerprint and `RDKit` descriptors across seven small `MoleculeNet` datasets, with paired scaffold bootstrap tests. For solubility and lipophilicity, **the representation effect exceeds the model effect in every main factorial design**, while results for hydration free energy and classification are mixed. With `RDKit` descriptors, the RF baseline surpasses the published solubility score of the graph transformer `DGT`, and the authors recommend reporting representation and model effects separately.

papers.title: Breaking Routing And Inter-device Dependencies in Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract: As Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale, Expert Parallelism (EP) becomes increasingly important for distributing experts across devices. However, the resulting token dispatch and combine operations can become a major bottleneck during inference. Overlapping these communication phases with computation is constrained by the sequential dependencies of standard MoE architectures. We introduce BRAID-MoE, an architecture that pairs laddered residual connections with early routing to relax these dependencies. Laddered residuals enable each expert combine to be deferred to the following block, while early routing computes the next routing decision from the pre-combine residual, with experts still receiving the updated post-combine hidden state. This creates an extended communication window in which the preceding combine and next dispatch can execute back-to-back on a dedicated communication stream, overlapping attention computation. On Qwen3-shaped MoEs with 0.4B-A0.1B and 2.5B-A0.5B parameters, BRAID closely matches sequential training at matched compute, with validation-loss increases of only 1% and 0.5%, respectively. We further demonstrate that existing MoE checkpoints can be adapted to BRAID with limited additional training, largely recovering their original accuracy. On a converted Qwen3-30B-A3B model, BRAID achieves speedups of up to 1.29$\times$ in prefill and 1.37$\times$ in decode, and at least 1.12$\times$ across diverse workloads and EP configurations on one or two four-H100 nodes. It outperforms competing overlap strategies in all tested settings, with the strongest gains when communication is a major latency bottleneck and its duration approaches the available computation window. These results demonstrate that early routing enables more effective communication-computation overlap in MoE inference at a modest cost in model quality.
papers.summary: When Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models spread experts across devices under Expert Parallelism (EP), the token dispatch and combine steps become an inference bottleneck that sequential dependencies prevent from overlapping with computation. `BRAID-MoE` pairs laddered residual connections with early routing, so each expert combine is deferred to the next block and the next routing decision is computed from the pre-combine residual, letting communication run alongside attention. Small `Qwen3`-shaped models trained this way show validation-loss increases of only 1% and 0.5%, and existing checkpoints can be adapted with limited extra training. On a converted `Qwen3-30B-A3B` across one or two four-H100 nodes, the design reaches speedups of **up to 1.29x in prefill and 1.37x in decode**, and at least 1.12x across the workloads tested.

papers.title: Boiling Down Uncertainty: Deep Generative Scenario Search with Decision-Guided Evolution Strategies for Two-Stage Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: One of the most common models for handling uncertainty is two-stage stochastic programming. Choosing the right number of scenarios is a trade-off between the uncertainty that can be represented and computational cost. A recent method, Deep Generative Scenario Search, generates synthetic scenarios and improves them by learning from the decisions they induce. The original approach used a black-box gradient estimate, since decisions are piecewise constant across scenarios. This paper provides the missing analytical foundation by deriving the gradient in closed form from recourse duality and an adjoint solve of the regularized reduced problem. The decision-focused direction, with a heuristic direction as a backup when duals are unavailable, defines the sampling subspace of a guided evolution strategy rather than being used as a direct update. For any guiding subspace, the expected update is a descent direction of the smoothed objective, so an inaccurate guide adds variance while the expected step still descends. For six problem families, both guided estimators outperform the baseline. The decision-focused version reduces the mean gap by three-quarters, and on the two families with the most integer variables the reduced sets beat the exact solver's two-hour incumbent in most runs, using a fifth of the time.
papers.summary: Two-stage stochastic programming must balance the number of scenarios against computational cost, and `Deep Generative Scenario Search` addresses this by generating synthetic scenarios and improving them based on the decisions they induce, originally with a black-box gradient estimate. The authors derive that gradient in closed form from recourse duality and an adjoint solve of the regularized reduced problem, then use it to define the sampling subspace of a guided evolution strategy instead of applying it as a direct update. They show the expected update is a descent direction of the smoothed objective for any guiding subspace, so an inaccurate guide only adds variance. Across six problem families the decision-focused version **reduces the mean gap by three-quarters**, and on the two families with the most integer variables it beats the exact solver's two-hour incumbent in most runs using a fifth of the time.

papers.title: Understanding the Importance of Massive Activations through Adversarial Robustness
papers.abstract: A common occurrence in Large Language Models (LLMs) is the emergence of so-called massive activations. This phenomenon is well known in the literature and has been connected to attention sinks, representational compression, as well as signal propagation. However, the reasons and consequences for their appearance are not yet well understood. In this paper, we explain the role of massive activations in deep learning by showing that they are connected to the region migration phenomenon in delayed robustness. Under the spline theoretic interpretation of deep networks, we show that massive activations push the representations away from the nonlinearity boundaries of the network, decreasing the complexity of its input-output map around data points. Furthermore, we uncover for the first time that this phenomenon is not unique to transformers and actually appears in a number of common architectures performing simple supervised learning tasks. We validate this connection through extensive experiments on a diverse set of architectures including residual MLP, ResNet18, Vision Transformers and GPT and datasets including MNIST, CIFAR10, Imagenette and Shakespeare Text. We consistently observe that massive activations and region migration co-occur with adversarial robustness. Furthermore, we illustrate that this connection holds in the large-scale pretraining of LLMs by showing that the rise of massive activations in LLMs closely tracks the adversarial accuracy of the model under perturbations of the token embeddings.
papers.summary: Massive activations, a few extremely large hidden values that emerge in Large Language Models (LLMs), have been linked to attention sinks and representational compression, but their cause and consequences are not well understood. Using the spline-theoretic view of deep networks, the authors argue that these activations push representations away from the network's nonlinearity boundaries, simplifying the input-output map around data points, and connect them to the region migration phenomenon in delayed robustness. Experiments on residual MLPs, `ResNet18`, Vision Transformers and `GPT`, over `MNIST`, `CIFAR10`, `Imagenette` and Shakespeare text, show the phenomenon is not unique to transformers. They report that **massive activations and region migration consistently co-occur with adversarial robustness**, including in large-scale LLM pretraining under perturbations of token embeddings.

papers.title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
papers.abstract: We prove that the following problem is \textbf{NEXPTIME}-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.
papers.summary: The question studied is a satisfiability problem for message passing neural networks (MPNNs) with local sum aggregation and ReLU activations: given such a network and a degree bound encoded in unary, decide whether some pointed graph with rational node labels and degree within the bound is accepted. The authors prove this problem is **NEXPTIME-hard, even for a fixed degree bound of 3**.

papers.title: On the Effectiveness of Resampling for Supervised Graph Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Class imbalance and scarce anomaly labels motivate oversampling in supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD), but its benefits across detectors and benchmarks remain unclear. In the low-label setting of GADBench, with 20 labelled anomalies and 80 labelled normal nodes, we compare class weighting and up to six oversampling strategies in ten detector configurations from three families: graph neural networks (GNNs), tree ensembles on neighbourhood-aggregated features, and tabular foundation models, on 17 datasets. On the eight datasets with organic anomalies, no strategy has a statistically resolved average gain in any configuration, and which nodes are labelled matters as much as the strategy. On the nine datasets with injected anomalies, Gaussian-noise oversampling (ROSE) gains up to 5.2 AUPRC points in four of the six tree and tabular foundation model configurations, and in all six only on attribute-swap anomalies; in four GNNs its gain is not distinguishable from zero. This gain depends on the injection recipe, which gives swapped nodes an atypical feature norm: it is no longer distinguishable from zero when the swap uses a single random donor or preserves the norm, although most detectors then also stop detecting the swaps. Over the 17 datasets, tuning the tree detectors adds about three points, as much as ROSE, and cuts ROSE's gain by about half or more. With the same source nodes and class weight, sampled graph views are not distinguishable from plain copies of those nodes. We recommend tuning baselines, repeating labelled splits, reporting organic and injected anomalies separately, and checking label-free degree and feature-norm baselines.
papers.summary: Oversampling is often used to counter class imbalance in supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD), but its benefit is unclear. In the low-label setting of `GADBench` (20 labelled anomalies, 80 labelled normal nodes), the authors compare class weighting and up to six oversampling strategies across ten detector configurations, spanning graph neural networks, tree ensembles, and tabular foundation models, on 17 datasets. On the eight datasets with organic anomalies, **no strategy shows a statistically resolved average gain in any configuration**, and the choice of labelled nodes matters as much as the strategy. Gaussian-noise oversampling (`ROSE`) gains up to 5.2 AUPRC points on injected anomalies, but only for attribute-swap anomalies and because of an artifact of the injection recipe, and simply tuning the tree detectors adds about as much.

papers.title: Gated Concept Adapters: Layer-Wise Concept Bottlenecks for Auditable Text Understanding
papers.abstract: Human-facing text understanding systems are used to infer affect, moderate harmful content, and support socially sensitive decisions. However, Transformer predictions are difficult to audit because they are produced from high-dimensional hidden states that do not provide a compact, inspectable interface for human analysis or intervention. We introduce Gated Concept Adapters (GCA), a layer-wise concept bottleneck framework that attaches gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected outputs of pretrained Transformers. Token representations are mapped into concept activations, filtered by learned gates, pooled into layer-level summaries, and exposed to the prediction head as a concept-mediated interface. The dimensions can be inspected through usage statistics, signature n-grams, post-hoc concept names, and targeted concept interventions. We evaluate GCA on fine-grained emotion classification, toxicity detection, topic classification, and a controlled verb-cloze stress test. In the affective and safety-relevant classification settings, GCA learns comparatively low-redundancy and intervention-sensitive concept representations while retaining useful predictive performance. On toxicity detection, it remains close to an unconstrained ModernBERT baseline while enabling concept-level inspection, targeted intervention, and lightweight post-hoc control. On GoEmotions, the end-to-end concept model incurs a macro-F1 cost relative to unconstrained RoBERTa, while a task-initialized frozen variant substantially reduces this gap. On AG News, GCA remains competitive with recent concept-based baselines, and the Qwen verb-cloze experiment clarifies the limits of concept-mediated full-vocabulary prediction. Overall, GCA provides a neural concept interface for auditable text understanding, prioritizing transparency, diagnosis, and intervention over unconstrained accuracy maximization.
papers.summary: Transformer text classifiers used for emotion inference and content moderation are hard to audit because their predictions come from high-dimensional hidden states. Gated Concept Adapters (`GCA`) attach gated, low-dimensional concept-producing readout adapters to selected layers of a pretrained Transformer, so that predictions pass through concept activations that can be inspected via usage statistics, signature n-grams, post-hoc names, and targeted interventions. On toxicity detection, `GCA` **stays close to an unconstrained `ModernBERT` baseline while enabling concept-level inspection and intervention**. On `GoEmotions` it incurs a macro-F1 cost relative to `RoBERTa` that a task-initialized frozen variant substantially reduces, and it remains competitive with concept-based baselines on `AG News`.

papers.title: ST-GNN-AAAS: Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for Anytime Automatic Algorithm Selection in the Traveling Salesman Problem
papers.abstract: Anytime Automatic Algorithm Selection (AAAS) aims to make solver choices under varying time budgets. The existing AAAS approaches largely rely on static instance characteristics and make limited use of temporal information revealed during solver execution. We propose ST-GNN-AAAS, a Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Network framework for AAAS in the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). The framework represents evolving incumbent tours using time-varying node features, including distances from each node to its neighbors in the current tour, and combines these features with solver performance observations over a short history window. Given this short history, ST-GNN-AAAS predicts solver selections over a longer future horizon. We evaluate the method on a subset of diverse TSP benchmarks from NATIONAL, TNM, TSPLIB, and VLSI, releasing the corresponding solver execution data to support reproducibility. Our model achieves a selection accuracy of 76.59% and closes 46.05% of the average rank gap between the single best solver (SBS) and the virtual best solver (VBS).
papers.summary: Anytime Automatic Algorithm Selection (AAAS) chooses which solver to run under varying time budgets, and existing approaches rely mostly on static instance features. `ST-GNN-AAAS` applies a spatio-temporal graph neural network to the Traveling Salesman Problem, representing evolving incumbent tours with time-varying node features and combining them with solver performance over a short history window to predict selections over a longer future horizon. On instances drawn from `NATIONAL`, `TNM`, `TSPLIB`, and `VLSI`, the model reaches 76.59% selection accuracy and **closes 46.05% of the average rank gap** between the single best solver (SBS) and the virtual best solver (VBS).

papers.title: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): How Faithfully Do LLMs Keep Privacy Constraints on In-Context Disclosure Granularity?
papers.abstract: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location (San Francisco) and disclosure is permitted only at the country level, an output at the state level (California) violates the constraint. Detecting such violations requires capturing not only direct privacy leakage (San Francisco) but also semantic leakage (California). However, existing benchmarks cannot measure the degree of leakage with respect to a given semantic constraint such as the country-level limit. We therefore formalize disclosure control as a constraint on the permitted ceiling over the hierarchy of a knowledge graph. Building on this formulation, we construct PDC-Bench, a benchmark of 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. In our experiments applying PDC-Bench to eleven LLMs, 62% of the constraint violations were semantic leakage. We further found that semantic leakage depends less on the model than on the permitted disclosure granularity and the task's need for the private attribute; reliable auditing must therefore target semantic leakage together with these two factors. Data, prompts, and code are available at https://github.com/fuji1655/PDC-Bench.
papers.summary: LLM outputs are sometimes restricted in how precisely they may reveal a personal attribute, for example a location that may be disclosed only at country level, so that naming the state is a violation even if the city is never mentioned. The authors formalize this as a permitted ceiling over the hierarchy of a knowledge graph and build `PDC-Bench`, a benchmark of 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. Testing eleven LLMs, they find that **62% of constraint violations were semantic leakage** as opposed to direct disclosure of the private value. Semantic leakage depended less on the model than on the permitted granularity and on how much the task needed the private attribute.

papers.title: When "Neutral" Means Irrelevant: A Construct-Validity Audit of NormAd-ETI
papers.abstract: NormAd-ETI scores a model's judgment of everyday actions as acceptable, unacceptable, or neither as the cultural context shrinks from a specific rule to a country name. We audit what that three-way score measures. It combines two decisions: whether a supplied norm applies, and whether the action conforms to it. Separating them shows that when only a country is shown, applicability falls to near chance while conformity stays well above it, because the prompt withholds the rule a Neutral label depends on. Because one answer carries both decisions, the score follows the steadier conformity and hides the weaker applicability, and no single prompt recovers the two separately. Dedicated forced-choice probes separate them for frontier models but not for small open models, where the applicability judgment still tracks the hidden acceptability label. Adding a written rationale reduces that conflation without removing it. We recommend reporting the two results separately and measuring the conflation gap.
papers.summary: The `NormAd-ETI` benchmark scores whether a model labels everyday actions as acceptable, unacceptable, or neither as cultural context shrinks from a specific rule to just a country name. This audit splits that three-way score into two decisions: whether a supplied norm applies, and whether the action conforms to it. With only a country shown, **applicability judgments fall to near chance while conformity stays well above it, and the combined score hides the weaker one**. Dedicated forced-choice probes separate the two for frontier models but not for small open models, so the authors recommend reporting both results separately along with the conflation gap.

papers.title: RoboRecast: Intent-Preserving Demonstration Augmentation via Diagnosis-Driven Optimization
papers.abstract: Collecting diverse real-world manipulation demonstrations is costly, motivating the use of simulation to augment existing demonstrations for robot policy learning. When objects, layouts, or robots change, transferring motions from a source demonstration can produce behavior that is semantically implausible or physically infeasible in the new setting. We introduce RoboRecast, an agentic optimization framework that preserves the interactions required by the source task while jointly optimizing the simulated scene and robot motion to make those interactions executable in the target setting. When an interaction fails, the agent uses simulation feedback to diagnose the cause, revise the relevant scene or motion parameters, and test whether the revision resolves the failure. This flexibility allows RoboRecast to generate synthetic data from both human and robot demonstrations and to adapt them to new layouts, objects, and robot embodiments. When target demonstrations are available, adding RoboRecast data improves policy success on both real-world single-arm and simulated bimanual tasks. Even without demonstrations in the target configuration, RoboRecast adapts source demonstrations to support policy learning with new objects or robot embodiments.
papers.summary: Transferring a manipulation demonstration to new objects, layouts, or robots in simulation often yields motions that are implausible or physically infeasible. `RoboRecast` is an agentic optimization framework that keeps the interactions the source task requires while jointly adjusting the simulated scene and the robot motion; when an interaction fails, the agent uses simulation feedback to diagnose the cause, revise parameters, and re-test. It works from both human and robot demonstrations. Adding its data improves policy success on real single-arm and simulated bimanual tasks, and **it supports policy learning for new objects or robot embodiments even with no demonstrations in the target configuration**.

papers.title: REBEAL: Human References Are No Longer the Best Translation, and Metrics Do Not Notice
papers.abstract: Reference-based MT evaluation assumes the human reference is correct and better than the systems it scores. Both assumptions now fail, since the human reference ranks first in none of the 2024 WMT MQM campaigns and carries annotated errors in 19% to 87% of its segments. What a metric does with a flawed reference is a question about the metric, and it would have been worth asking before reference quality came into doubt. We introduce REBEAL (Reference Bias EvALuation), a benchmark that probes how MT metrics respond to seven types of controlled reference contamination, drawn from the error categories those campaigns record. Across eight widely used metrics and three language pairs, recent learned metrics (xCOMET, MetricX) prove more robust than their predecessors, but each family fails in its own way. Surface metrics show no length sensitivity, so contamination hides in longer segments, while learned metrics accept references in unrelated languages as nearly correct. The failure they share is named-entity contamination, which no metric detects and which flips up to 8 of 36 system pairs when ranking nine MT systems.
papers.summary: Reference-based machine translation evaluation assumes the human reference is correct, yet in the 2024 `WMT` `MQM` campaigns the human reference ranks first in none of them and has annotated errors in 19% to 87% of its segments. `REBEAL` (Reference Bias EvALuation) is a benchmark that probes how metrics respond to seven types of controlled reference contamination, tested on eight metrics and three language pairs. Recent learned metrics such as `xCOMET` and `MetricX` are more robust than their predecessors, but surface metrics miss contamination in longer segments and learned metrics accept references in unrelated languages as nearly correct. **No metric detects named-entity contamination, which flips up to 8 of 36 system pairs** when ranking nine systems.

papers.title: HiCal: Offline Calibration for Hierarchical Scale Encoding in Accurate HiF4 Quantization
papers.abstract: Block floating-point (BFP) quantization is widely adopted for efficient low-bit large language model (LLM) inference, where the choice of block scales plays a critical role in quantization accuracy. HiFloat4 (HiF4) employs a hierarchical scale encoding scheme consisting of a global E6M2 scale and two levels of binary scale extensions. However, its conventional rounding rule and fixed scale extension thresholds may not fully capture the statistical characteristics of the quantized tensors in practice, leading to suboptimal scale representations. In this work, we propose HiCal, an offline calibration approach that improves HiF4 quantization accuracy by refining the encoding decisions across all three scale levels. Specifically, we introduce a calibrated rounding bias for the Level-1 E6M2 scale and optimize the scale-extension thresholds at Levels 2 and 3 based on the empirical distributions of local group magnitudes. The resulting calibration parameters are determined offline and remain fixed during inference, while the hierarchical encoding continues to adapt to individual blocks through their local values. This design eliminates the need for per-block multi-candidate scale search while preserving the original deterministic HiF4 encoding procedure. Experiments across five synthetic and real activation distributions show that the proposed method reduces quantization MSE by 9.91%-23.50% relative to the original HiF4 scheme, including a 13.00% reduction on real Qwen3-8B activations. End-to-end evaluations across six benchmarks further show average-score improvements of 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, respectively, without per-block multi-candidate search during inference.
papers.summary: Block floating-point (BFP) quantization for low-bit large language model inference depends heavily on how block scales are chosen, and the `HiFloat4` (`HiF4`) format uses a fixed rounding rule and fixed thresholds across its three-level hierarchical scale encoding. `HiCal` calibrates these offline, adding a rounding bias for the top-level scale and tuning the scale-extension thresholds at the two lower levels from the empirical distribution of local group magnitudes, with the parameters then fixed at inference so no per-block candidate search is needed. Quantization mean squared error drops by 9.91% to 23.50% across five activation distributions, including **13.00% on real `Qwen3-8B` activations**. End-to-end average scores over six benchmarks rise by 0.91 and 1.25 percentage points on `Qwen3-8B` and `Qwen3-30B-A3B`.

papers.title: MargEmbed-Akan: Bridging Twi Questions and English Knowledge through Cross-Lingual Score Distillation
papers.abstract:
Most information sought online by Twi (Akan) speakers is written in English, making cross-lingual retrieval essential. We evaluate eight systems: BM25, five open embedding models, and two proprietary models (gemini-embedding-001 and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large) on two Twi-English tasks. AfriQA contains 1,221 natively written Asante Twi questions that must retrieve their answering English Wikipedia passages. Bible translation retrieval requires a Twi passage to retrieve its English translation from 6,195 candidates.
  We introduce MargEmbed-Akan, a 560M-parameter open query encoder trained from AfriE5-Large-instruct using cross-lingual score distillation. The frozen base model scores each English training question against its answer passage and seven hard negatives. The student learns to reproduce these scores from both an NLLB-200 Twi translation that passes a round-trip translation check and the original English question, preserving English behaviour. During training, passages are encoded by the frozen base model; at evaluation, MargEmbed-Akan encodes questions and passages.
  On AfriQA, base AfriE5 and gemini-embedding-001 both achieve 66.6 nDCG@10; EmbeddingGemma 2, Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large achieve 56.6, 51.3, and 53.4, respectively. MargEmbed-Akan achieves 71.5, outperforming gemini-embedding-001 by 4.9 points, its base model by 5.0, and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large by 18.1. Its largest gain is on Twi typed without E and O (+7.5 over gemini-embedding-001). English retrieval does not differ significantly from the base model, although both proprietary models score 1.5-2.2 points higher. On Bible translation retrieval, MargEmbed-Akan and gemini-embedding-001 are statistically tied on standard Twi (97.2 vs. 96.5 nDCG@10); MargEmbed-Akan performs better on diacritic-free Twi (92.7 vs. 84.9). No AfriQA data was used for training or model selection.
papers.summary: Twi (Akan) speakers mostly have to search English content, so the authors compare eight retrieval systems on two Twi-to-English tasks: `AfriQA` question answering and Bible translation retrieval. `MargEmbed-Akan` is a 560M-parameter open query encoder trained from `AfriE5-Large-instruct` by cross-lingual score distillation, where the student reproduces the frozen base model's relevance scores from both an `NLLB-200` Twi translation and the original English question. On `AfriQA` it reaches **71.5 nDCG@10, against 66.6 for both its base model and `gemini-embedding-001`** and 53.4 for OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large`, with the largest gains on Twi typed without diacritics. English retrieval does not differ significantly from the base model, and no `AfriQA` data was used for training or model selection.

papers.title: Generating Schema-Aligned Synthetic Dialogues and Measuring Their Diversity
papers.abstract: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are expensive to annotate, and in sensitive domains they are also difficult to obtain at all. We therefore build them in the opposite order by sampling a schema-valid record first, then writing a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizing speech from the dialogue, so the label exists before the text and we need no annotation step. Naively prompting a language model for such dialogues yields small variations of a single conversation, so we add a sampled variation configuration, personas, and a topic plan that orders the fields of the record as explicit mechanisms for variation. We measure the variation that reaches the output through embedding space, where the embedding variance spreads over about two and a half times as many independent directions with our full configuration compared to without (participation ratio 23.3 against 9.2). Two corpora of medical dialogue give values of the same order, with sample size, text length and language being additional factors there. We also show the positive effect of our method in a downstream test, where an 8B extraction model reaches 64.8% field accuracy when fine-tuned on dialogues from our method, against 57.5% from naive generation. We release the generation library and the generated corpus of German clinical dialogues with aligned records.
papers.summary: Models that convert a conversation into a structured record need paired transcripts and records, which are costly to annotate and hard to obtain in sensitive domains. The pipeline here inverts the order: it samples a schema-valid record first, writes a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizes speech, adding a sampled variation configuration, personas, and a topic plan to keep outputs from collapsing into near-duplicates. Diversity is measured in embedding space, where the participation ratio rises from 9.2 to 23.3 with the full configuration. An 8B extraction model fine-tuned on the resulting dialogues reaches **64.8% field accuracy versus 57.5% with naive generation**, and the library and a corpus of German clinical dialogues are released.

papers.title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $\pi_{0.5}$. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.
papers.summary: Online reinforcement learning for vision-language-action policies gets little signal from sparse success or failure feedback on long manipulation tasks, and full-task rollouts give bottleneck stages too little practice. `ReFocus` alternates global and local training rounds: each task is decomposed into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subtasks whose progress reward both trains the policy and locates bottlenecks, and extra interaction is then allocated to task segments around those bottlenecks. It reaches **97.8% on `LIBERO-Long` and 51.3% on `RoboCasa365`, versus 90.6% and 39.3% for the `π0.5` baseline**. On a real-world task called `BreadBaker` it achieves 95% success compared with 30% for the baseline.

papers.title: BARE: Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion for Humanoid Robots
papers.abstract: Dynamic obstacle avoidance is essential for safely deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments, where rapidly approaching objects require immediate evasive responses. Recent advances in reflexive evasion have focused primarily on quadrupeds, which typically rely on large-scale whole-body maneuvers. In contrast, humanoids can exploit their rich body articulation to evade through small, localized body adjustments. By moving threatened body regions without repositioning the entire body, these responses may require less execution time and less surrounding free space. However, local adjustments can alter mass distribution or support conditions, making it challenging to achieve rapid evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. To this end, we propose BARE (Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion), a humanoid reflexive evasion framework guided by human motion priors that enables rapid local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. A risk-guided motion adapter is designed to select reference motions from a retargeted human evasive motion library based on the threatened body region and to adjust their temporal phases based on collision urgency, allowing the robot to reach evasive postures before potential contact. Conditioned on the adapted reference and link-level collision risk, a reflexive evasion policy learns through reinforcement learning to coordinate local body adjustments with whole-body stabilization. We validate BARE in simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating its ability to perform targeted local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability.
papers.summary: Humanoid robots dodging fast-approaching objects could move only the threatened body part instead of repositioning the whole body, but such local adjustments shift mass distribution and support conditions and can destabilize the robot. `BARE` (Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion) uses a risk-guided adapter to pick reference motions from a library of retargeted human evasive motions according to the threatened body region, and speeds up their timing according to collision urgency. A reinforcement-learned policy conditioned on that reference and on link-level collision risk coordinates the local motion with whole-body balance. Simulation and real-world experiments show **targeted local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability**.

papers.title: TeamFlowRL: Online Policy Optimization of Decentralized Flow Policies for Multi-Agent Coordination
papers.abstract: Complex cooperative tasks require coordinated multi-agent behavior. Offline generative policies learn expressive cooperative behaviors from trajectories but remain limited by fixed datasets. Online reinforcement learning can improve them through environment interaction. However, fine-tuning flow policies is difficult because action likelihoods are hard to compute. We propose TeamFlowRL, a two-stage framework that pretrains multi-agent flow policies offline and fine-tunes them online. We formulate team policy optimization over the complete denoising trajectories of decentralized flow policies, avoiding intractable action likelihoods. The resulting objective weights each agent's trajectory ratio with a shared team advantage and clips each ratio separately, aligning local policy updates with the common team return. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups, TeamFlowRL improves every offline initialization, with a 47.3% average gain in normalized score. It also achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning across 6 bimanual tasks.
papers.summary: Flow-based generative policies learned offline capture expressive cooperative multi-agent behavior but are limited by their fixed datasets, and fine-tuning them online is hard because action likelihoods are intractable. `TeamFlowRL` pretrains decentralized flow policies offline and then fine-tunes them by optimizing over complete denoising trajectories, weighting each agent's trajectory ratio by a shared team advantage and clipping each ratio separately. Across 51 paired configurations in seven simulation groups it improves every offline initialization, with a **47.3% average gain in normalized score**. On six bimanual tasks it achieves 33.1% higher average success under exploration noise than Gaussian-policy fine-tuning.

papers.title: A Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Official Statistics
papers.abstract: Official statistics are critical datasets for a wide variety of actors, including policymakers and businesses. For providers of official statistics, improving accessibility, governance, and disclosure of their data is of key importance. This can be improved by providing question-answering systems based on text-to-SQL approaches. However, existing text-to-SQL benchmarks do not resemble this setting. Official statistics are published as open-domain catalogs of thousands of wide tables whose columns and values are codes, and whose meaning is recorded in separate metadata rather than in a relational schema. To address this gap, we introduce LOCuST, a text-to-SQL benchmark that pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph. The graph describes the tables, measures, and dimension codes through labels, definitions, hierarchies, and units, and is the external knowledge a system needs to find the right tables and ground a question in the right codes. The benchmark includes expert-annotated questions for different query and aggregation types, including raw value retrieval, summations, proportion calculations, and joins. Alongside standard evaluation measures, we introduce an observation F1 metric that measures how close a query is to the ground truth even when the answers are different. We evaluate a variety of state-of-the-art LLMs and find that they struggle to write SQL that answers the questions correctly.
papers.summary: Official statistics are published as catalogs of thousands of wide tables whose columns and values are codes explained only in separate metadata, a setting existing text-to-SQL benchmarks do not cover. `LOCuST` pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph describing tables, measures, and dimension codes, plus expert-annotated questions spanning value retrieval, summations, proportions, and joins. It also introduces an observation F1 metric that scores how close a query is to the ground truth even when the answers differ. Evaluated state-of-the-art large language models **struggle to write SQL that answers the questions correctly**.

papers.title: ICLWorld: Benchmarking In-Context Learning of Agents from Digital to Physical Worlds
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets agents acquire new rules from context and adapt to user-specific requirements at inference time. The same frontier agents now operate both computers and robots, yet their ICL remains insufficiently assessed: existing benchmarks are largely offline, rely on text or static images, and risk training-data contamination, while robot evaluations are limited to method-level ablations. We present ICLWorld, an online benchmark that evaluates the ICL of agents from digital to physical worlds, covering computer use and robot use, together with UIverse, a unified harness that turns every environment into a user interface. We build 30 environments, record 630 demonstration videos (10+ hours), and design 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules that cannot be satisfied without learning from the context. Each task comes with three rule versions, given as text or video, and we test generalization at three levels, from replaying the demonstration to new instances and unseen environments. Across six frontier models, the strongest agents, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeed on 82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs, and a no-rule control reduces success to at most 8%. GPT-6 Astra succeeds under all three rule versions on only 38% of computer-use tasks, half its rate under a single rule, and answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of these tasks. Frontier agents learn rules comparably well from video and from text and transfer them across environments, whereas weaker agents rely on text and lose most of their video-based success once the demonstrated situation is resampled. These findings reveal substantial gaps between the digital and the physical world and between identifying a rule and acting on it.
papers.summary: `ICLWorld` is an online benchmark for in-context learning (ICL) in agents that operate both computers and robots, built on `UIverse`, a harness that exposes every environment as a user interface. It spans 30 environments, 630 demonstration videos, and 160 tasks with customized, often counter-intuitive rules given as text or video, tested at three levels of generalization. The strongest agents, `Claude Opus 5.5` and `GPT-6 Astra`, succeed on **82% and 76% of computer-use runs but only 27% and 26% of robot-use runs**, and removing the rule drops success to at most 8%. `GPT-6 Astra` answers 98% of robot rule questions correctly yet completes only 20% of those tasks, showing a gap between identifying a rule and acting on it.

papers.title: LATEC: Learned Axial TEnsor Compression for High-Dimensional Scientific Data
papers.abstract: With the growing scale of scientific simulation and infrastructure, part of the burden has shifted from producing scientific data to analyzing and storing it. Compression is a key step to expanding storage capacity, but requires dedicated techniques to enforce user-specified pointwise error bounds that ensure the validity of downstream scientific workflows. To further push the limits of compression, novel learned codecs have been developed, in particular for images and videos, but these methods often optimize for aggregated distortion and fail to meet error bound standards. Moreover, these methods often target fixed field dimensionality, failing to account for many scientific data use cases, or at the expense of large adaptation or retraining costs. In this work, we introduce the Learned Axial TEnsor Compression (LATEC) method, an error-bounded codec with a dimension-agnostic learned predictor based on a GNN architecture. LATEC is pretrained on synthetic 2-D and 4-D fields, and evaluated with and without domain fine-tuning on 13 scientific fields in 3-D to 5-D. Results show that LATEC is consistently competitive with SZ3, achieving an 18.1% average improvement and greater consistency across all domains than other compressors. These results demonstrate that a shared learned predictor can serve as a single error-bounded codec across tensor dimensionalities, competitive with specialized compressors, while retaining pointwise error guarantees.
papers.summary: Scientific data compression must respect user-specified pointwise error bounds, which learned image and video codecs generally do not guarantee, and such codecs are usually tied to a fixed field dimensionality. `LATEC` (Learned Axial TEnsor Compression) is an error-bounded codec whose learned predictor is a graph neural network that works across tensor dimensionalities. Pretrained on synthetic 2-D and 4-D fields and evaluated with and without fine-tuning on 13 scientific fields in 3-D to 5-D, it is consistently competitive with `SZ3`, with an **18.1% average improvement** and more consistent results across domains than other compressors.

papers.title: DexWAC: A Unified World-Actor-Critic Model for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.
papers.summary: World-action models extend vision-language-action policies by predicting future observations, but use that prediction only as an auxiliary loss, while policy-improvement methods typically train dynamics and value models separately. `DexWAC` jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in one pretraining stage on an image-editing backbone, predicting for each action chunk the endpoint visual latent, proprioception, reward, and continuation without generating intermediate video frames. The actor is then improved with `PPO` on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-N selection. It surpasses pretrained baselines in simulation and reaches **75% average success on two real-world tasks versus 45% for `π0.5`**.

papers.title: GeoSurge: Geometry-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning for Auditable Liver Resection Planning
papers.abstract: Surgical resection planning centers on generating executable resection surfaces from anatomical evidence and operative constraints. Medical multimodal foundation models enable anatomical understanding, and segmentation models predict resection regions, but neither translates these capabilities into explicitly constrained, executable resection surfaces. We present GeoSurge, an anatomy-grounded framework that combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens to generate executable, editable resection surfaces. To make resection geometry learnable and editable, GeoSurge maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar. Using this grammar, anatomy-oriented and tumor-centered templates generate candidates, which are filtered by hard constraints and semantic deduplication. Training supervision is then derived from candidate-expert geometric agreement and independently recomputed feasibility metrics. At inference, the reasoner uses patient evidence and surgical requirements to select or revise an action, which an independent geometry engine subsequently materializes and verifies. GeoSurge achieves the best overall scores on DeepTumour Liver and CRLM-QA, improving the constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on CRLM and from 56% to 99% on GeoSurge-Bench.
papers.summary: Planning a liver resection requires an executable cutting surface that satisfies anatomical and operative constraints, which neither medical multimodal foundation models nor segmentation models produce directly. `GeoSurge` combines mask-derived metrics with structure-aware point-cloud tokens and maps actions to parametric geometry through a surface-action grammar; candidate surfaces come from templates and are filtered by hard constraints, and at inference a reasoner selects or revises an action that a separate geometry engine materializes and verifies. It achieves the best overall scores on `DeepTumour Liver` and `CRLM-QA`, raising the **constraint satisfaction rate from 73% to 100% on `CRLM`** and from 56% to 99% on `GeoSurge-Bench`.

papers.title: Bathys: Advancing Deep Search Agents
papers.abstract: Deep search is a critical capability for agents tackling complex, open-ended tasks, where solving a problem requires iterative information gathering, query reformulation, and evidence-based verification rather than a single retrieval step. To address these requirements, we present Bathys 9B and 27B deep search agents built around a training framework that spans verifiable question synthesis, post-training, and online reinforcement learning (RL) under context compression. Our high-quality data construction ensures both search depth and reliability: each clue is reformulated as an indirect reference requiring independent retrieval, and retained evidence chains enable verification that the clues jointly determine a unique answer. Curated trajectories underpin a pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO), and Compaction-Managed Group Sequence Policy Optimization (CM-GSPO): SFT provides a stable foundation for tool use over long horizons and query reformulation; KTO uses binary feedback on trajectories to improve the selection of answers grounded in evidence; CM-GSPO optimizes execution sub-trajectories with length-normalized likelihood ratios on the recorded rollout contexts and reweights sub-trajectory advantages to correct the extra weighting introduced by independently averaging sub-trajectory losses. Bathys 9B and 27B attain 66.51% and 80.49% on BrowseComp, respectively, under an evaluation protocol with trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.
papers.summary: `Bathys` 9B and 27B are deep search agents trained for iterative information gathering, query reformulation, and evidence-based verification. Training data comes from verifiable question synthesis in which each clue is rewritten as an indirect reference requiring its own retrieval, with evidence chains kept to check that the clues determine a unique answer. The pipeline runs supervised fine-tuning, Kahneman-Tversky Optimization on binary trajectory feedback, and `CM-GSPO` (Compaction-Managed Group Sequence Policy Optimization), an online reinforcement learning stage that optimizes sub-trajectories under context compression. The two models score **66.51% and 80.49% on `BrowseComp`** under an evaluation protocol with trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.

papers.title: OpenWoud: Vendor-Unlocked Scalable Adaptive Random Forest Accelerator
papers.abstract: Online Machine Learning (ML) enables real-time decision-making on evolving data streams. These dynamic models learn continuously to adapt to new concepts, as previous ones become invalid, but their performance is often limited by throughput. The Adaptive Random Forest (ARF) is a state-of-the-art model for this setting, which naturally exposes parallelism and is therefore well-suited for hardware acceleration. However, prior Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based accelerators are vendor-locked and rely on resource-hungry Floating-Point (FP) arithmetics, limiting their scalability and portability. We present OpenWoud, a vendor-unlocked ARF framework for FPGAs. Our design replaces FP operators with a flexible FiXed-Point (FxP) arithmetic library and introduces fully transparent, manually scheduled dataflows for training and drift detection. This enables fine-grained time/area trade-offs and predictable behavior across platforms. A comprehensive evaluation on both synthetic and real datasets shows that OpenWoud maintains or increases accuracy (up to +12.89%), compared to a prior FPGA accelerator, while reducing the resource utilization by half. Competitive performance is observed compared to GPU (0.5 - 1.5x speed-up) and an FPGA baseline (0.2 - 0.5x), despite the latter being based on idealized simulation. Crucially, OpenWoud sustains true sample-by-sample inference, unlike GPUs that require batch insertion.
papers.summary: The Adaptive Random Forest is a leading model for online learning on evolving data streams, but existing Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) accelerators for it are tied to one vendor and rely on resource-heavy floating-point arithmetic. `OpenWoud` is a vendor-independent framework that swaps in a flexible fixed-point arithmetic library and manually scheduled dataflows for training and drift detection. Compared with a prior FPGA accelerator it maintains or improves accuracy (up to +12.89%) while **halving resource utilization**. Its throughput is 0.5 to 1.5 times that of a GPU and 0.2 to 0.5 times that of an FPGA baseline based on idealized simulation, and it sustains true sample-by-sample inference rather than batching.

papers.title: Economic World Model
papers.abstract: Can artificial intelligence reproduce the economic dynamics that emerge as households, firms and governments interact and adapt through markets and institutions? To answer this question, we define an economic world model (EWM) as an agent's internal representation of how an economic system works, enabling counterfactual simulation and decision-making under resource constraints. We then propose a general framework for studying EWMs that links three tasks: simulating agent behaviour, learning economic transitions and systematically evaluating the dynamics. As an initial implementation, we learn household policies from microeconomic data and calibrate a structural economic transition model using macroeconomic data, linking individual decisions to aggregate dynamics. Our micro-to-macro evaluation framework compares simulated individual actions and group distributions with observed microdata and assesses macroeconomic dynamics through forecasting and counterfactual experiments. Results show that simulated and observed household consumption distributions overlap by 94.9%, while EWM forecasts closely track real GDP and several other aggregate levels. In government-borrowing counterfactuals, the EWM reproduces the benchmark life-cycle model's short-run transmission from borrowing to consumption. For ex ante planning, the EWM enables an LLM agent to achieve 10.29% higher simulated GDP under the epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions. This initial EWM is only a starting point. We invite economists and AI researchers to build a stronger EWM together. Economists can contribute richer economic models and knowledge, while AI researchers can develop stronger data-driven methods for simulating agent behaviour and learning economic transitions. Together, we aim not only to reproduce real economic dynamics, but also to discover and test new mechanisms that support better decisions and benefit society.
papers.summary: An economic world model (EWM) is defined here as an agent's internal representation of how an economy works, supporting counterfactual simulation and decision-making under resource constraints. The initial implementation learns household policies from microeconomic data and calibrates a structural transition model on macroeconomic data, then evaluates from individual actions up to aggregate forecasts and counterfactuals. Simulated and observed household consumption distributions **overlap by 94.9%**, forecasts closely track real GDP, and government-borrowing counterfactuals reproduce a benchmark life-cycle model's short-run transmission to consumption. Planning with the model lets an LLM agent reach 10.29% higher simulated GDP under an epidemic shock than direct LLM decisions.

papers.title: Social Bias Neurons in Multilingual Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis
papers.abstract: Multilingual models exhibit social bias when processing inputs pertaining to societal stereotypes. We adapt emerging mechanistic interpretability methods to pinpoint and characterize model components that encode this bias. We conduct our analysis across three instruction-tuned models, four languages, and seven bias dimensions. Specifically, we leverage multilingual bias benchmarks in implementing two methods for identifying social bias neurons: activation probability entropy and integrated gap gradients. We find the latter method to be more effective, as the neurons it isolates (which are largely concentrated at the model's deepest layers) lead to sharper decreases in model bias when suppressed. Further analysis reveals neuron distribution patterns differ between high- and low-resourced languages, suggesting that a language's representation in pretraining data influences how its biases are represented within model internals. Our results also indicate that neurons linked to gender, nationality, and social class biases overlap the most with neurons related to other bias dimensions, pointing to the pivotal role these three dimensions play in how models learn and handle bias.
papers.summary: Two neuron-identification methods, activation probability entropy and integrated gap gradients, are adapted to locate the components that encode social bias in multilingual language models, across three instruction-tuned models, four languages, and seven bias dimensions. **Integrated gap gradients proves more effective: the neurons it isolates, mostly in the deepest layers, produce sharper drops in bias when suppressed.** Neuron distribution patterns differ between high- and low-resource languages. Neurons tied to gender, nationality, and social class overlap the most with those for other bias dimensions.

papers.title: CAPTA: Identifying LLMs Behind AI Agents
papers.abstract:
Large language model (LLM)-based agents access remote services through tools to complete user tasks, often via API calls. In this setting, a remote service may want to identify the backend LLM of an agent to launch model-specific attacks, including prompt injection or selective delivery of manipulated content. However, the service cannot directly query the backend model and must instead collect observable responses through its interactions with the agent, making identification challenging.
  In this paper, we present Completely Automated Preference Test to tell LLMs Apart (CAPTA), a model identification approach inspired by CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart), which distinguishes humans from automated programs. CAPTA presents multiple-choice questions as verification challenges, using differences in models' selection preferences to identify the backend LLM. It selects questions based on cross-model option-generation diversity and uses LLM-guided search to optimize their option sets. Our evaluation shows that CAPTA achieves 99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions across 25 LLMs from 10 model families. We further evaluate CAPTA with four widely used agents and seven representative LLMs, achieving 99.7% mean identification accuracy across all 28 agent-LLM combinations with 30 submitted answers.
papers.summary: A remote service that an LLM agent calls through tools may want to learn which backend model drives the agent, for example to mount model-specific prompt injection, but it can only observe the agent's responses. `CAPTA` (Completely Automated Preference Test to tell LLMs Apart) poses multiple-choice questions as verification challenges and identifies the model from its selection preferences, choosing questions by cross-model diversity and optimizing option sets with LLM-guided search. It achieves **99.0% mean identification accuracy with only 10 questions across 25 LLMs from 10 model families**. Across four widely used agents and seven LLMs it reaches 99.7% mean accuracy over all 28 combinations with 30 submitted answers.

papers.title: Are We Rewarding the Wrong Module? Module-Specific Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted to enhance the multimodal reasoning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods share a common limitation of Module-Level Credit Entanglement, in which the vision encoder, projector, and LLM modules are jointly optimized using the same advantage signals even when perceptual correctness and final-answer correctness differ. To address this limitation, we propose Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across model modules. Specifically, MSPO uses responses to perception checklists comprising auxiliary questions about visual information to derive an advantage for training the vision encoder. From these responses, MSPO computes the Confidence-aware Perception Reward (CaPR), using a perception sign obtained by thresholding checklist accuracy to determine reward direction and posterior confidence from a Beta distribution over latent perception accuracy to scale reward magnitude. We then derive the vision advantage through group-relative normalization of CaPR and scale it using main-task success rates. This advantage guides updates to the vision encoder, while the projector and LLM retain outcome-based GRPO updates. Extensive experiments on seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MSPO outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (`GRPO`) updates a multimodal model's vision encoder, projector, and language model with the same advantage signal, even when the model perceived the image correctly but answered wrongly or the reverse. Module-Specific Policy Optimization (`MSPO`) gives the vision encoder its own advantage derived from auxiliary perception-checklist questions, using a confidence-aware reward whose sign comes from thresholded checklist accuracy and whose magnitude comes from a Beta posterior. The projector and language model keep outcome-based updates. On seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks, `MSPO` **outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales**.

papers.title: Load Balancing Neurons: Firing-Rate Control Sustains Plasticity in Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Neural networks in continual learning often lose plasticity: some neurons become inactive, while others fire almost constantly. This limits adaptation to shifting data and wastes capacity. Prior work mitigates this by periodically reinitializing low-utility units, but such resets can destroy previously learned features and do not proactively prevent low utility. We study a simple diagnostic measure: the firing rate of ReLU units, defined as the fraction of positive pre-activations. Low rates identify dead units, while very high rates indicate linearized, always-on units. Based on this view, we introduce a lightweight load-balancing mechanism that adjusts per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range. Across continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, firing-rate distributions explain differences in plasticity across a range of approaches, including well-known techniques such as L2 regularization and non-affine normalization, and load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on both benchmarks. The same mechanism carries over to reinforcement learning, improving Rainbow DQN on Atari over a LayerNorm baseline.
papers.summary: Networks trained continually tend to lose plasticity as some ReLU units go dead and others fire almost constantly, and reset-based fixes can destroy learned features. The authors track each unit's firing rate (the fraction of positive pre-activations) and add a lightweight load-balancing mechanism that adjusts per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range.
