On continual `ImageNet` and class-incremental `CIFAR-100`, firing-rate distributions explain plasticity differences across methods such as L2 regularization and non-affine normalization, and **load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on both benchmarks**. The mechanism also improves `Rainbow DQN` on Atari over a `LayerNorm` baseline.

papers.title: A Hybrid Analytical-Neural Residual Surrogate for Fast Radio Propagation Prediction over Irregular Terrain
papers.abstract: Fast prediction of radio-wave propagation over irregular terrain is important for coverage analysis in mountainous environments, where many terrain and antenna configurations must be evaluated repeatedly. High-fidelity split-step parabolic equation (SSPE) solvers can capture terrain-induced shadowing and interference, but their computational cost is high for repeated planning studies. Learning-based surrogates reduce this cost, but direct field regression asks the network to learn both analytically tractable propagation trends and terrain-dependent residual structure. This paper proposes a hybrid analytical-neural residual surrogate that separates these two parts. A deterministic analytical baseline represents free-space spreading, antenna directivity, modified knife-edge diffraction, and terrain-aware specular reflection, while a compact coarse-to-fine neural network predicts the residual field. The network uses baseline-derived guidance channels, anisotropic convolutions, and feature-wise antenna conditioning to match the directional structure of terrain propagation fields. On synthetic SSPE data at 1.0 GHz, the proposed model achieves an MAE of 2.1061 dB, compared with 3.3955 dB for a standard U-Net and 3.2560 dB for a reproduced physics-guided CNN, while reducing the average inference time to 11.30 ms per sample. A zero-shot test at 1.8 GHz gives an MAE of 2.8692 dB without retraining, and a case study on the measured Hjorringvej terrain profile shows that the prediction remains consistent with the SSPE reference and follows the measured path-loss trend.
papers.summary: Coverage planning in mountainous terrain needs many radio-propagation evaluations, and high-fidelity split-step parabolic equation (SSPE) solvers are too slow for that. The proposed surrogate computes a deterministic analytical baseline (free-space spreading, antenna directivity, knife-edge diffraction, specular reflection) and has a compact coarse-to-fine network with anisotropic convolutions and antenna conditioning predict only the residual field. On synthetic SSPE data at 1.0 GHz it reaches **a mean absolute error of 2.1061 dB versus 3.3955 dB for a standard `U-Net`**, at 11.30 ms per sample. A zero-shot test at 1.8 GHz gives 2.8692 dB, and a case study on the measured Hjorringvej terrain profile follows the measured path-loss trend.

papers.title: Contrastive Proxy Forests: Completeness-Preserving Proxy Learning from Multimodal Records
papers.abstract: Proximal causal inference removes unmeasured confounding using two proxies of the confounder, an outcome-side W and a treatment-side Z. The proxies must satisfy exclusion restrictions and be complete, meaning that they reflect every aspect of the confounder. In practice, they are a few variables hand-picked from a structured table, even though clinical notes and physiological waveforms carry rich information about the confounder. Such records are too high-dimensional for a proximal estimator, and generic compression such as PCA may keep modality-specific variation (style) instead of the confounder, destroying completeness. Our key observation is that, under the proximal condition, the confounder is the only link between a treatment-side and an outcome-side modality beyond the covariates. Learning what they share therefore captures the confounder and filters out modality-specific style. Contrastive Proxy Forests (CPF) learns both proxies by contrasting the two modalities, given the covariates, on a separate unlabeled sample, and passes them to a proximal causal forest. This contrastive objective has an exact closed-form solution, ridge canonical correlation analysis. We prove that CPF preserves the exclusion restrictions exactly and that its proxies inherit the completeness of the raw records under conditions we characterize. Where style is strong, CPF lowers the error of conditional effects by 10-22% relative to PCA proxies, and on MIMIC-IV it is the only method whose point estimate of warfarin's effect on stroke falls inside the range of randomized trials.
papers.summary: Proximal causal inference removes unmeasured confounding using two proxies of the confounder, but these are usually a few hand-picked table variables, while clinical notes and waveforms are too high-dimensional and generic compression like PCA can keep modality-specific style instead of the confounder. `Contrastive Proxy Forests` (CPF) learns both proxies by contrasting a treatment-side and an outcome-side modality given the covariates, an objective solved in closed form by ridge canonical correlation analysis, and passes them to a proximal causal forest. The authors prove CPF preserves the exclusion restrictions and, under stated conditions, the completeness of the raw records. Where style is strong, **CPF lowers conditional-effect error by 10-22% relative to PCA proxies**, and on `MIMIC-IV` it is the only method whose estimate of warfarin's effect on stroke falls within the range of randomized trials.

papers.title: Red-Teaming a Sovereign LLM, Its Reasoning and Its Training Stages
papers.abstract: Open-weight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for applications with sensitive information. We investigate whether confidentiality instructions in system prompt can protect such information. We red-team Apertus v1.5, an open sovereign LLM, and five other model families across six languages and reasoning modes. We use synthetic personal records to evaluate direct disclosure, correction baits, yes/no verification, derived-value queries, reasoning leakage and authorisation checks. We also explore copyright attribution, historical misrepresentation and stereotyping. Despite confidentiality instructions, Apertus 8B and 70B leak information in 96% and 95% of requests, respectively, in correction-bait attacks. Verification and derived-value queries also expose protected information without necessarily revealing identifiers. Moreover, reasoning traces can leak confidential records even when final answers withhold them. Our experiments also show that post-training does not consistently improve safety. Our findings demonstrate that system prompts alone cannot ensure confidentiality and highlight the need for multilingual reasoning-aware safety evaluations.
papers.summary: Whether confidentiality instructions in a system prompt can protect sensitive data is tested by red-teaming `Apertus v1.5`, an open sovereign large language model (LLM), along with five other model families across six languages and reasoning modes. Using synthetic personal records, the study probes direct disclosure, correction baits, yes/no verification, derived-value queries, reasoning leakage, and authorisation checks. Despite the instructions, **`Apertus` 8B and 70B leak information in 96% and 95% of correction-bait requests**, verification and derived-value queries expose protected information without revealing identifiers, and reasoning traces can leak records even when final answers withhold them. Post-training did not consistently improve safety.

papers.title: FourStat: A Dual AutoEncoder Leveraging Frequency and Stationarity for Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: While numerous studies have focused on multivariate time series anomaly detection, many existing methods perform poorly or are not directly applicable to univariate settings. We introduce FourStat, a dual-model framework for univariate time series anomaly detection that combines two complementary approaches. The Fourier Autoencoder (FAE) captures global patterns like seasonality through frequency-domain analysis, while the Stationary Autoencoder (SAE) focuses on local structures by enforcing statistical stationarity. We also propose a new evaluation metric called Perfect Point that assesses whether perfect F1-scores can be achieved directly from anomaly scores, eliminating thresholding subjectivity. Results demonstrate that FourStat outperforms existing baselines, particularly on challenging anomaly types, while the new metric provides clearer insights into model performance gaps and advantages.
papers.summary: Many time series anomaly detectors target multivariate data and perform poorly or do not apply in univariate settings. `FourStat` pairs a Fourier Autoencoder (FAE), which captures global patterns such as seasonality in the frequency domain, with a Stationary Autoencoder (SAE), which models local structure by enforcing statistical stationarity. The authors also propose the `Perfect Point` metric, which checks whether a perfect F1-score is achievable directly from anomaly scores without choosing a threshold. They report that **`FourStat` outperforms existing baselines, particularly on challenging anomaly types**.

papers.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
papers.abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
papers.summary: Depth foundation models are vision transformers sized for GPUs, and when `Depth Anything V2` is quantised for the integer-only `Hailo-8L` accelerator on a Raspberry Pi 5 it loses large parts of the scene, because at 449 tokens 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. The authors instead distil `Depth Anything V2-Large` into an attention-free `ResNet-34` `U-Net` student with 24.5M parameters, whose int8 output matches its float version. **The student runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, versus 21.6 FPS for the vendor's `Depth Anything V2-Small` build**, with accuracy not resolvably different on a real outdoor drive. With mapping, hybrid-A* planning, and SLAM on the Pi's CPU, the full stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9±1.1 of 10 scenes in hardware-in-the-loop tests.

papers.title: ASCENT: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Advancing Stepwise Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models on Common Clinical Scenarios
papers.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) excel at medical question answering yet are rarely evaluated on the stepwise diagnostic reasoning that defines real clinical workflows, where impressions are revised as information accumulates. We build Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis (ASCENT), a clinician-annotated benchmark and training resource of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from MedQA-USMLE that decomposes each vignette into EMR-aligned steps (Findings, Impression, supporting Rationale), enabling evaluation of intermediate reasoning under incomplete information.
  Experiments and training with ASCENT revealed insights into how current LLMs handle stepwise diagnostic reasoning. Even strong reasoning models that perform well on MedQA-USMLE leave substantial headroom on ASCENT, and general-purpose frontier models trail further, exposing a persistent gap between fully informed and stepwise diagnosis. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B on ASCENT yields measurable F1 gains over both pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, with gains driven primarily by precision. Complementary robustness analyses (counterfactual perturbation, format-vs-content control, judge agreement, and rollout) further show that ASCENT-fine-tuned models rely on the diagnostic content of prior impressions rather than imitating their output format, while error propagation under rollout remains a key challenge for clinical deployment.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rarely evaluated on diagnostic reasoning where impressions are revised as information accumulates. `ASCENT` (Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis) is a clinician-annotated benchmark and training set of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from `MedQA-USMLE`, splitting each vignette into Findings, Impression, and Rationale steps. **Even strong reasoning models that do well on `MedQA-USMLE` leave substantial headroom on the stepwise task**, and general-purpose frontier models trail further. Fine-tuning `Qwen2.5-7B` and 32B on `ASCENT` raises F1 over pre-trained and `HuatuoGPT-o1` baselines, mostly through precision, while error propagation under rollout remains a problem.

papers.title: Quantum Community Detection for Data Analysis
papers.abstract: Community detection offers an alternative to conventional methods for data analysis tasks such as feature selection and clustering, and detecting communities with quantum algorithms is a promising avenue for quantum speedup. We investigate quantum spectral community detectors, such as the modularity-matrix algorithm deteQt, in pipelines for both tasks. We first generalise deteQt to multiple communities by recursive bisection, and show that it recovers planted communities, and hence redundant features, in synthetic and small datasets. We then propose projeQt, which applies a spectral filter to the encoded modularity matrix through the quantum singular value transformation, retaining higher-order eigenvectors that deteQt does not use. projeQt acts on the generalised modularity matrix and extracts several communities at once, without recursion, by k-means clustering of a Gram matrix built from quantum state overlaps. On MNIST we demonstrate both pipelines, selecting informative pixels and classifying images directly by clustering, and find them competitive with standard community detectors.
papers.summary: Quantum spectral community detection is examined as a component of feature-selection and clustering pipelines. The authors extend the modularity-matrix algorithm `deteQt` to multiple communities by recursive bisection, and propose `projeQt`, which applies a spectral filter to the encoded modularity matrix via the quantum singular value transformation and extracts several communities at once by k-means clustering of a Gram matrix built from quantum state overlaps. `deteQt` recovers planted communities, and hence redundant features, on synthetic and small datasets. On `MNIST`, used for pixel selection and clustering-based classification, **both pipelines are competitive with standard community detectors**.

papers.title: NCPU: Towards Cell-Inspired Spatial Computing
papers.abstract: Simple cellular automata (CAs) can be computationally universal, but their rules are designed by hand. We train Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs), which learn a local update rule by gradient descent, to compute exact digital logic. Bits are encoded as clusters of cells on a 2D grid, and a result reaches the output only by propagating through intermediate cells. One model is trained per task: logic gates, 4- and 8-bit ripple-carry adders, and a preliminary 8-bit arithmetic logic unit (ALU). All gate and adder models reach 100% bit correctness in 10 of 10 seeds, and exhaustive tests over all input pairs find at most 1 error in 256 (4-bit) and 7 in 65,536 (8-bit). Adders trained on operands of up to 3 bits generalize to 8 bits. The adders propagate the carry as a wave, with a delay of about 3.5 steps per bit of the carry chain. Outputs are correct only within the trained rollout length.
papers.summary: Simple cellular automata can be computationally universal, but their rules are hand-designed. Here Neural Cellular Automata (NCAs), which learn a local update rule by gradient descent, are trained to compute exact digital logic, with bits encoded as clusters of cells on a 2D grid and results reaching the output only by propagating through intermediate cells. Separate models are trained for logic gates, 4- and 8-bit ripple-carry adders, and a preliminary 8-bit arithmetic logic unit (ALU). **All gate and adder models reach 100% bit correctness in 10 of 10 seeds**, adders trained on operands of up to 3 bits generalize to 8 bits, and the carry propagates as a wave at about 3.5 steps per bit, though outputs are correct only within the trained rollout length.

papers.title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.
papers.summary: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) make a large language model (LLM) behave maliciously after quantization while staying benign at high precision. `ReQOR` is a training-free defense that runs the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, finds the dominant directions of the resulting discrepancies on benign calibration data, and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form as a factorized residual adapter. It needs no attack information or gradient-based optimization. Across four LLMs, three PGD-based attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats it substantially mitigates the backdoors while largely preserving benign utility, and **it remains effective on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack where existing baselines largely fail**.

papers.title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
papers.abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.
papers.summary: Classical analysis of stochastic gradient descent restricts the stepsize to below a curvature-dependent stability threshold, and it was an open question whether the acceleration that large stepsizes give deterministic gradient descent survives gradient noise. The authors answer affirmatively for cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing **an accelerated O(T^-2) convergence rate**. The analysis rests on a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics, which also yields tighter guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Numerical experiments illustrate the benefit of large learning rates.

papers.title: EviCraft: Can Minecraft Agents Find What They Cannot See?
papers.abstract: In Minecraft, a common testbed for embodied agents, semantic tools such as mineBlock pick targets from the simulator's loaded world state without a visibility test, so a buried ore the agent has never seen is one call away, and scores cannot show whether the agent searched. We formalize the missing requirement as evidence closure: every decision of an agent system, including those inside its tools, may depend on the world only through facts for which the agent holds evidence. EviCraft is a runtime and benchmark that enforces closure below the agent and makes the admission rule an experimental variable: a perception-grounded regime (G) admits only what is in line of sight or returned by the agent's own actions, and a loaded-state regime (L) reproduces standard tool stacks, with agents, tools, and worlds held fixed. On Survival, the regime effect exceeds the strongest agent's lead: under G, three mid-sized agents reach the diamond in 32%-40% of runs, against 76%-94% under L, and the strongest agent under G scores below each of them under L. In two models, removing only the line-of-sight test closes 93%-96% of the score gap, and loading state only inside tools recovers 70%-98%, so safeguards on observations and queries leave most of the leak open. In open-ended acquisition, the gain from L concentrates in items that depend on buried resources or mobs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/AllenReder/EviCraft
papers.summary: Minecraft agent tools such as `mineBlock` pick targets from the simulator's loaded world state without a visibility test, so an agent can reach buried ore it has never seen and scores do not show whether it searched. `EviCraft` is a runtime and benchmark built around evidence closure, the requirement that every decision, including those inside tools, depend only on facts the agent holds evidence for; it compares a perception-grounded regime against the standard loaded-state regime with agents, tools, and worlds held fixed. On Survival, **three mid-sized agents reach the diamond in 32%-40% of runs under perception grounding versus 76%-94% with loaded state**, a gap larger than the strongest agent's lead. Removing only the line-of-sight test closes 93%-96% of the score gap in two models, and loading state only inside tools recovers 70%-98%.

papers.title: RubikSQL-HB: Agentic Text-to-SQL with Knowledge in the Loop
papers.abstract: Database agents need more than schema structure: business meanings, stored values and reference queries supply knowledge that becomes relevant at different points in reasoning. We introduce RubikSQL-HB, which exposes these materials through queryable, database-specific knowledge workspaces built on the HeavenBase platform. Its knowledge interface remains available as an agent constructs and investigates an answer. Candidate agents interleave knowledge access with SQL construction and execution; a downstream Judge can reuse the same interfaces to investigate disagreements. A two-stage example interface separates discovering a reference question from expanding its SQL. On a 500-question BIRD Mini-Dev evaluation, the full pipeline reaches 75.2% execution accuracy, against 71.2% for first-candidate selection and 70.4% for execution-majority voting, with a correct candidate available on 79.0% of questions. The raw-knowledge condition, which also regenerates candidates without the built workspace, is 3.0 points lower, and adjudication with tools and revision accounts for most of the gain over selection baselines. A recorded execution probe shows how continued investigation resolves a candidate disagreement. Separate archived runs show semantic revision recovering answers absent from their original candidate pools. A versioned development study further illustrates how recurring corrections become reusable execution checks. The system and results connect knowledge-interface design to agent decision quality: queryable knowledge supports the construction of useful alternatives, and evidence-aware adjudication connects those alternatives to a final answer. Keeping knowledge in the loop lets agents acquire relevant observations as their reasoning develops.
papers.summary: Database agents need business meanings, stored values, and reference queries in addition to schema structure, and this knowledge becomes relevant at different points in reasoning. `RubikSQL-HB` exposes it through queryable, database-specific knowledge workspaces built on the `HeavenBase` platform, which candidate agents consult while constructing and executing SQL and which a downstream Judge reuses to investigate disagreements between candidates. On a 500-question `BIRD Mini-Dev` evaluation, **the full pipeline reaches 75.2% execution accuracy, against 71.2% for first-candidate selection and 70.4% for execution-majority voting**, with a correct candidate available on 79.0% of questions. Using raw knowledge without the built workspace is 3.0 points lower, and adjudication with tools and revision accounts for most of the gain.

papers.title: Learning World Models through Contrastive Identification of Actions
papers.abstract: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.
papers.summary: Latent world models trained from offline visual data do not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should keep, and inverse-dynamics regression rewards extra information only when it changes the conditional action mean. Contrastive Identification of Actions (`CIA`) instead trains the model to pick out the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal, targeting information the next latent supplies beyond history. The authors show that under exact behavior matching `CIA` can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and confirm this in a controlled example. **`CIA` achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks**, without modifying the planner.

papers.title: Beyond Fixed-Context Likelihood: Zero-Shot AI-Generated Text Detection via Context Perturbation Discrepancy
papers.abstract: The same increase in token log probability from earlier context can be typical at one position and unusually large at another. We introduce Context Perturbation Discrepancy (CPD), a zero-shot detector that measures this gain relative to what a single pretrained language model expects. Keeping the passage fixed, CPD scores each observed token under its full prefix and under a short window of recent tokens. Under the full-prefix distribution, the expected gain equals the KL divergence from that distribution to the restricted-prefix distribution. CPD subtracts this expectation from each observed gain and scales the sum of the signed deviations by its analytical reference standard deviation. On unedited human and AI texts from GEN, DetectRL-X, and HART, subtracting the expected gain raises AUROC by 32.78-35.81 percentage points at the same variance scale. CPD outperforms seven zero-shot baselines, averaging 94.80% AUROC and 79.60% recall at a 5% false-positive rate. On original and edited HART passages, the same scores separate texts more clearly by draft origin than by the benchmark's final-expression labels (89.15% versus 65.50% AUROC). Code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-tyf/CPD.
papers.summary: Context Perturbation Discrepancy (`CPD`) is a zero-shot detector of AI-generated text that scores each token under its full prefix and under a short window of recent tokens, using a single pretrained language model. It subtracts the expected log-probability gain from earlier context, which equals a KL divergence between the two distributions, from each observed gain and normalizes the sum by an analytical standard deviation. On unedited texts from `GEN`, `DetectRL-X`, and `HART`, subtracting the expected gain raises AUROC by 32.78-35.81 percentage points, and **`CPD` averages 94.80% AUROC and 79.60% recall at a 5% false-positive rate**, ahead of seven zero-shot baselines. On edited `HART` passages its scores separate texts more clearly by draft origin than by final-expression labels (89.15% versus 65.50% AUROC).

papers.title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.
papers.summary: In recommender systems built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), compression and cross-modal fusion are often assumed to add robustness against content manipulation. The authors argue the same process creates a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias, where signals that stay salient after compression and are supported across modalities gain disproportionate influence on ranking. Their inference-time attack `C3H` promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to match the decision criteria the recommender implicitly expresses, without noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning. Experiments show **`C3H` substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility**.

papers.title: NABLA: A Noise-Adaptive Blockwise Left-Right Preconditioning Algorithm for Stochastic Optimization
papers.abstract: We propose NABLA, a noise-adaptive blockwise left-right preconditioning algorithm for mini-batch stochastic nonconvex optimization. NABLA combines an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients with block-diagonal row and column preconditioners constructed from matrix-valued second-moment statistics. Unlike conventional matrix-preconditioned methods that use fixed decay parameters, NABLA adjusts the second-moment averaging coefficient through a closed-loop feedback rule determined by the cumulative stochastic-gradient energy and its running average. The first-moment coefficient remains fixed, allowing the trajectory-dependent adaptation to act directly on the structured preconditioners. The resulting method is horizon-free, requires no prior knowledge of the noise level, and automatically adjusts the memory of its second-moment estimators to the observed optimization dynamics. Under standard lower boundedness, smoothness, unbiasedness, bounded-variance, and spectral-boundedness assumptions, we establish uniform stability and variation bounds for the time-varying block preconditioners and control their interaction with momentum estimation and parameter updates. These results yield the noise-adaptive stationarity guarantee $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2}+\sigma^{1/2}T^{-1/4})$, which automatically reduces to the nearly deterministic $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ rate when the stochastic-gradient noise vanishes. NABLA therefore provides a principled approach to combining closed-loop trajectory feedback with memory-efficient structured matrix preconditioning.
papers.summary: `NABLA` is an optimizer for mini-batch stochastic nonconvex problems that combines an exponential moving average of gradients with block-diagonal row and column preconditioners built from matrix-valued second-moment statistics. Instead of a fixed decay, it adjusts the second-moment averaging coefficient through a closed-loop feedback rule driven by cumulative stochastic-gradient energy and its running average, requiring no knowledge of the horizon or noise level. Under standard smoothness, bounded-variance, and spectral-boundedness assumptions, the authors prove **a noise-adaptive stationarity rate of roughly O(T^-1/2 + sigma^1/2 T^-1/4) up to log factors**, which reduces to the near-deterministic O(T^-1/2) rate when gradient noise vanishes.

papers.title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
papers.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call $\sigma_{99}$), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) use the same feed-forward network (FFN) width in every layer, though layers at different depths may need different capacity. Applying principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection, the authors measure per-layer intrinsic dimensionality as the number of components needed to reconstruct activations to a fixed cosine similarity, scanning 58 open-weight LLMs from 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters. They find **a recurring middle-heavy profile, with middle layers carrying higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers**, robust to calibration corpus and fine-tuning. Using the profile to allocate widths in a distilled student at matched parameter budget beats uniform width by +2.3 points on `Qwen3-8B` and +2.5 on `Qwen2.5-3B`, with smaller gains on `Gemma-3-4B` and `LLaMA-3-8B`.

papers.title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.
papers.summary: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated proxy of the scene, on the untested assumption that the video shows what the proxy shows. `SimPWM` (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model) builds, from the first frame and a calibrated camera, a 3D robot model and 3D points for graspable objects, moves them with a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters, and has a video model render the result, so the simulated state can be perturbed. On `DROID` episodes from unseen setups, the arm follows the proxy with all three base video models (robot IoU 0.75-0.78), and simulated objects cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38% against a robot-only proxy. When the simulated objects are frozen, **the lift rate on rigid objects drops from 42% to 10% for `MiniMax-H3` but only from 57% to 49% for `LTX-2.3`**, indicating some base models infer the grasp from arm motion rather than the simulated state.

papers.title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores
papers.abstract: The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.
papers.summary: Brain scores measure how well model activations align with recorded brain activity, and because recordings are noisy there is an upper bound, the noise ceiling, on the score any model can reach. The authors introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and predict each one's behavior theoretically. They validate the predictions with simulations and compare against estimates from existing fMRI and EEG datasets. They find that **the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings**, and give best-practice recommendations for each situation.

papers.title: Is Prosody Encoded in the Neural Audio Codec Mimi?
papers.abstract: Neural audio codecs (NACs) have become a fundamental infrastructure for modern speech-language models, discretizing continuous speech signals into token sequences that enable large language models to process and generate audio. Most research evaluates codec quality at the decoding phase, assessing the naturalness of reconstructed speech. However, little research investigates what phonetic information is captured during encoding. In this paper, we investigated the potential correlates of prosody in the NAC Mimi, a codec used by conversational speech agents such as Moshi and Sesame and used in downstream tasks such as speech-to-speech translation (Hibiki).
papers.summary: Neural audio codecs (NACs), which turn continuous speech into token sequences for speech-language models, are usually judged by how natural their reconstructed audio sounds, with little study of what phonetic information they capture during encoding. The authors examine **whether correlates of prosody are present in the encodings of `Mimi`**, the codec behind conversational speech agents such as `Moshi` and `Sesame` and the speech-to-speech translation system `Hibiki`. The abstract does not state the outcome of the investigation.

papers.title: Scaling Laws of Ensemble Uncertainty in Language Models
papers.abstract: Many use cases for large language models (LLMs)---from AI safety to exploration and human interaction---can benefit from epistemic uncertainty estimates. We argue that existing Bayesian Deep Learning solutions, which are often restricted to a fixed model family, fail to capture the full epistemic uncertainty at practical LLM scales. This is because the error due to the bounded capacity of the model family remains invisible to disagreement among models supported by the prior. We relate this error to the well-known power-law scaling of LLM loss with model size. We then show that a second power law quantifies the shrinking disagreement within ensembles as model size increases. Its slower decay relative to the capacity law above suggests that ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty and become more competitive as an axis for scaling, compared to a single larger model. Finally, a third power law quantifies the loss of ensemble diversity as members share a larger fraction of training before branching, and therefore identifies a further limitation, beyond the capacity error, for LoRA ensembles and optimization-based or second-order methods that approximate uncertainty around a single training solution. At a high level, these findings suggest diverse ensembles can be a promising axis, both for scaling and uncertainty quantification at larger scales.
papers.summary: Bayesian deep learning methods that stay within a fixed model family are argued to miss part of the epistemic uncertainty of large language models (LLMs), because the error from the family's bounded capacity never shows up as disagreement between its members. The authors relate this capacity error to the known power-law scaling of loss with model size, then fit a second power law describing how disagreement within an ensemble shrinks as members grow. **Ensemble disagreement decays more slowly than the capacity error, so ensembles capture a growing share of epistemic uncertainty at larger scales.** A third power law shows diversity dropping as members share more training before branching, which limits `LoRA` ensembles and methods that approximate uncertainty around a single training solution.

papers.title: Sample-Efficient In-Context Adaptation via Sleep
papers.abstract: The ability to learn and generalize from limited experience, or sample efficiency, is a cornerstone of intelligence. How can we build language models that turn a few user interactions, a few snippets of unfamiliar code, or a handful of experimental results provided in context into knowledge that generalizes? Prior work has found that sleep, a process where the model performs $N$ recurrent forward passes to refine its representations of a chunk of context, can improve long-context reasoning (specifically, within SSM-attention hybrid models). We study whether this method also improves in-context adaptation on general, non-synthetic tasks for transformer language models. To this end, we pre-train language models up to 1.2B-parameters on up to 100B tokens with sleep mechanisms. Notably, longer sleep (i.e., using a larger number of recurrent forward passes $N$) enables the model to learn faster in-context on multiple few-shot algorithmic, question-answering tasks, while also achieving lower next-token prediction loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. On held-out code, models with $N=2$ and $N=4$ match the no-sleep baseline's loss using $2.10\times$ and $2.39\times$ fewer tokens in-context, respectively. More broadly, we view our work as a step toward building models that have better tradeoffs between in-context adaptation and decoding latency.
papers.summary: The question is whether sleep, a mechanism in which a model runs N recurrent forward passes to refine its representation of a chunk of context, improves in-context learning for ordinary transformer language models on non-synthetic tasks, having previously been shown to help long-context reasoning in hybrid state-space and attention models. The authors pre-train models of up to 1.2B parameters on up to 100B tokens with sleep mechanisms. Longer sleep speeds up in-context learning on few-shot algorithmic and question-answering tasks and lowers next-token loss on out-of-distribution evaluations. On held-out code, models with N=2 and N=4 match the no-sleep baseline's loss using **2.10x and 2.39x fewer in-context tokens**, respectively.

papers.title: MRBench: Benchmarking Physical Necessity Reasoning in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in multi-robot manipulation have shown how robots can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. However, successful coordination does not reveal which robots are actually needed. The same task may require different teams as robot capabilities change, resources become unavailable, or objects replace robotic support. We argue that reliable multi-robot manipulation requires physical necessity reasoning: understanding what a task demands, which resources can fulfill those demands, and which are truly necessary. We introduce MRBench, a benchmark for physical necessity reasoning in heterogeneous multi-robot manipulation. It comprises eight tasks with distinct concurrency and reach constraints, each evaluated under five configurations that change the required resources while preserving the task goal. Our evaluation reveals that existing coordination agents perform well with reference teams but struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can replace robotic support. To address this gap, we propose MRScissors, which separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities and identifies minimal feasible teams through constrained search. Across two model backbones, MRScissors achieves 85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy, outperforming the strongest baselines by 10.4 and 9.5 points, respectively. Together, these findings expose a critical gap between coordinating robots and understanding their physical necessity.
papers.summary: Successful multi-robot coordination does not show which robots a task actually needs, so the authors define physical necessity reasoning: working out what a task demands, which resources can meet those demands, and which are truly required. Their benchmark `MRBench` has eight manipulation tasks with different concurrency and reach constraints, each run under five configurations that change the required resources while keeping the goal fixed. Existing coordination agents do well with reference teams but struggle when robot embodiments change or passive objects can stand in for robots. The proposed `MRScissors` separates task requirements from measured physical capabilities and searches for minimal feasible teams, reaching **85.4% and 91.2% team-selection accuracy** on two model backbones, 10.4 and 9.5 points above the strongest baselines.

papers.title: From Grammar Deltas to Token Masks: Incremental Constrained Decoding under Runtime Grammar Evolution
papers.abstract: Grammar-constrained decoding enables large language models to generate outputs that satisfy formal constraints, but in code and domain-specific language generation, the relevant constraints are not always fully available before decoding and may emerge progressively from new declarations, inferred type information, or runtime analysis feedback. Existing structured-decoding engines efficiently handle fixed, predeclared, or previously seen constraint structures; however, when a first-seen grammar update changes the parser state induced by an already committed prefix, the straightforward solution reconstructs the constraint state under the updated grammar, repeating parsing work already performed over the prefix. We introduce GramDelta, an incremental framework for constrained decoding with append-only runtime grammar updates. GramDelta maintains parse state over the committed prefix and propagates only changes induced by newly added grammar rules through historical dependencies, avoiding prefix replay. It then maps the updated parse state to exact next-token masks via compilation-free factorized projection over shared historical charts, avoiding per-update mask-cache recompilation. GramDelta therefore preserves the result of full reconstruction while making update cost sensitive to the actual impact of a grammar change. Experiments across four model configurations show that GramDelta adds negligible overhead without updates; under sustained runtime grammar evolution, it reduces median first-seen grammar-update latency by 10.7--11.5x and reduces the additional TPOT overhead over unconstrained decoding by 53.1--81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline. These results enable efficient constrained decoding when constraints progressively emerge and evolve with the generated prefix.
papers.summary: Grammar-constrained decoding normally assumes the grammar is fixed before generation, but in code and domain-specific language generation new constraints can appear mid-decoding from declarations, inferred types, or runtime analysis, and existing engines then rebuild the parser state by replaying the whole committed prefix. `GramDelta` handles append-only grammar updates incrementally: it keeps the parse state over the prefix, propagates only the changes caused by newly added rules, and derives exact next-token masks without recompiling a mask cache. Across four model configurations it adds negligible overhead when no updates occur. Under sustained grammar evolution it **cuts median latency for first-seen grammar updates by 10.7-11.5x** and reduces the extra per-token time over unconstrained decoding by 53.1-81.9% relative to the strongest reconstruction baseline.

papers.title: EPRO: Robust Policy Optimization Through an Imperfect Execution-Policy Predictor
papers.abstract: RL for LLMs often separates rollout generation from policy training. Although the two numerical engines share model parameters, they can induce different policies. This creates a challenge beyond correcting a known training-inference mismatch: during learner updates, the execution policy corresponding to the current parameters cannot be directly observed. We view this as optimizing an unobserved execution policy through an imperfect predictor of its evolution. This perspective raises two fundamental questions: how can we estimate the execution policy's response to learner updates, and how much should we trust that estimate when optimizing the actual execution policy? We introduce Execution-Policy Robust Optimization (EPRO) to address these challenges. Starting from the observed rollout-time execution policy, we use training-policy changes to construct a differentiable predictor of the current execution policy, whose score yields Transported Score Centering (TSC). Our robust-improvement analysis reveals how prediction error limits the magnitude of reliably justified updates. For practical implementation, we introduce Policy Shift as an observable proxy for prediction risk and use Shift-Aware Soft Clipping (SSC) to attenuate risky updates. Across four Qwen3 model settings, EPRO achieves the highest average held-out accuracy among the compared methods on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning for large language models often generates rollouts with one numerical engine and trains with another, and although both share parameters they can induce different policies, so the policy that will actually execute after a learner update cannot be observed directly. Execution-Policy Robust Optimization (`EPRO`) treats this as optimizing an unobserved execution policy through an imperfect predictor: it builds a differentiable predictor from the rollout-time policy and training-policy changes, giving a correction called Transported Score Centering (TSC). An analysis shows how prediction error limits the size of updates that can be reliably justified, and Shift-Aware Soft Clipping (SSC) attenuates risky updates using an observable policy-shift proxy. Across four `Qwen3` model settings, `EPRO` achieves **the highest average held-out accuracy among the compared methods on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks**.

papers.title: Interactive Neural Computers
papers.abstract: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.
papers.summary: Instead of training an agent to operate an existing computer, the authors train a generative model to act as the computer itself, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Their `Interactive Neural Computer`, structured like a Neural Turing Machine, combines a surprise-gated slot memory supervised by latent next-frame prediction (`MEMORY-JEPA`) for off-screen content, a query bridge to a pretrained vision-language model for reasoning, and a residual renderer that predicts only latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts it recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%) versus at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines, and it **raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%**. Because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.

papers.title: Breaking the Joint Action Space Dependence in Distributionally Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We study the sample complexity of learning robust coarse correlated equilibria (CCE) in finite-horizon, general-sum, distributionally robust Markov games with known rewards and a generative model of the nominal transitions. Each player evaluates a policy by its worst-case return over total-variation (TV) balls centered at the nominal transition distribution of every stage, state, and joint action; this is the standard $(s,a)$-rectangular uncertainty set. Existing generative-model guarantees for this model scale with the number $\prod_iA_i$ of joint actions, where $A_i$ is the number of actions of player~$i$. Since this number grows exponentially with the number of players, these guarantees suffer from the curse of multiagency. We design an algorithm whose sample complexity depends on the action sets only through the largest individual action-set size $A_*:=\max_iA_i$. The algorithm uses $\widetilde O(SA_*H^5D^4/\varepsilon^4)$ transition samples and, with probability at least $1-\delta$, returns a Markov policy that is an $\varepsilon$-robust CCE from every initial state. Here $S$ is the number of states, $H$ is the horizon, and $D:=\max_i\min\{H,1/\rho_i\}$, where $\rho_i$ is the TV radius of player~$i$. Two ingredients make this possible: a plug-in estimate of the robust backup whose mean error does not depend on the number of states, and a single batch of samples per round that serves as bandit feedback for all players at once. The result shows that the dependence on $\prod_iA_i$ can be avoided without modifying the $(s,a)$-rectangular uncertainty set.
papers.summary: Existing sample-complexity guarantees for learning robust coarse correlated equilibria (CCE) in distributionally robust Markov games scale with the number of joint actions, which grows exponentially in the number of players. For the finite-horizon, general-sum setting with total-variation (TV) uncertainty balls around each stage, state, and joint action, and a generative model of the nominal transitions, the authors design an algorithm whose **sample complexity depends on the action sets only through the largest individual action-set size**. Its bound is polynomial in the number of states, that largest action-set size, the horizon, and the inverse TV radius, with a 1/epsilon^4 dependence on the target accuracy. Two ingredients make this possible: a plug-in estimate of the robust backup whose mean error is independent of the number of states, and a single batch of samples per round that serves as bandit feedback for all players at once.

papers.title: E(n)-Equivariant Spherical Decision Surfaces
papers.abstract: We present a constructive derivation of exactly E(n)-equivariant spherical decision surfaces by extending prior O(n)-equivariant hypersphere neurons to include translations. To achieve this, we present a decomposition of the features of the O(n)-equivariant neurons and provide explicit representations for translation and E(n)-transformations to fulfil the respective equivariance constraints. The resulting decision surfaces are exactly E(n)-equivariant without input centring or explicit pairwise differences, and admit explicit closed-form matrix representations. In addition, we numerically verify the correctness of the derivations and perform a downstream check of the resulting geometric primitives.
papers.summary: Earlier hypersphere neurons are equivariant to rotations and reflections, the group O(n), but not to translations. The authors give a constructive derivation that extends them to the full Euclidean group E(n) by decomposing the neurons' features and providing explicit representations for translations and E(n) transformations. The resulting spherical decision surfaces are **exactly E(n)-equivariant without input centring or explicit pairwise differences** and have closed-form matrix representations. The derivations are verified numerically and checked on a downstream task.

papers.title: Data-driven Reduced-order Modeling of a Multistable Viscoelastic Flow
papers.abstract: Viscoelastic flow past two side-by-side microcylinders has been shown to exhibit geometry-dependent transitions among symmetric, converging, diverging, and asymmetric-diverging flow states, together with regions of bistability and tristability. Here, we develop a data-driven framework for learning a two-dimensional, parameter-dependent normal form for this bifurcation structure from sparse measurements of stable flow states. We use the flow asymmetry parameters $I'$ and $I''$ as state variables, with the gap ratio $G$ and Weissenberg number $Wi$ as control parameters. In the absence of trajectory data, the measured steady states are enforced as stable equilibria of the learned vector field through equilibrium and local-stability constraints. We examine both polynomial and neural-network representations of the associated normal form and incorporate the physical reflection symmetry directly into the model. The resulting models recover the main geometry-dependent transitions and the overall structure of the experimental phase diagram. To reduce additional stable equilibria that are not constrained by the measurements, we introduce an iterative negative-sample procedure that refines the predicted equilibrium structure. Combining equilibrium data, local stability, physical symmetry, and negative samples yields the closest agreement with the experimental phase diagram among the models considered. The remaining discrepancies reflect the limited information available, solely in the form of sparse equilibrium measurements. Overall, the framework aims to showcase a prototypical example of both the potential and the limitations of inferring nonlinear flow dynamics from sparse equilibrium measurements and highlight the importance of physical constraints and additional dynamical information for reconstructing complex bifurcation structures.
papers.summary: Viscoelastic flow past two side-by-side microcylinders switches between symmetric, converging, diverging, and asymmetric-diverging states, with regions where two or three states are stable at once. The authors learn a two-dimensional, parameter-dependent normal form for this bifurcation structure from sparse measurements of stable steady states alone, using polynomial and neural-network models that enforce the measured states as stable equilibria and build in the physical reflection symmetry. An iterative negative-sample procedure removes spurious extra equilibria that the data do not constrain. **Combining equilibrium data, local stability, symmetry, and negative samples gives the closest match to the experimental phase diagram** among the models considered, with remaining discrepancies attributed to having only sparse equilibrium measurements and no trajectory data.

papers.title: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation
papers.abstract: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.
papers.summary: Streaming video generators that produce video chunk by chunk often keep following the old prompt after a user switches prompts mid-generation. The authors trace this to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt, and find it persists even when the cache holds only that one chunk. Their training-free Residual Guidance (`RG`) denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache, then adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk. Across single-switch and long multi-switch settings it improves prompt switching on existing streaming models while largely retaining visual quality, at a cost of **one extra forward pass per chunk with no training or per-model tuning**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Streaming video generators that produce video chunk by chunk often keep following the old prompt after a mid-stream prompt switch, a failure the authors trace to "context inertia": the cached previous frames act as a prior that suppresses the new prompt. `Residual Guidance` (RG) is a training-free fix that measures the new prompt's effect without the cache and adds it to the cache-conditioned prediction, so the cache itself is left untouched.

- The inertia comes from what the cached frames depict rather than from stale prompt information: at the first denoising step the full context retains only **0.18** of the context-free prompt response on `Self Forcing` and **0.27** on `LongLive`, even after `LongLive` re-caches under the new prompt.
- For each post-switch chunk, RG re-noises the previous chunk (τ=850), denoises it once under the new prompt with an empty KV cache, and adds the difference from the original chunk to the first two of four denoising steps with weights 1 and 0.5, using the same configuration for every model.
- Across seven streaming baselines distilled from `Wan2.1-1.3B`, average switch achievement rises from **21% to 58%** on `T2V-CompBench` dynamic-attribute switches, from **47% to 66%** on `StoryEval` three-event stories, and from **66% to 81%** on 60-second `InteractiveBench` scripts, with VBench quality staying within about 0.02 of the base model.
- The cost is one extra forward pass per post-switch chunk, which lowers throughput by about **6%** on a 5-second single-switch video, and 20 raters preferred RG **70.7%** of the time overall and 73.1% for prompt adherence.
- Consistency is the trade-off, with raters preferring RG on consistency only 44.3% of the time and unintended change rising above the base model, while object removal remains difficult and achievement is scored by a VLM judge that agreed with human labels on 86% of the authors' analysis-set videos.

papers.title: Reliable and grounded reporting of any computed tomography scan with FORA
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems for computed tomography (CT) remain largely restricted to specific anatomical regions, examination types or predefined abnormalities, limiting their ability to provide comprehensive and spatially grounded interpretations. Here we present FORA, a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across the 28 CT protocols represented in our cohort. Trained on 304,962 routine CT examinations supervised by their accompanying reports, FORA learns to localize abnormalities without manually annotated lesions. Its architecture combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck that connects spatial evidence, radiological findings and report generation. We first developed and benchmarked the architecture on chest radiographs, achieving state-of-the-art performance, before training a separate model on three-dimensional CT examinations. On 36,619 held-out CT examinations, FORA achieved a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918 for radiological concept recognition, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21. FORA also ranked first on three public benchmarks, outperforming Merlin on its own test set without training on that institution's data (AUROC 0.907 versus 0.826). On independent localization benchmarks for pulmonary emboli, renal masses and rib fractures, FORA's strongest spatial evidence fell within annotated lesions at rates up to 348 times greater than chance. FORA achieved more than threefold higher macro-averaged finding recall than the strongest existing report generator. These results show that a single model can combine broad abnormality recognition, spatial localization and report generation across 12 CT examination types, using routine reports without lesion-level supervision.
papers.summary: Computed tomography (CT) models are mostly limited to particular anatomical regions, exam types, or predefined abnormalities. `FORA` is a general-purpose CT model that recognizes and spatially localizes 1,028 hierarchically organized radiological concepts and generates reports across 28 CT protocols, trained on 304,962 routine examinations supervised only by their accompanying reports, with no manually annotated lesions. It combines multiple-instance learning with an interpretable concept bottleneck linking spatial evidence, findings, and report text. On 36,619 held-out examinations it reaches **a macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918, exceeding the strongest of 18 existing CT models by 0.21**; it also outperforms `Merlin` on that model's own test set (0.907 versus 0.826) and achieves more than threefold higher finding recall than the strongest existing report generator.

papers.title: PtychoFM: A Foundation Model for Ptychographic Imaging
papers.abstract: Ptychography provides high-resolution lensless imaging across X-ray, electron, and optical microscopy, but reconstructing images from diffraction measurements generally requires computationally intensity iterative phase retrieval. These methods often require experiment-specific analysis, limiting real-time feedback as data acquisition rates increase. Here, we demonstrate PtychoFM, a physics-aware foundation model for ptychographic imaging that combines large-scale pre-training with experiment-specific fine-tuning to reconstruct complex object images directly from individual diffraction patterns. Trained using a differentiable forward model without object-space labels, PtychoFM transfers from step-scan training data on one sample to fly-scan measurements of other samples with different feature sizes, morphologies, and refraction indices. At a synchrotron beamline, diffraction frames were streamed from the detector to a single GPU for inference at up to 200 frames per second and returned for real-time visualization. PtychoFM provides a practical route to rapid, transferable ptychographic reconstruction and live experimental feedback under nonideal conditions.
papers.summary: Ptychography is a lensless imaging technique used in X-ray, electron, and optical microscopy, and reconstructing its images normally requires slow iterative phase retrieval tuned to each experiment. `PtychoFM` is a physics-aware foundation model that reconstructs complex object images directly from individual diffraction patterns, combining large-scale pre-training with experiment-specific fine-tuning and training through a differentiable forward model without object-space labels. It transfers from step-scan data on one sample to fly-scan measurements of other samples with different feature sizes, morphologies, and refraction indices. At a synchrotron beamline, frames streamed from the detector to a single GPU were reconstructed at **up to 200 frames per second** for real-time visualization.

papers.title: Field Life: Particle Life as Interacting Chemical Fields
papers.abstract: Field Life is a cellular automaton inspired by the interaction dynamics of Particle Life. In Particle Life, each particle has a colour, and an interaction matrix sets how strongly each colour attracts or repels each other colour. In Field Life, each colour is a channel of the automaton, and each cell holds a concentration of every colour. One step of the rule has three parts. Each colour is convolved with a ring-shaped kernel, which measures how much of that colour surrounds a cell. The interaction matrix combines these measurements into an attraction for each colour. The mass of each colour then moves toward higher attraction, in a way that conserves mass. A random matrix and a random initial state are usually enough to produce moving structure: bodies that glide, bodies that shed diffuse clouds, and gliders that break up into smaller gliders. We sample rules at random, keep the rules that move and form structure, and describe the patterns that appear: colours that sort into regions, colours that form stripes, and gliders, compact bodies that travel across the grid. The simulation and 120 saved rules, which we call worlds, are released.
papers.summary: `Field Life` is a cellular automaton that recasts `Particle Life`, where coloured particles attract or repel each other according to an interaction matrix, as continuous concentration fields with one channel per colour. Each step convolves every colour with a ring-shaped kernel to measure its surrounding concentration, combines those measurements through the interaction matrix into an attraction per colour, and moves each colour's mass toward higher attraction while conserving it. **A random matrix and a random initial state are usually enough to produce moving structure**, including colours that sort into regions or stripes and gliders that travel across the grid or split into smaller gliders. The simulation and 120 saved rule sets are released.

papers.title: Measurement Artifacts in Trustworthiness Evaluations of Quantized Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Evaluations of quantized language models attribute the change in a benchmark score to quantization. We write the measured change as the true change plus a term contributed by the instrument. Instrument error that is the same at every precision can shrink a paired comparison but cannot create or reverse an effect. Error that interacts with quantization can do both, and it is reported as an effect of quantization. We estimate this interaction for four measurement choices in 8 instruction-tuned models below two billion parameters, at float16, LLM.int8() and NF4, on identical items. Measured against labels from two human annotators, the 4-bit rise in harmful compliance is about half to two-thirds of the rise in non-refusal that a corrected key word detector records. Cloze and lettered multiple-choice scoring disagree about the effect of quantization far more than their noise allows: their estimates correlate at \r{ho} = 0.10, against a ceiling of about 0.77. LLM.int8() answers and generations depend on which items share a batch, and padding alone changes its answers. Rounding activations to 8 bits is enough to produce this dependence. NF4 is batch-invariant. The two largest reported calibration losses are response-bias shifts.
