We release item-level predictions, option scores and human annotations, and give recommendations for evaluating compressed small models.
papers.summary: Benchmark score changes in quantized language models are usually attributed entirely to quantization, but the authors show that part of the measured change can come from the measurement instrument interacting with quantization. They estimate this interaction for four measurement choices across 8 instruction-tuned models under two billion parameters at float16, `LLM.int8()`, and `NF4` on identical items. Against labels from two human annotators, **the 4-bit rise in harmful compliance is only about half to two-thirds of the rise in non-refusal recorded by a corrected keyword detector**, and cloze versus lettered multiple-choice scoring give estimates of the quantization effect that correlate at just rho = 0.10 against a ceiling of about 0.77. `LLM.int8()` outputs also depend on which items share a batch and on padding, while `NF4` is batch-invariant; item-level predictions and human annotations are released.

papers.title: Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables
papers.abstract: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure methods used to generate their training data, and refining them against experimental measurements provides a direct route beyond this limit. However, such refinement remains difficult for dynamical observables because differentiating chaotic molecular trajectories yields unstable gradients. Here, we introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories themselves. The resulting gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as the trajectory length increases. We validated the gradient estimator against finite-difference calculations and used it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves the predictions of shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which is included in the optimization objective. Alignment at a single temperature also improves the apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing their temperature dependences closer to experiments. Moreover, the optimized potential exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent, higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating that alignment with experiments improves the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets. PathGrad thus establishes a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force field optimizations.
papers.summary: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure calculations they are trained on, and refining them against experimental dynamical measurements is hard because differentiating through chaotic molecular trajectories gives unstable gradients. `PathGrad` differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories, producing a gradient estimator accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives whose variance stays stable as trajectories lengthen. The authors use it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, **jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which was in the objective**, and reduces force errors against an independent higher-level quantum-chemical reference.

papers.title: What Does a Skill Vocabulary Cost? A Closed-Loop Decomposition over Demonstrated Motions
papers.abstract: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.
papers.summary: Robot policies that pick from a learned latent codebook of skills are hard to debug, since a closed-loop failure cannot be attributed to the vocabulary, the choice of skill, or its execution. Movement Prototype Quantization (`MPQ`) instead places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy: each predicted action chunk is replaced by its nearest library element and corrected toward the prediction within a bound, with no trained parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original, which makes it a reference baseline for attributing a skill selector's shortfall component by component. On `LIBERO-90`, **quantization costs nothing and skill choice at most 2 points, while the selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap of up to 12 points**; offline reconstruction error predicts none of these differences.

papers.title: Tabra Blends: Improving the Accuracy--Latency Trade-off with Complementary Tabular Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models make different trade-offs between prediction accuracy and latency. We study whether a compact ensemble can deliver higher accuracy in less time. Across 816 TabArena splits, our blend of four-estimator Kumo and one LimiX pipeline reaches 2063.8 Elo, 45.4 points above the top published entry in the same fit. Its normalized fit + predict time is 15% lower than Kumo-16's and 98% lower than full LimiX's. We find that greater prediction diversity between the two models helps explain the reduction in error.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models trade prediction accuracy against latency in different ways, and the authors test whether a compact ensemble can improve on both. Across 816 `TabArena` splits, a blend of a four-estimator `Kumo` model and one `LimiX` pipeline reaches **2063.8 Elo, 45.4 points above the top published entry**. Its normalized fit-plus-predict time is 15% lower than `Kumo-16`'s and 98% lower than full `LimiX`'s. Greater prediction diversity between the two models helps explain the error reduction.

papers.title: Fresh Keys, Stale Secrets: Numeric Leakage across Linked LLM Prompts
papers.abstract: Small businesses repeatedly ask cloud language models about the same confidential prices, unit costs and margins. Numeric prompt disguises for such numbers are evaluated one prompt at a time, but a provider sees a firm's history, in which each fresh secret gives a new, independent view of the same numbers. Since real costs are not public, we measure on synthetic firms with known values how much an honest-but-curious provider recovers when it knows the disguise algorithm, holds sector-level price and margin statistics, and links a firm's queries. In one prompt, per-field scaling, a fixed-axis instantiation of Zhang et al.'s order-preserving substitution and Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt's released sanitizer keep the attacker's margin-hit advantage over a prior-only guess between -0.6 and +4.4 percentage points. After 16 linked queries with fresh secrets, every disguise we test (Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon\geq 0.5$) has a target recovered significantly more often: under the order-preserving substitution, margin recovery rises from 25.0% to 59.4%. The same attacker recovers 29.4 percentage points more margins with fresh maps than with one reused map. Theory explains the contrast: one reused secret bounds all queries by a single full-precision view of the fields shown, whereas fresh scaling keys are identifiable. Except for Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon=0.5$, the gains persist when the attacker's prior comes from another population model and when values drift by up to 5% between queries; on our firms, whose prose cues are weak, reading the prose with a language model adds at most 2.5 points. Code and data: https://github.com/Jamli58/fresh-keys-stale-secrets
papers.summary: Schemes that disguise confidential numbers such as prices, costs, and margins before sending them to a cloud language model are evaluated one prompt at a time, yet a provider sees a firm's whole query history, where each fresh secret key gives another independent view of the same values. Using synthetic firms with known values, the authors measure what an honest-but-curious provider recovers when it knows the disguise algorithm, holds sector-level statistics, and links a firm's queries, testing per-field scaling, an order-preserving substitution, and the `Preempt` sanitizer. On a single prompt the attacker gains at most 4.4 percentage points over a prior-only guess, but after 16 linked queries every disguise tested leaks significantly more: under order-preserving substitution, **margin recovery rises from 25.0% to 59.4%**. Fresh maps let the attacker recover 29.4 points more margins than one reused map, which the authors explain theoretically: a reused secret bounds all queries by a single view, whereas fresh scaling keys are identifiable.

papers.title: Weight Scale Rebalancing: Transferable Training Recipes for Transformers
papers.abstract: Training Transformers requires careful hyperparameter tuning, which becomes increasingly costly for large models. We introduce UDV-Rebalance (UDVR), a reparameterization that inserts an auxiliary diagonal matrix $D$ between naturally paired weight matrices $(U,V)$ appearing throughout Transformer architectures. UDVR periodically rebalances the factors to maintain unit-norm columns in $U$ and unit-norm rows in $V$, with $D$ absorbing the corresponding scales. With rebalancing, a single hyperparameter setting of UDVR remains effective across model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This yields a tuning-free rule that adapts to each weight matrix using only its dimensions. We fit this rule once on ViT models trained on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and it remains valid when the activation function or the optimizer is changed. The same rule transfers to new image domains in DomainNet, to ViT, Swin, and MaxViT on ImageNet, and to language-model pretraining with up to 1.3B parameters. UDVR consistently outperforms Weight Normalization and $\sigma$Reparam and matches a vanilla baseline whose hyperparameters are swept on each target model.
papers.summary: Hyperparameter tuning for Transformers gets more expensive as models grow. UDV-Rebalance (`UDVR`) inserts an auxiliary diagonal matrix between naturally paired weight matrices and periodically rebalances the factors so one keeps unit-norm columns and the other unit-norm rows, with the diagonal absorbing the scales. This yields a tuning-free rule that sets hyperparameters for each weight matrix from its dimensions alone; it is fit once on `ViT` models trained on `CIFAR-10` and `CIFAR-100` and transfers to `DomainNet`, to `ViT`, `Swin`, and `MaxViT` on `ImageNet`, and to language-model pretraining up to 1.3B parameters. `UDVR` consistently outperforms `Weight Normalization` and `sigmaReparam` and **matches a vanilla baseline whose hyperparameters are swept separately on each target model**.

papers.title: MXFP4 for LLM Inference: Complementary Post-Training Quantization Techniques and Their Interactions
papers.abstract: Recent advances in low-precision representation have introduced several microscaling numerical formats for LLM quantization. By sharing a scale factor across groups of 16 or 32 elements, these formats enable aggressive low-precision quantization with minimal accuracy degradation, particularly when combined with modern PTQ algorithms. Their accuracy depends on how the numerical format interacts with rotation, PTQ, and scale selection. We study the composability of PTQ configurations across six LLMs and three microscaling formats: MXFP6, MXFP4, and NVFP4, systematically varying Hadamard rotation granularity, PTQ algorithm, and scale-selection strategy. Our central finding is that effective quantization recipes are format dependent: both MXFP4 and NVFP4 support accurate 4-bit inference, but techniques that benefit one do not necessarily transfer to the other. MXFP4 benefits substantially from rotation and error-correcting PTQ, whereas NVFP4 gains less from rotation, consistent with its finer-grained scales capturing more within-block variation. Building on these findings, we introduce Midmax, a calibration-free scale-selection strategy that mitigates clipping error in power-of-two block scales and improves accuracy across a majority of the evaluated MXFP4 configurations. We show that pairing MXFP6 activations with MXFP4 weights recovers most of the accuracy lost at 4-bit and, on Llama-3.1-8B, matches or exceeds our in-house BF16 baseline. An additional study finds that augmenting MXFP4 with a per-tensor macroscale, a mechanism intrinsic to NVFP4, does not improve average accuracy, suggesting that global rescaling alone does not address the limitations of E8M0 block scales for MXFP4 quantization. Together, these results provide practical guidance for combining numerical formats, rotation, PTQ, and scale selection for accurate low-precision LLM inference.
papers.summary: Microscaling number formats share one scale factor across blocks of 16 or 32 values, and their accuracy depends on how they interact with rotation, post-training quantization (PTQ) algorithms, and scale selection. A study across six LLMs and three formats (`MXFP6`, `MXFP4`, `NVFP4`) finds that **effective quantization recipes are format dependent**: `MXFP4` gains substantially from Hadamard rotation and error-correcting PTQ, while `NVFP4` gains less from rotation. The authors introduce `Midmax`, a calibration-free scale-selection strategy that reduces clipping error and improves most `MXFP4` configurations. Pairing `MXFP6` activations with `MXFP4` weights recovers most of the 4-bit accuracy loss and matches or exceeds a BF16 baseline on `Llama-3.1-8B`.

papers.title: Adaptive Electromagnetic Transient-level Digital Twins for Data Centers via In-Context Learning with LLMs
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) workloads has significantly increased data center (DC) power demand. Frequent operational and configurational changes, such as load surges caused by dynamic workload allocation, can induce electromagnetic transients (EMTs) whose accurate prediction is critical for reliable DC operation and maintenance. Although high-fidelity EMT solvers are widely adopted for transient analysis, their computational cost limits large-scale and multi-scenario studies. Digital twins address this computational bottleneck by emulating the behavior of a physical system and enabling fast prediction in place of expensive high-fidelity simulation. However,data-driven digital twins are non-adaptive and fail to generalize once the DC configuration changes. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an adaptive EMT-level digital twin for DCs based on in-context learning (ICL) with large language models (LLMs). We formulate the EMT prediction task as a system identification problem under parametric uncertainty and develop a GPT-2-based framework that adapts to unseen DC configurations at inference time from a small set of EMT trajectory samples, without model retraining. The proposed framework is validated on three representative EMT scenarios and benchmarked against three baseline non-adaptive twins. Results demonstrate superior prediction accuracy, improved adaptability to unseen operating conditions, and substantial computational speedups compared to high-fidelity EMT simulation.
papers.summary: Load surges in data centers can cause electromagnetic transients (EMTs) that are costly to simulate with high-fidelity solvers, and data-driven digital twins stop generalizing once the data center configuration changes. The authors frame EMT prediction as system identification under parametric uncertainty and build a `GPT-2`-based framework that uses in-context learning (ICL) to adapt at inference time. The model **adapts to unseen data center configurations from a small set of EMT trajectory samples without retraining**. On three EMT scenarios it reports better accuracy than three non-adaptive baseline twins and substantial speedups over high-fidelity simulation.

papers.title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
papers.abstract: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.
papers.summary: Agents on long tasks often commit to an answer before gathering enough evidence, even when their own stated belief still lists several candidates, and an end-of-episode outcome reward cannot teach when to commit. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (`RLVB`) uses the simulator's exact posterior over the answer to reward further steps while evidence is insufficient and committing once it suffices, with no judge or reward model. Across three vision-language models and three benchmarks, including the new `Pro Worlds` visual puzzle benchmark, `RLVB` **improves the base model in all nine settings by 17.1% on average**, while `GRPO` and `PPO` with outcome reward fall below the base model on average. It also beats `PPO` with an LLM-judge process reward by 9.3% on average using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours.
papers.highlight_summary:
Agents on long evidence-gathering tasks often commit to an answer while their own stated belief still names several candidates, and an end-of-episode outcome reward cannot fix this because a lucky guess is paid the same as a supported answer. `RLVB` (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs) uses the training simulator's privileged knowledge to compute the exact posterior over the hidden answer at every step, and rewards the agent for gathering more evidence while that posterior is open and for committing once it is settled.

- At each history the agent samples several turns, each scored by the log-probability of its action under a teacher that does lookahead on the exact posterior, and a group-relative policy gradient (or an EM variant) raises the higher-reward turns; no judge, critic or reward model is needed, and the reward never reads the belief line the agent writes, although the update trains it alongside the action.
- Across three vision-language models (`Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking`, `Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking`, `Qwen3.5-4B`) and three benchmarks (`HiddenGames`, plus the unseen `Pro-Worlds` and `RoboQuest`), `RLVB` improves the base model in **all nine settings** by **17.1 points on average** (**10.4** with EM), while `GRPO` and `PPO` trained on the outcome reward fall below the base model on average.
- Against `PPO` with a per-turn process reward from an LLM judge, `RLVB` wins in eight of nine settings by **9.3 points on average** while using **1.6× fewer GPU-hours** (74.2 against 120.1 on `Qwen3.5-4B`), and the EM variant uses about 4× fewer.
- The gain comes from when the agent answers, not how well it reads evidence: it answers with sufficient evidence in **51%, 12% and 74%** of episodes on the three benchmarks against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model, and commits at only **0.1–2.2%** of turns where evidence is insufficient and its belief line still names several answers, against 3–68% for the base model.
- The method requires a simulator that can enumerate the hidden state to give an exact posterior, the trained agent's belief line is not consistently more exact and its steps are no more informative than the base model's, adding an explicit reward on the belief line does not raise accuracy, and absolute accuracy stays far below the posterior teacher (about 29–32% against 100% on `Pro-Worlds`).

papers.title: Joint Detection of Constructive Speech, Hate Speech and Agreement in Online Conversations
papers.abstract: Online hate speech is an ever-growing issue with negative impacts on both groups and individuals, potentially causing users to withdraw from online conversations and debate. With some prominent social media platforms reducing their moderation efforts, constructive speech has emerged as an alternative strategy for countering hate. Automated detection of constructive and hateful speech can aid monitoring and improve understanding of their prevalence and online dynamics. In this work, we collect and annotate a large dataset of English and Danish social media comments for hateful tone, constructive tone, and agreement with parent comments. We fine-tune several multilingual LLMs to classify along these three dimensions and compare context-enriched and non-context-enriched model architectures. The E5-large LLM performs best on both the context-enriched (82% average F1) and non-context-enriched (81.6% average F1) classification tasks, demonstrating the potential of multilingual LLMs for scalable detection of hateful and constructive speech across languages.
papers.summary: Automated detection of both hateful and constructive speech could support monitoring of online conversations as some platforms reduce moderation. The authors collect and annotate a large dataset of English and Danish social media comments for hateful tone, constructive tone, and agreement with the parent comment, then fine-tune several multilingual models with and without conversational context. `E5-large` performs best, reaching **82% average F1 with context** and 81.6% without.

papers.title: Shared information governs multi-view planted matching
papers.abstract: We study when the rows of $K$ shuffled views of the same $n$ objects can be matched, where each object is observed once in every view through a Gaussian feature vector with known covariance. For every fixed $K$, all views can be matched up to $o(n)$ errors if the shared information $J$ of one object's $K$ observations exceeds $(1+\epsilon)\log n$, and not if it is below $(1-\epsilon)\log n$; this can hold although no two views can be matched on their own. Below the threshold, two views can still be matched if some set of views containing both has shared information above $\log n$; otherwise every estimator, even one that reads all views, has vanishing overlap between them. Matching every row is governed by the weakest bipartition of the views: with weak correlations the threshold is $2\log n$ for the mutual information across it. For a weak common signal observed through independent noise, the two thresholds are $4/K$ and $4/(K-1)$ in units of $\sum_\ell\rho_\ell^2/\log n$, which answers a question of Wee, Yang, Fan and Mao. Beyond weak correlations the bipartition condition is not sufficient: rare subpopulations impose a R\'enyi condition for every partition into at least three blocks. We conjecture that the two conditions together characterize exact recovery for Gaussian laws, and prove this for three views with equal correlations and in several further cases, in part with computer assistance. With equal correlations, layered screening attains $4/K$ for $K=3,4$ in $O(Kn^2d)$ operations, and for general laws a recursive decoder attains $J$. The almost-exact thresholds extend to known product laws and to objects observed in random subsets of the views.
papers.summary: The question is when the rows of K shuffled views of the same n objects, each observed through Gaussian feature vectors with known covariance, can be matched back together. For fixed K, **all views can be matched up to o(n) errors when the shared information of one object's K observations exceeds (1+epsilon) log n, and not when it is below (1-epsilon) log n**, which can hold even when no pair of views is matchable on its own. Exact matching of every row is governed by the weakest bipartition of the views, with a threshold of 2 log n on the mutual information across it under weak correlations, plus additional Rényi conditions from rare subpopulations beyond that regime. The authors conjecture that these two conditions characterize exact recovery, prove it in several cases partly with computer assistance, and give algorithms attaining the thresholds.

papers.title: Label leakage through file headers: geometry and batch confounds in public mammography datasets, and a pre-training acceptance gate
papers.abstract: A dataset whose diagnostic label can be recovered from non-diagnostic information yields high, reproducible and uninformative model performance. We applied pre-training controls that see only image geometry, global texture, a sub-collection identifier or one covariate to six public mammography datasets, against a stop threshold of AUC 0.60. In KAU-BCMD, geometry alone predicted the BI-RADS class at AUC 1.0000 in a local copy and at a mean of 0.979 in a public Kaggle archive; after resizing, texture alone gave 0.847. In CMMD, the sub-collection prefix predicted malignancy at 0.7753; the restricted sub-collection passed geometry (0.5000) and texture (0.5810) but failed an identifier-order control added post hoc (test AUC 0.9926). CBIS-DDSM exceeded the stop on geometry (pooled mean 0.654 over 20 splits), a verdict statistic chosen post hoc; its official mass and calcification splits did not. M-SYNTH, INbreast and a partial VinDr-Mammo copy passed the few controls run. We release the code and derived tables. There is no quantum component in the inference path.
papers.summary: A dataset whose diagnostic label can be predicted from non-diagnostic information produces high but uninformative model performance. The authors run pre-training controls that see only image geometry, global texture, a sub-collection identifier, or a single covariate on six public mammography datasets, with a stop threshold of AUC 0.60. In `KAU-BCMD`, **image geometry alone predicted the BI-RADS class at AUC 1.0000** in a local copy, and in `CMMD` the sub-collection prefix predicted malignancy at 0.7753 while an identifier-order control reached 0.9926. `CBIS-DDSM` exceeded the threshold on geometry in pooled splits, whereas `M-SYNTH`, `INbreast`, and a partial `VinDr-Mammo` copy passed the controls that were run.

papers.title: Motion Conditioned World Modeling for Embodied Visual Tracking
papers.abstract: World models support embodied decision-making by predicting future environment states. In embodied visual tracking, uncertain target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes jointly affect visual observations, making future-state prediction challenging. We propose Motion-Conditioned World Modeling, which incorporates predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion into latent state transitions. A Geometry--Progress module jointly models geometric paths and single-step travel distances through shared motion modes and path-conditioned progress distributions. This formulation captures uncertainty in route selection and motion progress while preserving their dependence. Action-induced coordinate transformations express predicted paths in the next robot frame, providing geometrically grounded conditions for future visual-state prediction. Future visual feature reconstruction supervises the motion predictor through the conditioned transition branch, linking explicit motion representations to subsequent observations. The model is jointly optimized with motion likelihood, feature reconstruction, and expert-action supervision, enabling the tracking policy to combine visual context with predictive motion cues.Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks demonstrate improved tracking performance and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight $0.5$B backbone.
papers.summary: In embodied visual tracking, uncertain target motion and the robot's own viewpoint changes both alter what the robot sees, which makes predicting future states difficult. `Motion-Conditioned World Modeling` feeds predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion into latent state transitions, using a Geometry-Progress module that jointly models geometric paths and single-step travel distances. Predicted paths are transformed into the next robot frame to condition future visual feature prediction, and the model is trained jointly on motion likelihood, feature reconstruction, and expert-action supervision. Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks show **improved tracking and cross-environment generalization with a 0.5B backbone**.

papers.title: SOARS: System One Assisted Reranking for Agentic Search
papers.abstract: Deep search agents address complex information needs through iterative retrieval and reasoning, where the relevance of retrieved evidence influences downstream performance. Existing rerankers improve retrieval effectiveness but introduce substantial latency and cost when invoked throughout the search trajectory. We introduce SOARS, a training-free framework leveraging a System One model for fast, calibrated relevance estimation. At each search step, SOARS selects query-relevant passages from long documents and reranks candidates in a single call, jointly considering the original question and agent-generated sub-query. Across six LLM backbones on BrowseComp-Plus and WebShaper, SOARS consistently improves answer accuracy and evidence recall while reducing search calls, end-to-end latency, and inference cost. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves GPT-5.4 Mini's accuracy from 73.9% to 84.7% while reducing search calls from 23 to 14, demonstrating the potential of System One reranking for more effective and efficient deep search.
papers.summary: Deep search agents depend on the relevance of retrieved evidence, but invoking rerankers throughout a search trajectory adds latency and cost. `SOARS` is a training-free framework that uses a fast System One model to select query-relevant passages from long documents and rerank candidates in a single call, considering both the original question and the agent's sub-query. Across six LLM backbones on `BrowseComp-Plus` and `WebShaper`, it improves answer accuracy and evidence recall while reducing search calls, latency, and inference cost. On `BrowseComp-Plus` it **raises `GPT-5.4 Mini` accuracy from 73.9% to 84.7% while cutting search calls from 23 to 14**.

papers.title: InstructReplay: Replaying Assistant Turns to Preserve General Behavior During Factual Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning an instruction-tuned language model on new facts often erodes its general abilities. We find that standard fine-tuning lowers instruction-following, reasoning and coding benchmarks by 35 points on average, and that these losses track a collapse in answer length: fine-tuned models at least halve their responses, and the further a response drifts from the initial model's length, the more often it fails. We propose InstructReplay: the initial model answers a set of general instructions once, and during fine-tuning the model is kept close to the initial model on these answers. Across three model families and two domains, InstructReplay reduces the average decline on five general benchmarks from 28.1 to 2.4 points and keeps answer length close to the initial model's, while learning the new facts as well as standard fine-tuning. It balances learning and retention better than seven adaptation methods in all six settings. Controlled comparisons attribute the gain to replaying the model's own answers to general instructions rather than to the form of the loss.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning an instruction-tuned language model on new facts lowers instruction-following, reasoning, and coding benchmarks by 35 points on average, and the losses track a collapse in answer length. `InstructReplay` has the initial model answer a set of general instructions once and then keeps the fine-tuned model close to those answers during training. Across three model families and two domains, it **reduces the average decline on five general benchmarks from 28.1 to 2.4 points** while learning the new facts as well as standard fine-tuning. Controlled comparisons attribute the gain to replaying the model's own answers rather than to the form of the loss.

papers.title: Theory-Informed Quantum Error Mitigation for Shor Order Finding with Fourier Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Quantum noise distorts the distribution of circuit measurement outcomes, often leaving enough information to infer the algorithm's correct result. To recover this latent information from the noisy distribution in Shor order finding, we introduce a theory-informed quantum error mitigation method. We model how circuit errors shift, broaden, or weaken peaks in the output distribution. These models guide both the generation of synthetic training data and the design of a Fourier neural operator with a learned gain that attenuates or amplifies higher retained Fourier modes. We score each candidate order by averaging the correlations between its ideal distribution and the distributions measured in three circuit executions. The network adjusts these scores to guide the order estimate and determine the weights of a normalized mixture of the ideal distributions. On 1,351 simulated test cases for general modular exponentiation, held out by circuit configuration, exact order recovery rises from 19% to 34%, and the median Jensen-Shannon divergence from the ideal distribution falls by 50%, from 0.64 to 0.32. On 101 Mersenne rotation circuits executed across five IBM quantum processors, a separate model trained and calibrated in simulation increases the number of correct order estimates from 35 to 53. Algorithmic structure can remain recoverable even when noise makes it barely visible.
papers.summary: Quantum noise distorts the measurement distribution of Shor order-finding circuits, but often leaves enough information to infer the correct result. The authors model how circuit errors shift, broaden, or weaken output peaks, and use these models to generate synthetic training data and to design a Fourier neural operator that adjusts correlation-based scores for each candidate order. On 1,351 held-out simulated cases, **exact order recovery rises from 19% to 34%** and median Jensen-Shannon divergence from the ideal distribution falls from 0.64 to 0.32. On 101 Mersenne rotation circuits run on five IBM quantum processors, a model trained in simulation raises correct order estimates from 35 to 53.

papers.title: Reading Decisions Before Spans: Efficient Generative Verification
papers.abstract: A developer checking an assistant's report may need only an alarm that a claim is unsupported. A generative verifier, however, can continue decoding to quote and classify the errors. We study how much of that output is needed to recover its decision. In a frozen 2B span verifier, the choice between an empty error list and its first object precedes all localization. Native8 stops generation at this branch. The preceding seven syntax tokens are fixed, so Prefill1 supplies them as input and generates only the unrestricted branch token, using the same native instruction. On 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 reduces eager resident service by 84.84% relative to full generation, with released-reference F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41. It saves 31.98% over Native8 even though their logical token totals are identical. Under default compiled execution, the extra saving is 6.74-26.73% on the complete workload, with small decision changes. Controlled evidence interventions and first-location decoding establish what these shorter readouts retain and what requires further generation.
papers.summary: A generative verifier that checks whether an assistant's claims are supported can keep decoding to quote and classify errors, but a developer may need only the alarm. In a frozen 2B span verifier, the choice between an empty error list and a first error object comes before any localization, so `Native8` stops generation at that branch and `Prefill1` supplies the seven fixed syntax tokens as input and generates only the branch token. On 2,015 code-agent test responses, `Prefill1` **cuts eager resident service by 84.84% relative to full generation with F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41**, and saves 31.98% over `Native8` despite identical logical token totals. Further experiments establish what the shortened readouts retain and what needs more generation.

papers.title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation
papers.abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.
papers.summary: Long-video understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) requires finding relevant evidence while processing few tokens, and existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods do not account for how much each additional token is worth. `Lembas` treats video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget, modeling diminishing returns within an item and across similar evidence, and solves it with an iterative water-filling algorithm with a convergence guarantee. In multi-turn conversations it reuses tokens from earlier turns and refines relevance using the VLM's attention. It **improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over baselines at comparable compute**, and in multi-turn settings gains up to 1.5 points with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.

papers.title: One Style Fits All? Cultural Values Embedded in Conversational AI via a People-Pleasing Lens
papers.abstract: Conversational AI systems trained on large-scale web corpora inevitably encode the cultural values and interactional norms embedded in their training data, yet our understanding of how deployed LLMs reflect or reinforce culture-specific social expectations remains limited. This study examined how supportive versus challenging chatbot interaction styles shape user experience and continuance intention, and whether people-pleasing tendency (PPT) moderates these effects across cultures. Taiwanese (N = 49) and Korean (N = 52) participants completed a collaborative tourism-planning task. Results showed that: (1) supportive chatbots consistently led to higher continuance intention, satisfaction, and trust; (2) PPT did not moderate these effects; and (3) cultural variation emerged only in perceived threat, where higher PPT was associated with greater baseline threat in the Taiwanese but not the Korean sample. These findings reveal how a general-purpose LLM style may differentially activate culturally situated social scripts, raising implications for culturally inclusive conversational AI design.
papers.summary: A user study examines how supportive versus challenging chatbot interaction styles affect user experience and intention to keep using the system, and whether people-pleasing tendency (PPT) moderates these effects across cultures. Taiwanese (N = 49) and Korean (N = 52) participants completed a collaborative tourism-planning task with a chatbot. **Supportive chatbots consistently produced higher continuance intention, satisfaction, and trust**, and PPT did not moderate these effects. Cultural variation appeared only in perceived threat, where higher PPT was associated with greater baseline threat in the Taiwanese sample but not the Korean one.

papers.title: Do Vision-Language Models Know Their Own Visual Weaknesses? Probing Capability-Level Metacognition
papers.abstract: Metacognition includes knowing one's own strengths and weaknesses across kinds of tasks, not only judging whether a single answer is correct. We test whether vision-language models (VLMs) know in advance which kinds of visual tasks and image conditions are hard for them, across a wide range of open and proprietary models. Because some tasks are hard for every model, we separate what a model knows about this shared difficulty from what it knows about itself. We find that VLMs know little in advance about their visual weaknesses. They misjudge their overall accuracy and do not even know which kinds of tasks are hard for every model, and most misjudge how degraded images affect them. We further train VLMs to predict their own accuracy, which teaches them their own level of accuracy on kinds unseen in training but not which kinds are hard for them. However, information about these weaknesses appears once a model starts solving. On a few unlabeled questions of a kind, the probability a model assigns to its own answers follows weaknesses particular to the model, across kinds of tasks and image conditions. VLMs thus hold information about their own weaknesses that their stated predictions do not yet reflect. By separating what is particular to a model from what holds for every model, our evaluation offers a test for methods that aim to teach VLMs their own weaknesses, and the answer probability offers them a signal to start from.
papers.summary: The study tests whether vision-language models (VLMs) know in advance which kinds of visual tasks and image conditions are hard for them, separating knowledge of difficulty shared by all models from knowledge specific to one model. Across open and proprietary models, **VLMs know little in advance about their visual weaknesses**: they misjudge their overall accuracy, do not know which task kinds are hard for every model, and mostly misjudge the effect of degraded images. Training models to predict their own accuracy teaches their overall accuracy level on unseen kinds but not which kinds are hard for them. Once a model starts solving, however, the probability it assigns to its own answers on a few unlabeled questions tracks its model-specific weaknesses.

papers.title: Quantum kernels on breast data: concentration, surrogates, and two ways an advantage gets manufactured
papers.abstract: Quantum-kernel advantage claims on breast data are usually a single number: one quantum arm, one comparator, one test split. We asked what that number measures once the full comparator set and selection history are visible. We report three active benchmarks, all exact classical statevector simulations of 8-qubit fidelity kernels with no quantum component in the inference path: a sample-efficiency sweep on Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer at ten training-set sizes; raw-versus-processed arms on 1,200 M-SYNTH simulated mammograms with a matched closed-form dequantisation surrogate, five classical methods at the same input and eleven kernel families; and a 30-seed selection-inflation measurement on BreastMNIST. A CMMD D1 clinical arm is withdrawn as a result arm because its frozen splits leak the label through patient serial order, a defect reported in a separate study; it is retained only as a worked example. All three active arms are negative. On M-SYNTH raw an apparent +0.1736 (p = 5.2e-06) against a tuned RBF-SVM falls to +0.0019 (p = 0.937) against a random forest at the same input, and a Laplacian kernel wins on validation. On WDBC, with model selection confined to training data, the quantum kernel is below the selected classical arm at every training-set size, with 2 of 200 paired subsamples ahead. Best-of-30 seed selection adds +0.0210 on BreastMNIST. One result does not fit: at bandwidth 2pi the matched closed-form Gaussian surrogate failed to reproduce the M-SYNTH raw kernel (0.5410 against 0.7045, p = 6.3e-06). Comparator choice and selection each produce effects larger than any quantum-classical difference we measured; we give a reporting standard that removes both.
papers.summary: Claims of quantum-kernel advantage on breast data usually rest on one quantum arm, one comparator, and one test split. The authors run three benchmarks using exact classical simulations of 8-qubit fidelity kernels on `Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer`, `M-SYNTH`, and `BreastMNIST`, with full comparator sets and selection history exposed, and **all three come out negative for the quantum kernel**. On `M-SYNTH`, an apparent +0.1736 gain over a tuned RBF-SVM shrinks to +0.0019 against a random forest on the same input, and best-of-30 seed selection alone adds +0.0210 on `BreastMNIST`. Comparator choice and selection each produce effects larger than any quantum-classical difference measured, and the authors propose a reporting standard that removes both.

papers.title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation
papers.abstract: Clustering is a foundational tool for exploratory data analysis across the sciences. We argue that clustering methods should be evaluated along four dimensions: fidelity to the data's underlying structure, interpretability of the recovered groups, stability under data perturbations and algorithmic randomness, and scalability to modern scientific datasets. Yet existing methods rarely satisfy all four criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PHM-ensemble, a general probabilistic framework for multiresolution clustering that estimates the underlying data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits and subsequently constructs a clustering hierarchy through hierarchical merging of the mixture components. On simulated datasets and the MNIST benchmark, PHM-ensemble matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms in agreement with ground truth, produces more stable results across runs, and reveals complex underlying structures. Applied to 1.82 million peripheral blood cells from the Human Immune Health Atlas, PHM-ensemble achieves higher agreement with expert-curated major cell-type annotations than the Leiden clustering used in the original study (adjusted Rand index 0.965 versus 0.789), while requiring only half the computing time. Beyond identifying major immune lineages, it reveals biologically coherent relationships among cell types and resolves finer structure within individual lineages, uncovering subtypes and cellular states consistent with known biology.
papers.summary: Clustering methods rarely combine fidelity to underlying structure, interpretability, stability, and scalability. `PHM-ensemble` is a probabilistic multiresolution clustering framework that estimates the data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits, then builds a hierarchy by merging mixture components. On simulated data and `MNIST` it matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms and gives more stable results across runs. On 1.82 million blood cells from the `Human Immune Health Atlas`, it reaches **an adjusted Rand index of 0.965 versus 0.789 for Leiden clustering in half the computing time**.

papers.title: ShellBench: What Matters More for AI Agents, Models, or Harness for Everyday Tasks
papers.abstract: The use of AI agents among the general public has been increasing exponentially throughout 2026, though it is often hard for users to determine which configuration is most effective for their personal use. To help provide clarity here we introduce ShellBench, 100 day-to-day tasks based on more than 10 million user requests, each set in a realistic workspace with messy files and competing data sources, and graded for both correctness and safety. We evaluate 12 models across 5 agent harnesses at 3 reasoning levels for a total of 53,100 rollouts, 20% of which are on tasks designated for public release. We find that model choice impacts performance more than harness choice, but the three leading models differ by only 1.1 percentage points. GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% of attempts at about one-sixth of GPT-6 Astra's estimated token cost per attempt, while GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%. We also found that harness choice had little effect on either performance or safety with all harnesses scoring between 42.9 (Claude Code) and 45.2 (OpenClaw) for pass@1.
papers.summary: `ShellBench` is a benchmark of 100 everyday tasks derived from more than 10 million user requests, each set in a realistic workspace with messy files and competing data sources and graded for correctness and safety. The authors evaluate 12 models across 5 agent harnesses at 3 reasoning levels, totalling 53,100 rollouts. **Model choice affects performance more than harness choice**, though the three leading models differ by only 1.1 percentage points: `GPT-6 Astra` leads at 62.5% and `GPT-6.1 Sol` passes 61.4% at about one-sixth of the estimated token cost per attempt. Harnesses all score between 42.9 (`Claude Code`) and 45.2 (`OpenClaw`) on pass@1, with little effect on safety.

papers.title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch's treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.
papers.summary: `V-learning` estimates optimal treatment policies from offline trajectories, but mobile health policies are updated online in batches, which makes the data adaptively collected and patient trajectories dependent. The authors develop statistical theory for batch-updated `V-learning` with varying deterministic batch sizes, establishing consistency of the estimated value function and policy, a functional central limit theorem, asymptotic normality of the learned policy's value, and a consistent variance estimator. **To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch**. Simulations show near-nominal confidence interval coverage under adaptive assignment and steady policy improvement for small cohorts followed over many batches.

papers.title: Beyond Expected Value: PPO with Distributional Critics for Systematic Conservation Planning
papers.abstract: Systematic conservation planning must allocate limited protection budgets sequentially under ecological and climatic uncertainty. Static tools cannot adapt as conditions change, and policies optimised only for expected outcomes can fail on the worst-case trajectories climate change makes increasingly likely. CAPTAIN was the first framework to cast this as sequential reinforcement learning, but its gradient-free Evolution Strategies (ES) optimiser lacks per-timestep credit assignment. We replace ES with Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) via a Plackett-Luce solution to CAPTAIN's non-differentiable action space, and replace its scalar critic with an Implicit Quantile Network (IQN) modelling the full return distribution. A matched-granularity comparison shows decision granularity, not the optimiser, drives most of the ecological gain, so the real contribution is training efficiency and extensibility to risk-sensitive objectives. On a New Zealand marine dataset, it matches or exceeds ES's outcomes at a fraction of the training cost, offering a template for future work ES's black-box design could not support
papers.summary: Conservation planning must allocate limited protection budgets sequentially under ecological and climate uncertainty, and the `CAPTAIN` framework addresses this with gradient-free Evolution Strategies (ES) that lack per-timestep credit assignment. The authors replace ES with Proximal Policy Optimisation (`PPO`), using a Plackett-Luce formulation for the non-differentiable action space, and swap the scalar critic for an Implicit Quantile Network (`IQN`) that models the full return distribution. A matched-granularity comparison shows that decision granularity, not the optimiser, drives most of the ecological gain, so the contribution is training efficiency and support for risk-sensitive objectives. On a New Zealand marine dataset the method **matches or exceeds ES outcomes at a fraction of the training cost**.

papers.title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels: external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests, and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85-0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path, leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged, and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4x larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache's LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x raw's goodput and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7x via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw's queue and goodput at 8. On an AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24x and 1.59x. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3's numerical accuracy.
papers.summary: LLM serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so that multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes, but capacity limits both prefix reuse and concurrent long requests, and lossy compression changes outputs. `LoomKV` applies lossless KV compression to both the external tiers and the GPU pool on an unmodified engine, using a calibrated per-head 3-bit code over the high bytes of BF16 values to **store BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models**. Built on `LMCache` and `vLLM`, its tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x the goodput of raw storage and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT) on `AgentX` near the eviction cliff, and its pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens. Where raw capacity already suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput.

papers.title: "I Do Intend to Deliver": Will LLMs Run a Marketplace Advance-Fee Scam?
papers.abstract: Online fraud is traditionally limited by the cost of the human labor needed to talk to potential victims. We ask whether hosted large language models will now supply that labor. We prompted ten off-the-shelf models to play the seller in the "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam common on buy-and-sell sites, using a plain system prompt with no jailbreak. Each model played 30 conversations against each of four buyer personas, from credulous to guarded, with the same model playing the buyer (1,200 conversations). We label each conversation by what happened to the buyer's money, and validate the labels against two human coders. 737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance. Eight of the ten models played in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Only the guarded buyer, who wanted a findable identity, resisted, and the most willing sellers got past it by inventing names and phone numbers. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, usually reasoning about their own honesty rather than the buyer's risk. Several models protected the buyer without refusing, by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety. We release the benchmark, prompts, code and labels.
papers.summary: Online fraud has been limited by the human labor needed to talk to victims, so the authors test whether hosted large language models (LLMs) will supply that labor. Ten off-the-shelf models were asked, with a plain system prompt and no jailbreak, to play the seller in a "free item, just pay delivery" advance-fee scam across 1,200 conversations against four buyer personas ranging from credulous to guarded. **737 conversations (61%) ended with the buyer paying in advance**, eight of the ten models played along in almost every conversation, and running both sides cost about 2.5 cents per payment. Sellers that recognized the scam still took the money in 133 conversations, while several models protected the buyer without refusing by conceding payment on delivery, so refusal rates alone misstate safety.

papers.title: Attestation is All You Need: Toward a Zero-Trust Architecture for HPC AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents are beginning to automate data analysis, orchestration, and simulation steering in HPC environments, but they introduce a security problem that existing cluster defenses do not address: the hijacked authorized agent. An adversary can subvert an agent through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. We propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense for this setting. Our system, AEGIS, compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, monitors agent actions with ebpf-based syscall interception, verifies evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers slurm-level containment. On the real attestation path, AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency at a 1-second interval and low measured verifier overhead. Controlled experiments show full attack-suite coverage, stronger detection than representative baselines, and no observed false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.
papers.summary: AI agents automating analysis and orchestration on high-performance computing clusters can be hijacked through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. `AEGIS` defends against this with behavioral attestation: it compiles constraints derived from the task, monitors agent actions through `eBPF`-based syscall interception, verifies the evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers containment at the `Slurm` level. On the real attestation path it **detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency** at a 1-second interval, with low verifier overhead and no observed false positives on the benign workflows evaluated.

papers.title: Polynomial-Time Learning of Random Automata from One Label per Word
papers.abstract:
We study a binary deterministic finite automaton whose $2n$ transitions are chosen independently and uniformly from its $n$ states. The learner observes independent uniform words of length $m$, each labeled with a single bit indicating acceptance. For every fixed $\beta>0$ we give a polynomial-time algorithm that works outside a set of transition tables of probability $o(n^{-\beta})$. On each remaining table, for any start state and accepting set, the predictor has error at most $\epsilon$ on fresh uniform words of length $m$ with probability at least $1-\gamma$ over the training sample and the learner's random choices. Its sample size and running time are polynomial in $n$, $m$, $1/\epsilon$ and $\log(2/\gamma)$, with degree depending only on $\beta$. Although each word reveals only one output, comparing label moments at two consecutive history lengths lets us estimate the expected product of the signed outputs of two continuations from the same hidden state.
  We also refute Conjecture 4 of Fish and Reyzin on meeting times. For two distinct states fixed before the table is drawn and every fixed $c>0$, the fraction of words of length $\lfloor cn\rfloor$ that send them to different states converges in probability to $e^{-c}$. On a typical table, driving this fraction down to $1/n$ takes asymptotically $n\log n$ letters. Selected proof steps are formalized in Lean.
papers.summary: The setting is a binary deterministic finite automaton with n states whose transitions are chosen uniformly at random, where the learner sees uniform random words of length m, each labeled only with a single accept/reject bit. The authors give **a polynomial-time algorithm that learns all but a vanishing fraction of such transition tables** to error epsilon, for any start state and accepting set, by comparing label moments at two consecutive history lengths to estimate correlations between continuations from the same hidden state. They also refute Conjecture 4 of Fish and Reyzin on meeting times, showing that the fraction of words of length cn sending two fixed states to different states converges to e^-c. Selected proof steps are formalized in `Lean`.

papers.title: Benchmarking Evidence Sufficiency in Vision-Language Models for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Reliable driving VLMs must do more than answer correctly or localize relevant scene actors: they must determine whether the available visual evidence is sufficient to support an answer. Existing evaluations largely treat grounding and answerability as separate measurements, making it difficult to distinguish well-supported predictions from those localized to relevant but insufficient evidence. We introduce DriveAnswer, a benchmark of 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families, that operationalizes this distinction using matched strong- and weak-evidence configurations. Each pair preserves the underlying scene fact and semantic answer while changing whether the observations support answering, making abstention the appropriate response under weak evidence. On the six-family evaluation, the strongest zero-shot baseline reaches 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy, yet only 21.55% of matched questions satisfy both answer-abstain behavior and complete grounding. With controlled adaptation, Gemma-4-12B reaches 63.29% on this joint capability, nearly tripling its zero-shot performance. Qwen3-VL-8B exhibits the same broad improvement in evidence-sensitive answering and grounding. These results show that semantic correctness, evidence sufficiency, and grounding are distinct capabilities that should be evaluated jointly.
papers.summary: Driving vision-language models are usually scored separately on answering and on grounding, which hides cases where a model localizes relevant actors but the visual evidence is insufficient to support an answer. `DriveAnswer` is a benchmark of 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families built from matched strong- and weak-evidence pairs that keep the scene fact fixed, so that abstaining is correct under weak evidence. The strongest zero-shot baseline reaches 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy, yet **only 21.55% of matched questions satisfy both correct answer-or-abstain behavior and complete grounding**. Controlled adaptation lifts `Gemma-4-12B` to 63.29% on this joint measure, with `Qwen3-VL-8B` improving similarly.

papers.title: Eliciting the Recall Capacity of Linear Attention
papers.abstract: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.
papers.summary: Linear attention models lag softmax attention on associative recall, the ability to retrieve information seen earlier in context. Synthetic recall tasks show that recall capacity scales with state size similarly across the linear-attention architectures tested, and that **even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances**, yet standard language model training does not reliably teach these models to copy from context. Adding in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting during training narrows the long-distance recall gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling.

papers.title: File Size as a Potential Dataset Bias in Audio-Visual Deepfake Data
papers.abstract: Deepfake detection benchmarks are commonly designed to evaluate whether models can distinguish authentic from manipulated audiovisual content. However, benchmark construction pipelines may introduce unintended associations between class labels and simple file-level properties. In this work, we identify a potential file-size bias in two widely used audio-visual deepfake datasets. In the 1M-Deepfakes Detection Challenge dataset, a score derived from file size alone achieves 70.13% AUC on the validation set. When file size is considered together with video duration, simple file-level methods exceed 90% AUC on 1M and 85% AUC on FakeAVCeleb. Although the same pattern is not observed in DFDC, the results suggest that the observed association is dataset-dependent rather than an inherent property of deepfake videos. We discuss several possible explanations, including differences in encoding, compression, source data, manipulation procedures, and post-processing, although the present analysis does not establish the underlying cause. We further discuss whether the factors associated with file size may also leave traces in decoded video or audio, and consequently whether they could influence content-based deepfake detection, as an important direction for future work. Our findings highlight the importance of examining simple file-level properties when constructing and evaluating deepfake datasets and benchmarks.
papers.summary: Deepfake detection benchmarks can leak the label through simple file-level properties that have nothing to do with the content. In the `1M-Deepfakes Detection Challenge` dataset, a score derived from file size alone reaches 70.13% AUC on the validation set, and **combining file size with video duration exceeds 90% AUC on `1M-Deepfakes` and 85% on `FakeAVCeleb`**. The pattern does not appear in `DFDC`, indicating that it stems from how specific datasets were built rather than from deepfakes themselves, and the analysis does not establish the underlying cause.

papers.title: When Repair Accuracy Misleads: Training a VLM on Its Own Failures
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a vision-language model on its own failures is a direct way to repair it, but accuracy on held-out failures, the obvious measure of success, misleads. Many mined failures are not model errors: a human audit of 100 failures of Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on questions generated from COCO and GQA found label errors in 37. And mined failures share wording regularities: question-only classifiers get both answers right on 73.2% of held-out failure pairs. We study both traps with verified failure-driven repair (VFR): typed minimal-pair failure mining, verification by three LLM judges that answer without seeing the stored labels, answer-first corrective targets, and LoRA fine-tuning with replay. VFR repairs 82.8% of held-out failures (base model: 10.0%), and on independently labeled, unconditioned pairs it raises overall accuracy from 87.4% to 92.4% through spatial relations, whose accuracy rises from 66.7% to 96.8% even where the wording points to the wrong answer. Yet on negation, of which it repairs 88.9% of held-out failures, its accuracy on unconditioned pairs falls from 88.7% to 79.7%: it breaks negations about absent objects, rare in its training set. Without verification, accuracy on unconditioned pairs falls to 80.8%, below the base model's 87.4%, through a negation shortcut our development benchmarks miss; without failure selection, it stays at 92.0% (one seed) while repair falls to 73.4%. Training also lowers two-image relation accuracy (74.3% to 49.6%; replay data alone: 48.4%); multi-image replay partly and unevenly reverses this. Paraphrasing the spatial questions keeps most of the gain (87.3% vs. the base model's 62.0%), though rewording lowers spatial repair on held-out failures from 92.9% to 76.8%. On What'sUp's independent photos of objects under others, caption choice stays perfect while accuracy on our yes/no pairs falls from 84.5% to 26.4%.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a vision-language model on its own mined failures looks like a direct repair, but accuracy on held-out failures misleads: a human audit of 100 failures of `Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct` found label errors in 37, and question-only classifiers answer 73.2% of held-out failure pairs correctly from wording alone. The authors study verified failure-driven repair (`VFR`), which mines typed minimal-pair failures, verifies them with three LLM judges that do not see the stored labels, and fine-tunes with `LoRA` plus replay. `VFR` repairs 82.8% of held-out failures and raises accuracy on independently labeled pairs from 87.4% to 92.4%, driven by spatial relations, but **negation accuracy on those independent pairs falls from 88.7% to 79.7% even though 88.9% of held-out negation failures are repaired**. Skipping verification drops independent-pair accuracy to 80.8%, below the base model, and training also lowers two-image relation accuracy.

papers.title: CAPER: PartGround and PlanRefine for Reliable Manual-Guided Robotic Assembly Planning
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) used in robot task planning to derive assembly procedures from existing manuals may correctly interpret individual assembly actions yet confuse exact part identities, predict unsupported Part IDs, or produce inconsistent parts across assembly steps. Thus, we propose CAPER (Capacity-Aware Part-grounding and Evidence Refinement), a manual-guided robotic assembly framework that enables VLMs to generate assembly procedures with two modules--PartGround and PlanRefine. PartGround aligns step-level manual evidence with product-specific inventory and part-reference information to identify exact Part IDs and quantities, transforming free-form hardware prediction into evidence-guided assignments represented in a shared Assembly Intermediate Representation (Assembly IR). PlanRefine audits PartGround assignments against finite inventory by removing the lowest-confidence assignments. Uncertain identity cases remain marked for review in the Assembly IR. We evaluate CAPER on the IKEA Assembly in the Wild (IAW) dataset. Experiment results show that CAPER reaches a Finite-inventory Consistency Rate of 83.33% and produces zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences. At the plan level, PlanRefine removes all observed inventory-overuse pairs (9 -> 0) and excess units (51 -> 0). Overall, the results indicate that PartGround and PlanRefine improve part reliability, while also enhancing finite-inventory consistency and local prediction accuracy. Project page and video: https://xhzzzz123.github.io/CAPER/
papers.summary: Vision-language models that derive robot assembly procedures from instruction manuals often understand each action but confuse exact part identities, predict parts that are not in the kit, or use parts inconsistently across steps. `CAPER` (Capacity-Aware Part-grounding and Evidence Refinement) adds two modules: `PartGround` aligns step-level manual evidence with the product's inventory to assign exact part IDs and quantities in a shared intermediate representation, and `PlanRefine` audits those assignments against the finite inventory, removing the lowest-confidence ones and flagging uncertain cases for review. On the `IKEA Assembly in the Wild` dataset it reaches a finite-inventory consistency rate of 83.33% with no out-of-inventory part IDs, and **`PlanRefine` removes all observed inventory-overuse pairs (9 to 0) and excess units (51 to 0)**.

papers.title: AVQ-Attention-2: Adaptive Vector-Quantized Attention with Exact Local Blocks and Linear-Cost Training
papers.abstract: Attention costs $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ in the number of tokens. Vector-quantized attention reduces this to $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ by clustering the $N$ keys, attending to the $M$ codewords instead, and its adaptive form, AVQ-attention, concentrates codebook resolution where a query's attention mass actually falls. We present AVQ-Attention-2, a better design that merges it with exact local attention and attends to the mean of each cluster's keys rather than to a codeword. We show three improvements: consistently better quality at comparable cost; training that now also costs $\mathcal{O}(NM)$ rather than $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$; and an approximation accurate enough that the layer can be dropped into a pretrained transformer without fine-tuning. Across a variety of sequence lengths the result is competitive not merely with other approximate attention but with exact dense attention, running faster than FlashAttention at little to no loss in quality.
