papers.summary: Vector-quantized attention cuts the quadratic cost of attention to O(NM) by clustering the N keys and attending to M codewords instead. `AVQ-Attention-2` revises the adaptive variant by combining it with exact local attention and attending to the mean of each cluster's keys rather than to a codeword, which also brings training cost down to O(NM). The approximation is accurate enough that the layer can be dropped into a pretrained transformer without fine-tuning, and across a range of sequence lengths it is reported as **running faster than `FlashAttention` at little to no loss in quality** relative to exact dense attention.

papers.title: On Potentiality and Actuality Of Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Foundation models are built through large-scale pretraining, often followed by post-training, and are then adapted to specific tasks and behaviors. But, does the adaptation add truly new capabilities, or the base model already holds it? We decompose the update induced by different adaptations into a component shared across all inputs and a residual that varies with the input. We find that the shared component suffices for most of the adaptation gain and can be learned directly: a shift adapter that learns a constant vector per layer, identical for every input, reproduces the behavior of LoRA and full fine-tuning. We call this the potentiality principle of foundation models: the base model already contains the capacity needed for task-specific expertise. To adapt to a new task, the model just needs to be actualized, i.e., pushed in a certain direction via a constant, input-independent shift. We show the implications of this principle on parameter-efficient adaptation, steering, and convergence across models, and how it explains the neural thickets phenomenon.
papers.summary: The question is whether adapting a foundation model adds new capabilities or surfaces ones the base model already holds. The authors decompose the update induced by an adaptation into a component shared across all inputs and an input-dependent residual, and find that the shared part accounts for most of the gain. **A shift adapter that learns one constant vector per layer, identical for every input, reproduces the behavior of `LoRA` and full fine-tuning**, which they call the potentiality principle. They discuss implications for parameter-efficient adaptation, steering, convergence across models, and the neural thickets phenomenon.

papers.title: Modelling Billingual Learning Through LLM Training: A Critical-Period Exploration
papers.abstract: Critical-period accounts of second-language (L2) acquisition suggest that the ability to learn a new language may depend on how easily previously acquired first-language (L1) knowledge can be modified. This exploratory computational study extends a neural language-model approach to critical period effects by examining internal representations rather than behavior. A small two-layer GPT-2 model was trained on English and then on German (a relatively related L2) or Finnish (a relatively distant L2) through either Sequential training or Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), which limits change in parameters important for English. Mean-pooled hidden states for 20 held-out probe sentences per language were compared with those of the English-only model using cosine similarity at the embedding layer and two transformer layers after one and two L2 epochs. English similarity remained high in the transformer layers but became negative in the embedding layer. L2 similarity increased in the transformer layers, and German and Finnish differed more in the second transformer layer than in the first. EWC reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% but changed transformer-layer similarity by less than .001. With one training run per condition, these findings are preliminary.
papers.summary: Critical-period accounts of second-language (L2) acquisition suggest that learning a new language depends on how easily first-language (L1) knowledge can be modified. A two-layer `GPT-2` model was trained on English and then on German or Finnish, either sequentially or with Elastic Weight Consolidation (`EWC`), which limits change in parameters important for English, and its hidden states were compared to an English-only model by cosine similarity. English similarity stayed high in the transformer layers but turned negative in the embedding layer, and **`EWC` reduced Fisher-weighted parameter drift by about 6% while changing transformer-layer similarity by less than .001**. With one training run per condition, the authors describe the findings as preliminary.

papers.title: One, No One and One Hundred Thousand CTs: Testing Anatomical Control in Text-to-CT Generation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in deep learning and the public availability of computed tomography (CT) datasets with paired reports have enabled many Text-to-CT generators. However, their evaluations almost always differ in preprocessing and metrics, which hinders comparison. Moreover, their protocols almost never test how editing the report changes the CT, not even at the same seed, so the report is often assumed to control the anatomy without evidence of how much and how consistently it does. We therefore propose CtrlCT, a toolkit that tests two properties of a generator, Credibility and Control. Credibility tests compare generated CTs, as a population, with real CTs and reports; Control tests are metamorphic and need no reference CT: at a fixed seed, editing one finding should change it as requested, keep negated findings absent and shift distant anatomy no more than a new seed, and the change should hold across seeds. A Report Card summarises all measures and insights for each generator. We benchmark five public generators on 940 chest CTs and 687 edits of pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, holding out a sixth to test the toolkit. Among them, the most credible generators barely respond to an added effusion, while the most responsive produce less realistic and less diverse CTs. The analyses proposed in the literature do not reveal this. We release CtrlCT, its edits, seeds and 30,525 synthetic CTs after acceptance.
papers.summary: Generators that produce computed tomography (CT) scans from radiology reports are evaluated with inconsistent preprocessing and metrics, and almost never tested on whether editing the report actually changes the anatomy in the output. `CtrlCT` is a toolkit that scores a generator on credibility, comparing generated scans as a population against real scans and reports, and on control, using reference-free metamorphic tests in which one finding is edited at a fixed seed and the rest of the scan should stay put. Benchmarking five public generators on 940 chest CTs and 687 edits of pleural effusion and cardiomegaly shows that **the most credible generators barely respond to an added effusion, while the most responsive produce less realistic and less diverse scans**.

papers.title: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) generation with a lightweight draft model, but existing methods are compared as complete recipes under different training setups, which obscures what each design choice contributes. `LEGOSpec` decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components on a shared training infrastructure and varies them under matched conditions, finding that the best backbone depends on context length and memory budget, that proposal design trades acceptance against latency, and that the objective should match token distributions locally while optimizing acceptance length across the block. The resulting general-purpose draft, `DFlux`, **improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads** across `Qwen` and `Gemma` models. The framework also raises training throughput by up to 79% and speeds offline supervision preparation by up to 3.11x over `SpecForge`.

papers.title: Leto: Utility-Centric Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents rely on external memory to retain and reuse information across interactions. Existing memory systems treat memory as a record of the past and evaluate it by fidelity to the conversation. However, the value of memory lies in whether it improves the agent's response. A memory system decides what to memorize and what to serve before that response exists, and fidelity checks neither decision against it. Faithful memory can therefore fail to improve the response. We instead view memory as a prediction problem and present \textbf{\emph{\leto{}}}, a memory system for LLM agents that focuses on the utility of memory to the future rather than on its fidelity to the past. Because future requests are unknown, \emph{\leto{}} preserves access to conversation details through memory indexing, allowing information to remain available through its sources. When a request arrives, memory replay draws on this index to anticipate and supply the context the agent needs beyond what the request explicitly states. The utility of the served context remains uncertain until the response is generated, motivating a utility loop that uses response outcomes to refine future memory selection. We evaluate our system against six memory systems on five benchmarks across three scenarios. In personalization, it outperforms the strongest compared memory system by 16.3 percentage points in accuracy on PrefEval and by 3.1 points in task completion on PERMA. For long-horizon tasks, it achieves the best overall performance on MemoryArena averaged over five environments with a gain that increases with the chain depth. In long-context understanding, it is on par with retrieval over the raw history while serving fewer context tokens.
papers.summary: Memory systems for large language model (LLM) agents are usually built and judged on how faithfully they record past conversation, which does not guarantee that the stored memory improves the agent's next response. `Leto` treats memory as a prediction problem: it indexes conversation details so they stay reachable through their sources, replays memory at request time to anticipate context beyond what the request states, and uses response outcomes in a utility loop to refine future selection. Against six memory systems on five benchmarks, it **beats the strongest compared system by 16.3 percentage points in accuracy on `PrefEval`** and by 3.1 points in task completion on `PERMA`, gives the best overall result on `MemoryArena`, and matches retrieval over raw history on long-context understanding while serving fewer tokens.

papers.title: Train What You Run: Probabilistic Convolutions for Learning Token Compaction in State Space Models
papers.abstract: Visual token compaction reduces inference cost by passing only selected image patches or video tokens to later layers. In sequence models with local convolutions, each removal changes which tokens are neighbors. Learning which tokens to keep therefore requires a training signal that accounts for the new neighborhoods. We introduce ProbConv, which computes the exact expected convolution before activation at a kept position under independent keep decisions. The operator is differentiable in the keep probabilities. With binary decisions, ProbConv and step gating reproduce the compacted Mamba block. Across image, vision--language and video backbones, ProbConv is strongest under strong compaction: its advantage over matched training controls grows as more tokens are removed. In Cobra, it also outperforms adaptations of published vision--language pruning methods at matched inference budgets. ProbConv also improves over matched zero-mask training in video frame selection and speech frame dropping. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gmum/probconv
authors: Piotr Kubaty (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
Doctoral School of Exact and Natural Sciences
Mikhail Saladkou (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
Jacek Tabor (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
{\L}ukasz Struski (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science
papers.summary: Dropping visual tokens to cut inference cost is awkward in sequence models with local convolutions, because each removal changes which tokens are neighbors, and training needs to account for that. `ProbConv` computes the exact expected pre-activation convolution at a kept position under independent keep decisions, which is differentiable in the keep probabilities and, with binary decisions, reproduces the compacted `Mamba` block used at inference. Across image, vision-language, and video backbones, **its advantage over matched training controls grows as more tokens are removed**, and in `Cobra` it outperforms adaptations of published vision-language pruning methods at matched inference budgets. It also improves over zero-mask training for video frame selection and speech frame dropping.

papers.title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $\pi_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.
papers.summary: Robot manipulation policies are tested on scenes containing mirrors, inspired by the mirror self-recognition test from animal cognition. `RoboDojo-Mirror` keeps the tasks, success criteria, and policy checkpoints of `RoboDojo` fixed while adding single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions, and evaluates five policies spanning vision-language-action models, world action models, and agentic policies. **Every mirror condition lowers success, with average drops of 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies** and up to 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Comparisons with matched non-reflective panels show that 50–88% of mirror-specific failures occur without robot-panel contact, pointing to phantom targeting of reflected objects and mislocalization of real ones, and real-robot runs with `pi0.5` and `FastWAM` show lower success as well.
papers.highlight_summary:
Whether an ordinary mirror breaks robot manipulation policies is tested with `RoboDojo-Mirror`, a benchmark that keeps `RoboDojo` tasks, success criteria and policy checkpoints fixed while adding a single mirror, dual mirrors or a mirrored tabletop. Every mirror condition lowers aggregate success for all five policies tested, with behaviour consistent with reaching for reflected objects and mislocating real ones.

- The protocol pairs layouts and policy seeds across four scene conditions on eight tasks for five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action, World Action and agentic types (`WALL-OSS`, `VPP2`, `Awomo-0.5`, `Rex-M1 Preview`, `GPT-6-Astra`), with geometry-matched non-reflective panels as a physical-obstruction control for two of them.
- Averaged over the three mirror conditions, success rates fall by **10.8 to 56.7 percentage points** depending on the policy, and the worst single case is a **62.5-point** drop on the mirrored tabletop, where `Rex-M1 Preview` goes from 66.7% to 4.2%.
- In the panel comparison for `WALL-OSS` and `Awomo-0.5`, **50–88%** of mirror-specific failures occur without any recorded robot–panel contact, so collisions alone do not explain the degradation, and in a tabletop grasping diagnostic `VPP2` falls from 97.8% to 4.4% success while empty close-and-lift episodes rise from 0% to **95.6%**.
- Real-robot trials on a Franka show the same trend, with `π0.5` dropping from **77.5%** to 52.5% (upright mirror) and 27.5% (mirrored tabletop), and `FastWAM` from **60.0%** to 30.0% and 10.0%.
- The work diagnoses the failure without proposing a fix, execution budgets differ so the results are not a cross-policy ranking, the agentic `Astra` results rest on only five rollouts per cell (average drop 10.8 points, 95% interval 1.7–20.0), and mirror-related prompt hints gave no consistent improvement when the main camera saw targets only by reflection.

papers.title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
papers.abstract: As clinical AI agents begin to interact with electronic health records (EHRs), large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate their actions. But how reliably can these judges recognize clinically dangerous mistakes, especially when an agent appears to have completed its task successfully? We investigate this question using MedAgentBench by introducing controlled clinical errors into verified agent trajectories. The experiments include 416 faulty trajectories, eight error categories, and six open-weight LLM judges. By comparing each faulty trajectory with its correct counterpart, we measure whether judges genuinely recognize errors rather than simply flagging more actions as unsafe. The findings show that access to clinical evidence significantly improves judge reliability. When shown only the final answer, judges cannot distinguish errors that leave it unchanged, while flagging 56% of correct trajectories. With full trajectory information, the ability to distinguish unsafe actions from correct ones reaches a score of 0.75, and providing actual EHR responses improves discrimination by 0.39. Surprisingly, including the agent's reasoning does not improve overall performance and reduces detection of incorrectly reported clinical values by 0.18, which remain the hardest errors to detect. MedGemma performed worse than the general-purpose model and was the only judge to miss potentially dangerous medication overdoses. We also find that the benchmark's original grader accepts all 38 trajectories with an intentionally skipped laboratory check, while combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker informed by the full EHR record detects 97% of injected faults.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to judge the actions of clinical agents working with electronic health records (EHRs), raising the question of whether they catch dangerous mistakes in runs that appear successful. The authors inject controlled clinical errors into verified `MedAgentBench` trajectories, producing 416 faulty trajectories across eight error categories, and compare six open-weight judges on each faulty trajectory and its correct counterpart. Judges shown only the final answer cannot distinguish errors that leave it unchanged and flag 56% of correct trajectories, whereas full trajectories bring discrimination to 0.75, and including the agent's reasoning does not help overall. The benchmark's original grader accepts all 38 trajectories with a skipped laboratory check, while **combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker informed by the full EHR record detects 97% of injected faults**.

papers.title: RecordRoute: Auditing Agent Failures with Localization-Guided Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Auditing failed agent executions requires identifying the responsible actor, the earliest decisive step, and the error mode. Representative supervised methods either focus on step localization or predict multiple attribution targets from shared trajectory representations. These methods do not use the localization result to select the text for mode diagnosis. To address this limitation, we propose RecordRoute, which couples comparative localization with local diagnosis. Specifically, it represents each record with word and character features and learns to rank records through comparisons within each trajectory. The selected record supplies the actor and step, while its text and metadata drive mode prediction. On controlled-injection Who&When Pro, RecordRoute outperforms StepFinder and ASCon on all four official metrics. With actor and step predictions fixed, local diagnosis reaches 77.47% pooled joint accuracy versus 69.28% for full-trace diagnosis. On natural failures from TraceElephant and CatchBench POST, it outperforms these baselines and three open LLMs in localization.
papers.summary: Auditing a failed agent run means identifying the responsible actor, the earliest decisive step, and the error mode, but existing supervised methods do not use the localized step to choose which text the mode diagnosis reads. `RecordRoute` ranks records within each trajectory using word and character features, takes the actor and step from the selected record, and predicts the error mode from that record's text and metadata. On `Who&When Pro` it outperforms `StepFinder` and `ASCon` on all four official metrics, and with actor and step predictions fixed, **local diagnosis reaches 77.47% pooled joint accuracy versus 69.28% for full-trace diagnosis**. On natural failures from `TraceElephant` and `CatchBench POST` it also beats these baselines and three open LLMs at localization.

papers.title: PAC-style Bounds on the Conditional Validity of Conformal Predictors
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction sets are guaranteed to be marginally valid over the attribute space, but local coverage can diverge from the user-defined target $1-\alpha$. Constructing conditionally valid prediction sets with finite calibration data is impossible for a general data-generating distribution. We derive PAC-type probabilistic lower bounds on the input-conditional coverage of any conformal predictor, without assumptions on the data distribution. They are based on the Markov and Cantelli inequalities and adapt to both calibration-marginal and calibration-conditional setups. A tighter, model-dependent Cantelli bound depends on the variance of the conditional coverage and is estimable from data using a fully non-asymptotic Hoeffding argument. The results suggest conditional-coverage variance as a scalable and theoretically motivated empirical measure of conditional validity.

papers.title: Best Arm Identification with Unknown Post-Action Context Distribution
papers.abstract: We study best arm identification (BAI) with post-action context in the fixed-confidence setting. After choosing an action, the learner observes a post-action context together with a reward whose distribution depends only on this context. Incorporating such intermediate information can substantially reduce the sample complexity of identifying the best arm. While Shahverdikondori et al. (2026a) analyzed the case where the distribution of contexts given actions is known, we address the more challenging and practically relevant case where this distribution is unknown. We derive an instance-dependent sample complexity lower bound and propose a Track-and-Stop algorithm that matches it asymptotically with access to an optimization oracle. Our stopping rule uses a new concentration inequality that jointly controls uncertainty in the context distributions and reward means, removing the factor of two incurred by separate concentration bounds. Implementing the algorithm generally requires solving nonconvex optimization problems. We propose a convex relaxation with instance-dependent approximation guarantees, including asymptotic tightness on hard Gaussian instances. Experiments demonstrate that exploiting post-action context reduces the sample complexity relative to baselines that ignore it, even when the context distributions are unknown.
papers.summary: placeholder

papers.title: Score-Based Diffusion for Hypergraph Signals in the t-Spectral Domain
papers.abstract: We introduce the first score-based generative model for signals on a fixed hypergraph, formulated in the spectral domain of t-product hypergraph signal processing (t-HGSP). The naive tensor heat semigroup is ill-posed, since after palindromic symmetrization the spectral slices of the Laplacian tensor are no longer positive semidefinite. A per-mode frequency shift repairs it, yielding a forward Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion that decouples per (eigenmode, slice) pair with closed-form marginals, exact score targets, and an exactly isotropic stationary law. A lightweight slice-conditioned denoiser is trained on the resulting real spectral grid. Sampling combines its score on data-active modes with the closed-form score elsewhere, which proves essential for stability at scale. A closed cosine-form observation operator turns missing-node recovery into linear-Gaussian guidance with stabilized posterior sampling. On hypergraphs of up to 500 nodes, our model beats a clique-expansion baseline by margins growing from $2\times$ to $27\times$ in covariance error, matches the graph-spectral statistics of the data better than the graph-basis model itself, and reaches the finite-sample estimation floor on data rotated off the t-spectral axes. Posterior sampling reduces missing-node NMSE to 0.28-0.64 (classical baselines 0.87-1.1) at conservative coverage, and cuts the framework's own denoising baseline by up to $3.6\times$.
papers.summary: Generating signals on a fixed hypergraph is addressed with a score-based diffusion model built in the spectral domain of t-product hypergraph signal processing (`t-HGSP`). A per-mode frequency shift fixes the ill-posed tensor heat semigroup, giving a forward Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion that decouples per eigenmode and slice with closed-form marginals and exact score targets, and a lightweight slice-conditioned denoiser is combined with the closed-form score during sampling. On hypergraphs of up to 500 nodes, the model beats a clique-expansion baseline by **margins growing from 2x to 27x in covariance error**. Posterior sampling for missing-node recovery lowers normalized mean squared error to 0.28-0.64, against 0.87-1.1 for classical baselines.

papers.title: SALSA: Sampling Adversarial Suffixes from Learned Distributions for LLM Safety Assessment
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where adversaries append optimized suffixes to otherwise benign looking prompts to bypass safety alignment. Existing optimization-based GCG-style attacks can be effective, but they are expensive at inference time, and suffer from poor transfer. We present, SALSA, a generative framework that learns a distribution over jailbreak suffixes from optimization-derived attack corpora. Once trained, the model supports efficient sampling-based attacks. On open-source targets, it achieves attack success rates comparable to state-of-the-art optimization baselines, while reducing generation time from 3.46s to 0.04s per prompt. In black-box transfer, it remains highly effective against proprietary systems, including 99% ASR on GPT-3.5-Turbo, and reaches 45% ASR on the substantially harder GPT-4o, more than doubling the strongest baseline at an equal sampling budget. We further offer an intuition for why generative sampling can preserve high attack success, when the learned suffix distribution is close to the distribution of optimization outputs. Overall, our results show that learning adversarial suffix distributions yields a scalable, and practically efficient foundation for continuous LLM vulnerability discovery.
papers.summary: Optimization-based jailbreak attacks in the style of `GCG` append adversarial suffixes to prompts but are slow at inference time and transfer poorly. `SALSA` instead trains a generative model on corpora of optimization-derived suffixes and then attacks by sampling from the learned distribution. On open-source targets it matches the attack success rate (ASR) of optimization baselines while cutting generation time from 3.46s to 0.04s per prompt. In black-box transfer it reaches 99% ASR on `GPT-3.5-Turbo` and **45% ASR on `GPT-4o`, more than double the strongest baseline at an equal sampling budget**.

papers.title: Can a Frontier LLM Repair a Quantized Network by Tool-Free Weight-Space Programming?
papers.abstract: We give four large language models (LLMs) of the Claude family the complete weights of a 20k-parameter CIFAR-10 CNN as text and ask them to produce a 4-bit network without tools, data or the ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization to 4 bit lowers the test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%. We design four evaluation protocols that differ in the input and task description given to the LLMs and analyze their responses. In the first two protocols the LLMs are given the float and the 4-bit RTN network and are told that the accuracy has dropped significantly. In the last two they receive only the float network and the task to quantize it, which tests whether they apply an optimization on their own or fall back to plain RTN. Our analysis shows that a frontier LLM can recover most of the lost accuracy. Given one answer per layer, Opus 5.5 raises the accuracy of the 4-bit network to 77.95% by balancing the rounding errors within each 3x3 kernel, reasoning over the integer weights without tools. This is 3.5 pp below the float network and 2.8 pp below AdaRound, which learns the rounding from calibration data. Given only the float network, the LLMs name error-cancelling corrections but do not apply them and fall back to plain RTN, at most with mildly clipped scales, which still lifts Fable 5.2's quantized network to 70.0%. We analyze in detail what the LLMs did and why it works. Code and prompts can be found at https://github.com/urbste/weight-space-programming-ptq
papers.summary: Four Claude-family large language models (LLMs) receive the full weights of a 20k-parameter `CIFAR-10` convolutional network as text and must produce a 4-bit version with no tools, data, or ability to run inference. Standard round-to-nearest (RTN) quantization drops test accuracy from 81.4% to 60.4%, and four protocols vary whether the models see the RTN network and are told about the accuracy loss. Answering one layer at a time, `Opus 5.5` **raises the 4-bit accuracy to 77.95%** by balancing rounding errors within each 3x3 kernel, which is 2.8 points below the data-driven `AdaRound`. Given only the float network, the models name error-cancelling corrections but fall back to plain RTN with mildly clipped scales, which still brings `Fable 5.2`'s network to 70.0%.

papers.title: Hybrid AI for AI-Native RAN Control: A Functional Perspective
papers.abstract: AI-native radio access network (RAN) control involves interdependent decisions across network entities, protocol layers, and timescales. Understanding how AI and conventional methods can jointly support these decisions requires a common basis for comparing their functional roles. This survey introduces a technique-agnostic taxonomy of RAN decision-making organized around four complementary capabilities: Representation and Reasoning, Prediction and Simulation, Adaptive Control, and Decision Synthesis. These capabilities are defined by their roles in the control process, independently of the techniques used to implement them. Through this perspective, we examine representative AI and model-based approaches, including foundation models, world models, reinforcement learning, and optimization. We then apply the taxonomy to representative RAN control solutions across slow, medium, fast, and cross-timescale applications to identify which capabilities they implement and how these capabilities are combined in hybrid AI systems. We also review datasets, benchmarks, simulators, digital twins, and experimental platforms according to their support for the decision-making process and reproducible evaluation. The review highlights a gap between the availability of resources for closed-loop experimentation and the standardization of tasks, metrics, and evaluation protocols needed for meaningful comparisons.Finally, we identify research directions for hybrid AI in AI-native RAN, including capability integration, multi-agent and cross-timescale coordination, constraint handling, and reproducible closed-loop evaluation. A curated list of surveyed works and evaluation resources is available at https://github.com/pegahani/Hybrid-AI-RAN-Survey.
papers.summary: Control of AI-native radio access networks (RAN) involves interdependent decisions across network entities, protocol layers, and timescales, which makes AI and conventional methods hard to compare. This survey proposes a technique-agnostic taxonomy built on four capabilities: Representation and Reasoning, Prediction and Simulation, Adaptive Control, and Decision Synthesis. It applies the taxonomy to foundation models, world models, reinforcement learning, and optimization across slow, medium, fast, and cross-timescale RAN control, and reviews datasets, simulators, digital twins, and testbeds. The review finds **a gap between available resources for closed-loop experimentation and the standardized tasks, metrics, and protocols needed for meaningful comparison**.

papers.title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.
papers.summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for large language model (LLM) rankers in recommendation are hard to compare because the rankers lack a standard classification head and the methods act at different stages of the pipeline. A fixed-ranking benchmark evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract, across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones. **The ordering of UQ methods changes across backbones even on the same reference instances**, and the ranking-aligned `Top10Mass` signal gives the strongest scalar `Error@10` detection in several conditions. Scalar signals are weak at identifying which controlled evidence change hurts `NDCG@10` more, where source-specific signals such as `Perturbation Rank Instability` do better.

papers.title: When Is Product Decoding of ECOC MAP-Consistent? Pair Structure and the n-vs-Rest Codes
papers.abstract: Error-Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) combine binary classifiers by the sum decoder, which totals probabilities, or the product decoder, which totals log-likelihoods. In the noiseless setting, where the binary classifiers output the true posteriors, we ask on which code matrices each decoder always agrees with the Bayes-optimal (MAP) class. For the sum decoder the answer is known: the code must be equidistant (James and Hastie, 1998). We answer the question for the product decoder. Two classes are compared through the votes of the columns on which they differ: the sum decoder decides by their sample mean, the product decoder by an M-estimator with influence function artanh, and each vote is the MAP margin plus a bias determined by the other classes alone. Our main theorem states that the product decoder is MAP-consistent if and only if, for every class pair, the columns on which the two classes differ are matched with the columns obtained by swapping the two classes (or their complements), and equivalently if and only if the code is a union of n-vs-Rest codes. Efficient equidistant codes are therefore excluded: Hadamard codes ($M\ge 8$), which meet the Plotkin bound with $M-1$ columns, have no such pairs, and for the Sylvester type the reversal margin can be at least a constant 0.0182 independent of $M$. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. On six real datasets with estimated probabilities, the product decoder is slightly more accurate when each column is calibrated, and the sum decoder is better when the calibration error differs across columns; in either case the decoders disagree only near ties.
papers.summary: Error-Correcting Output Codes (ECOC) combine binary classifiers using either a sum decoder or a product decoder, and the question is on which code matrices the product decoder always agrees with the Bayes-optimal maximum a posteriori (MAP) class when the binary classifiers output true posteriors. The main theorem shows the product decoder is **MAP-consistent if and only if the code is a union of n-vs-Rest codes**, equivalently when the columns separating each class pair are matched with their class-swapped counterparts. Efficient equidistant codes such as Hadamard codes with at least 8 classes are therefore excluded, and all theorems are machine-checked in `Lean 4`. On six real datasets the two decoders disagree only near ties, with the product decoder slightly ahead when every column is calibrated.

papers.title: Latent Merger: Latent-Space Composition of Hypernetwork-Generated LoRAs
papers.abstract: Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.
papers.summary: Hypernetworks that turn a document into a low-rank adapter (LoRA) in one forward pass let new knowledge be injected into a frozen language model, but keeping one adapter per document does not scale in streaming settings. A study of two such systems, `Doc-to-LoRA` and `SHINE`, finds their generated adapters are more spectrally concentrated and more aligned across documents than directly fine-tuned ones, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal. Based on this, the hypernetwork's intermediate latents are merged and then decoded through the frozen LoRA-generation head. This **latent-space merging consistently improves over weight-space and factor-space baselines** while keeping a single fixed-rank adapter.

papers.title: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement
papers.abstract: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.
papers.summary: Whether response speed and streaming affect how people judge chatbot answers is tested with three sources of natural variation. In `compar:IA`, a French government chatbot arena, repeated prompts were randomly answered either with a freshly streamed reply or a stored reply from the same model shown at once, and **the replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points**, with the same text winning 57% of votes when streamed and 29% when replayed. Across 324,029 arena conversations, congestion-slowed answers earned no detectable credit in votes but reduced follow-up questions. In 4,378,514 `WildChat` replies from `ChatGPT` use, slower replies likewise made users less likely to continue.

papers.title: Local Indices Are Not Enough: Synchrony and Global Information in Bandit Algorithms
papers.abstract: Standard index-based stochastic bandit algorithms such as KL-UCB and Thompson Sampling achieve optimal $O(\log T)$ regret over a horizon $T$. The former uses the global timestep to construct each arm's index, while the latter samples each arm's belief distribution at every timestep. The necessity of global information and synchronous index updates for achieving optimal regret has not been examined yet. In this paper, we investigate the fundamental limits of asynchronous local index algorithms---those that recalculate an arm's index only upon pulling it, using solely that arm's own reward history and a local randomness budget. We prove that no such algorithm can achieve $O(\log T)$ regret across all bandit instances. We then analyse the functional equations arising from asynchronous updates, and show that the achievable regret lies in a sub-polynomial, super-polylogarithmic regime. We propose an asynchronous local index policy whose regret upper bound also lies in this regime. Turning to synchronous local algorithms, which sample every arm's index at all timesteps as in Thompson Sampling, we show that a locally determined randomness budget per arm suffices to retain $O(\log T)$ regret, demonstrating that synchrony, albeit with some randomness, is essential to the optimality of Thompson Sampling.
papers.summary: Optimal stochastic bandit algorithms such as `KL-UCB` and `Thompson Sampling` rely on either the global timestep or on resampling every arm at every step, and it has been unclear whether that is necessary. For asynchronous local index algorithms, which update an arm's index only when it is pulled and use only that arm's reward history and local randomness, the authors prove that **no such algorithm can achieve O(log T) regret across all bandit instances**. The achievable regret is shown to lie in a sub-polynomial, super-polylogarithmic regime, and a policy with a matching-regime upper bound is given. Synchronous local algorithms that sample every arm's index each step retain O(log T) regret with a locally determined randomness budget.

papers.title: ClusterVAD: Threshold-Free Unsupervised Voice Activity Detection with Pre-Trained Neural Representations
papers.abstract: Voice activity detection (VAD) is one of the first steps in speech processing pipelines, from transcription and diarization to speech language models. Supervised detectors need labelled data and inherit the domain and annotation conventions of their training corpora. Existing unsupervised detectors rely on hand-crafted acoustic features which cannot benefit from data and degrade in far-field, noisy or atypical speech. We propose ClusterVAD, an unsupervised VAD built on frozen speech foundation model representations. Fitted once on a small set of untranscribed speech, it clusters the representations and labels each cluster as speech or non-speech with sonority, an acoustic measure. At inference, a frame-level speech probability is computed from the cluster assignments, and a two-state hidden Markov model fitted to each recording enables threshold-free detection. Across benchmarks covering meetings, far-field and noisy recordings, Mandarin and dysarthric speech, ClusterVAD obtains the lowest detection error on pause-level references and is competitive on speaker turn-level references. These results indicate that speech foundation models inherently capture the distinction between speech and non-speech, which can be leveraged without training a detector.
papers.summary: Voice activity detection (VAD) usually depends on either labelled training data or hand-crafted acoustic features that degrade in far-field, noisy, or atypical speech. `ClusterVAD` is an unsupervised detector that clusters frozen speech foundation model representations from a small set of untranscribed audio and labels each cluster as speech or non-speech using sonority, an acoustic measure. At inference a two-state hidden Markov model fitted per recording removes the need for a decision threshold. Across benchmarks covering meetings, far-field and noisy recordings, Mandarin, and dysarthric speech, it obtains **the lowest detection error on pause-level references** and is competitive on speaker turn-level references.

papers.title: Understanding Clipping In Zeroth-Order Optimization
papers.abstract: Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a resource-efficient alternative to Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) when fine-tuning LLMs, thanks to the inherent low dimensionality of the loss landscape. It relies on a two-point estimate of the gradient that only accesses the function value and not the gradient, bypassing the resource-heavy backpropagation. Recently, it was accidentally discovered that per-sample clipping can improve the performance of the trained model, while running a differentially private version of zeroth-order optimization \cite{zhang2024dpzero} with a very large privacy parameter $\epsilon$ (corresponding to very little privacy). In this paper, we systematically investigate this phenomenon and demonstrate that ($i$) the optimal choice of learning rate $\eta$ is inversely proportional to the clipping threshold $c$, satisfying $\eta c =$ constant; ($ii$) clipping drives the zeroth-order optimization to a different solution with higher test accuracy; and ($iii$) this phenomenon is only observed with per-sample clipped zeroth-order optimization and not other zeroth-order alternatives that also provide robust estimates of the gradient. Further analyses with artificially injected label noise reveals that clipping leads to more robust predictions, which stems from the implicit down weighting of hard-to-fit training examples. Our code is available at https://github.com/SewoongLab/ClipZero
papers.summary: Zeroth-order optimization fine-tunes large language models using two-point function-value estimates of the gradient instead of backpropagation, and per-sample clipping was previously observed by accident to improve its results. A systematic study finds that the optimal learning rate is inversely proportional to the clipping threshold, that clipping steers optimization to a different solution with higher test accuracy, and that the effect appears only with per-sample clipping and not with other robust zeroth-order gradient estimators. Experiments with injected label noise indicate that **clipping yields more robust predictions by implicitly down-weighting hard-to-fit training examples**.

papers.title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.
papers.summary: Group relative policy optimization (`GRPO`) is widely used to train reasoning models and agents, but its group size is typically picked by trial and error. Using the U-statistic structure of the `GRPO` policy gradient, group size selection is recast as estimating a variance ratio, and a pessimistic ratio estimator is proposed that accounts for uncertainty in a small denominator, with its properties characterised across three sample-size regimes. On synthetic tasks from `Reasoning Gym` and on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, the **adaptive group size reduces the mean squared error of the policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines** at modest extra compute.

papers.title: Auditing the Judge: Human-Derived Bias Discovery, Quantification, and Mitigation in LLM Judges
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators in evaluation and training pipelines, their judgements are often affected by systematic biases that conflict with human preferences. Although prior work has identified various biases and proposed methods for detecting and mitigating them, less attention has been paid to using human preferences to inform bias identification and mitigation. Moreover, these approaches rely heavily on pre-discovered bias lists, overlook bias strength, and depend on costly interventions. In this work, we propose HUB-J, an integrated framework based on human-derived bias factors that detects, quantifies, and mitigates biases in LLM-as-a-Judge systems. Our approach leverages human-LLM judgement disagreement cases to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, and utilizes agreement cases to quantify bias strength through controlled input modifications and resulting shifts in model decisions. Finally, building on these quantified biases, we introduce a lightweight, training-free regression-based mitigation strategy that estimates the influence of each bias factor on model judgments and corrects bias-influenced decisions by removing its estimated effect. Empirical results show that HUB-J uncovers both known and novel bias factors, reveals meaningful differences in model susceptibility, and consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) used as automated judges show systematic biases that diverge from human preferences, and existing methods depend on pre-compiled bias lists, ignore bias strength, and need costly interventions. `HUB-J` mines cases where human and LLM judgements disagree to automatically discover interpretable bias factors, then measures each factor's strength on agreement cases through controlled input modifications. A training-free regression step estimates each factor's influence on a judgement and removes it. The framework uncovers both known and novel bias factors and **consistently reduces bias-driven decision flips while generalizing across models**.

papers.title: The Reliability Function of Error-Correcting Output Codes with Noisy Binary Classifiers
papers.abstract: Error-correcting output coding (ECOC) builds a multi-class classifier from binary classifiers. We study the excess error rate of ECOC over the Bayes (MAP) classifier when each binary classifier outputs a posterior estimate whose log-odds is corrupted by Gaussian noise. Recasting decoding as a test over a Gaussian channel, we derive an upper bound from the union and Chernoff bounds and a lower bound from the nearest competing category and the Mills ratio. The bounds show that a large Hamming distance is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the excess error rate. The excess error rate stays bounded away from zero, by a constant that depends on the two largest posteriors and the noise level but not on the number of categories $M$, whenever the distance between the code words of the two most probable categories is bounded; for equidistant codes this distance is $d_{\min}$. Conversely, it is at most $M-1$ times a factor that is exponentially small in the minimum distance $d_{\min}$, and it vanishes whenever $\kappa\,d_{\min}-\ln(M-1)\to\infty$ for an explicit $\kappa$ (for general codes, under a posterior condition). For $n$-vs-rest codes with $n\geq2$, the upper and lower exponents coincide asymptotically, which determines the reliability function of ECOC in closed form. The results extend to correlated Gaussian noise with the Hamming distance replaced by an effective distance; when noise is shared at the level of categories, the effective distance stays bounded and the excess error rate does not vanish for any code. All theorems are machine-checked in Lean 4. In a semi-synthetic setting, the measured decay agrees with the predicted exponent. On ResNet-50 features of CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-1k, the excess error over a log-likelihood decoding reference decreases with $d_{\min}$ and, for larger $M$, levels off at a moderate distance, while codes with $d_{\min}=1$ degrade as $M$ grows.
papers.summary: Error-correcting output coding (ECOC) builds a multi-class classifier from binary ones, and the analysis here concerns its excess error over the Bayes classifier when each binary classifier's log-odds is corrupted by Gaussian noise. Treating decoding as a test over a Gaussian channel gives upper and lower bounds showing that **a large Hamming distance is both necessary and sufficient for reducing the excess error rate**, which decays exponentially in the minimum distance. For n-vs-rest codes with n at least 2 the exponents coincide asymptotically, giving the reliability function in closed form, and all theorems are machine-checked in `Lean 4`. On `ResNet-50` features of `CIFAR-10/100` and `ImageNet-1k`, excess error falls as minimum distance grows and levels off at a moderate distance.

papers.title: On the Creation of Object-Centric Event Logs from Patient Journeys
papers.abstract: Interactions between patients and health systems as well as conditions that individuals experience during a disease are represented in patient journeys. Therefore, patient journeys are important assets to investigate how care is being provided, and how health systems can be designed to better suit the needs of patients. While there is initial work on patient journeys from a process mining perspective with traditional case notions, object-centric process mining techniques have yet to be covered. This is unfortunate, since due to the rich structure of objects and their relationships, object-centric process mining approaches are particularly promising in this context. This paper addresses this gap by investigating object-centric event log (OCEL) generation from patient journeys. Based on a list of challenges and requirements, the paper presents an approach for the creation of OCELs from patient journey data. The approach is evaluated on a synthetic patient cohort provided by our industry partner.
papers.summary: Patient journeys record interactions between patients and health systems, and prior process mining work on them has used traditional single-case notions rather than object-centric techniques. Starting from a list of challenges and requirements, the authors present **an approach for creating object-centric event logs (OCELs) from patient journey data**. The approach is evaluated on a synthetic patient cohort supplied by an industry partner.

papers.title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) that translate natural language into first-order logic (FOL) can produce unfaithful formulas that corrupt downstream reasoning. `FOL-Proof` derives a pool of candidate readings deterministically with linguistic tools such as the `English Resource Grammar` and `Minimal Recursion Semantics`, then uses a satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solver to check whether any reading is logically equivalent to the LLM's formula, accepting, rejecting, or optionally repairing it and abstaining when checks are inconclusive. On `ProofWriter`, `RuleTaker`, `PrOntoQA`, and a new adversarial benchmark, `LongFaithCheck`, it attains **near perfect selective accuracy**, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines perform substantially worse.

papers.title: Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation
papers.abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.
papers.summary: Groupwise quantization improves LLM accuracy at low bit widths but prevents standard integer matrix kernels from covering the full dot product on GPUs. `Shifter Quantization` (`SQ`) rebuilds native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits, and a variant, `Shifter Integer` (`SHI`), targets INT4 kernels. At 2 bits, `SQ2` and `SHI2` reach **2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of `llama.cpp` on a `Q2_K` checkpoint** while reducing `WikiText-2` KL divergence by 6.6-7.8%. At 4 bits `SQ4` gets 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of `NInfer` baselines with 24-40% lower KL, and at 8 bits `SQ8` has 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than `vLLM`'s online FP8.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence
papers.abstract: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty.
papers.summary: Entity resolution pipelines usually commit early to a single span and type from Named Entity Recognition (NER), discarding ambiguity that downstream Entity Linking (EL) could use. In this proof of concept, a `BERT`-based NER model with two auxiliary span-boundary heads is run with Monte Carlo dropout to produce averaged start- and end-boundary probabilities and a fuzzy entropy signal, which then adapt the fuzzy-matching cutoff during candidate generation. On the `AnnoCTR` cyber threat intelligence dataset linked to the `MITRE ATT&CK` knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal approaches **improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966**.

papers.title: The Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) Dataset
papers.abstract: Monitoring Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) supports safety and well-being for people living at home, especially older adults, and radar sensing is gaining increasing attention in the field of activity recognition for its ability to ensure privacy in the home while also surpassing technical limitations of other sensing modalities. However, radar-based activity recognition remains constrained by the limited availability of large-scale datasets. We introduce the Radar-based Activities of Daily Living (R-ADL) dataset to addresses the gaps identified in existing work: 1) it expands the scale of available data by providing over eight hours of annotated recordings in which a person performs eight distinct activities; 2) it overcomes room configuration limitations by recording from five different locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment; and 3) it extends beyond primitive actions to focus on high-level ADLs. In addition to the dataset, this paper introduces practical guidance for future ADL dataset construction. We conducted a detailed analysis of how ADLs are prioritized across academic research, health survey tools, and clinical trials to identify clinically significant ADLs. Furthermore, we provide our experimental design, data collection and annotation strategies, post-processing pipeline for forming the R-ADL dataset from raw data, and baseline results on standard machine learning architectures. The R-ADL dataset serves as a valuable resource for advancing ADL recognition systems as we continue building larger and more diverse datasets.
papers.summary: Radar-based recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) offers privacy-preserving home monitoring, particularly for older adults, but is held back by a shortage of large datasets. The `R-ADL` dataset provides **over eight hours of annotated radar recordings of one person performing eight high-level activities**, captured from five locations in a two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment. The authors also analyze which ADLs are prioritized across research, health surveys, and clinical trials, and document their collection, annotation, and post-processing pipeline along with baseline results on standard architectures.

papers.title: AIChipBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Automated AI Accelerator Design
papers.abstract: A language-model decoder carries state between decoding steps, and in hardware a wrong state update can leave the current token correct and corrupt the output several tokens later, so a design can pass output tests and still be wrong. AIChipBench asks what LLM coding agents need to build such hardware correctly. Agents implement quantized Qwen3.5, Gemma 3, Gemma 4, and Llama 3.2 decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code against an executable integer reference that specifies the outputs and the stored state at every decoding step. They debug against public tests under fixed budgets; their frozen designs are graded on held-out token sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, and a second track asks them to speed up a correct design at nearly fixed area. Across 9,136 attempts by four coding agents, the difficulty lies in stored state. Feedback that points to the first state mismatch raises acceptance over output-only feedback in all 12 agent--task cells of a matched study, by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points, and halves the agent-hours per accepted design. Regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required. More than a third of attempts to speed up a correct design end without one. An overall score ranks Sol 5.6 and Fable 5.1 above Astra 6 and Opus 5.5, and both halves of the instances give this order in all 200 random splits. Hardware agents therefore need debugging feedback that exposes stored state, and their benchmarks need final tests well beyond the development cases.
papers.summary: `AIChipBench` tests whether LLM coding agents can implement quantized `Qwen3.5`, `Gemma 3`, `Gemma 4`, and `Llama 3.2` decoders in synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) code, where a wrong stored-state update can pass output tests yet corrupt tokens several steps later. Agents debug against public tests and an executable integer reference under fixed budgets, and frozen designs are graded on held-out sequences, resets, memory stalls, and synthesis, with a second track for speeding up a correct design. Across 9,136 attempts by four agents, feedback pointing to the first state mismatch **raises acceptance by 25.0 to 46.9 percentage points over output-only feedback** and halves agent-hours per accepted design. When regraded on new sequences and conditions, 45 of 69 accepted designs fail within the 32 steps their tests required, and the overall score ranks `Sol 5.6` and `Fable 5.1` above `Astra 6` and `Opus 5.5`.

papers.title: EventDiffusion: Learning Native Event Stream Distribution from Videos
papers.abstract: Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes at high temporal resolution, but scarce recordings constrain data-driven research. Sparse RGB observations cannot uniquely determine intervening events since identical frames may correspond to streams with different activity, polarities, and timing. Existing simulators largely rely on prescribed sensor dynamics and estimated brightness trajectories, whose assumptions limit the diversity and fidelity of plausible event streams. We introduce EventDiffusion, a hierarchical generative framework that directly learns the conditional distribution of native asynchronous event streams from real recordings. EventDiffusion decomposes generation into three probabilistic processes: Event Activity Diffusion (EAD) learns stochastic discrete event counts; Event Spatial Allocation (ESA) distributes these counts to individual pixels while preserving cardinality; and Event Timing Diffusion (ETD) learns continuous asynchronous timestamp distributions. We also introduce CEFS, an event-stream realism metric combining event activity and polarity with multiscale space-time structure and temporal fidelity. Across all datasets, EventDiffusion achieves double the accuracy of SOTA methods and demonstrates robustness across different cameras at any resolution.
papers.summary: Event cameras record asynchronous brightness changes, but real recordings are scarce and simulators rely on prescribed sensor dynamics that limit the diversity and fidelity of synthetic event streams. `EventDiffusion` is a hierarchical generative model that learns the conditional distribution of native event streams from video in three stages: Event Activity Diffusion (`EAD`) for stochastic event counts, Event Spatial Allocation (`ESA`) for distributing counts to pixels, and Event Timing Diffusion (`ETD`) for continuous timestamps. The authors also introduce `CEFS`, a realism metric combining event activity, polarity, space-time structure, and temporal fidelity. They claim **double the accuracy of prior state-of-the-art methods across all datasets**, with robustness across cameras and resolutions.

papers.title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
papers.abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent
papers.summary: Agents built on frontier language models are costly because the frontier model re-reads its full context and performs every subtask itself, however easy. `Delegent` is a harness built on `Claude Code` in which the frontier model stays in charge of each task but hands focused subtasks such as code investigation, test runs, and corpus search to small language model (SLM) subagents running on hardware the user already owns, with no trained router. With a 27B FP8 SLM, the authors report that it **cuts frontier cost by 67% on long-horizon coding** and by 59% on agentic search with no loss in task performance, and a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop still cuts coding cost by 66%. A short instruction that keeps the main coding work with the frontier model accounts for most of the saving.

papers.title: GREMLIN: Generating Random Environments for Meta-Learning with Interacting Networks
papers.abstract: Can randomly parameterized neural environments supply useful experience for learning a reinforcement learning algorithm? We investigate this question using DiscoRL's rule-discovery framework, replacing human-designed training games with sixteen selected neural environments. Each game combines bounded vector dynamics with a random strategy-based reward and an independent outcome reward. After 224.8 million agent-environment steps, we froze the teacher and trained fresh agents. DQN outscored GREMLIN on most games, both generated and human-designed. GREMLIN nevertheless outperformed the untrained teacher on all 26 games, showing that generated experience can improve a learning rule. It remains unclear whether this approach can yield a competitive rule with longer meta-training.
papers.summary: The question studied is whether randomly parameterized neural environments can provide useful experience for meta-learning a reinforcement learning algorithm. Using the rule-discovery framework of `DiscoRL`, the authors replace human-designed training games with sixteen selected neural environments that combine bounded vector dynamics with a random strategy-based reward and an independent outcome reward, meta-train for 224.8 million steps, then freeze the teacher and train fresh agents. `DQN` outscored the resulting `GREMLIN` rule on most games, both generated and human-designed, but **`GREMLIN` beat the untrained teacher on all 26 games**, indicating that generated experience can improve a learning rule. Whether longer meta-training would yield a competitive rule is left open.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
papers.abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves.
