A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived rather than freshly generated rollouts, but this leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy: maximum likelihood on the archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training usually discards its rollouts after each update, and this work asks how much of the learned capability is retained in those rollouts rather than only in the weights. Replaying the original RL algorithm on archived rollouts collapses catastrophically, so the authors instead apply plain maximum likelihood to the archived rollouts in their original order, starting from the same base model and making no distinction between correct and incorrect responses. They report that **a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL**, and that training on only the last few steps' rollouts often recovers the final model's performance. Their interpretation is that most RL compute goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.

papers.title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
papers.abstract: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.
papers.summary: Behavioral cloning models of human chess play typically predict moves from the board alone and ignore the clock, even though time pressure strongly affects human decision quality. The authors extend a `Chessformer`-style transformer with learned conditioning tokens for player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, plus output heads for thinking time and resignation, and train it on large-scale online game data. Temporal conditioning gives modest overall accuracy gains but **substantially larger gains under time pressure**, along with better thinking-time and resignation predictions. The model also matches how human move quality degrades when time is short, reducing the systematic over-strength of time-agnostic models.

papers.title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model (LLM) inference by letting a small draft model propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, with the speedup governed by how closely the draft distribution matches the target's. The authors observe that open-source draft models often pick the right top token but are systematically underconfident relative to the target, and they test post-hoc calibration methods including temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Standard temperature scaling of the draft distribution **improves acceptance length by up to roughly 10%** at almost no added cost across tasks, and throughput measurements confirm the serving gain. Analysis of more general calibration methods suggests further headroom.

papers.title: MetaFORGE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Harness Optimization in Automated Code Generation for Parallel Computing
papers.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs.
  Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.
papers.summary: The correctness and performance of parallel programs generated by large language models (LLMs) depend heavily on the instructions guiding generation. `MetaFORGE` iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation, folding correctness tests, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, with an external memory that distills and retrieves optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, it **improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance over zero-shot generation** and generally exceeds a `TextGrad` baseline, including when its refinement model is reduced to `gpt-4o`. Retrieval ablations and leakage-controlled held-out experiments indicate that the learned knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and the memory.

papers.title: SAG-Mem-1.0 Technical Report
papers.abstract: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, including intermediate evidence with limited similarity to the original question. Existing approaches often rely on derived memory representations or persistent relational structures, introducing construction costs and potentially losing source details. We present SAG-Mem, a conversational memory framework that preserves complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks and discovers complementary evidence through query-time lexical expansion. Memory construction requires no model inference, using a lexical index without LLM-based extraction, summarization, or semantic relation construction. At query time, BM25 retrieves initial candidates, an evidence evaluator identifies useful chunks, and lexical cues from selected evidence guide an additional retrieval round. Retrieved dialogue is further annotated with calendar interpretations of supported relative-time expressions, preserving the original wording and temporal granularity. We also introduce SAG-Mem-Lite, an alternative configuration that replaces evidence scoring with embedding-based candidate scoring, achieving lower operational cost than Full Context and all memory-based baselines across both benchmarks with low query latency. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval, SAG-Mem achieves overall scores of 83.08 and 80.20, respectively, the highest among the evaluated methods on both benchmarks. On LongMemEval, it exceeds the strongest compared baseline by 7.20 points. SAG-Mem-Lite achieves scores of 77.09 and 77.20, respectively. These results support dialogue preservation and evidence-guided retrieval expansion as an effective design for long-term conversational memory.
papers.summary: Long-term conversational memory requires retrieving complementary facts scattered across dialogue sessions, and existing systems often build derived summaries or relational structures that cost inference and can lose source detail. `SAG-Mem` instead keeps complete dialogue messages in non-overlapping chunks behind a lexical index built without any model inference; at query time `BM25` retrieves candidates, an evidence evaluator selects useful chunks, and lexical cues from that evidence drive a second retrieval round, with relative-time expressions annotated with calendar interpretations. It scores 83.08 on `LoCoMo` and 80.20 on `LongMemEval`, the highest among evaluated methods, **beating the strongest compared baseline on `LongMemEval` by 7.20 points**. A cheaper `SAG-Mem-Lite` variant that uses embedding-based candidate scoring reaches 77.09 and 77.20 at lower operational cost than full-context and the memory-based baselines.

papers.title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $\beta$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.
papers.summary: Robot policies learn mostly from human demonstrations of competent behavior, which leaves poor coverage of the low-level recovery behaviors needed for autonomous improvement. The authors introduce `β-Data`, collected through adversarial teleoperation in which a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while an operator keeps working toward completion without resets, then relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. Across simulated manipulation tasks and three real-robot platforms, this midtraining stage yields more favorable data scaling, better zero-shot generalization, and better use of extra rollout time than standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, the resulting policies **need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates**.

papers.title: A Bias in Disguise: Tiny Gradient Edits Stop a Small Language Model's Thinking Loops and Complement a Frontier Model's Weight Edit
papers.abstract: Qwen3.5-0.8B rarely finishes reasoning in thinking mode: at a 4,096-token budget only 1 or 2 of 500 MATH-500 answers close their think block (two seeds), and accuracy is 15.4%. A recent demonstration had GPT-6 Astra edit 131,072 of the model's weights without gradients and reported MATH-500 rising from 7.9% to 48.1% at a 32,768-token budget. We provide the missing gradient baseline, then combine the two edits. Fine-tuning only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient, on the model's own correct answers to MATH training problems, raises thinking-mode MATH-500 at 4k tokens to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes of training on one GPU; 50 training examples suffice, and 1,398 random positions give only 16.3%. The gradient concentrates the edit on the most nearly constant channel of each of the first three layers. Because the model has no bias terms, an edit confined to those channels acts as a constant vector added to the residual stream: adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches the accuracy of such an edit. Under the Astra protocol (32k tokens, presence penalty 1.5), the Astra edit scores 52.1% (finished and correct) in our reproduction and our full-strength edits reach 45.6-45.7%, but ours win at every budget up to 16k tokens (39.5% against 6.7% at 4k). The two edits are complementary. The Astra edit plus our 139,750-weight edit at half strength scores 62.2% at 32k, 10 points above the Astra edit alone (p = 3e-9), with half as many tokens; our half-strength edit alone scores 46.7%.
papers.summary: `Qwen3.5-0.8B` almost never finishes reasoning in thinking mode, closing its think block on only 1 or 2 of 500 `MATH-500` answers at a 4,096-token budget and scoring 15.4%. As a gradient baseline for a recent gradient-free edit of 131,072 weights made by `GPT-6 Astra`, the authors fine-tune only the 140 to 139,750 weights with the largest gradient on the model's own correct answers, raising accuracy at that budget to 39.0-45.5% after 2-9 minutes on one GPU with as few as 50 examples. Because the model has no bias terms, the edit behaves like a constant vector added to the residual stream in the first three layers, and adding three fixed vectors to the unedited model matches it. The two edits are complementary: **combining the `GPT-6 Astra` edit with the gradient edit at half strength scores 62.2% at a 32k-token budget**, 10 points above the `GPT-6 Astra` edit alone.

papers.title: BriConstrain: Geometrically Constrained Decoding for Autoregressive Brick Assembly Generation
papers.abstract: Language models can generate LEGO$^\circledR$ assemblies from text, but their builds often contain parts that collide or attach to nothing. The usual approach of rejecting and resampling invalid placements discards decoded tokens without guaranteeing a valid build. We present BriConstrain, a constrained decoding method that restricts a pretrained language model's next-token probabilities before sampling, steering it towards valid placements. Because the validity of a brick placement depends on the non-predetermined build state, it cannot be compiled into a fixed grammar and must be checked dynamically. However, checking the validity of a brick before sampling is challenging as the space of valid placements is combinatorially large and cannot be enumerated exhaustively. Our key idea is to narrow the search space by constraining how parts attach rather than which parts attach to each other. Concretely, given the model's predictions of the currently placed part, and the previously placed parent it wants to connect to, we constrain the model's choice of how they attach. This allows us to span the space of part attachments, using a precomputed geometric oracle, and to effectively filter out colliding options. With valid attachment candidates in hand, we bias the model's next-token distribution towards the remaining valid candidates. We evaluate our method on two LEGO$^\circledR$ formats and models: BrickNet, which annotates connectivity explicitly, and our proposed Implicit Connectivity LDraw Format (ICLF), which uses numeric values for placements and leaves connectivity implicit. Our method raises collision-free builds from 31% to 91% on BrickNet and from 15% to 65% on ICLF, and outperforms rejection sampling on both formats at about 60% of its decoding cost.
papers.summary: Language models that generate LEGO assemblies from text often place bricks that collide or attach to nothing, and rejection sampling wastes decoded tokens without guaranteeing a valid build. `BriConstrain` is a constrained decoding method that takes the model's predicted part and the parent it wants to connect to, uses a precomputed geometric oracle to enumerate how the two can attach, filters out colliding options, and biases next-token probabilities toward the remaining valid candidates. It is evaluated on `BrickNet`, which annotates connectivity explicitly, and on the proposed Implicit Connectivity LDraw Format (`ICLF`), which leaves it implicit. Collision-free builds rise **from 31% to 91% on `BrickNet`** and from 15% to 65% on `ICLF`, beating rejection sampling at about 60% of its decoding cost.

papers.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.
papers.summary: World-action models (WAMs) build robot policies on pretrained video-generation models, but generating future frames is too slow for real-time control. `iWAM` conditions the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation instead of a fully denoised future frame: it inverts each training future into its latent noise vector using the reversible dynamics of flow matching, then learns a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future generation so one evaluation yields informative features. At inference, a noise vector is sampled from the prior and the policy is conditioned with **just one video-backbone forward pass**. On simulated benchmarks and real robots, the authors report that it recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs at substantially lower inference cost.

papers.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
papers.abstract: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a student on a stronger teacher's agent trajectories normally imitates both actions and chain-of-thought, but the strongest teachers are closed models whose reasoning is hidden. The authors train the student on the teacher's actions alone with its reasoning block left empty, plus a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations to limit drift, and find the learned policy carries over to inference with thinking enabled, an effect they call cross-format transfer. Distilling `Qwen3.6-27B` raises `Qwen3-4B` on `AppWorld` from 7% to 18% and `Qwen3-32B` from 12% to 25%, and adding `CoT-proxies`, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning, lifts `Qwen3-4B` to 35%. Distilling the closed `GPT-5.6 Luna` from its visible outputs and API reasoning summaries raises `Qwen3-4B` **from 7% to 48% on `AppWorld`** and from 3% to 28% on `SWE-bench Verified`.

papers.title: BioLoom: Scaling Biomedical Vision-Language Models by Learning from the Structure of Scientific Articles
papers.abstract: The development of biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) with contrastive image-text pretraining has been driven by scaling to increasingly large and diverse image-text datasets. Beyond scaling, further progress can come from learning richer representations from existing data. We hypothesize that the structure of scientific literature itself provides an additional source of supervision: figures, panels, captions, and accompanying article text encode rich relationships across modalities. Yet, treating these as independent image-text pairs overlooks their relationships. To address this limitation, we incorporate these structural relationships into contrastive image-text supervision. We preserve exact image-text matches while introducing weaker positive supervision for related pairs, such as a panel and the caption of a sibling panel. We upweight cross-article negatives of the same content type to encourage finer discrimination. We also enrich panel descriptions using visual content, original figure captions, and mentioning paragraphs. Pairing panels with these descriptions and whole figures with their original captions yields Loom52M, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs spanning scientific charts and biomedical images. Using Loom52M, BioLoom (DFN-2B) achieves 56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks from 43 datasets in 10 domains, compared with 48.77% for MedPMC-CLIP. On BioLoomBench with concise captions and BioMedFlickr, it achieves bidirectional mean Recall@1 of 63.20% and 10.59%, versus 46.37% and 7.55% for the respective strongest evaluated baselines, BiomedCLIP and MedPMC-CLIP. Code, datasets, benchmarks, and models are available at https://bioloom-clip.github.io/.
papers.summary: Biomedical vision-language models (VLMs) trained with contrastive image-text pretraining usually treat figures and captions as independent pairs, ignoring the relationships among figures, panels, captions, and article text. The authors add this structure to the contrastive objective by keeping exact matches, giving weaker positive supervision to related pairs such as a panel and a sibling panel's caption, upweighting same-type negatives from other articles, and enriching panel descriptions, which yields `Loom52M`, a dataset of 52.4 million image-text pairs. `BioLoom` reaches **56.82% domain-balanced mean accuracy across 67 zero-shot classification tasks, versus 48.77% for `MedPMC-CLIP`**. Its bidirectional mean Recall@1 is 63.20% on `BioLoomBench` and 10.59% on `BioMedFlickr`, against 46.37% and 7.55% for the strongest evaluated baselines.

papers.title: DiaCap: Jointly Learning Who Speaks When for Audiovisual Dialogue Captioning
papers.abstract: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
papers.summary: `DiaCap` is an audiovisual large language model for dialogue captioning that outputs the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video, treating utterance timing and audiovisual diarization as one coupled task. It is first trained on 225K curated clips with dense synthetic captions, then refined with reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips using feedback on utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On `DiaDemBench`, extended with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, it performs on par with `Gemini 4 Argon` in audiovisual diarization while **outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME)**. The authors also report strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos and transfer to audiovisual question answering.

papers.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
papers.abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/
papers.summary: A single manipulation policy that controls many different robots must adapt its strategy to each robot's morphology, which shared action representations do not necessarily capture. `OmniAct` conditions on a kinematic graph of the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity tied to its visual observation, and uses a flow-matching policy to predict relative joint motions per node; it is trained on simulated trajectories from one million procedurally generated, physically feasible embodiments. On 2,000 held-out embodiment-scene episodes it achieves **63.0% success, versus 57.9% for the strongest baseline** and 17.8% for `pi 0.5`, and on the task families where `GPT-6 Astra` was evaluated it scores 64.7% against 41.1%. On a previously unseen real robot it reaches nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, `MolmoAct2`, and it learns distinct strategies for different morphologies.

audio.title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies
audio.script: Today's pick from the AI Paper Digest. Can an ordinary mirror confuse a robot? The authors took an existing benchmark for robot manipulation and added mirrors to the scene. Every mirror setup lowered success for all five models tested. The robots appeared to reach for reflections and misjudge where real objects were. Plain panels of the same shape showed collisions alone do not explain it. Real robot trials showed the same trend. The paper diagnoses the problem but offers no fix. Hints in the prompt did not reliably help.
